surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed prior FY organic CC guidance of “+6.5–8.0%” and said a raise that only flowed through the Q1 beat was the base case, while lifting the H2 organic assumption would be a bull trigger.

surprises.description: Cost savings are running ahead of the preview’s $55 million 2026 target: management now expects $75 million of 2026 savings and about $200 million at run rate, with a $50 million Q4 P&L benefit largely already in hand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cost actions are expected to yield $75 million in 2026 savings and approximately $200 million in run-rate savings … ahead of schedule, with a $50 million Q4 P&L benefit largely already in hand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$55M targeted for 2026” and expected “results beginning in Q3.”

surprises.description: The acquired businesses generated 90 basis points of net price realization, above their historical 50 basis points. The preview did not specify an expectation for this pricing metric.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net price realization in the acquired businesses reached 90 basis points in Q2, up from a historical 50 basis points, on the path toward a 150 basis point target.”

surprises.description: GLP-1 testing demand was substantially stronger than the prior contribution assumption: revenue grew over 40%, with growth above 30% in the Americas, above 36% in Europe, and nearly doubling in India. Management said this was running well ahead of the roughly 30-basis-point contribution assumption.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GLP-1 testing revenue grew over 40% in the quarter” and was “running well ahead of the prior ~30 basis point contribution assumption.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The call referenced a “prior ~30 basis point contribution assumption.”

surprises.description: China microbiology declined only at a low-teens rate, considerably less than the modeled 30% decline. This was a better outcome than the expectation cited on the call.
surprises.fact_evidence: “China microbiology declined only low-teens versus a modeled 30% decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The call referred to “a modeled 30% decline.”

surprises.description: Management quantified a sizable U.S. pharma reshoring pipeline: 76 expansion sites representing about $100 billion of CapEx, with roughly 70% tied to existing Waters accounts. The preview expected a reshoring tailwind but did not cite a pipeline of this scale or account penetration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is tracking 76 U.S. pharma reshoring expansion sites (about half under construction, ~$100 billion CapEx) with roughly 70% tied to existing Waters accounts,” expected to benefit Analytical Sciences from 2027 to 2030.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described drug-manufacturing exposure as “structurally advantaged by reshoring” and anticipated instrument placements in late 2027–2028.

surprises.description: A stronger U.S. dollar is expected to reduce full-year adjusted EPS by roughly $0.25. The preview did not flag a headwind of this size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A stronger U.S. dollar consumed roughly $0.25 of EPS on the full-year outlook.”

in_line: Q2 adjusted EPS was $3.05, at the high end of the $2.95–$3.05 guide and only modestly above the $3.01 consensus, broadly consistent with the preview’s expected range.
Full-year adjusted EPS guidance of $14.45–$14.65 was within the preview’s anticipated post-update range of about $14.50–$14.65, despite the newly disclosed dollar headwind.

surprises.description: Non-GAAP diluted EPS was $0.45, far above the preview’s $0.26 consensus and management’s pre-announcement floor of $0.23. Adjusted EBITDA margin also reached 40%, versus the preview’s roughly 38% expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$0.45 non-GAAP diluted EPS” and “a 40% adjusted EBITDA margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP diluted EPS: Consensus $0.26”; management had said “at or above the high end” of its $0.20–0.23 range; adjusted EBITDA margin consensus was “~38%.”

surprises.description: DOCN disclosed record incremental ARR of $93 million, nearly triple the amount added in the same quarter last year, with little contribution from pricing. The preview focused on revenue, AI ARR and RPO, but did not anticipate this scale of new ARR bookings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A record $93 million in incremental ARR, nearly triple the amount added in the same quarter last year,” with “pricing had very little impact on this figure.”

surprises.description: RPO reached $894 million, well above the preview’s expected roughly $800–820 million. Its 3.7-year average life is consistent with the preview’s expectation of more than three years, though the preview had flagged the possibility that long-duration RPO could push revenue recognition further out.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Remaining performance obligations surged more than 12x year-over-year to $894 million with a 3.7-year average life.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: RPO was expected to be “$800M+” and the base scenario anticipated “~$800–820M”; the preview watched whether the “weighted-average life extension to >3 years” pushed recognition right.

surprises.description: The company equitized $472 million of its 2030 convertible notes with effectively no dilution and brought pro forma net leverage to about 0.7x. This was a favorable answer to the preview’s concern about funding capacity and its warning that new equity or convert financing would be a major downside risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In July, the company equitized $472 million of its 0% 2030 convertible notes with effectively no dilution,” bringing “pro forma net leverage to approximately 0.7x.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “any hint of a new equity or convert raise” was the “biggest single downside tail” and cited a net leverage target of “~3x by YE26.”

surprises.description: Large-customer ARR growth was especially strong: ARR for customers spending over $1 million grew 214%, up from 179% growth in the Q1 baseline, and the top cohort’s share of ARR rose from 9% to 23%. That signals accelerating large-account demand, while also sharpening the concentration issue the preview had highlighted.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$100,000-plus customer ARR growing 98%, $500,000-plus growing 160%, and $1 million-plus growing 214%,” with “the top cohort” rising “from 9% to 23% of total ARR year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 “$1M+ customer ARR $183M (+179%)” and said quantified customer concentration would be a “meaningful new datapoint.”

surprises.description: The new inference engine had attracted more than 6,000 customers since its late-April launch, and inference services were growing nearly 800% year over year. The preview expected AI ARR and an inference-heavy mix, but did not set an expectation for this product-level adoption.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inference services grew nearly 800% year-over-year” and the “inference engine” attracted “over 6,000 customers since its late-April launch.”

surprises.description: DOCN recently raised list prices by about 30% on numerous GPU fleets, an action not anticipated in the preview. The call facts do not establish how much of the increase will translate into realized revenue or margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recently raised list prices on numerous GPU fleets by approximately 30%.”

surprises.description: Management said it will no longer highlight net dollar retention as a key metric, despite reporting 102% for Q2. The preview did not anticipate this change in the company’s metric disclosure, so its significance is unclear from the provided facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “will no longer highlight net dollar retention (102% in Q2) as a key metric.”

in_line: Revenue of $281 million was close to the preview’s $279 million consensus and within its $279–282 million base scenario.

AI customer ARR of $234 million was within the preview’s $230–260 million watch range; 85% from non-bare-metal inference services and core cloud was consistent with the expected inference/core-cloud-heavy mix.
The FY2026 revenue guide of $1.17–1.18 billion met the preview’s expectation of at least $1.17 billion, and the Q4 exit growth rate of 35% or more was within or above its anticipated 33–35% range.
Confidence in 50%+ growth for 2027 reiterated the preview’s expectation of a greater-than-$1.7-billion, approximately 50%-growth framework.
Committed capacity of approximately 155 megawatts matched the preview, which already noted the July signing that brought capacity to about 155 megawatts.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $2.15, well above the preview’s $1.41 consensus—about 53% higher. This was a substantial beat against the stated estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Andersons reported Q2 2026 adjusted EPS of $2.15.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 FY2026 consensus EPS: $1.41.

surprises.description: The Houston soybean meal export terminal was expected to be completed in Q3 2026, but management now expects it to be fully operational in Q4, indicating a one-quarter delay.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Houston soybean meal export terminal is expected to be fully operational in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Project timing: Port of Houston soybean meal export capacity (completion guided Q3 2026).”

surprises.description: Agribusiness adjusted pretax income rose only modestly, to $20 million from $17 million, but fertilizer performed above expectations despite domestic prices dropping late in the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Agribusiness adjusted pretax income rose modestly to $20 million from $17 million, with fertilizer performing above expectations despite domestic fertilizer prices dropping late in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Fertilizer performing above expectations.”

in_line: The $24 million of Q2 45Z credits was broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of a similar or larger quarterly contribution given $26.2 million in Q1 and ratable recognition. The forecast of $90–100 million for the full year supplies the requested annual quantification.
Full-year capital spending of approximately $225 million excluding acquisitions matched the preview’s expectation of about $225 million.
Management reaffirmed the $7 run-rate EPS target exiting 2028, as the preview expected.
Long-term debt-to-EBITDA of 1.3x was below the company’s 2.5x target, consistent with the preview’s expectation that leverage would remain below that threshold.
The favorable renewables operating backdrop anticipated in the preview was reflected in record second-quarter ethanol production, higher margins, and strong domestic and export demand.

surprises.description: Whirlpool reported Q2 ongoing EPS of negative $0.21, versus the preview’s $0.08 consensus, turning an expected profit into a loss. Q2 net sales were also $3.5 billion versus $3.61 billion expected, a smaller miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales were $3.5 billion with ongoing EPS of negative $0.21.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | Q2 FY2026 consensus | $3.61B”; “Ongoing EPS | Q2 FY2026 consensus | $0.08.”

surprises.description: Full-year EPS guidance was lowered because expected interest expense rose from $300 million to $350 million. The preview highlighted the existing $3.00–$3.50 EPS outlook as a key question, but did not report an expected reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year EPS guidance was lowered solely due to raised interest expense (from $300 million to $350 million),” while the operational outlook was reaffirmed.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Is $3.00–$3.50 ongoing EPS still live? Consensus of $0.08 in Q2 leaves essentially the entire year's earnings in H2. Any trim, or a shift to the low end, is the single biggest swing factor.”

surprises.description: Whirlpool said tariffs were an unfavorable 200 basis points in Q2 and expects similar costs in Q3 and Q4, making the headwind explicit and persistent into the second half. The preview noted surviving tariffs and input-cost exposure but did not quantify or forecast this impact.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net tariff impact was an unfavorable 200 basis points in Q2 driven by Section 232 implementation, and management expects similar tariff costs in Q3 and Q4.”

surprises.description: SDA Global had strong underlying demand, but a temporary trade-inventory burn after a late-quarter order depressed reported top-line results, a potential shortfall against the preview’s expected sales growth. The underlying U.S. POS growth of 16% and high-teens global sell-through make the reported weakness a timing-driven, mixed signal rather than a demand collapse.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SDA Global delivered ~12% EBIT margin with underlying U.S. POS growth of 16% and high-teens global sell-through, but a temporary Q2 trade inventory burn from a late-quarter order depressed reported top-line results.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “SDA Global sales | $226.5M”; “Implied Y/Y | +12.7%”; and “Latin America and SDA as the only consensus growth lines.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a sale of its minority stake in Beko Europe BV for about $128 million, yielding roughly $84 million in net cash—an asset-sale cash source not identified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Whirlpool sold its minority stake in Beko Europe BV for approximately $128 million, generating roughly $84 million of net cash consideration.”

surprises.description: In addition to the expected 2026 cost program, Whirlpool cited a further $60 million of annualized EBIT benefit from consolidating distribution centers from 126 to 90. That specific incremental benefit was not in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An added $60 million annualized EBIT benefit from consolidating distribution centers from 126 down to 90.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “>$150M structural cost takeout in 2026.”

surprises.description: Whirlpool executed a promotional price increase of more than 10% versus Q1 and announced a roughly 4% list-price increase effective in July; two-thirds of the promotional benefit was realized in Q2, with more carryover expected. This offered evidence of pricing realization and future benefit against the preview’s concern that competitors’ price cuts could force Whirlpool to give back increases.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A promotional price increase of more than 10% versus Q1 effective late April, plus a ~4% list price increase effective July, with only two-thirds of the promo pricing benefit realized in Q2 and more carryover expected.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Post-IEEPA pricing dynamics — whether competitors' price cuts forced Whirlpool to give back the announced increases.”

in_line: MDA North America sales of $2.4 billion were close to the preview’s $2.419 billion consensus; its sequential margin recovery was also consistent with the preview’s focus on pricing actions and cost takeout supporting a recovery.
The operational outlook of roughly 4% full-year EBIT margin was reaffirmed, consistent with the preview’s stated guidance.
The common dividend had already been suspended according to the preview, so its suspension was not new.

surprises.description: Q2 continuing-operations revenue was $740.3 million, far below the preview’s $848.6 million consensus and the company’s $840–860 million guide, despite 12.7% year-over-year growth. The gap is especially notable because the preview expected reported Q2 revenue to remain comparable to consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net revenue from continuing operations was $740.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net revenue | $848.6M” consensus; company guide “$840–860M.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $132.0 million, versus roughly $160 million expected, and the 17.8% margin missed the approximately 19% guide. That reverses the preview’s expectation that Q1’s labor-driven margin weakness would be transitional and that the capitated contract would contribute at high incremental margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin compressed to 17.8% ($132.0 million) from $136.4 million a year earlier due to elevated West Coast capitated contract costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$160M (implied)” and “~19% margin”; the preview said “19%+ = thesis intact” and expected the capitated contract to “drop[] through at high incremental margin.”

surprises.description: Full-year continuing-operations adjusted EBITDA guidance fell to $490–520 million from $680–730 million. That is well below even the preview’s rough $656–706 million ex-Diabetes bridge, indicating a much deeper reset than the expected effect of selling Diabetes Health alone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company slashed full-year continuing operations adjusted EBITDA guidance to $490-520 million from a prior $680-730 million,” driven by “divestiture, capitated contract issues, and a supplier price hike.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s rough ex-Diabetes frame was “$656–706M EBITDA,” and it said a recast “materially below that band” would be a cut under cover of the divestiture.

surprises.description: The West Coast capitated contract is materially more costly and slower to reach profitability than the preview’s high-incremental-margin thesis implied: it underperformed by $15 million in Q2, is expected to cost another $40 million in H2, and is not expected to reach run-rate profitability until next year. Management still targets a 20% long-term margin, but the near-term H2 ramp is substantially weaker than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The West Coast capitated contract underperformed by $15 million in Q2 and is expected to cost an additional $40 million in the second half”; it is “only reaching run-rate profitability next year,” while management targets a “20% long-term margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the contract was expected to “drop[] through at high incremental margin” and described the H2 margin ramp as the crux of the bear case.

surprises.description: A major manufacturer terminated its contract and imposed an immediate price increase, creating a $30 million H2 impact with no mitigation secured. The preview did not identify this supplier disruption as a risk, and the cost is already included in the sharply reduced guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A major manufacturer terminated its contract and imposed an immediate price increase effective July 1, creating a $30 million second-half impact that is currently fully reflected in guidance with no mitigation yet secured.”

surprises.description: The Diabetes Health sale leaves about $60 million of stranded corporate overhead in continuing operations, with only roughly half expected to be removed within 12 months of closing. That is a concrete and prolonged cost burden beyond the preview’s rough ex-Diabetes bridge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Diabetes Health divestiture leaves roughly $60 million of stranded corporate overhead in continuing operations, of which only about half is expected to be removed within 12 months of closing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked “what stranded overhead remains” and used a rough ex-Diabetes EBITDA bridge “before stranded costs,” but did not anticipate this $60 million figure or removal timetable.

surprises.description: Full-year free cash flow guidance is now $80–120 million, well below the preview’s $175–225 million expectation. The reduced outlook makes the preview’s anticipated strong back-half cash generation much less attainable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year free cash flow guided to $80-120 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 FCF consensus of “—” and cited the company’s prior “$175–225M” guide, while saying the guide depended on “~$100M in each of Q3 and Q4.”

surprises.description: Q2 free cash flow was negative $20.9 million, weaker than the preview’s expectation of modest Q2 FCF and its near-breakeven scenario. The company attributed the result to $166.2 million of capex, including about $25 million of one-time equipment and vehicle purchases.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow was negative $20.9 million in Q2 driven by $166.2 million of capex (including ~$25 million of one-time equipment/vehicle purchases).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q2 FCF was expected to be “modest” with elevated capex and described “Q2 near breakeven” as part of the FCF cadence to watch.

surprises.description: The company recorded a $144.2 million noncash goodwill impairment tied to reallocating costs following the Diabetes Health divestiture. The preview mentioned a prior-quarter impairment but did not flag another impairment in this release.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recorded a $144.2 million noncash goodwill impairment tied to the diabetes divestiture cost reallocation.”

surprises.description: The company executed a $19 million annualized cost restructuring in Q2, an additional savings action not anticipated in the preview. Its benefit is positive, though the call facts do not specify how much has already flowed through the reported results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company executed a $19 million annualized cost restructuring in Q2.”

in_line: Capitated revenue reached $103.3 million, within the preview’s expected clean-quarter range of about $95–110 million, although it represented about 14% of revenue rather than the preview’s 11–13% estimate.
The preview explicitly anticipated that management might announce a new capitated partnership; the call reported a signed Humana OneHome agreement covering 478,000 members in South Florida and Texas.

The $235 million Diabetes Health sale and the intention to use proceeds largely for debt reduction were already known or expected in the preview; the call cited a current 3.06x net leverage ratio and a 2.5x target.

surprises.description: Capital solutions fees reached $277 million, well above the $223 million consensus and also above the preview’s $250–270 million upside expectation. Management said the fees were a record and that the business is running ahead of its five-year Investor Day target roughly three years early.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Capital solutions fees reached a record $277 million”; “running ahead of the 5-year Investor Day target roughly three years early.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Capital solutions (ACS) fees & other” consensus was “$223M”; the preview said ACS “should clear $250–270M.”

surprises.description: Fee-related earnings were $785 million, above the preview’s expected $745–765 million range, and the FRE margin also expanded. The preview expected strong FRE and reaffirmed growth guidance, but not a quarterly result this high.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record fee-related earnings of $785 million”; “FRE margin expanded to 58.5%, up ~80 bps sequentially and ~120 bps year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a “2–4% sequential step gets to $745–765M” and flagged “20%+ FY26 FRE growth” reaffirmation as important.

surprises.description: Reported Athene net spread improved to 114 bps from 97 bps last quarter, above the preview’s anticipated 95–110 bps range for reported spread. The 124 bps figure adjusted to the 11% alternatives assumption was in line with the full-year outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Athene's reported net spread rose to 114 bps from 97 bps last quarter”; adjusted to the 11% alternatives return assumption, it “would have been 124 bps.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said reported spread would “likely stay in the 95–110bps band” and highlighted the 120–125 bps full-year guide.

surprises.description: Q3 redemption requests for the ADS non-traded BDC were running at roughly half the level seen at the same point in Q2, a clear improvement on the preview’s concern about continued high requests. The preview identified Q3 redemption commentary as a key debate but had no specific expectation of a halving.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 redemption requests are running at roughly half the level seen at the same point in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted Q2 requests of “16.8%” and said to watch whether Q3 requests remained “>10%” in its bear scenario.

surprises.description: Adjusted net income per share was $2.11, below the preview’s primary $2.18 consensus estimate, despite record fee- and spread-related earnings. The gap was small, and the preview also cited an alternate estimate of $2.05.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total adjusted net income of $1.3 billion ($2.11/share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “$2.18 is the number to beat,” while noting an alternate compilation of “$2.05.”

surprises.description: Q2 origination reached $74 billion, below the preview’s expected $80–90 billion range and below its base-scenario $80–85 billion, although it was above Q1’s $71 billion. This was offset in part by $50 billion of signed and announced deals for future quarters.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Origination hit $74 billion in Q2”; “an additional $50 billion in signed and announced deals … set to benefit future quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said origination “should land $80–90B” and gave a base case of “$80–85B”; it also noted management had said Q2 would be “even stronger” than Q1’s $71 billion.

surprises.description: Apollo disclosed a $35 billion Broadcom AI financing, described as the largest private credit deal ever, but the associated fees will arrive over multiple quarters rather than immediately, weighted toward late 2026 and the first three quarters of 2027. The preview had anticipated strong origination and multiple-draw financing solutions, but not a deal of this size or its timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The $35 billion Broadcom AI financing—the largest private credit deal ever—will be recorded and generate fees as capital is drawn down over multiple quarters, weighted toward Q4 2026 and the first three quarters of 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview referred to “multiple draw financing solutions” and expected Q2 origination of “$80–90B,” but did not mention the Broadcom financing.

surprises.description: Apollo reported record dry powder of $82 billion, including $62 billion of future management fee potential that could produce about $400 million of annual management fees once deployed. The preview mentioned Athene’s roughly $40 billion of cash as origination capacity, but did not forecast this firm-wide fee opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A record $82 billion of dry powder including $62 billion of future management fee potential”; approximately “$400 million of annual management fee income once deployed.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “~$40B cash as origination dry powder” at Athene.

surprises.description: Flagship private equity Fund XI had surpassed $12 billion through July, with management fees expected to begin once capital is fully invested in the back half of the first half of 2027. The preview did not discuss Fund XI fundraising or its fee-start timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Flagship private equity Fund XI has surpassed $12 billion through July”; fees are expected to activate “once capital is fully invested” in the back half of the first half of 2027.

surprises.description: The ADS non-traded BDC reported an 8% annualized inception-to-date return, compared with 4% for high-yield. The preview focused on redemption pressure and did not set an expectation for relative investment performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ADS non-traded BDC has delivered an 8% annualized inception-to-date return (vs. 4% for high-yield).”

in_line: Management reaffirmed 20%+ FRE growth and 10% SRE growth guidance for the year, as the preview expected.
Athene’s 124 bps net spread after adjustment to the 11% alternatives return assumption was within the 120–125 bps full-year outlook highlighted in the preview.

surprises.description: Wayfair grew Q2 revenue 7.5% year over year, ahead of the preview’s 5.7% consensus growth estimate and above its 6–7% base scenario. The gap was modest rather than a full bull-case result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net revenue grew 7.5% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net revenue” consensus: “+5.7%” year over year; the base scenario anticipated “+6–7%.”

surprises.description: The U.S. business accelerated to 8.7% growth, while the preview expected the home category to remain down mid-single digits. The reported flat-to-slightly-positive U.S. category growth also marked a much stronger backdrop than anticipated, though the recovery was concentrated among higher-income customers.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The U.S. segment accelerat[ed] to 8.7% growth” and Q2 was “the first quarter of flat-to-slightly-positive year-over-year U.S. category growth since 2021, with a K-shaped skew favoring higher-income segments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management framed Q2 as “category down mid-single digits” and noted that April category data “was still negative.”

surprises.description: International revenue declined instead of sharing in the U.S. acceleration, with Canada and the U.K. identified as weak spots. The preview flagged UK/Canada Rewards traction as something to watch, but did not anticipate a decline in the International segment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International declined 1.3% due to weakness in Canada and the U.K.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “UK/Canada Rewards traction” among the narrative wildcards to watch.

surprises.description: Orders rose 6% year over year and more than 12% sequentially, including the strongest Q2 sequential order growth since 2020. That exceeded the preview’s call for acceleration beyond Q1’s 3% order growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Orders rose 6% year-over-year and over 12% sequentially versus Q1—the strongest Q2 sequential order growth since 2020.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull case required “order growth accelerating past Q1's +3%,” and cited Q1 “new orders +7%.”

surprises.description: Active customers grew more than 3%, above the preview’s modeled 1–3% year-over-year increase and its estimated 21.3–21.6 million customer range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Active customers rose more than 3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled “Active customers ~21.3–21.6M” and “+1–3%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $242 million at a 6.9% margin, above the preview’s base expectation of roughly $230 million and 6.5%, though still within the company’s 6–7% guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Wayfair delivered Q2 adjusted EBITDA of $242 million at a 6.9% margin, the best margin since 2021,” with “100 basis points of SOTG&A leverage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario expected “EBITDA ~6.5% (~$230M)”; its bull scenario called for “EBITDA margin ≥7%.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow reached $301 million, substantially more than the return to positive cash flow the preview said was needed and above the $230 million Q2’25 comparison cited there.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow reached $301 million (cash from operations of $360 million less $59 million CapEx), up more than 30% year-over-year and the best quarterly cash generation since Q2 2020.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “a return to positive FCF” was needed and noted “Q2'25 was +$230M.”

surprises.description: Q3 revenue guidance was high-single-digit growth, above the preview’s expectation of mid-single-digit-or-better growth and above management’s historic mid-single-digit guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided Q3 to high single-digit revenue growth—above its historic mid-single-digit guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the buy-side wanted “mid-single-digit-or-better revenue growth.”

surprises.description: Alongside the stronger Q3 revenue outlook, management expected gross margin at the low end of the 29.5–30.5% range. That is a cautious margin signal against a preview that emphasized holding margin within the range and warned that margin trajectory was central to the debate.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q3 gross margin was “expected at the low end of the 29.5%-30.5% range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called gross margin versus “the 29.5–30.5% guide” the key debate and described the base case as “GM ~30%.”

surprises.description: Perigold and the specialty brands substantially outgrew the core mass-market business, a brand-level growth result the preview did not set expectations for. Perigold’s scale and customer spending were also disclosed, adding evidence of a sizable higher-end business.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Specialty retail brands grew nearly 20% and Perigold grew more than 35% in Q2, both meaningfully outpacing the core mass Wayfair business”; Perigold had “just over $400 million in annual sales” and “near 400,000” active customers.

surprises.description: The 2026 store opening count was three, below the preview’s expectation of more than three, but Wayfair also disclosed five leases for 2027 and favorable store economics: over half of store customers were new, with supplier-owned inventory keeping capital needs low.
surprises.fact_evidence: “3 large-format stores opening in 2026 and 5 leases signed for 2027”; “over 50% of store customers are new to the file” and “inventory is supplier-owned, keeping combined CapEx in the low single-digit percentage of revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview referred to “more than 3” stores in 2026 and said “Any store-level economics would be new information.”

surprises.description: Rather than further convertible repurchases, Wayfair issued a $400 million high-yield note to redeem 2028 converts. The transaction moves the company away from convertible debt, but the preview had specifically identified additional convert repurchases as a possible catalyst; the Fitch upgrade and lower stock-based compensation were additional favorable disclosures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed its shift away from convertible debt by issuing a $400 million high-yield note to redeem 2028 converts”; it “earned a 2-notch Fitch upgrade” and cut trailing-12-month stock-based compensation “~40% versus two years ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “further convertible repurchases (~$300M principal retired in Q1)” as a narrative wildcard.

in_line: Q3 adjusted EBITDA margin guidance remained at 6–7%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the margin guide would not step down.
Q2 fixed costs were $361 million, within the preview’s $360–370 million SG&A guidance range.

surprises.description: North and Central America operating earnings declined 2.4%, rather than growing around 8% as the preview’s $225 million estimate implied. The reported low-single-digit volume growth did not prevent Millersburg start-up costs and capacity constraints from weighing on the segment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “North and Central America segment operating earnings declined 2.4% year-over-year,” as “roughly $5 million in Millersburg start-up costs and capacity constraints offset low-single-digit volume growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “NCA comparable op. earnings $225M” versus “$208M” a year earlier; the preview said consensus implied “+8%.”

surprises.description: EMEA operating earnings rose just 6.6%, well short of the preview’s $161.2 million estimate, which implied roughly 25% growth from the cited $129 million prior-year base. Benepack’s contribution was largely offset by the divested Saudi Arabian business.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EMEA volumes grew mid-single digits with segment operating earnings up 6.6%, though Benepack contributions were largely offset by the divested Saudi Arabian business.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EMEA comparable op. earnings $161.2M” versus “$129M” a year earlier; the preview’s dollar figures imply roughly 25% growth.

surprises.description: South America operating earnings surged 64%, far above the preview’s $53 million estimate versus $51 million a year earlier, which implied only about 4% growth. World Cup-driven customer demand helped produce the outsized result against a flattish regional market.
surprises.fact_evidence: “South America was the standout region with mid-teens volume growth and a 64% surge in segment operating earnings, aided by World Cup-driven customer demand against a flattish regional market.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “S. America comparable op. earnings $53M” versus “$51M” a year earlier, or “+4%.”

surprises.description: Comparable EPS growth was 14.4%, above the roughly 10% growth implied by the $0.99 consensus estimate against the $0.90 year-ago result. The call did not provide the Q2 EPS dollar amount, so the precise beat versus consensus cannot be established from these facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable diluted EPS grew 14.4% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Comparable diluted EPS” consensus was “$0.99” versus “$0.90” a year earlier, implying “+10%.”

surprises.description: Global can-volume growth was 4.3%, ahead of the preview’s 3%-or-better threshold for validating the full-year build. Growth across all three regions also extended the volume-growth streak to six consecutive quarters.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Global shipped beverage can volumes increased 4.3% year-over-year in Q2 2026 with growth across all three regions, marking the sixth consecutive quarter of volume growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 needs +3% or better to validate the full-year build.”

surprises.description: South American volume growth reached the mid-teens, below the preview’s estimate of about 20.4% and its expectation of a roughly 20% Q2 snapback. The segment still delivered strong growth, but the recovery was less pronounced than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “South America” had “mid-teens volume growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated South America volume growth at “+20.4%” and said the “South America” segment was expected to deliver “the +20% snapback.”

surprises.description: North and Central America volume growth was low-single-digit, better than the preview’s 0.8% estimate, even though segment earnings fell. This was a modest volume upside in a region the preview described as capacity-constrained.
surprises.fact_evidence: Capacity constraints “offset low-single-digit volume growth” in North and Central America.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated NCA volume growth at “+0.8%.”

surprises.description: Ball said it expected to return about $800 million to shareholders in 2026, including at least $600 million of buybacks, but had completed only about $100 million of repurchases in the first half. That is well below the preview’s roughly $150 million-per-quarter pace and leaves a substantial amount to execute in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ball plans to return approximately $800 million to shareholders in 2026, including at least $600 million in buybacks and roughly $200 million in dividends, with only ~$100 million of repurchases completed in the first half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “≥$600M repurchase / $800M total returns implies roughly $150M/quarter of buyback”; the preview said an H1 run rate below that “raises questions about capital deployment priorities.”

surprises.description: Millersburg start-up costs are expected to total about $35 million for 2026, with roughly $30 million in the second half. The preview flagged the plant ramp and FCF trajectory, but did not anticipate this specific expense burden or its concentration in the back half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year Millersburg start-up costs are expected to total approximately $35 million, with roughly $30 million landing in the second half and no start-up costs anticipated in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the Millersburg, Oregon plant ramps in 2H26” and highlighted “FCF and capex commentary against >$900M / capex ≈ D&A” as a key watchpoint, but gave no start-up-cost estimate.

surprises.description: The call placed Millersburg’s full ramp and delivery of full value in 2027, later than the preview’s description of the plant ramping in the second half of 2026. Commercial production had begun, but the full contribution was not expected until the following year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Millersburg, Oregon plant began producing commercial cans last month” and is “expected to reach full ramp and deliver full value in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the Millersburg, Oregon plant ramps in 2H26.”

surprises.description: The expected South American full-year volume outlook was at the low end of the 4%-6% range, rather than a stronger position within the range suggested by the preview’s emphasis on the recovery. This is a cautious forward signal alongside the weaker-than-expected Q2 volume recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expected South America to be “at the low ends of their respective 1%-3% and 4%-6% ranges.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said South America was guided to “4–6% with April volumes already running +20%” and identified the Q2 “+20% snapback” as an important test.

surprises.description: Interest expense guidance was around $310 million, below the preview’s approximately $320 million expectation. This is a modest favorable change to the full-year outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: Ball reaffirmed “interest expense around $310 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the FY2026 guidance as “interest expense ~$320M.”

in_line: Ball remained on track for its full-year 10%-plus comparable EPS growth target; the preview expected that target to be reaffirmed, while noting that an upgrade was possible.
The company reaffirmed free cash flow greater than $900 million, consistent with the preview’s stated target.
EMEA volume growth was mid-single-digit, broadly in line with the preview’s 6.1% estimate; its full-year outlook remained above the 3%-5% range as previously guided.
North and Central America remained at the low end of its 1%-3% full-year volume-growth range, as the preview expected.
The tax-rate outlook of slightly above 23% and year-end net debt/EBITDA of about 2.7x matched the preview’s stated expectations.

surprises.description: Broadridge finished FY26 closed sales at $305 million, above the preview’s $240–290 million guide, with a record $158 million in Q4. The $470 million backlog and year-end pipeline growth also made the sales result stronger than a simple recovery to the expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 closed sales hit a record $158 million, lifting full-year closed sales to $305 million and the closed sales backlog to $470 million (up $40 million year-over-year)”; “year-end sales pipeline was up more than one-third from a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 closed sales landing inside $240–290M”; the preview also said Q4 closed sales of “$93–143M” were implied by the guide.

surprises.description: FY27 recurring revenue guidance starts at 6%, below the preview’s 7% mental anchor, although the 6%–8% range includes 7% and matches the preview’s stated base-case range. The low end therefore leaves more room for growth below the level the preview said investors needed to defend the compounder narrative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal '27 guidance calls for 6%-8% recurring revenue growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy side needs ≥7% recurring”; the preview also said “Anything with a 5- or 6-handle on recurring validates the bear case,” while its base case anticipated “FY27 recurring 6–8% cc.”

surprises.description: The year-end sales mix showed strong adoption of platform-enabled and next-generation products: they rose more than 50% and made up nearly 40% of closed sales. The preview anticipated pipeline conversion as an important test, but did not forecast this degree of contribution from newer products.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Platform-enabled and next-generation products [were] rising over 50% and accounting for nearly 40% of closed sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 is the proof quarter” for the claim that larger, complex deals were timing rather than demand weakness; the preview called for evidence the pipeline was converting.

surprises.description: Broadridge gave concrete, rapidly growing tokenized-repo activity rather than only the general tokenization proof points the preview was looking for: DLR processed $360 billion in daily volume in June, three times May’s level, with nearly 20 institutions onboarding and further growth expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The DLR tokenized repo platform processed $360 billion in daily volume in June (3x the prior May), with nearly 20 institutions onboarding and management guiding to 50% further growth by December.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Explicit management framing on AI and tokenization” was a key watch item; “tokenization expanding the opportunity. Reiteration with proof points matters more than any EPS line.”

surprises.description: The reported position-growth metrics strengthened versus the Q3 figures highlighted in the preview: equity position growth reached 17% (14% revenue-generating) versus the prior 11% equity growth, and fund growth was 7% versus 6%. That provides a stronger near-term data point against the disintermediation concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 equity position growth was 17% with 14% revenue-generating position growth, while fund positions grew 7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q3 “equity record growth +11%, fund/ETF positions +6%” and said these were “the hard-data rebuttal to disintermediation fears; any crack here is disproportionately damaging.”

surprises.description: A proposed SEC e-delivery rule introduced a new medium-term trade-off not raised in the preview: management expects no FY27 impact, but sees a possible modest recurring-revenue headwind over two to three years, partly offset by new solutions, alongside a reported-margin benefit from lower low-margin distribution revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The SEC's proposed e-delivery rule is expected to have no impact in fiscal '27 but may create a modest recurring revenue headwind over 2-3 years (offset by new solutions) while boosting reported margins by reducing low-margin distribution revenues.”

surprises.description: Broadridge disclosed $25 million of expected AI-driven productivity gains in FY27, presenting AI as a source of operating efficiency as well as a risk discussed in the preview. Because the company plans to reinvest the gains in growth initiatives, this is not a direct increase to expected earnings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company embedded $25 million in expected AI-driven productivity gains in fiscal '27, primarily in the technology organization, which it plans to reinvest to fund growth initiatives.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “AI-disintermediation” as a longer-dated fear and called for explicit management framing on AI; it did not anticipate quantified productivity gains.

surprises.description: Broadridge returned more than $9 per share in FY26, including record buybacks and a 12% dividend increase, and expanded its buyback authorization to $1.5 billion. The preview identified an enlarged authorization as a possible confidence signal, but did not specify this scale of total returns or the dividend increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Broadridge returned over $9 per share to shareholders in fiscal '26 via a record $600 million in buybacks and $443 million in dividends, and raised the dividend 12% to $4.36 while increasing buyback authorization to $1.5 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “An enlarged repurchase authorization at these levels would be a credible confidence signal.”

in_line: FY26 adjusted EPS grew 12% to $9.60, in line with the upper end of the 10%–12% FY26 growth guidance and the preview’s expectation that consensus was effectively assuming the high end.
FY26 recurring revenue grew 8% in constant currency, consistent with the preview’s estimate of roughly 7.5%–8% reported growth and its expectation of at least 7% constant-currency growth.
FY27 adjusted EPS growth guidance of 8%–12% matched the preview’s base-case range of 8%–12%.

FY27 adjusted operating margin guidance of approximately 21%, up from 20.5%, is consistent with the preview’s focus on whether margin expansion would resume and its cited objective of at least 50 basis points of annual expansion.

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance was cut to $275–$295 million, from $315–$335 million, despite the preview focusing on whether the company would avoid another cut. The new outlook implies an adjusted EBITDA margin of only about 12%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “adjusted EBITDA is now guided to $275-$295 million with a margin of only about 12%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance hold or cut again — the release explicitly includes an updated FY2026 outlook; a third cut this fiscal year would confirm the bear case.” The preview also cited the then-current $315–$335 million guide.

surprises.description: Q3 adjusted gross margin fell to 27.7% from 35.1% a year earlier, and adjusted EBITDA margins were below guidance. The preview flagged the margin trajectory as a key debate, but the reported shortfall and the 180-basis-point inventory charge added to the cost pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin collapsed to 27.7% from 35.1% a year ago,” driven by “protein and freight inflation, tariffs, and an excess bottled shake inventory charge that alone was a 180 basis point headwind”; adjusted EBITDA margins “came in below guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin trajectory — whether the Q2 collapse (27.0%) was the trough; tariff, whey-protein and freight cost commentary.”

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin is expected to be only about 10%, with promotions, costs ahead of pricing, and bottle inventory weighing on results. The preview discussed margin pressure generally but did not indicate a margin outlook this weak for Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin is expected to be only about 10%,” reflecting “heavy seasonal promotions, commodity/freight inflation ahead of pricing, and a ~100 bp bottle-inventory headwind.”

surprises.description: The company raised its full-year net sales outlook to $2.335–$2.375 billion, or 1–3% growth, from $2.325–$2.365 billion, or flat-to-2% growth. That was better than the preview’s concern that the company might cut guidance again.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year net sales guidance was raised to $2.335-$2.375 billion (1-3% growth) from prior flat-to-2%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance hold or cut again” and “a third cut this fiscal year would confirm the bear case.”

surprises.description: Q3 net sales grew 4% year over year, above the preview’s 1.6% growth consensus. Both Premier Protein and Dymatize also exceeded expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 net sales rose 4% year-over-year, with both Premier Protein and Dymatize exceeding expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $556.0M … +1.6% YoY.”

surprises.description: Excess bottled-shake inventory created a substantial, newly disclosed cost and required further discounting: the full-year outlook includes $28 million of unfavorable inventory impacts, with additional Q4 promotional markdowns. The preview flagged retailer inventory and destocking risk, but not this specific excess bottle inventory and associated charges.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The full-year outlook includes $28 million of unfavorable inventory-related impacts ($21 million already recorded)”; Premier required a “$10 million reserve (2% of total inventory) plus additional Q4 promotional markdowns.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Retailer inventory/weeks-of-supply — destocking triggered the 2025 downdrafts and is central to the pending securities class action.”

surprises.description: Dymatize sales surged 27%, including 6% volume growth and 21% favorable price/mix, and exceeded expectations. That is a sharp recovery from the 1.9% sales decline reported for Q2, although the company cautioned that Q4 faces a tough comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Dymatize net sales surged 27% on 6% volume growth and 21% favorable price/mix from earlier inflation-driven price increases, though it faces a tough Q4 comparison.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Dymatize exceeding expectations.”

surprises.description: The company announced a double-digit price increase on Premier shakes and further powder pricing for Q1 FY2027, but expects volume elasticity to be slightly greater than 1—suggesting volume pressure could outweigh the price increase. The preview highlighted the tension between pricing, promotions, and consumer sensitivity but did not anticipate this specific price action or elasticity estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A double-digit price increase on Premier shakes plus additional powder pricing effective Q1 fiscal 2027,” with “expected volume elasticity slightly greater than 1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Price/mix vs. volume — can promotion be dialed back without losing Premier Protein shelf space” and the preview cited “price-sensitive consumers.”

surprises.description: A sizable Q4 legal settlement payment is expected to push net leverage from 3.2x at quarter-end to approximately 4x by fiscal year-end. The preview mentioned a pending securities class action but did not anticipate a settlement payment or this leverage increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net leverage stood at 3.2x at quarter-end but is expected to rise to approximately 4x by fiscal year-end due to a sizable legal settlement payment in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Retailer inventory/weeks-of-supply — destocking triggered the 2025 downdrafts and is central to the pending securities class action.”

surprises.description: A June organizational realignment incurred a $5 million charge but is expected to produce $10–$12 million in annualized operating expense savings, mostly in fiscal 2027. The preview identified a possible new-CEO strategic reset but did not forecast this specific restructuring charge or savings plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A June organizational realignment incurred a $5 million charge and is expected to generate $10-$12 million in annualized operating expense savings, mostly realized in fiscal 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “New CEO's strategic reset — Axelrod … may rebase expectations.”

surprises.description: Revenue was expected at $19.31 billion, with even the preview’s bull case set at $19.8 billion or more; Caterpillar reported a record $20.5 billion, its first quarter above $20 billion. That is a substantially stronger top-line result than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 sales and revenues reached a record $20.5 billion, up 24% year-over-year,” and this was “the first time Caterpillar surpassed $20 billion in a single quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $19.31B”; the bull scenario was “Revenue | ≥$19.8B.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was expected at $6.25, with the preview’s inferred buy-side bar at $6.45–$6.60 and its bull case at $6.75 or more. The reported $8.17 was well above all of those benchmarks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted profit per share rose 73% to $8.17, exceeding company expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS: $6.25”; the preview described the functional buy-side bar as “$6.45–$6.60 EPS” and the bull case as “≥$6.75.”

surprises.description: Backlog was expected to grow by only $1–3 billion in the base case, while the preview’s bull case called for $5 billion or more of sequential growth. Instead, backlog rose $9 billion to a record $72 billion, with contributions from all three primary segments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog grew sequentially by $9 billion to a record $72 billion,” up “approximately 92% versus Q2 last year,” with “all three primary segments contributing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case anticipated “backlog $64–66B (+$1–3B q/q),” while the bull case anticipated “Backlog ≥$67–68B (+$5B q/q).”

surprises.description: The consolidated adjusted operating margin was expected to be about 19.1%; the reported 21.9% was materially higher. The result included $392 million of IEEPA tariff recoveries, an important contributor the preview had not identified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating profit margin was 21.9%, a 430 basis point increase over the prior year, boosted by $392 million in IEEPA tariff recoveries.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. operating margin | ~19.1% | 17.6% | +150bps.”

surprises.description: The full-year sales-growth outlook was raised from low double-digit growth to mid- to high-teens growth, a larger upgrade than the preview’s example of a raise to low-teens growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its full-year 2026 sales and revenues growth outlook to mid- to high-teens, up from prior guidance, driven by demand across all three primary segments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The standing guide was “low double-digit” sales growth; the preview said an explicit raise “to ‘low-teens’ growth” would be a bull trigger.

surprises.description: Power-generation sales to users surged 72% on data-center demand, far stronger than the preview’s expectation that growth would hold around 35–40%. This is a pronounced acceleration in the demand metric the preview identified as central to the Power & Energy outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sales to users in power generation surged 72% on data center demand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bull scenario expected “power gen still +35–40%”; the preview also said Q1 power-generation sales were “+41% y/y” and that sustaining that growth rate mattered.

surprises.description: Construction Industries sales growth substantially exceeded the preview’s directional estimate, and its reported margin was also above the displayed estimate. The $400 million dealer-inventory increase is a qualification, but sales to users grew for a sixth consecutive quarter, so the result was not just dealer restocking.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Construction Industries sales jumped 35% to $8.3 billion with a 23.3% margin, aided by a $400 million dealer inventory increase and sixth consecutive quarter of sales-to-users growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The segment table showed Construction Industries sales of “$7.24B,” “+18.0%,” and an operating-margin estimate of “22.4%.” The preview also said to watch whether CI was being “flattered by dealer restocking versus end-user demand.”

surprises.description: Power & Energy orders were being taken as far out as 2030, extending beyond the preview’s reference to orders well into 2028 and its request for quantified forward-order visibility. That provides stronger evidence of demand duration than the preview’s expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: Caterpillar was “taking Power and Energy orders as far out as 2030.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted Q1 orders were “well into 2028” and called for “Explicit 2027 order commentary / data-center regulatory response,” including quantified new power-generation bookings.

surprises.description: Caterpillar is restarting production of its 10-megawatt gas reciprocating-engine platform, adding about 1.5 gigawatts of capacity with shipments due to begin in Q4. The preview discussed capacity investment generally but did not anticipate this specific restart or near-term shipment timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is restarting production of its 10-megawatt gas reciprocating engine platform, bringing about 1.5 gigawatts of capacity online with shipments beginning in Q4.”

surprises.description: Full-year tariff costs were guided to the low end of the preview’s $2.2–$2.4 billion range. This is a favorable reduction in expected costs, although the facts do not provide the actual Q2 tariff cost needed to compare with the preview’s roughly $700 million quarterly guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 tariff costs are now expected to be around $2.2 billion (low end of the prior range), while Q3 tariff costs are estimated at roughly $600 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified “the FY $2.2–$2.4B range” and said “Another trim is a clean, high-quality margin beat.”

surprises.description: The company reported record MP&E free cash flow of $5.1 billion and returned $2.2 billion to shareholders, including an 8% dividend increase. The preview flagged cash flow and capacity spending as issues to watch but gave no Q2 cash-flow or shareholder-return expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Caterpillar generated record MP&E free cash flow of $5.1 billion and returned $2.2 billion to shareholders via $1.5 billion buybacks and dividends, including an 8% dividend increase.”

in_line: Power & Energy segment sales rose 17%, broadly in line with the preview’s directional estimate of 15.1% growth.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $93.3 million, about $4.8 million below the preview’s $98.1 million consensus. That was a miss even though revenue grew 1% year over year, rather than showing the roughly 6% reported decline implied by the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue grew just 1% year-over-year to $93.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: ~$98.1M … vs. $104.6M in Q2 2025 — an implied ~6% reported decline.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.08, below the preview’s $0.10 consensus. Full-year adjusted EPS guidance was also lower than the preview’s cited range, at $0.31–$0.36 rather than $0.35–$0.41.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS held flat at $0.08; full-year adjusted diluted EPS is guided to $0.31-$0.36.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS: $0.10”; FY2026 guidance was “$0.35–0.41.”

surprises.description: The company reaffirmed full-year revenue guidance at $367–$382 million, below the preview’s cited $395–$405 million range. The preview expected confirmation of that range, although it also noted a 0–4% growth target excluding the divested business.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reaffirmed its full-year 2026 revenue guidance of 0% to 4% growth ($367 million to $382 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance … revenue $395–405M”; the preview also asked whether “the $395–405M revenue … ranges are reiterated.”

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted EBITDA margin guidance was lowered to 29%–31%, rather than holding at the preview’s cited 30%–32% range. Management attributed the reduction to divestiture-related stranded costs, not weaker underlying performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year EBITDA margin guidance was lowered to 29%-31% from the prior 30%-32%, attributed to divestiture-related stranded costs rather than underlying performance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin 30–32%”; the preview asked whether the range would be reiterated.

surprises.description: Bookings momentum was stronger than the preview’s cautious setup suggested: normalized trailing-12-month bookings growth accelerated to 7% exiting the first half, from 0.8% at the end of 2025, and pipeline grew 27% year over year. The preview had highlighted weak Q1 bookings and sought evidence of a second-half bookings-to-revenue recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Normalized for the Chemaxon acquisition, trailing 12-month bookings growth accelerated to 7% exiting the first half, up sharply from 0.8% exiting 2025, and sales pipeline grew 27% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that “Total bookings fell 2%” in Q1 and said to watch for “second-half bookings-to-revenue conversion commentary.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a May workforce reduction of about 5% and said combined operational actions should produce roughly $13 million of run-rate savings, more than the previously identified plan. The preview did not flag this expanded savings program.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A May reduction in force cut approximately 5% of the global workforce, and combined operational actions are expected to yield roughly $13 million in run-rate savings, an increase over the prior identified plan.”

surprises.description: Alongside completing a $100 million buyback, the Board authorized a new $50 million repurchase program, a capital-allocation action the preview did not discuss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed a $100 million buyback (including $17.4 million repurchased in Q2), and the Board authorized a new $50 million share repurchase program.”

in_line: Software remained the stronger business while services remained softer: software revenue grew 4% and services revenue declined 3%, consistent with the preview’s framing of software strength and services demand as the key swing factor.

Services bookings were nearly flat at down 1%, a marked improvement from the 14% decline cited for Q1 and a stabilization signal the preview specifically said to watch for; the reported services book-to-bill was still only 1.07.

surprises.description: The preview identified a pending Breakthrough Therapy request as a potential catalyst, including a grant in its bull case. The FDA declined BTD for the cVM program based on the initial 12-week data package, although management said this does not change the development path.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The FDA declined to grant Breakthrough Therapy Designation for the cutaneous venous malformation (cVM) program based on the initial 12-week data package, though management says this does not alter the development path.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Phase 3 start guided 2H26 with a Breakthrough Therapy request pending”; the bull case included “TOIVA Ph3 dosing + BTD granted for CVM.”

surprises.description: The preview framed FY26 cash burn at about $80 million and warned that a higher burn could reopen financing concerns. Management raised planned 2026 cash spend to approximately $85–95 million, citing expanded commercial and medical affairs investment, while saying the existing cash supports operations through potential approval and a standalone launch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its 2026 cash spend guidance to approximately $85-95 million due to expanded commercial and medical affairs investments”; the company said its cash funds operations “through potential approval and a standalone launch.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Prior framing was ~$80M FY26 burn”; the preview said burn above that level could imply a 2027 equity raise.

surprises.description: The preview focused on the more than 30,000 diagnosed U.S. MLM patients and the MLM opportunity. Management described a potential expansion of QTORIN rapamycin’s addressable U.S. population to more than 300,000 across multiple mTOR-driven indications, with cVM approval targeted for 2029 and angiokeratomas for 2031.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The pipeline-in-a-product strategy could expand QTORIN rapamycin's addressable U.S. population from over 30,000 MLM patients to over 300,000 across multiple mTOR-driven indications,” with cVM targeted for 2029 and angiokeratomas for 2031.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “>30,000 diagnosed U.S. mLM patients” and a “$1B+ peak U.S. sales” claim, and discussed pipeline expansion without quantifying a population above 300,000.

surprises.description: The preview flagged pricing and payer framing as items to watch but gave no specific favorable expectation. Management cited orphan-drug pricing of $100,000–$200,000 per patient per year for MLM and payer research indicating strong coverage support with no expected step-throughs of unapproved therapies.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Orphan drug pricing of $100,000-$200,000 per patient per year for MLM,” with “strong coverage support and no expected step-throughs of unapproved therapies.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for: ... payer/pricing framing.”

surprises.description: The preview discussed commercial hiring and patient identification but did not report physician-demand survey findings. Management said more than 80% of surveyed physicians would consider QTORIN as first-line therapy across all four indications, and 96% would incorporate it for angiokeratomas.
surprises.fact_evidence: “More than 80% of surveyed physicians said they would consider the QTORIN candidate as first-line therapy across all four indications, and 96% said they would incorporate QTORIN rapamycin into their practice for angiokeratomas.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “patient-identification progress” and commercial buildout, but stated no expectation for physician survey results.

surprises.description: The preview anticipated DSAP pitavastatin entering Phase II, but did not mention a third product candidate. Management also said the company expects to announce a third product candidate later this year, adding a pipeline disclosure beyond the preview’s specific expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Expects to announce a fourth indication (QTORIN pitavastatin for DSAP entering Phase II in Q4 2026) and a third product candidate later this year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “QTORIN pitavastatin (DSAP) Ph2 initiation 2H26” and said two new indications were promised for 2H26; it did not mention a third product candidate.

surprises.description: Management introduced a plan to pursue FDA Platform Designation after the first approval to expedite future programs, a regulatory strategy not discussed in the preview. The potential benefit is prospective rather than a near-term change to the stated timelines.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Plans to pursue FDA Platform Designation after its first approval to expedite future programs.”

in_line: The first NDA module had already been submitted before the preview; management remained on track for full submission in 2H 2026 and potential approval in 1H 2027, matching the preview’s baseline timeline.

Cash of approximately $251 million was within the preview’s estimated $245–252 million range, and management said it funds operations through potential approval and a standalone launch, consistent with the preview’s no-raise framing.
The planned sales force of approximately 40 reps was at the upper end of the preview’s 30–40-rep range.
TOIVA’s 73% improvement result had already been reported in the preview, and the expected Q4 2026 Phase III start falls within the preview’s 2H 2026 guidance.
The preview already expected QTORIN pitavastatin DSAP Phase II initiation in 2H 2026; the call’s Q4 2026 timing is within that window.
The Phase III SELVA win was already known before the release; the call reiterated that the study met its endpoints and reported 95% improvement on the primary endpoint.

surprises.description: Enpro raised its 2026 outlook further than the preview’s bull case: sales growth is now 14%-16%, adjusted EBITDA $330-$340 million, and adjusted EPS $9.30-$9.80. The preview’s bull case contemplated roughly $325-$338 million of EBITDA and $9.20-$9.70 of EPS, while its current baseline guidance was lower still.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its full-year 2026 guidance,” with total sales growth of 14%-16% (up from 10%-14%), adjusted EBITDA of $330-$340 million (up from $315-$330 million), and adjusted diluted EPS of $9.30-$9.80 (up from $8.85-$9.50).
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull scenario expected a raise to “~$9.20–9.70 EPS / $325–338M EBITDA”; its current guidance was 10%-14% sales growth, $315-$330 million EBITDA, and $8.85-$9.50 EPS.

surprises.description: Q2 sales were well above both published consensus and the preview’s higher buy-side estimate: $338.8 million versus consensus of about $323 million and a suggested buy-side bar near $328 million. The 17.6% reported growth also exceeded the preview’s roughly 12% consensus growth expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 sales rose 17.6% year-over-year to $338.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 revenue consensus was “$322.9M – $323.7M”; the preview said the buy-side bar sat closer to “~$328M revenue.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EPS substantially exceeded expectations, reaching $2.50 versus $2.30 consensus and even above the preview’s estimated $2.35-$2.40 buy-side bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS reached $2.50 in Q2, up 23.2% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Adj. diluted EPS” consensus of “$2.30” and estimated a buy-side bar of “$2.35–2.40 EPS.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA also beat the preview’s derived estimate, and the margin was slightly above its projected range: $86.9 million versus roughly $80-$82 million expected, at 25.6% versus a derived 24.9%-25.4%.
surprises.fact_evidence: Adjusted EBITDA was “$86.9 million” and the margin was “25.6%,” up 90 basis points.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s derived estimates were “~$80–82M” of adjusted EBITDA and a “~24.9% – 25.4%” adjusted EBITDA margin.

surprises.description: Enpro recorded an unanticipated roughly $60 million environmental reserve for legacy Arizona uranium mines. The long delay before meaningful cash outflows limits the near-term cash impact, but the reserve build is a sizeable unexpected charge and long-duration remediation obligation.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company recorded a “roughly $60 million environmental reserve build” tied to legacy uranium mines in Arizona; no meaningful cash outflows are expected for about 3 years and remediation could span up to 10 years.

surprises.description: The company raised 2026 capital expenditure expectations from about $50 million to $60-$65 million, pulling AST cleaning-capacity investments forward. The preview discussed the AST ramp but did not anticipate this higher spending plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised 2026 capital expenditure expectations to $60-$65 million (up from ~$50 million),” pulling forward AST cleaning capacity investments in Arizona, Milpitas, California, and Taiwan.

surprises.description: Net leverage came down to 1.6x, below the preview’s cited 1.9x level, after $80 million of revolving debt repayment. That is better deleveraging than the preview’s starting point implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: Enpro “reduced net leverage to 1.6x” after repaying “$80 million in revolving debt” and generated “over $60 million in year-to-date free cash flow.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “net leverage (1.9x)” as a metric to watch.

surprises.description: Management said AST visibility now extends through 2027, adding a longer-dated visibility signal beyond the preview’s focus on the near-term H2 ramp and whether management would quantify orders or backlog. The preview did not anticipate visibility extending that far.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management said “visibility [is] now extending through 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview focused on the H2 ramp and said to watch “whether management quantifies backlog/order growth again.”

in_line: AST’s 21.8% Q2 revenue growth was within the preview’s expected 18%-22% range; its 23.9% margin was within the expected 23%-24% range. Management’s expectation of approximately 20% AST growth in H2 and margins approaching 25% exiting the year also matched the preview’s anticipated H2 ramp and year-end margin target.

Sealing Technologies’ 33.2% adjusted EBITDA margin was above the preview’s >32.5% watch level and within its expected 32.5%-33% range; its 10th consecutive quarter above 30% continued the expected durability.

Commercial vehicle markets remained soft and guidance did not assume a significant recovery, as the preview expected. Management’s early-stabilization comments were consistent with the preview’s expectation that the market might be nearing a bottom.

The $50 million share repurchase authorization remained in place; the preview had noted it as untouched and identified a buyback activation, rather than mere continuation, as a potential new development.

surprises.description: Revenue was $130 million, about 6% above the preview’s $122.1 million consensus estimate and above its $118–125 million base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue was $130 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Q2 FY26 Consensus | $122.1M”; the base case projected “Revenue $118–125M.”

surprises.description: The company lifted the low end of both FY26 guidance ranges: GOV’s floor rose from $2.2 billion to $2.3 billion, and adjusted EBITDA’s floor rose from $30 million to $34 million. The upper ends were unchanged.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised or set full-year fiscal 2026 guidance to Marketplace GOV of $2.3 billion to $2.6 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $34 million to $40 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 Marketplace GOV $2.2–2.6B, Adj. EBITDA $30–40M — reaffirmed at Q1.”

surprises.description: World Cup volume was exceptionally concentrated: the call compared its transaction volume with the entire Taylor Swift Eras Tour, while noting that the World Cup volume came in one quarter. The preview anticipated a World Cup boost but warned that falling resale prices could mean weak sell-through.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The World Cup generated transaction volume comparable to the entire Taylor Swift Eras Tour but concentrated in a single quarter rather than spread across two years”; it also drove “a mid-teens percentage of Q2 GOV.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The FIFA World Cup ... falls across Q2 and Q3”; the preview asked “how much GOV came from World Cup” and cautioned that pricing was “in free fall” with “possibly weak sell-through.”

surprises.description: World Cup orders had a greater than 99.7% successful fulfillment rate, a customer-experience result the preview did not identify as an expected outcome or key metric.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Vivid Seats maintained a greater than 99.7% successful fulfillment rate for World Cup orders,” contrasting its experience with “publicized fulfillment problems at a competitor.”

surprises.description: Outside the World Cup, industry volumes were softer, with theater weakness attributed to rising competition and soft Las Vegas leisure travel among lower-end consumers. The preview discussed competitive pressure generally but did not flag these specific demand headwinds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Industry volumes outside the World Cup were softer in Q2, with theater weakness driven by rising competitive intensity and soft Las Vegas leisure travel among lower-end consumers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a “crowded” competitive set and said “other competitors remain aggressive,” but did not identify theater and lower-end Las Vegas travel as specific Q2 pressures.

surprises.description: The revolving credit facility was renewed with maturity extended through August 2029, a concrete financing extension not anticipated in the preview’s discussion of stalled recapitalization talks and ongoing lender negotiations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with $137 million in cash and renewed its revolving credit facility with an extended maturity through August 2029.”
