surprises.description: Revenue was $173.5 million, below the preview’s $177–179 million consensus range, despite 21.9% reported growth. The preview had already warned that revenue consensus might be too high, but the actual result still fell short of that stated market expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue grew 21.9% to $173.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $177–179M.”

surprises.description: ODR organic revenue declined 3.4%, rather than inflecting to positive growth as the preview said it needed to do; the reported revenue increase came entirely from Pioneer Power.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The entire increase was driven by a $30.9 million contribution from the Pioneer Power acquisition, as ODR organic revenue actually declined 3.4%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “ODR organic growth…must inflect positive tonight” and modeled “ODR organic ~+3%.”

surprises.description: Limbach completed a $30 million CYMCOR acquisition, adding an immediate cash-and-revolver-funded transaction where the preview had warned that further M&A activity could be a negative. The company sees potential data-center and cross-selling benefits, but expects no CYMCOR contribution in current guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company acquired CYMCOR for $30 million (funded by cash and revolver borrowings)” and expects it to generate “$12 million of program management revenue and $4 million of adjusted EBITDA in 2027,” with “no contribution included in current guidance.” CYMCOR oversees budgets exceeding “$8 billion”; management cited roughly “$3 million” of services revenue pulling through “approximately $60 million” of bookings.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview warned that “more M&A talk tonight would read as a negative” given rising leverage and unproven integration.

in_line: Bookings remained strong at $182 million in the quarter and $616 million over the trailing three quarters, consistent with the preview’s emphasis that bookings and backlog had to hold up.
Pioneer Power’s gross margins improved about 150 basis points versus acquisition, broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of gradual improvement over a two-to-three-year period.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $1.90, far above the preview’s $1.60 “real bar” and the $1.55 published consensus. The result also exceeded the preview’s implied $1.58–$1.64 range based on management’s prior Q2 growth framing.
surprises.fact_evidence: Materion delivered record adjusted EPS of $1.90 in Q2 2026, up 39% year-over-year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat $1.60 as the real bar”; the preview also says management’s Q1 framing implied “$1.58–$1.64” for Q2.

surprises.description: Materion raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $6.80–$7.20, well above the preview’s existing $6.00–$6.50 range and even its bull-case guidance scenario of $6.35–$6.65.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management raised full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $6.80–$7.20, up from $6.00–$6.50.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed current guidance of “$6.00–$6.50” and a bull-case outcome of “guidance narrowed/raised to $6.35–$6.65.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow was much stronger than the preview’s base-case expectation of modestly positive cash flow, and exceeded even its bull-case threshold of $40 million. This was a strong reversal from the preview’s emphasis on weak Q1 cash flow and the risk of another negative quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company generated $59 million in free cash flow, approximately 150% conversion.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “FCF modestly positive,” while the bull case specified “FCF positive $40M+”; the preview also warned about “Two consecutive negative-FCF quarters.”

surprises.description: The company raised its full-year top-line outlook to mid-teens sales growth, adding a second consecutive quarterly increase. The preview focused on a possible EPS guidance raise but did not anticipate this top-line outlook increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company raised its full-year top-line outlook to mid-teens sales growth, marking the second consecutive quarterly guidance increase.

surprises.description: Record value-added sales of $308.2 million topped the preview’s roughly $300.8 million implied consensus and cleared its stated $305 million threshold for a strong underlying quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: Record value-added sales reached $308.2 million, up 15% year-over-year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave implied VA sales of “~$300.8M” and said “a $305M+ VA sales print is” what matters.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 23.3%, above the preview’s implied estimate of about 21.3%. The beat was partly helped by roughly $2–3 million in one-time positive items, which qualifies the strength of the underlying result.
surprises.fact_evidence: Adjusted EBITDA margin hit a record 23.3% ($71.8 million), with 250 basis points of year-over-year expansion, “though aided by roughly $2-3 million in one-time positive items.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview implied adjusted EBITDA of “~$64M / ~21.3% of VA.”

surprises.description: Electronic Materials’ adjusted EBITDA margin reached 32%, substantially exceeding the preview’s 27% segment consensus and its expectation of at least 28.5% for continued expansion. Management cautioned that Q2 was likely the richest mix of the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: Electronic Materials achieved a record 32% adjusted EBITDA margin, up nearly 900 basis points year-over-year; management flagged Q2 as likely the richest mix of the year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The segment consensus listed a “27%” margin; the preview expected “28.5%+” for a fifth consecutive quarter of margin expansion.

surprises.description: Precision Optics’ margin was 21.4%, above the preview’s 16% consensus estimate. However, its 26% sales growth was slightly below the preview’s 30% sales-growth expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: Precision Optics surpassed 20% EBITDA margin at 21.4%, while adjusted EBITDA rose 206% year-over-year on 26% sales growth.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s segment consensus forecast Precision Optics sales growth of “+30%” and a “16%” margin.

surprises.description: Backlog growth accelerated beyond the preview’s already strong expected pace: it was up roughly 30% year-over-year and 20% since the start of the year, versus expectations of about 20% year-over-year and 15% year-to-date.
surprises.fact_evidence: Record backlog grew roughly 30% year-over-year and 20% since the start of the year, with first-half incoming orders up nearly 30%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 backlog was “+20% YoY and +15% YTD” and asked whether backlog would “hold the +20% YoY pace.”

surprises.description: The defense RFQ pipeline expanded substantially beyond the preview’s $300 million reference point, with more than $500 million in open RFQs. The preview had highlighted conversion from the existing pipeline as something to watch, but did not anticipate this increase in its size.
surprises.fact_evidence: Defense had over $500 million in open RFQs, up from approximately $300 million last quarter.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$300M in open RFQs” and said to watch how much of that pipeline converted.

surprises.description: Space orders doubled year-over-year and now account for roughly a quarter of aerospace and defense sales, a specific strength not anticipated in the preview’s discussion of defense orders and overall A&D order rates.
surprises.fact_evidence: Space orders doubled year-over-year and now represent roughly 25% of aerospace and defense sales.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted A&D order rates running “+50% YoY” and focused on defense orders and RFQs, but did not state an expectation for space orders or their sales mix.

surprises.description: The $65 million beryllium capacity investment will push CapEx above the preview’s stated $75 million forecast, but incoming customer funds will offset the added spending. The funding offset makes the higher reported CapEx less of a cash-flow burden than the preview’s spending figures alone suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: A $65 million customer-funded beryllium capacity investment will flow through CapEx above the disclosed $75 million forecast but be offset by incoming funds.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “$75M capex plus $25M mine development” and said to watch for an update on “the $65M US defense investment.”

in_line: Electronic Materials delivered its fifth consecutive quarter of margin expansion, as the preview expected; the size of the margin increase was substantially above expectation.
All three business segments posted double-digit growth, consistent with the preview’s broad expectation for strong segment growth outside the specific Performance Materials recovery debate.

surprises.description: KHC increased the planned incremental investment by another $100 million, almost entirely for marketing, on top of the preview’s $600 million plan. That is more spending than investors were told to expect, though management framed it as an investment from a position of strength.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management announced “an additional $100 million in incremental spending—almost entirely marketing—on top of the prior $600 million,” framing it as “spending from a position of strength.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a “$600M reinvestment” in the U.S. business and focused on whether that spend was “buying volume and share.”

surprises.description: Only about one-third of the original $600 million investment had been spent, leaving most of the outlay for the second half. The preview emphasized whether the spending was already translating into volume and share, so the back-loaded timing makes that proof point later than investors might have hoped.
surprises.fact_evidence: Only “roughly $200 million” of the planned $600 million had been spent; the remaining roughly $500 million was weighted to the second half, broadly evenly between Q3 and Q4.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said that “1H tracking to the upper half” would be a bull unlock and that the key question was whether the $600 million was “buying volume and share.”

surprises.description: Management said the 2026 investment year would not be followed by a wraparound of investment spending in 2027, presenting 2026 as the margin trough setup for 2027 growth. The preview called 2026 a trough year but did not specify whether elevated spending would continue into 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management reiterated that “2026 is the base investment year with no wraparound of investment spend into 2027,” positioning it as the “margin trough setup for 2027 growth.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed 2027 inflation of 4% to 5%, a future cost pressure not flagged in the preview. It said the pressure was manageable and that productivity would offset as much as possible while margins were maintained and strengthened, tempering the adverse cost signal.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects “2027 inflation in the 4% to 5% range” but said it is manageable and intends to offset as much as possible through productivity while “maintaining and strengthening margins.”

surprises.description: U.S. consumption improved from a roughly 2.5% decline in Q2 to about a 1% decline in July, and management expects sequential improvement in Q3 and Q4. That is a more constructive demand trend than the preview’s roughly 4.3% expected company volume/mix decline suggested, although consumption and KHC’s volume/mix are not identical measures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. consumption declined about 2.5% in Q2 but improved to roughly -1% in July,” with management guiding to sequential improvement in Q3 and Q4.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed expected volume/mix of “~-4.3%” and identified volume as “the whole thesis.”

surprises.description: Heinz and U.S. condiments showed notable growth: Heinz was up 3% worldwide year-to-date, and U.S. condiments were up 3% year-to-date versus flat in the prior year. The preview highlighted Taste Elevation and emerging markets as areas to watch, but did not anticipate these specific growth figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Heinz grew 3% worldwide year-to-date” with a 12% increase in emerging markets in the quarter, and “U.S. condiments grew 3% year-to-date versus flat last year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “Taste Elevation (Heinz, Philadelphia, sauces)” and described emerging markets as the growth narrative, but gave no expectation for these Heinz or condiment figures.

surprises.description: KHC paid down $1.9 billion of debt during the quarter and another $1 billion after quarter-end, while raising its cash-conversion expectation. The preview focused on roughly 100% FCF conversion and dividend cover, so the higher conversion expectation is favorable; free-cash-flow guidance in dollars, however, was essentially unchanged.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “paid down $1.9 billion of debt in the quarter plus another $1 billion after quarter close, raised its cash conversion expectation, and kept free cash flow guidance essentially unchanged in dollar terms.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited an FY “FCF conversion guide ~100%” and flagged “FCF and dividend cover” as a key watch item.

surprises.description: At the midpoint, the second-half organic-sales outlook looks weaker than the first half on the surface, but management said underlying performance improves by roughly 70–80 basis points after adjusting for the Q1 snowstorm benefit and Q2 shipment phasing. The preview did not lay out this specific second-half profile, so the apparent slowdown and the more favorable normalized comparison are both new context.
surprises.fact_evidence: “At the midpoint, second-half organic sales appear weaker than the first half,” but normalizing for the “~0.7 pp Q1 snowstorm benefit” and “~0.8 pp Q2 shipment phasing into Q3” shows underlying performance improving by roughly 70–80 bps.

in_line: Market-share losses narrowed to 30 bps in the first half and roughly 20 bps in recent weeks, consistent with the preview’s base case of share stabilizing and its reference to improving market-share trends.
KHC absorbed the built-in 100 bps SNAP-related headwind while protecting market share, as the preview said the 2026 guidance included that headwind and expected it to be absorbed.

surprises.description: Continuing-operations revenue was just under $2.0 billion, far below the preview’s $2.68 billion consensus, which included an $804 million Food Ingredients estimate. The scope difference makes this a large reported-revenue gap, not evidence by itself of an underlying sales collapse; on the continuing-operations basis, revenue was up roughly 6%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 continuing operations revenue was just under $2 billion, up roughly 6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales: $2.68B”; the segment table includes “Food Ingredients: $804M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted operating EBITDA was $408 million, well below the preview’s roughly $538 million segment-sum bogey, which also included Food Ingredients. The comparison is therefore heavily affected by the changed reporting perimeter, although the continuing-operations figure itself rose 6%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted operating EBITDA rose 6% to $408 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Implied adj. op. EBITDA (sum of segment consensus): ~$538M”; the segment table includes Food Ingredients.

surprises.description: The full-year dollar guidance reset sharply lower than the preview’s expected ranges: sales to $7.4–$7.6 billion from an expected $10.5–$10.8 billion, and EBITDA to $1.53–$1.6 billion from $2.05–$2.15 billion. The scale of the gap is large, but it reflects a different business perimeter following the Food Ingredients divestiture rather than a like-for-like reduction in the outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance was raised to sales of $7.4-$7.6 billion ... and EBITDA of $1.53-$1.6 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management reaffirmed FY2026 guidance of $10.5–10.8B sales and $2.05–2.15B adjusted operating EBITDA.”

surprises.description: Despite the lower nominal guidance, IFF raised its sales-growth outlook: the range became 2%–4%, with the low end up from 1%, rather than the preview’s expectation that the prior range would be reaffirmed at its low end. That is a positive change in the outlook on the continuing-operations basis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sales of $7.4-$7.6 billion (2%-4% growth, up from 1%-4%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Comparable CN sales growth would land at the low end of the 1–4% range”; the base case expected guidance to be “reaffirmed at low end of sales range.”

surprises.description: The preview asked for a capital-allocation framework but did not anticipate a $2.5 billion repurchase authorization with roughly $500 million planned before the transaction closes and the remaining $2 billion afterward. The size and staged timing make this a substantial return-of-capital commitment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Board authorized a $2.5 billion share repurchase program”; “about $500 million expected in H2 2026” and “the remaining $2 billion following close by end of 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy side wants a framework: buyback size vs. further deleveraging vs. bolt-on M&A.”

surprises.description: IFF also committed more than $1 billion of divestiture proceeds to debt reduction and set a net-leverage target of 2.0x–2.5x by the end of 2027. The preview highlighted the need for a proceeds framework but did not specify an expected debt-repayment amount or target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Use more than $1 billion of divestiture proceeds to reduce debt,” targeting “net debt to credit-adjusted EBITDA of 2.0x-2.5x by end of 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy side wants a framework: buyback size vs. further deleveraging vs. bolt-on M&A.”

surprises.description: Scent grew at a high-single-digit rate, above the preview’s 3.5% sales-growth consensus. However, Fragrance Ingredients’ growth of more than 20% was boosted by an easy comparison and opportunistic synthetics sales, and management expects it to normalize lower in the second half, tempering the positive Q2 result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “High single-digit Scent growth”; “Fragrance Ingredients grew over 20% in Q2, boosted by an easy comparison ... and opportunistic synthetics sales,” with growth expected “to normalize lower in H2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Scent consensus was “$624M” and “+3.5%” year over year; the preview also described commodity Fragrance Ingredients pressure.

surprises.description: Fine Fragrance finished slightly positive in Q2 even though the referenced guidance had called for a mid-single-digit decline. But management warned of a softer Q3 against a 20% prior-year comparison, less encouraging than the preview’s expectation of gradual second-half improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fine Fragrance finished Q2 slightly positive despite guidance for a mid-single-digit decline,” while “a softer Q3 is expected against a 20% prior-year comparable.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Fine Fragrance weakness in the Middle East” and said “gradual 2H improvement” was expected.

surprises.description: Management disclosed a couple-hundred-million-dollar working-capital headwind in the second half from the separation. The preview focused on whether working-capital discipline would support free cash flow, but did not flag this sizable separation-related cash use.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A couple-hundred-million-dollar working capital headwind [is] anticipated in H2 from the separation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Confirmation that working capital discipline is structural, not one-quarter.”

surprises.description: The company quantified roughly $100 million of temporary stranded corporate and functional costs after the Food Ingredients separation, with only about two-thirds targeted for elimination within 12 months after close and the rest by year two. The preview specifically sought a stranded-cost number but had no amount or reduction timeline to compare against.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately $100 million in stranded corporate/functional costs” will temporarily pressure margins; management targets eliminating “about two-thirds within 12 months post-close and the remainder by the second year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “a number on stranded costs” but did not give an expected amount or timeline.

surprises.description: Higher incentive-compensation accruals tied to strong first-half performance reduced Q2 EBITDA growth by a couple of percentage points. The preview did not identify this compensation expense as a drag on the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: EBITDA growth was “muted by higher incentive compensation accruals tied to strong first-half results,” costing “a couple of percentage points of EBITDA growth.”

in_line: Management had already said Q2 absolute EBITDA dollars would be below Q1’s $568 million; the preview treated that sequential decline as pre-announced.
The preview anticipated continued price-to-input-cost pressure and said surcharges were not yet fully implemented. Q2 growth was driven entirely by volume, with negligible pricing.

The preview highlighted free cash flow and the possibility that working-capital improvement could support it. First-half free cash flow was $378 million, up $284 million year over year, driven by net working-capital improvements.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue, adjusted EBITDA margin, and adjusted EPS all substantially exceeded the preview’s expectations: revenue was $2.8 billion versus consensus of about $2.65 billion, margin was 24% versus about 21.3%, and EPS was $3.93 versus $3.06–$3.07.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $2.8 billion with adjusted EBITDA of $660 million, delivering a 24% adjusted EBITDA margin, while adjusted EPS came in at $3.93.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales: $2.65–2.66B”; “Adj. EPS: $3.06–3.07”; “Adj. EBITDA margin (implied): ~21.3%.”

surprises.description: The Q3 outlook is weaker than the preview’s anticipated H2 price/cost recovery: management expects a 20–22% adjusted EBITDA margin, below Q2’s 24%, and said Iran-related cost pressure will rise to roughly $40 million. The preview expected cost recovery in Q3–Q4, making the increasing Q3 cost burden a negative deviation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance” projects “revenue of $2.6–2.7 billion (slightly below prior year) and an adjusted EBITDA margin of only 20–22%, down from 24% in Q2”; “the Iran cost impact [is] expected to worsen to roughly $40 million in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “negative price/cost across most segments, with recovery in Q3–Q4 as pricing catches up”; the preview also says the key question is whether “the H2 catch-up is reaffirmed, pushed out, or upsized.”

surprises.description: Roofing faces a sharper Q3 setback than the preview anticipated: management expects revenue to fall mid- to high single digits as shipments decline after demand was pulled into Q2 ahead of price increases, and expects the margin to fall to about 30% from 34% in Q2. This contrasts with the preview’s expectation of H2 price/cost recovery following the June increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Roofing Q3 revenue is guided down mid- to high single digits with ARMA shipments expected down high single digits due to demand pulled forward into Q2 ahead of price increases, and Roofing EBITDA margin is expected to fall to ~30% from 34% in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management expected “recovery in Q3–Q4 as pricing catches up” and described the June increase as a potential source of “better-than-modeled realization.”

surprises.description: Insulation outperformed the preview’s modeled decline: revenue grew 4% to $971 million versus an estimate of about $915 million, while EBITDA was $213 million at a 22% margin versus the preview’s $183 million and 20% margin estimate. Lower pricing and inflation still weighed on profitability, but the reported segment results were better than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Insulation delivered 4% revenue growth to $971 million driven by strong nonresidential and European volumes, though EBITDA fell to $213 million (22% margin) on lower pricing and inflation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s segment model estimated Insulation revenue of “~$915M,” EBITDA of “$183M,” and a “20%” margin.

surprises.description: Doors revenue was weaker than the preview’s model, but profitability was better: revenue was $513 million versus an estimate of about $526 million, while the 11% EBITDA margin exceeded the modeled 8.5%. The company attributed the margin beat largely to tariff refunds, so it was not solely an underlying operating improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Doors Q2 revenue fell 7% to $513 million due to strategic divestitures, with EBITDA of $57 million (11% margin) beating guidance largely because of tariff refunds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled Doors revenue at “~$526M” and a margin of “8.5%,” and expected revenue to be down mid-single digits.

surprises.description: Q2’s Iran-related cost pressure was less severe than the preview’s roughly $60 million estimate, and tariff refunds provided an additional offset. The call cited $30 million of Iran-related cost inflation and $25 million in tariff refunds, including half in Doors.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 EBITDA included $25 million in tariff refunds (half in Doors) that partially offset $30 million in net Iran-related cost inflation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had quantified “~$60M of Q2 inflation tied to the Iran conflict.”

in_line: The company achieved $135 million in run-rate Doors synergies, matching the preview’s expectation that the $135 million target would be reached by midyear; the additional $75 million of structural cost improvements also matched the preview’s stated program.

The $200 million of Q2 buybacks and continued commitment to return $1 billion in 2026 were consistent with the preview’s expectation of a meaningful Q2 repurchase and the company’s previously stated return commitment.
The $800 million 2026 capital investment plan matched the preview’s FY capex expectation of about $800 million.
The CFO handoff to Jonathan Collins on August 10 matched the preview’s stated transition timing.

Management declined to comment on Carlyle acquisition speculation, consistent with the preview’s description that Owens Corning had not substantively engaged and had not formally rejected the approaches.

surprises.description: North America subscribers came in at 5.75 million, about 350,000 above the preview’s estimated 5.4 million. Instead of the expected seasonal and blackout-related sequential decline, subscribers rose by about 25,000 sequentially, with management attributing the step-change to the World Cup.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total North America subscribers reached 5.75 million”; “The World Cup drove a step-change in subscriber trajectory, producing a sequential gain of about 25,000 subscribers versus a roughly 250,000 sequential decline in the year-ago third quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base case -250K to -350K sequentially to ~5.35–5.45M.”

surprises.description: EPS was a substantially larger loss than the preview’s approximate consensus: a loss of $0.25 per share versus an expected loss of about $0.09. The preview warned that EPS estimates were stale and inconsistently rebased, but the reported gap was still sizeable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed to $25.7 million (a loss of $0.25 per share) from $38 million in the prior-year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS ~-$0.09”; the preview also cautioned that “consensus EPS dispersion is wide and partly stale.”

surprises.description: Fubo raised the low end of its FY2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance by $10 million rather than simply reaffirming the existing range. The high end remained $100 million, so the improvement was a higher floor rather than a higher maximum.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised fiscal 2026 pro forma adjusted EBITDA guidance to $90-$100 million (up $10 million at the low end).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a “reaffirm[ation] at $80–100M” was the base case and identified a raise as the bull case.

surprises.description: The call disclosed that COO Alberto Horihuela will leave the operating role and move to a Founder Advisor role by year-end, a leadership transition the preview did not flag. His continued involvement through 2027 provides some continuity, making the news mixed rather than wholly negative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Co-Founder and COO Alberto Horihuela will transition to a Founder Advisor role by year-end and remain through 2027.”

surprises.description: Advertising results included an unexpectedly strong concrete marker: June was the best month of ad growth in at least two years, with double-digit year-over-year increases in CPM and fill rates. The preview anticipated ad upside and faster-than-expected improvement, but did not anticipate this best-in-two-years result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Migration to the Disney ad server delivered double-digit increases in CPM and fill rates versus last year, with June marking the best month of ad growth in at least two years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “watch for ad upside called out here” from the World Cup, while noting CPMs and fill rates had improved “faster than expected.”

surprises.description: Management said current cash exceeds the face value of the 2029 convertible notes, giving the company refinancing optionality. The preview discussed cash levels and the year-end cash threshold, but not this specific balance-sheet position or financing option.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $236.4 million in cash” and current cash “exceed[s] the face value of its 2029 convertible notes, providing refinancing optionality.”

in_line: Revenue was $1.474 billion versus the preview’s roughly $1.50 billion consensus and $1.48–$1.52 billion base-case range; the preview noted that about $30 million of revenue variation could be noise.
Adjusted EBITDA of $19.1 million was within the preview’s estimated $10–$25 million range.
Management reaffirmed the fiscal 2028 adjusted EBITDA target of at least $300 million, as the preview identified reaffirmation as the key outcome to watch.
The Disney ad-server migration was tracking ahead of plan with faster-than-expected CPM lift, consistent with the preview’s expectation of faster improvement and a full migration by year-end.
Management reaffirmed positive free cash flow expectations for fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028; the preview had identified softened FCF-positive language as a downside risk.
The company expected to finish fiscal 2026 with more than $200 million in cash, consistent with the preview’s stated cash commitment and expected roughly $215–$235 million range.
The new CEO deferred detailed strategy across the four growth pillars until the November call, consistent with the preview’s expectation of constructive but non-committal first-call commentary.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $83.9 million, below both the $85–90 million company guide and the $87.44 million consensus. Management attributed about $3 million of the shortfall to KELK shipments delayed by the ERP implementation, with most expected to ship in Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $83.9 million”; revenue was “reduced by approximately $3 million due to temporarily delayed KELK shipments caused by a new ERP system implementation,” with those orders expected to ship “mostly in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview: “Net revenue | Consensus | $87.44M”; company guidance was “$85–90M (const. FX).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was just $0.04, well below even the preview’s lower alternative estimate of $0.108 and far below the $0.19 consensus. The quarter also had a GAAP net loss of $1.7 million, although adjusted earnings remained positive.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net earnings of $586,000 ($0.04 per diluted share)” and “a GAAP net loss of $1.7 million (-$0.13 per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview: “Adjusted EPS | $0.19”; alternative estimate “$0.108.”

surprises.description: Sensors bookings and demand were stronger than the preview’s confirmation threshold: the segment’s book-to-bill rose to 1.44 from 1.36 in Q1, with record bookings and 26% year-over-year revenue growth. This is evidence of further acceleration in the AI, data-center, semiconductor and defense-related business.
surprises.fact_evidence: Sensors had a “very strong 1.44 book-to-bill ratio,” “record quarterly bookings of $48.1 million (up 6% sequentially),” and “26% year-over-year revenue growth” driven by AI infrastructure, data center, semiconductor and defense demand.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview: “Watch Sensors specifically”; a “second consecutive quarter above 1.15 confirms” the order-cycle thesis, and the bull case said “Sensors AI/semi orders accelerate again.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed that its initial humanoid robotics customer formally nominated VPG as a vendor and projected a steep production ramp—from tens of bots per week to hundreds and potentially thousands by year-end. The preview anticipated watching for a move to production, but did not describe a nomination or this scale of ramp.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received a formal vendor nomination letter from its initial humanoid robotics customer,” which projects a ramp “from tens of bots per week to hundreds and even thousands per week by the end of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview: watch for “any move from pre-production to production at the two established humanoid makers.”

surprises.description: Backlog increased by roughly $10–11 million sequentially to $135.8 million, an additional sign of demand beyond the preview’s focus on book-to-bill. The preview expected book-to-bill above 1.0 but did not specify a backlog increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog grew approximately $10-11 million sequentially to $135.8 million.”

surprises.description: Foreign exchange was a sizable operating-profit headwind, reducing profit by about $900,000 sequentially and $3.3 million year over year. The preview highlighted margin and EPS sensitivity but did not flag this specific drag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Foreign exchange was a significant headwind, reducing operating profit by approximately $900,000 sequentially and $3.3 million year-over-year.”

surprises.description: Management expects full-year 2026 organic growth to exceed the 8%–10% target in its three-year plan. The preview discussed the plan’s longer-term margin and EBITDA targets but did not anticipate full-year growth exceeding its target.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “expects full-year 2026 organic growth to exceed the 8%-10% target in its 3-year plan.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Call: “expects full-year 2026 organic growth to exceed the 8%-10% target in its 3-year plan.”

surprises.description: Price increases will provide only a limited near-term benefit because they apply only to new orders; management expects the Q3 ASP benefit to be just a few hundred thousand dollars. The preview did not flag this constraint on near-term pricing benefits.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Price increases can only be applied to new orders, limiting near-term ASP benefit to a few hundred thousand dollars in Q3.”

in_line: Consolidated book-to-bill was 1.14, above 1.0 as the preview expected, and marked the seventh consecutive quarter at or above 1.0; it was, however, just below the preview’s 1.15 confirmation threshold.
Q3 revenue guidance of $84–89 million after Q2 revenue of $83.9 million implies a broadly in-line to modestly higher quarter, consistent with the preview’s base case of an in-line Q3 guide.

The company reported first-half cost savings of $1.6 million and said it remained on track for $6 million this year within the three-year cost-reduction program, consistent with the preview’s expectation that progress on the program would be a secondary item.

surprises.description: Vishay guided Q3 revenue to $945–975 million, a $960 million midpoint. That is above the preview’s $920–950 million base-case range and reaches its $960 million bull-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 revenue guidance is $945–975 million,” implying “4.5% sequential growth at the midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case called for a “Q3 guide $920–950M,” while its bull case called for “Q3 guide ≥$960M.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted revenue was $919 million, above the preview’s operative consensus cluster of $895–897 million and even above the company’s $905 million guidance ceiling. The result also exceeded the preview’s bull-case revenue range of $910–925 million’s lower bound, though it remained within that range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted revenue reached $919 million, exceeding guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed consensus of “$895M (Zacks) / $897M (MarketBeat)” and company guidance of “$875–905M”; its bull scenario was “$910–925M.”

surprises.description: Vishay said Q3 gross margin should reach 24%, one quarter earlier than planned. That is ahead of the preview’s focus on a margin trajectory toward 23%, indicating a faster-than-expected recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management guided Q3 gross margin to “24%, achieving that target one quarter earlier than planned.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified “Gross margin trajectory toward 23%” as a catalyst and said the bull case required “GM ≥22.5%.”

surprises.description: Q2 EPS was $0.19, four cents above the preview’s $0.15 GAAP consensus estimate. The beat was meaningful relative to the estimate, though the preview had characterized the reported quarter as likely in line to better.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 EPS was $0.19 (both GAAP and adjusted).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “EPS (GAAP) $0.15” and said the quarter was “likely in-line-to-better.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin reached 22.6%, above the 22.0% guide and the preview’s roughly 22.0% consensus. It also cleared the preview’s 22.5% threshold for validating operating leverage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin expanded to 22.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed consensus gross margin of “~22.0%,” company guidance of “22.0% ±50bp,” and said “Anything above 22.5% validates operating leverage.”

surprises.description: Orders and backlog remained especially strong: book-to-bill was 1.32 and backlog coverage expanded to 6.1 months. The book-to-bill was slightly below Q1’s 1.34, but above the preview’s expected 1.15–1.30 base range, while coverage extended rather than flattening.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Book-to-bill hit 1.32” and “total backlog [grew] 18% to $1.9 billion, representing 6.1 months of coverage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said book-to-bill “Above ~1.15–1.20 = recovery intact,” gave a base-case range of “1.15–1.30,” and said to watch for backlog coverage “extending vs. flattening.”

surprises.description: Industrial revenue surged and accounted for more than half of the total revenue increase, with smart grid, AI power and high-voltage DC demand cited as drivers. The preview noted that segment-level detail was thin and flagged AI sizing as an open question, but had no specific expectation for this degree of industrial strength.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Industrial revenue jumped 16.2% sequentially and 30.1% year-over-year,” accounting for “over half of the total revenue increase,” driven by “smart grid, AI power and high-voltage DC demand.”

surprises.description: The reported offering raised $830 million net through 17.25 million shares, more than the preview’s stated $750 million raise. The proceeds fund accelerated capacity expansion and M&A, but the larger share issuance also means more dilution than the preview described.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed a public stock offering of 17.25 million shares, raising $830 million net,” boosting cash to $1.3 billion and funding “accelerated capacity expansion and M&A.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “A $750M equity raise priced at $50 on July 1” and said proceeds were “earmarked for growth plus revolver paydown.”

surprises.description: Vishay expects negative free cash flow for 2026. The preview already anticipated $400–440 million of capex and the German fab investment, but did not flag negative full-year free cash flow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “2026 CapEx is guided at $400–440 million” and “the company expects negative free cash flow for the year.”

surprises.description: Vishay disclosed price increases on about one-third of running part numbers, tied to higher metals, materials and logistics costs, with some increases already reflected in Q2. The preview had noted a 1.5% ASP contribution as an operational assumption, but did not anticipate this broad pricing action or the associated cost pressures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “About one-third of running part numbers have had announced price increases tied to rising metals, materials and logistics costs, with some already reflected in Q2 results.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the bull case required “the ~1.5% ASP contribution management guided to actually land.”

in_line: 2026 CapEx of $400–440 million, roughly half for the 12-inch German fab, and the mid-2027 nonautomotive production target matched the preview’s stated capex and fab expectations.

surprises.description: Adjusted OIBDA was about $12 million, far below the preview’s roughly $59 million base case, and the company reported a $19 million operating loss rather than the prior-year $42 million operating profit. The preview anticipated cost pressure, but not a decline in OIBDA of this size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted OIBDA collapsed to approximately $12 million from $66 million year-over-year,” and the company “swung to a $19 million operating loss from $42 million of operating income.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case was “Adj. OIBDA ~$59M”; it also said, “I’d expect [Baseball segment Adj. OIBDA] $40–45M.”

surprises.description: Q2 had 34 regular-season home games, two fewer than the preview’s estimate of 35–36. Baseball event revenue consequently fell $19 million; the preview expected fewer games, but estimated a smaller shortfall against the 40-game comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: The quarter included “only 34 regular season home games versus 40 in Q2 2025,” and baseball event revenue “fell $19 million to $161 million due to six fewer home games.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Q2 2026 lands at roughly 35–36 vs. 40,” or “~4 lost dates.”

surprises.description: Management said BravesVision will remain an elevated expense going forward and cited increased MLB revenue sharing among rising baseball costs. The preview expected payroll and in-house production costs to pressure margins, but did not flag revenue sharing or explicitly anticipate that BravesVision expense would remain elevated over time.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects “BravesVision to be an ongoing elevated expense going forward,” and confirmed higher costs from “rising Major League player salaries, production costs, and increased MLB revenue sharing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said, “Player payroll is up, and BravesVision production costs are now in-house opex,” and expected both to compress Baseball segment margin.

surprises.description: The preview expected more detailed BravesVision metrics in Q2, such as subscribers, household reach, or ad sales. The reported facts instead give management’s confidence in the network’s economics and say DTC results are ahead of early projections, but provide no quantified KPI.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management said it is “confident BravesVision will replicate or exceed the annualized revenue from its prior third-party local rights partner,” with “direct-to-consumer results outpacing early projections”; no subscriber, reach, or ad-sales figure is reported in the provided call facts.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “explicitly promised more detailed metrics in Q2” and called for “any quantified BravesVision KPI (subs, distribution households, ad revenue).”

surprises.description: The preview put revenue at $297.7 million consensus and about $303 million in its base case; reported revenue was $305 million. That was a modest beat to consensus and roughly in line with the preview’s modeled case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue declined to $305 million from $312 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Revenue $297.7M” consensus and a base case of “~$303M.”

surprises.description: Despite the Q2 game-count headwind, baseball event revenue grew roughly $4 million over the first six months, attributed to higher average attendance and contractual season-ticket rate increases. The preview discussed the need for strong per-game revenue and favorable Q1 attendance, but did not forecast this first-half growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: Baseball event revenue “grew roughly $4 million over the first six months on higher average attendance and contractual season ticket rate increases.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said per-game revenue “needs to grow ~11% just to hold the line” in Q2 and noted Q1 attendance of about 33,000 per game.

surprises.description: Management introduced the MLB national media deal’s January 1, 2029 expiration as a growth catalyst and cited the NBA’s annual media revenue increase from $2.7 billion to $7.7 billion. The preview focused on BravesVision and did not identify this future league-rights opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management cited “the MLB national media deal expiring 1/1/29 as a growth catalyst,” referencing the NBA’s increase “from $2.7 billion to $7.7 billion annually.”

surprises.description: Management raised the Section 162(m) salary tax-deduction limitation as an unintended consequence and said it expects a legislative or regulatory fix. The preview did not mention this issue, and the reported facts do not quantify its financial effect.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management flagged the “salary tax deduction limitation (Section 162m) as an unintended consequence they expect to resolve via a legislative or regulatory fix.”

in_line: Media-related revenue was $73 million versus the preview’s roughly $74 million base case. The preview anticipated BravesVision revenue-recognition timing effects and a slower collection cadence.

Mixed-use development revenue was $29 million, close to the preview’s roughly $30 million base case. The reported growth, occupancy above 93%, and higher visitor count were broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation for continued Battery Atlanta growth.

surprises.description: Ardent reported Q2 adjusted EBITDA of $115 million, below the preview’s roughly $125 million estimate and below its stated clean-Q1-based expectation of about $118–$125 million. The result was only slightly above the preview’s estimated clean Q1 level of $113 million, rather than the anticipated step-up.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $1.62 billion with adjusted EBITDA of $115 million, down from Q1's $124 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA *not published* (my est. ~$125M)”; “Clean Q1 was ~$113M”; “Anything below ~$118M breaks the FY bridge.”

surprises.description: Q2 activity was weaker than the preview’s base case of softness concentrated in ER or low-acuity volumes with surgical mix holding: surgeries declined 2.9% and admissions declined 1%. The weakness was concentrated in April and May, though volumes returned to modest growth in June and July.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Surgeries and admissions declining 2.9% and 1% respectively, driven by material weakness in April and May before rebounding to modest growth in June and July.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: Volume softness is real but confined to ER/low-acuity; surgical mix holds.”

surprises.description: Despite the Q2 EBITDA shortfall, management said Q3 EBITDA should approach Q1’s $124 million level. That points to a stronger Q3 than the preview’s expectation that Q2 and Q3 would be more comparable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guiding Q3 EBITDA to approach the Q1 level.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 and Q3 ‘more comparable to each other.’”

surprises.description: Ardent raised its 2026 impact-program savings target to at least $70 million, above the preview’s $55 million starting target. Workforce actions are already in place, with a stated full annualized impact of $30–$35 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its 2026 impact program savings target to at least $70 million, up from $55 million previously and $40 million originally, with structural workforce actions carrying a full annualized impact of $30-$35 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$55M FY target (raised from $40M)”; the bull scenario expected “an IMPACT raise above $55M.”

surprises.description: Management held the exchange-related EBITDA headwind at $35 million even though the preview’s base case anticipated an increase to $45–$55 million. It also said many members losing exchange coverage are moving to other insurance rather than self-pay, a potentially more favorable outcome than the preview’s feared uninsured migration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reaffirmed its $35 million exchange headwind for the year,” and said “a material portion of members losing exchange coverage are migrating to other insurance rather than self-pay.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: ... exchange headwind nudged to $45–55M but absorbed”; the preview also described concern that displaced patients could go uninsured “almost one for one.”

surprises.description: A June payer renewal is expected to add $5–$10 million to 2026 adjusted EBITDA, and management described further multi-year repricing potential because rates are below the 50th percentile in most markets. The preview highlighted payer mix and exchange exposure but did not anticipate this specific contract-driven upside.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A single June payer contract renewal in one market is expected to add $5-$10 million to 2026 adjusted EBITDA,” with “rates below the 50th percentile across most markets as a multi-year repricing opportunity on 2-3 year renewal cycles.”

surprises.description: Q2 operating cash flow was $197 million, up from $117 million a year earlier, while cash, total liquidity, and net leverage were reported at $724 million, $992 million, and 0.8 times. The preview had noted $610 million of cash and 1.0x net leverage at March 31 but did not flag this quarterly cash-flow strength.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 operating cash flow rose to $197 million from $117 million a year ago,” with “$724 million cash, $992 million total liquidity, and net leverage of 0.8 times.”

surprises.description: Ardent repurchased $13 million of stock in Q2 and said it was inclined to continue buybacks, with $34 million still authorized. The preview identified capital-allocation changes as something to watch but did not anticipate continued repurchases.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Repurchased $13 million of stock in Q2 with $34 million remaining under authorization,” and signaled “a bias to continue buybacks amid perceived undervaluation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “watch for ... capital-allocation changes,” without predicting buybacks.

surprises.description: Management cited plans for more than 20 specialist physician starts in one market in the second half. The preview did not identify this hiring and growth plan as an expected call item.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cited over 20 specialist physician starts planned in one market for the second half.”

in_line: Q2 revenue of $1.62 billion exceeded the preview’s $1,589.7 million consensus estimate, but only by about 1.9%, a modest positive deviation.

The company reaffirmed its $485–$535 million FY2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance range, as the preview’s base case expected an unchanged range. The stated bias of revenue toward the lower end was consistent with the preview’s warning that the outlook could be “trending toward the lower half.”
Contract labor spending fell 42%, broadly matching the preview’s expectation of a decline of 40% or more.

surprises.description: U.S. RevPAR grew 1.3%, below the preview’s +2% to +3% base case and +2.5% estimate, despite the preview’s expectation of a favorable comparison and supportive industry data. The result was closer to the preview’s implied +1% to +2% consensus range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. RevPAR increased 1.3% year-over-year” and the FIFA World Cup contributed “about 60 basis points to Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base case +2.5%”; the base scenario expected “U.S. RevPAR” of “+2 to +3%.”

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted EPS guidance fell to $6.86–7.10 from $6.92–7.14, even as EBITDA guidance increased. The preview had highlighted Q1’s higher tax rate as temporary and expected it to normalize, so the higher expected tax rate and interest expense are a negative departure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted diluted EPS guidance was set at $6.86-7.10, reflecting higher expected interest expense and a higher effective tax rate partially offset by share repurchases.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The FY2026 guidance in force listed adjusted diluted EPS of “$6.92” to “$7.14”; the preview said Q1’s “temporary tax rate elevation” was “expected to normalize.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $175 million, above the preview’s derived consensus of $166–169 million and its own $170 million estimate. It reached the preview’s bull-case figure, rather than the expected base-case level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA rose 6% year-over-year to $175 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA *not published* — ~ $166–169M derived”; “My estimates (above consensus): … Adj. EBITDA $170M”; the bull scenario listed “$175M.”

surprises.description: The company raised full-year EBITDA guidance, but the new $635–650 million range only modestly exceeds the prior $632–647 million range and does not narrow to the preview’s anticipated upper-half range of roughly $640–650 million. The direction was better than a reaffirmation, but the raise was less decisive than the preview’s base-case framing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 guidance for adjusted EBITDA to $635-650 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected the guide to be “narrowed to upper half (~$640–650M)”; it described an outright raise as the bull trigger.

surprises.description: The full-year U.S. royalty-rate expansion outlook of 7–9 basis points is stronger than the preview’s expected mid-single-digit-basis-point growth. Q2’s 11-basis-point increase also indicates stronger current rate expansion than that outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: Guidance for “U.S. royalty rate expansion to 7-9 basis points”; “U.S. average royalty rate increased 11 basis points on favorable brand mix shift.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “U.S. effective royalty rate hit 5.22% in Q1 (+11bp); guide is mid-single-digit-bp growth.”

surprises.description: Global net rooms growth guidance rose to approximately 1.5% from about 1%, a stronger outlook than the preview’s roughly 1% full-year expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: Guidance for “global net rooms growth to approximately 1.5% (up from ~1%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Global net rooms ~+1%” in the FY2026 guidance in force.

surprises.description: The U.S. conversion pipeline was up 24% year over year and 6% sequentially, with most expected 2026 openings and signed agreements converting to openings this year. That provides a more encouraging U.S. conversion and near-term opening picture than the preview’s concern about a shrinking global pipeline, although the preview had noted strong Q1 agreement growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The U.S. conversion pipeline is up 24% year-over-year and 6% sequentially,” with conversions expected to represent “~90% of 2026 U.S. openings” and about 75% of year-to-date signed agreements expected to open this year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the “Global pipeline” was “>77,700 rooms at Mar-26 vs. 93,000+ at Jun-25” and called the absolute contraction “a legitimate bear talking point”; it also noted Q1 franchise agreements awarded were up 65% in the U.S.

surprises.description: The call disclosed that Q3 EBITDA comparisons will lose roughly $9.5 million of prior-year liquidated damages. That creates a near-term comparison headwind not discussed in the preview, although management linked it to improved franchisee retention.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 EBITDA comparisons face a headwind from roughly $9.5 million of prior-year liquidated damages that are not expected to recur, reflecting improved franchisee retention.”

surprises.description: Management gave a first-asset-disposition timetable for the hotel-ownership exit: the first sale is expected in the first half of 2027, with about $450 million of owned hotels among $650 million of related balance-sheet assets. The preview anticipated lower capital spending but did not specify a disposition timetable or the assets involved.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Capital outlays for hotel development declined 80% year-over-year in the first half as the company exits hotel ownership, with the first asset disposition expected in the first half of 2027 (~$450 million of owned hotels among $650 million in related balance sheet assets).”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EPS of $2.02 exceeded the preview’s cited consensus of $1.96–1.97, although it was essentially in line with the preview’s own $2.03 estimate. This is a modest beat against consensus, not against the preview’s central estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS increased 5% to $2.02.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS” consensus was “$1.96–1.97”; the preview’s estimate was “Adj. EPS $2.03.”

in_line: U.S. net rooms growth was nearly flat year over year, broadly matching the preview’s base case that U.S. net rooms would remain slightly negative but improve; the strong openings and lower exits supported that expected improvement.
The raised full-year U.S. RevPAR outlook of 0–1.25% was broadly in line with the preview’s base-case expectation of moving the range to roughly 0% to +1%.
The reiterated $175–225 million 2026 share-repurchase plan was in line with the preview’s stated buyback guidance; the preview had described acceleration beyond that plan as a possible bull signal.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $6.5 million, above the preview’s $5.5 million base case and its $6.0 million “real test,” though slightly below the preview’s suspect $6.71 million consensus. The result also reversed the preview’s expectation of a seasonal trough and a likely revenue miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated Q2 2026 revenues rose 17% to $6.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | My Base | $5.5M”; “The real test is >$6.0M”; published consensus “$6.71M,” which the preview cautioned was “a weak anchor.”

surprises.description: APC revenue grew 11% year over year, rather than declining from the prior-year quarter as the preview’s $2.2 million estimate implied. The preview expected thin backlog and “no new deliveries,” making the reported growth a positive surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “APC up 11%” year over year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “APC revenue | $2.2M”; “vs. $2.5M Q2’25; thin backlog, no new deliveries.”

surprises.description: FuelChem grew 21% year over year, well ahead of the preview’s roughly $3.3 million estimate versus $3.1 million a year earlier. That was stronger than the modest growth implied by the model despite the expected seasonal trough.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FuelChem up 21%” year over year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FUEL CHEM revenue | $3.3M”; “vs. $3.1M Q2’25”; the preview described Q2 as “FUEL CHEM’s seasonal trough.”

surprises.description: APC backlog reached $14.3 million, far above the preview’s $6.9 million March-quarter starting point and the roughly $7 million level it identified as a bullish threshold. The preview highlighted backlog as the most important disclosure, so the increase was a substantial positive surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “APC backlog reached $14.3 million at June 30, 2026—the largest quarter-end backlog since 2018”; “about $10.5 million expected to be recognized in the next 12 months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “APC entered the quarter with only $6.9M backlog”; the preview said a backlog “with a ‘7’ or higher handle at 6/30” would be a bull signal.

surprises.description: Margins came in materially below the preview’s 44% gross-margin estimate, with APC margin falling rather than improving. Management attributed APC’s sharp decline to project mix and execution costs, while the preview had anticipated improving APC mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated gross margin declined to 41% from 46%”; “APC margin dropping sharply to 36% from 44% due to project mix and execution costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | 44.0%”; “APC mix improving, FUEL CHEM softening.”

surprises.description: The preview expected $3–5 million of data-center business to close by the end of Q2 or early Q3, but the update described only one inquiry that may convert before the end of Q3, with potentially material revenue in 2027. That leaves a prospective opportunity rather than a reported award and pushes the possible timing later than the preview’s stated window.
surprises.fact_evidence: “One data center inquiry may convert to a commercial award before the end of Q3 2026 via a capacity reservation agreement, potentially generating material revenue in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$3–5M expected to close ‘by end of Q2 or early Q3’”; the preview asked whether a data-center SCR award had converted.

surprises.description: The data-center opportunity was described at a much larger scale than the preview’s $75–100 million total pipeline: the reported figure was approximately $75–100 million per project, with projects potentially involving 30–40 units. This is a major increase in the stated potential size, although it remains pipeline rather than awarded revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The data center sales pipeline approximates $75–$100 million per project,” with units priced at “$1–$4 million” and projects ranging “up to 30–40 units.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited a “$75–100M pipeline” and “8–10 projects at $1–3M per unit.”

surprises.description: The FuelChem demonstration had not converted and was paused; it was now expected to restart only in mid-Q4. That is later and less advanced than the preview’s near-term conversion watch, though the potential annualized revenue if it converts remained in the same range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A paused FuelChem demonstration is expected to restart in mid-Q4 2026” and, if converted, “could add $2.5–$3 million in annualized revenue in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a demonstration “that started November 2025” and flagged conversion as a near-term item; it said conversion adds “$2.5–3.0M annualized” and noted management had said “later in the year.”

surprises.description: The CEO’s retirement, effective just days after the release, and the appointment of a successor were not anticipated in the preview. The successor’s M&A and operating experience could support the company’s acquisition strategy, but the transition itself adds uncertainty.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CEO Vincent Arnone will retire effective August 10, 2026, after 27 years, succeeded by Ramesh Nagahali,” who brings “M&A and operational experience relevant to potential acquisition strategy.”

in_line: Full-year 2026 revenue guidance remained for revenue to exceed 2025, with FuelChem approximating prior-year levels and APC exceeding 2025; this matched the preview’s stated company guidance and base case. The preview also expected most of the large new APC contract revenue to fall in 2027.

The Q2 loss was broadly in line with the preview’s own model: reported EPS was $(0.04), versus its modeled $(0.04)–$(0.05), although it was worse than the published $(0.02) consensus that the preview expected to miss.
Cash and investments of approximately $29.6 million were within the preview’s expected range of approximately $28.5–29.5 million; no debt was consistent with the preview’s stated zero-debt position.

surprises.description: Continuing-operations revenue was $334 million, below the preview’s $369–376 million consensus range and its $360–375 million base estimate. The preview anticipated provisional-pricing pressure, but the reported result was also affected by Greens Creek concentrate produced in Q2 but not sold until early August, shifting revenue into Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue from continuing operations fell to $334 million from the record $411 million in Q1, driven by lower metal prices and a timing gap where Greens Creek silver concentrate was produced but not sold until early August, shifting that revenue into Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $368.8M – $375.5M”; “Revenue $360–375M” in the preview’s base estimate.

surprises.description: Hecla cut Keno Hill’s full-year silver outlook to 2.2–2.6 million ounces and said meaningfully higher production is not expected until roughly the end of 2029. The preview expected full-year production guidance to be reaffirmed and described the ramp as gated by permit amendments not expected until mid-2029.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Keno Hill's full-year silver guidance was cut to 2.2-2.6 million ounces as the company deliberately runs the mine at a lower rate, with a ramp-up to meaningfully higher production not expected until roughly the end of 2029 pending permits and infrastructure investment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Production guidance 15.1–16.5 Moz Ag / 51–55 koz Au reaffirmed”; “the 440 tpd ramp remains gated on permit amendments not expected until mid-2029. Watch for any pull-forward.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the quarter’s free cash flow to be $90–130 million and to decline from Q1’s record $144 million. Instead, Q2 free cash flow was $136 million, slightly above that estimate range and nearly matching the Q1 record.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow of $136 million nearly matched last quarter's record $144 million with all three mines contributing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Free cash flow $90–130M” and “Down from Q1's record $144M.”

surprises.description: Greens Creek guidance improved: full-year silver production guidance was raised to 8.0–8.3 million ounces and cash-cost guidance improved to negative $12.15 to negative $12.00 per ounce. The preview expected production guidance to be reaffirmed and identified better-than-guidance costs as a possible positive.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year Greens Creek guidance to 8.0-8.3 million ounces of silver with cash costs improving to negative $12.15 to negative $12.00 per ounce.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Production guidance 15.1–16.5 Moz Ag / 51–55 koz Au reaffirmed”; “A cost guidance cut is plausible and would be a genuine positive.”

surprises.description: Lucky Friday lowered its full-year cash-cost guidance to $9.00–$9.75 per ounce, while the preview had highlighted possible cost-guidance reductions generally rather than this specific mine-level improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “[Management] lowered Lucky Friday cash cost guidance to $9.00-$9.75 per ounce.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cost guidance revision — a cut to AISC guidance partially offsets the price shock and is the most likely positive surprise.”

surprises.description: Greens Creek and Lucky Friday each set new site-level quarterly free-cash-flow records, and Lucky Friday also produced a record 1.5 million ounces of silver. The preview expected total silver production to be roughly in line, but did not anticipate these mine-level records.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Greens Creek and Lucky Friday each set new site-level quarterly free cash flow records of $130 million and $88 million, respectively, and Lucky Friday posted a record 1.5 million ounces of silver on higher mill rates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Silver production 3.8–4.1 Moz” and “~3.9 Moz” consensus.

surprises.description: Management described a potential Greens Creek pyrite-concentrate circuit that could add about 1.0–1.2 million ounces of silver and 10,000–15,000 ounces of gold annually for relatively low capital investment. The preview did not flag this potential production project.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The proposed Greens Creek pyrite concentrate circuit could add roughly 1.0-1.2 million ounces of silver and 10,000-15,000 ounces of gold annually at low capital intensity of $40-60 million and incremental operating costs of $10-15 million per year, with first production targeted for Q4 2027 to H1 2028.”

surprises.description: Management highlighted a large but still unproven tailings-reprocessing opportunity at Greens Creek: more than 600,000 ounces of gold in the tailings and Phase 3 metallurgical testing beginning this month. The preview did not mention this opportunity, and the call facts do not establish that the gold can be recovered economically.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Greens Creek tailings reprocessing project contains over 600,000 ounces of gold with an in-situ value estimated near $6.1 billion at June 30 prices, with Phase 3 metallurgical test work commencing this month to determine viability.”

surprises.description: Management said fuel is only about 3% of consolidated costs, limiting the effect of oil-price spikes. The preview raised cost inflation at Lucky Friday and Keno Hill as a risk but did not identify this degree of fuel-cost insulation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fuel represents only about 3% of the consolidated cost structure due to high-grade underground mining and hydro-based power, insulating margins from oil price spikes relative to peers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cost inflation at Lucky Friday/Keno Hill” was listed as a bear-case driver.

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA was $199 million, within the preview’s $180–220 million estimate range.

Management presented a lower-price-deck free-cash-flow projection rather than affirming the prior >$700 million figure based on $75 silver and $4,500 gold; the preview’s base case anticipated that the FCF outlook would be re-based to spot prices.

surprises.description: Revenue was $25.7 million, about 9% above the preview’s $23.56 million consensus. The preview’s bull case was also close at $25.5 million, but the reported result substantially exceeded its base-case expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 fiscal 2027 revenue grew 32% year-over-year to $25.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Consensus | ~$23.56M”; the preview’s base scenario was $23.0M.

surprises.description: The quarter produced $2 million of net income and $0.47 per diluted share, far above the preview’s near-break-even base EPS estimate and the dispersed consensus range. The preview cautioned that EPS estimates were unreliable, so the size of the beat should be treated cautiously.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 net income turned positive at $2 million (47 cents per diluted share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Published consensus EPS ranged from “$(0.01) to $0.07”; the preview’s base scenario estimated “~$0.00” EPS.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $2.5 million, well above the preview’s $0.6 million base-case estimate. The preview expected the positive-EBITDA streak to continue, but the reported quarterly amount was much stronger than its modeled outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose to $2.5 million from $200,000 year-over-year,” the seventh consecutive positive quarter.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario projected “Adj. EBITDA ~$0.6M”; it also said a seventh straight positive quarter was part of the base case.

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 34.6%, well above the preview’s expectation of roughly 30%. About 130 basis points came from a one-time tariff-related net benefit, but margin still exceeded the expected level after accounting for that benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Overall gross margin expanded to 34.6% from 30.1%, though roughly 130 basis points came from a one-time net benefit of tariff changes and refunds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “~30% (guided)” and said a 30–31% result was fully guided.

surprises.description: Backlog fell to approximately $24 million from $30.1 million at the end of Q4, a larger sequential drop than the preview’s base-case range of $28–32 million. The preview had warned that a decline toward the mid-$20 millions would undermine confidence in the full-year outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog exiting Q1 stood at approximately $24 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said backlog holding “≥$30M” was the bull case, while its base scenario anticipated “backlog ~$28–32M”; it warned that a decline “toward the mid-$20Ms” would undermine the guide.

surprises.description: Management said it does not expect the intra-year revenue ramp seen in prior years because Q1 benefited from a roughly $15 million exterior-lighting project recognized largely across Q4 and Q1. That makes the strong Q1 result more project-timing-dependent than a steady quarterly run rate, while the preview had derived consensus from an even annual cadence and described Q1 as structurally the weakest quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management does not expect the intra-year revenue ramp seen in prior years, as Q1 was bolstered by a ~$15 million exterior lighting project largely recognized across Q4 and Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had indicated FY27 should “play out relatively evenly over the year” and derived an even-quarter range of “$23.75–24.25M”; it also said “Q1 is structurally the weakest quarter.”

surprises.description: LED revenue was $17.7 million, above the preview’s already-strong bull-case threshold of more than $15 million and well above the roughly $12 million FY26 first-three-quarter run rate cited in the preview. LED margin also improved substantially year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LED lighting segment revenue grew to $17.7 million from $12.9 million with margin improving to 37.8% from 31.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 LED needed to be “meaningfully above the ~$12M FY26 run-rate” and set “LED >$15M” as a bull-case marker.

surprises.description: EV charging revenue rose to $4 million, beating the preview’s bull-case marker of at least $3.5 million and reversing the sharply declining trend the preview highlighted. The increase was partly offset by weaker segment profitability.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EV charging revenue rose to $4 million from $2.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q4 revenue of $2.3 million, down 61% year over year, and used “Voltrek stabilizes ≥$3.5M” as a bull-case assumption.

surprises.description: EV charging gross margin fell to 26.9% from 33.8%, a significant deterioration alongside the revenue rebound. The preview focused on whether segment revenue would stabilize and did not anticipate this margin decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EV charging ... gross margin fell to 26.9% from 33.8% amid sector-wide market uncertainty.”

surprises.description: The hyperscale data-center opportunity appears to contribute later than the preview had suggested: management now expects most revenue in fiscal 2028, rather than the preview’s expectation of revenue landing in late fiscal 2027. The update also describes potentially multi-million-dollar opportunities per building, which adds scale to the longer-term opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The newly entered hyperscale data center lighting business is expected to generate most of its revenue in fiscal 2028, with each building potentially representing seven-figure (multi-million dollar) opportunities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said data-center revenue “lands in late FY27” and expected “~zero Q1 revenue contribution.”

surprises.description: Management said a potential interior Home Depot project was progressing, providing a specific additional project lead that the preview did not mention. It remains unbooked, so it is not yet backlog or secured revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A potential interior Home Depot project remains unbooked but progressing.”

in_line: Management reiterated FY27 revenue guidance of $95–97 million with positive adjusted EBITDA, as the preview identified reiteration as its base-case expectation.
The positive adjusted-EBITDA streak continued for a seventh quarter, as the preview expected the streak to reach seven quarters.
The preview expected approximately zero Q1 revenue from the data-center business; the reported update instead places most of its expected revenue in FY28.

surprises.description: OSS raised its FY2026 revenue-growth outlook to 25%–30% from 20%–25%, rather than reaffirming the old range. The higher range moves beyond the preview’s most likely case, though its lower end is still 25%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Increased full-year 2026 revenue growth guidance to 25%-30%, up from prior guidance of 20%-25%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a reaffirmation was the base case and that a raise was the cleanest bull catalyst; its bull case called for “above 25% growth / to $42M+.”

surprises.description: Q2 continuing-operations revenue was $9.3 million, above the preview’s roughly $8.8 million estimate and its $8.5–9.0 million beat/miss range. That is a modest beat, rather than merely the roughly 50%–60% growth expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue from continuing operations grew 62.3% year-over-year to $9.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 revenue | ~$8.8M (derived, not published consensus)”; the caveat says to treat the threshold as “a range ($8.5–9.0M).”

surprises.description: Bookings remained exceptionally strong: $15.1 million and about 1.7x book-to-bill were above the preview’s base-case range of roughly 1.0–1.2x and well above the level it said should be achievable from the defense award. The ratio was just below Q1’s 1.8x, but did not show the expected possible deceleration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record bookings of $15.1 million in Q2 and over $30 million year-to-date, yielding a book-to-bill ratio of approximately 1.7.”
