surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “book-to-bill ~1.0–1.2x”; it said above 1.0x should be achievable, while Q1 was “~$15M bookings / 1.8x.”

surprises.description: A previously unmentioned $6.25 million legal settlement charge drove a $7.3 million GAAP loss, but excluding that charge the loss was only $0.01 per share—better than the preview’s expected $0.02–$0.03 loss. The unexpected charge and the better underlying result make this a mixed surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A $6.25 million legal settlement charge drove a GAAP net loss from continuing operations of $7.3 million ($0.29/share),” while excluding it “the non-GAAP net loss narrowed to just $0.2 million ($0.01/share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 EPS estimates of “~$(0.02) to $(0.03)” and modeled a net loss of about “$(0.03)”; it did not mention a legal settlement charge.

surprises.description: OSS reported support for 14 multi-year programs with combined estimated revenue potential above $42 million, a more concrete and substantial program base than the preview had specified. The preview focused on conversions of named programs and possible new adds but gave no comparable count or combined value.
surprises.fact_evidence: “OSS is now supporting 14 multi-year programs with estimated combined revenue potential exceeding $42 million,” up from one such program three years ago.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview watched for “program-level conversions” and “any new prime-customer program adds,” but did not give an expectation for 14 programs or $42 million of potential.

surprises.description: The call included a $2.2 million robotics production booking, whereas the preview explicitly treated the announced robotics order as a Q3 booking rather than a Q2 one. If included in Q2 bookings as stated, the order arrived earlier than the preview expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New bookings included … a $2.2 million robotics production order with $10-15 million five-year potential.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the July 21 “$2.2M autonomous construction/mining order” as “a Q3 booking, not Q2.”

surprises.description: OSS also reported a renewable-energy data-center order that could scale toward a $10 million opportunity, a specific new order and opportunity not identified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New bookings included … a renewable energy data center order scaling toward a $10 million opportunity.”

in_line: Gross margin was 39.1%, close to management’s approximately 40% pre-guide and within the preview’s expected normalization range; the preview specifically warned that a Q2 margin well below Q1’s 51.6% was not itself a miss.
Customer-funded development revenue was about $944,000, roughly 10% of revenue, remaining a meaningful contributor near the preview’s roughly $1 million Q1 reference point.
The company maintained expectations for approximately 40% gross margin and positive full-year EBITDA, as the preview expected.
H1 cash use was accompanied by a $7.1 million inventory build to hedge against memory supply constraints; the preview said an inventory build ahead of the H2 ramp was expected and defensible.

surprises.description: Hagerty raised its FY2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook to $270–280 million, well above the preview’s expected range of roughly $245–255 million in the base case and even above its $255–265 million bull case. The increase is substantially larger than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its full-year 2026 ... adjusted EBITDA guidance to $270-280 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case anticipated guidance “raised modestly to ~$245–255M”; its bull case anticipated “$255–265M.”

surprises.description: Hagerty now expects FY2026 GAAP net income of $18–30 million, rather than the preview’s expected full-year GAAP net loss of $41–51 million. That is a substantial reversal in the expected bottom-line outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Set GAAP net income guidance of $18-30 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Standing FY2026 guidance was a “GAAP net loss $(51)M–$(41)M incl. ~$190M pre-tax transitional costs.”

surprises.description: First-half written premium growth was 19%, above the preview’s roughly 17% Q2 estimate and the then-current 15–16% full-year growth guide. Hagerty also raised its full-year written premium growth outlook, though only to 16–17%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half 2026 written premium grew 19%”; full-year guidance was raised “to 16-17% (up from prior 15-16%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated written premium at “$415M (+17%)” for Q2 and identified the standing FY guide as “+15–16%.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue appears materially above the preview’s estimate: first-half revenue of $667 million less the already reported Q1 revenue of $311.8 million implies about $355 million for Q2, versus the preview’s $320 million estimate. The preview cautioned that revenue was mechanically affected by the fronting transition, so the beat is less informative about underlying performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reported GAAP revenue fell 6% to $667 million” in the first half; Q1 revenue was reported as $311.8 million in the preview, implying approximately $355 million in Q2.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q2 revenue at “$320M (range $305–335M)” and cited consensus of “$315.4M – $316.2M.”

surprises.description: New business accelerated sharply, with quarterly counts rising from roughly 100,000 to 160,000, largely through State Farm conversions, and first-half member additions reaching a record 279,000. That runs against the preview’s concern that the record pace could decelerate as the prior-year comparison became harder.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Added a record 279,000 new members in the first half” and quarterly new business count jumped “from roughly 100,000 to 160,000 largely due to State Farm conversions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the +102% comp gets harder from here” and urged investors to watch “the run-rate of new business.”

surprises.description: Hagerty Re’s first-half loss ratio was 41%, below the preview’s roughly 42% seasonal expectation. The reported 88% combined ratio also indicates somewhat better underwriting results than the preview’s cited Q2 2025 combined ratio of 89.6%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Hagerty Re's first-half combined ratio was 88% (90% in Q2) with a loss ratio of 41%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected a Q2 loss ratio of “41–42%” in its base case and described “~42% seasonal normal”; it cited Q2 2025 combined ratio of 89.6%.

surprises.description: Retention was 88%, below the preview’s 88.5% threshold, and declined both year over year and sequentially. The shortfall is modest, but it is a negative quality signal alongside rapid new-member growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retention held at an industry-leading 88%, though it declined 50 basis points year-over-year and 30 basis points sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview set “retention ≥ 88.5%” as a key metric and called “Sub-88%” a yellow flag.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA appears slightly below the preview’s $78 million base estimate: the reported first-half $160 million less the preview’s already reported Q1 $85.2 million implies about $75 million for Q2. This modest quarterly shortfall contrasts with the much stronger full-year guidance raise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half adjusted EBITDA grew 32% to $160 million”; the preview reported Q1 adjusted EBITDA of $85.2 million, implying approximately $75 million for Q2.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q2 adjusted EBITDA at “$78M” (range “$65–88M”).

surprises.description: Marketplace results were stronger than the preview’s concern that high auction sales might fail to translate into revenue: Q2 marketplace revenue rose 48%, and first-half marketplace sales increased 17%. Broad Arrow’s growth and sell-through rate were also strong, although private sales declined against a prior-year large collection sale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Marketplace total sales grew 17% to $65 million with Q2 marketplace revenue up 48% to $40 million,” led by “Broad Arrow's 74% first-half sales increase and a 91% sell-through rate”; private sales declined against a prior-year large collection sale.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged Q1’s “record $135.4M aggregate auction sales (+80%)” alongside marketplace revenue down 12%, and said “Strong headline auction totals with weak marketplace revenue is the pattern to watch for.”

in_line: Reported revenue weakness and the accounting effects of the Markel fronting arrangement were anticipated: the preview warned that the transition eliminated commission revenue and said reported revenue carried “very little signal.”

The increase in earned premium was consistent with the expected effect of moving to 100% economics under the Markel fronting arrangement; the preview specifically warned that the transition would inflate earned premium.

The Bennetts acquisition was expected to close in Q3 for £34 million and to triple Hagerty’s UK scale; the call reported the acquisition after quarter-end for the same price and with that scale impact.

surprises.description: Q2 oil and total production both exceeded company guidance, and Talos raised its full-year stand-alone production ranges despite excluding the pending Gulf of America acquisition and including the shelf divestment. The preview expected 2026 guidance to be reiterated rather than revised before the acquisition closed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 oil production averaged approximately 69,000 barrels per day and total production nearly 94,000 BOE per day, both exceeding guidance”; Talos “raised full-year 2026 stand-alone production guidance to 64,000-68,000 barrels of oil per day and 87,000-91,000 BOE per day.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 guidance of oil “63–67 MBbl/d” and total “88–92 MBoe/d,” and said, “Management said it will update 2026 guidance after closing, so expect guidance to be reiterated rather than re-cut on Aug 4/5.”

surprises.description: BP declined to exercise its preferential right, preserving the Na Kika interests in the Gulf of America acquisition and allowing Talos to operate Coulomb. The preview identified an exercise of the right—and losing the Na Kika interests—as a material risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “BP declined to exercise its preferential right, allowing Talos to operate the Coulomb field and become a partner in the Na Kika platform.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said, “If exercised, Talos gets Coulomb only — roughly halving the deal’s scope,” and called the outcome “the single highest-information item of the event.”

surprises.description: The Gulf of America acquisition is now expected to close in Q3 2026, earlier than the preview’s expectation of closing by year-end 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: The acquisition “is expected to close in Q3 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the acquisition was “Expected to close by year-end 2026.”

surprises.description: The acquisition’s stated production contribution is approximately 18,000 BOE per day, above the preview’s approximately 16,000 BOE per day estimate. The call also described accretive oil cut, operating expense, and EBITDA margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: The acquisition adds assets “producing approximately 18,000 BOE per day and roughly 20% oil production growth, with accretive oil cut, operating expense, and EBITDA margins.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the acquisition as adding “~16 MBoe/d (Q1’26, ~77% oil).”

surprises.description: Talos reported record adjusted free cash flow and adjusted EBITDA, for which the preview said it had no consensus estimates. The results therefore add a strong reported financial outcome without a preview benchmark to quantify a beat against.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company generated record adjusted free cash flow of approximately $232 million and adjusted EBITDA of approximately $402 million in Q2 2026.”

surprises.description: The gas-weighted shelf divestment removed approximately $54 million of future abandonment obligations and improved the portfolio’s oil weighting; the preview did not flag this transaction or these benefits.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The noncore gas-weighted shelf divestment eliminated approximately $54 million of future abandonment obligations and improved portfolio oil weighting.”

surprises.description: Talos refinanced its 9% notes due 2029 with 8% notes due 2034, lowering the coupon and extending maturities—an unanticipated financing action in the preview, which discussed acquisition funding but not this refinancing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company issued $800 million of 8% senior notes due 2034 to redeem $625 million of 9% notes due 2029, lowering the coupon and extending maturities.”

surprises.description: Before the acquisition close, cash and leverage were stronger than the preview’s Q1 balance-sheet figures: cash was about $578 million and leverage was 0.5x, versus $386.4 million and 0.8x cited in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Leverage declined to 0.5x with cash of approximately $578 million and total liquidity of approximately $1.2 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 balance-sheet figures of “$386.4M cash” and “0.8x net debt/LTM EBITDA.”

surprises.description: Talos made no share repurchases in Q2 because of an acquisition-related blackout, whereas the preview highlighted Q1 buybacks and identified the pace of buybacks during the acquisition as an open question. The call also reported that cumulative returns since Q2 2025 had reduced the share count by about 7%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Talos returned approximately $135 million to shareholders since Q2 2025, reducing share count by about 7%, but repurchased no shares in Q2 2026 due to an acquisition-related blackout.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted Q1 buybacks of “2.7M shares / $38.2M (34% of FCF)” and said, “With $450–500M of cash going out the door for Shell, the buyback pace is a live question.”

surprises.description: Talos disclosed a roughly 4-million-acre Honduras position and a first-ever 3D seismic program beginning in the second half of 2026, a new exploration program not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Honduras position spans roughly 4 million acres (equivalent to 700 Gulf of America blocks) with a first-ever 3D seismic program starting in the second half of 2026.”

in_line: Mexico’s Block 29 plans were broadly in line with the preview: the call cited a 2027 FID target anchored by the Polok and Chinwol discoveries and roughly 200 million BOE of gross resource, while the preview described a 2027 FID target and more than 200 MMBoe gross recoverable.

surprises.description: Voya reported adjusted operating EPS of $1.51, well below the preview’s $1.88–$1.99 range. The preview had already estimated a $0.50–$0.60-per-share alternative-investment drag, but the reported combined drag was about $0.90 per share and included severance costs that the preview did not identify.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted operating earnings of $1.51 per diluted share ($140 million), which included an approximate $0.90 per share drag from below-expectation alternative investment performance and severance costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat ~$1.90 as the number to beat and $2.00 as the whisper”; the preview’s bridge estimated an “Alt investment income shortfall” of “-$0.50 to -$0.60” and implied Q2 EPS of “~$1.90–2.00.”

surprises.description: Voya released $8 million of stop-loss reserves, whereas the preview’s base case anticipated no new release. The release is positive evidence on claims, though smaller than the prior quarter’s $25 million release noted in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company released $8 million of stop-loss reserves while holding reserves at the high end of its best estimate range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case said “stop loss on track, no new release”; it identified a second reserve release as part of the bull scenario.

surprises.description: Quarterly excess-capital generation was about $150 million, below the roughly $200 million per quarter the preview expected. This is a shortfall in generation even though year-to-date generation was $350 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately $150 million of excess capital in Q2 ($350 million year-to-date).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “~$200M/quarter generation.”

surprises.description: Voya bought back about $200 million of shares in Q2, exceeding the $150 million Q2 buyback the preview said had been committed. It also plans at least $100 million more in Q3, for which the preview gave no specific expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Voya returned approximately $200 million to shareholders in Q2 ($300 million in buybacks year-to-date…) and plans at least $100 million of additional buybacks in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$150M committed for Q2.”

surprises.description: Cash conversion came in above 100%, better than the preview’s expectation of roughly 90% or more.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash conversion above 100%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “~90%+ cash conversion.”

surprises.description: Management said Q2 severance costs should be fully offset by expense savings by year-end, with a six-month payback, and expressed confidence in meaningfully higher second-half earnings. The preview did not anticipate this cost-savings timing or earnings outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects the Q2 severance costs to be fully offset by expense savings by year-end (a six-month payback), supporting confidence in meaningfully higher second-half earnings.”

surprises.description: A legacy sub-advised relationship wind-down will pressure Investment Management flows in the second half, an issue not flagged in the preview. Management said the 2026 revenue impact would be immaterial, limiting the near-term significance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A legacy sub-advised relationship wind-down will pressure H2 flows with immaterial 2026 revenue impact.”

in_line: The Q2 alternative-investment return was a 2.5% annualized loss, consistent with the preview’s account of Voya’s July 8 preannouncement of an approximately -2.5% annualized result.
The 24% 2026 stop-loss rate increase matched the preview’s stated 24% increase at 1/1/26.

surprises.description: Government Services 2026 adjusted operating income guidance was updated to $55–65 million, below the preview’s $70–80 million expectation. Management also said delayed AW189 deliveries and prolonged transition costs would reduce 2026 adjusted operating income by about $8 million, rather than the transition-cost roll-off the preview was watching for.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Government Services 2026 guidance was updated to $475 million-$495 million in revenue and $55 million-$65 million in adjusted operating income”; delayed Leonardo AW189 deliveries “adversely impacted 2026 Government Services adjusted operating income by approximately $8 million through elevated KPI penalties and prolonged transition costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 segment guide is $70–80M”; the preview said to watch whether “UKSAR2G transition costs ... are rolling off.”

surprises.description: Offshore Energy Services adjusted operating income guidance was raised to $235–245 million, above the preview’s $225–235 million range, on stronger rates and activity and contracts lasting longer than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Offshore Energy Services segment's 2026 adjusted operating income guidance was raised to $235 million-$245 million on stronger rates, activity, and longer-than-expected contracts.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “OES needs ~$58–62M/quarter of adj. op income ... to hit the $225–235M guide.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was implied at about $79.8 million—$59.3 million in Q1 plus the reported $20.5 million sequential increase—slightly above the preview’s $73–78 million estimate. The increase was supported by lower repairs and maintenance costs, contrary to the preview’s concern about a second consecutive quarter of R&M inflation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA increased $20.5 million sequentially, driven by higher utilization, fuel revenues, and lower repairs and maintenance costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: ~$73–78M”; the preview warned that “a second consecutive quarter of R&M inflation breaks the guidance bridge.”

surprises.description: A jet-fuel price spike reduced Government Services profitability by $1.5 million through the UKSAR2G deferred price adjustment mechanism. The preview did not flag this cost, although the company said a contract amendment had tightened the mechanism and the issue should not recur.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A jet fuel price spike hurt Government Services profitability by $1.5 million due to a UKSAR2G deferred price adjustment mechanism, which has since been tightened via contractual amendment and should not recur.”

surprises.description: Operating cash flow turned positive at $41.4 million in Q2 after an $8.3 million use in Q1, a stronger indication of working-capital normalization than the preview had quantified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow swung to $41.4 million positive in Q2 from an $8.3 million use in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the CFO “guided to working-capital normalization,” while noting Q1 operating cash flow was “−$8.3M.”

in_line: Bristow affirmed its full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $295–325 million, consistent with the preview’s base case of an affirmed guide.

Q2 revenue was implied at about $411.8 million from Q1 revenue of $388.7 million plus the reported $23.1 million sequential increase, within the preview’s cited consensus range of $407.3–415.6 million.
Berry Aviation closed on July 13, in Q3 as the preview expected, and its immediate accretion to earnings, free cash flow, and EBITDA margins was already anticipated.

surprises.description: The preview expected management to reaffirm 15–20% Belmont Core growth, but the call reaffirmed growth of about 15%, the bottom of that range. With first-half growth at only 3%, reaching the reaffirmed target requires very strong growth in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management reaffirmed full-year Belmont Core gross written premium growth of ~15% over 2025, despite only 3% growth in the first half, implying very strong double-digit growth is required in the second half.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management guided on the Q1 call to 15–20% full-year growth in Belmont core gross premium. The preview said the bull case required management “reaffirming 15–20% Belmont core growth.”

surprises.description: The expense ratio was materially worse than the preview’s on-track threshold: it was 40.9%, versus an expectation that Q2 would be below 39%. Management also put the return to roughly 36% in the latter half of 2028, later and more precisely than the preview’s description of optimization over the next seven quarters.
surprises.fact_evidence: The expense ratio is elevated at 40.9%, running roughly 4.5 points above long-term targets due to Catalyx/Kaleidoscope technology investments, with management targeting a return to ~36% by the latter half of 2028.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 is seasonally better (38.8% in Q2 2025). Sub-39% is on-track; 40%+ again says the program isn't converting.” The preview also said optimization was a “major tactical objective over the next seven quarters.”

surprises.description: Valiant Re assumed reinsurance grew sharply, a segment development the preview did not flag: Q2 premiums rose 79%, and the treaty count expanded with three additions. This is a notable source of growth beyond the preview’s focus on Belmont Core and Wholesale Commercial.
surprises.fact_evidence: Valiant Re assumed reinsurance premiums surged 79% in Q2 to $21.5 million (43% for the half), with in-force treaties expanding to 22 after adding 3 new treaties in the quarter.

surprises.description: Specialty products premiums fell sharply because products were terminated, a decline not anticipated in the preview. The ongoing programs were nearly stable, so the reported drop was concentrated in discontinued products rather than broad weakness across the remaining programs.
surprises.fact_evidence: Specialty products premiums fell 36% in Q2 to $7.8 million due to terminated products, though the 11 ongoing programs were only down 1%.

surprises.description: Penn-America returned to growth at 2% after two quarterly declines, but management’s accompanying warning of intensifying E&S competition and moderating rate momentum tempers that improvement. The preview discussed softening market conditions, but did not anticipate this specific segment’s return to growth or the call’s rate commentary.
surprises.fact_evidence: Penn-America returned to growth (+2% in Q2) after two consecutive quarterly declines, but management flagged intensifying E&S competition with flat first-half rate change and moderating rate momentum.

surprises.description: The investment portfolio’s book yield was somewhat better than the preview’s roughly 4.3% estimate, and management gave a 4.9% year-end 2026 target. The reported 1.08-year duration, however, remained close to the short-duration positioning the preview described.
surprises.fact_evidence: The fixed income book yield rose to 4.42% with a short 1.08-year duration, with $177 million of maturities reinvested at 5.45%, and management targets a 4.9% book yield by year-end 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the portfolio as having a “roughly 1-year duration, 4.3% book yield” and said management had signaled possible extension within 12–24 months.

surprises.description: Discretionary capital was $302 million, above the preview’s $290 million figure, but management said fully deploying it would take 2 to 2.5 years. The preview already expected no buybacks, so that part of the capital stance was not a surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: Discretionary capital stood at $302 million, with management expecting a 2 to 2.5-year ramp to fully deploy it and no share buybacks currently planned.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$290M of discretionary capital” and said “No buybacks planned for 2026.”

in_line: Q2 accident-year combined ratio of 94.7% was broadly in line with the preview’s modeled ~94.5% calendar-year combined ratio and expectation for a low-to-mid-90s current accident-year result.

Management’s statement that book reserves remain solidly above actuarial indications matched the preview’s expectation that reserves were “solidly above” indications; no adverse development was reported in the supplied call facts.
No share buybacks were planned, as the preview already expected.

surprises.description: FY2026 sales guidance jumped to $1.02–1.06 billion from $890–970 million. Much of the increase is sulfur-cost pass-through—now expected to be $220 million rather than $155 million—so the higher sales outlook does not translate proportionally into EBITDA.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 sales guidance was raised to $1.02-1.06 billion (from $890-970 million), driven partly by higher sulfur pass-through now expected at $220 million versus $155 million prior.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 consensus revenue of $966.7M is within $3M of the top of the $890–970M range”; the prior company guidance assumed “~$155M of sulfur cost pass-through.”

surprises.description: Q2 sales were $250 million, about $12 million above the $237.54 million consensus estimate, but most of the year-over-year increase came from sulfur pass-through with no material EBITDA impact. The revenue beat was therefore less substantial economically than the headline suggests.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 sales were $250 million, up $74 million year-over-year, though approximately $55 million of that increase was sulfur cost pass-through with no material EBITDA impact.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Q2 2026 Consensus: $237.54M.”

surprises.description: The updated EBITDA outlook included a modest improvement in the legacy business, rather than only adding Calabrian to the prior forecast: the legacy-business low end rose from $180 million to $185 million. The overall $195–207 million range is close to the preview’s expected additive range, so the upside is mainly this organic floor increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance was raised to $195-207 million, with legacy business guidance low end lifted to $185 million and Calabrian expected to contribute $10-12 million in the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a clean additive update would be “roughly $190–205M” and described its base case as “~$185–197M organic plus ~$11M Calabrian → ~$196–208M; no organic raise.”

surprises.description: FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance rose to $0.58–0.72 from the prior $0.50–0.65 range, putting the consensus estimate of $0.66 inside the updated range rather than above its top end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS is guided to $0.58-0.72.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed prior adjusted diluted EPS guidance of “$0.50–0.65” and noted that “FY26 consensus EPS of $0.66 sits above the top of the company's $0.50–0.65 guide.”

surprises.description: Adjusted free-cash-flow guidance increased at the low end to $45 million from $40 million, despite capex guidance also moving up. This reverses the preview’s concern that cash flow was the likeliest place for a quiet disappointment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted free cash flow guidance was raised to $45-55 million … with capex now $85-95 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave prior adjusted FCF guidance of “$40–55M” and said, “This is the most likely place for a quiet disappointment.”

surprises.description: Virgin sulfuric acid volume grew at a double-digit rate, a stronger reported volume signal than the preview’s expectation that mining-driven demand would hold and its call to watch for volume evidence.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Virgin sulfuric acid volume grew double digits year-over-year, aided by the Waggaman plant acquired in May 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “mining-driven virgin acid demand” as a tailwind and said to watch whether “mining virgin acid demand” was holding.

surprises.description: Management warned of a possible temporary destocking-related demand impact, adding a specific near-term risk to the sulfur outlook. The preview had flagged industrial softness and expected sulfur easing in Q4, but did not identify destocking as a risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects sulfur prices to plateau or moderate modestly with a risk of temporary destocking-related demand impact.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “potential softness in some industrial applications” and said management “expects easing in Q4.”

in_line: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $53 million, within the company’s $50–55 million guide and close to the preview’s roughly $52–53 million implied consensus.
Calabrian was expected to contribute roughly $11–12 million for the second half; the reported contribution outlook was $10–12 million.
Leverage rose to about 2x after the acquisition funding, consistent with the preview’s estimate of roughly 2.0x pro forma leverage.

The reported $3–4 million of Calabrian synergies and the resulting reduction in the effective purchase multiple from about 8x to 7x were consistent with the preview’s expectation of quantified synergy details and a path below 7x.

surprises.description: The preview expected modest or moderate full-year operating profit, but management now expects a moderate operating loss for 2026. That is a clear deterioration from the recovery outlook investors were told to expect.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects a “moderate operating loss for full-year 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management was expected to reiterate “modest/moderate full-year 2026 operating profit guidance” and described a guidance cut to the “modest full-year operating profit” outlook as a bear-case risk.

surprises.description: Bookings rose 17% sequentially and more than doubled from Q2 2025, reaching their highest quarterly level in three years. The preview expected momentum to confirm an H2 inflection, but did not anticipate growth of this scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: Bookings reached $680 million, “up 17% sequentially and more than double Q2 2025,” and were the “highest quarterly level in 3 years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “bookings/backlog momentum confirming the H2 inflection” as a key watch item; Q1 bookings had increased 7% sequentially.

surprises.description: Despite the preview’s expectation that Q2 would be the low point for operating profit, the operating loss improved by about $10 million from Q1. This was a better quarter-to-quarter operating result than the trough framing implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: The consolidated operating loss improved to $18 million, “roughly $10 million better than Q1 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Q2 2026 is expected to be the low point for operating profit and net income.”

surprises.description: Cash flow turned positive rather than continuing the cash burn highlighted in the preview. Operating cash flow improved by about $50 million from Q1, when it was negative.
surprises.fact_evidence: Operating cash flow “turned positive at $17 million,” an improvement of “approximately $50 million from Q1 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “cash burn and leverage” as a Q2 watch item and described continued cash burn as a bear-case concern.

surprises.description: The $35 million tariff refund did not provide straightforward relief: it was largely offset by unfavorable capitalized material costs and higher gross tariff expense. The preview was looking for tariff mitigation, so the offsetting costs limit the benefit investors might have expected from refunds.
surprises.fact_evidence: The quarter included “$35 million in tariff refunds,” largely offset by “unfavorable capitalized material costs and $10 million in higher gross tariff expenses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “progress on [tariff] mitigation” as a key watch item and noted “~$40M of tariff refund applications and $15–20M expected from suppliers.”

surprises.description: Bookings have not yet translated into shipments as quickly as the preview’s H2 recovery framing might suggest: production is temporarily lagging, with trucks being reshored to North America and customer deliveries rescheduled. This adds a specific near-term execution constraint to the expected backlog-led recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management said production growth is “temporarily lagging bookings” because trucks planned for Europe are being reshored to North America after the April Section 232 tariff change and customer delivery rescheduling.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview anticipated a “meaningful second-half recovery driven by rebuilding backlog, tariff mitigation, and restructuring savings” and highlighted bookings/backlog momentum as confirmation of the H2 inflection.

surprises.description: Management added a longer-range recovery marker not covered in the preview: it expects trailing 12-month EBITDA to exceed pre-COVID levels in the second half of 2027 and targets 7% operating profit over the cycle. The targets are positive, though they are distant and depend partly on footprint savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects trailing 12-month EBITDA to exceed pre-COVID levels in the second half of 2027, cites $15–$20 million in annualized benefits from manufacturing footprint optimization, and targets “7% operating profit over the cycle.”

in_line: Revenue was $813 million versus the preview’s $804.6 million consensus estimate, a small beat.
The 2025 restructuring program remained on track for $40–$45 million of annualized savings, consistent with the preview’s expectation that savings were tracking toward that range.
Management continued to weight the most significant improvement to the second half, consistent with the preview’s expected H2 recovery timing.

surprises.description: DK reported adjusted EBITDA of about $639 million and adjusted EPS of $5.48, far above the preview’s implied $400–425 million EBITDA bar and the most current $2.39–$2.67 EPS estimates. Even excluding the 50% RVO adjustment, EBITDA was about $490 million and EPS about $3.64, still a substantial beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net income of approximately $344 million ($5.48 per share) and adjusted EBITDA of approximately $639 million, though excluding the 50% RVO adjustment, adjusted EBITDA was ~$490 million and adjusted EPS ~$3.64.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$2.39” and “$2.67” Q2 adjusted EPS estimates; “adjusted EBITDA of roughly $400–425M.”

surprises.description: DKL produced about $144 million of EBITDA, slightly above the preview’s $130–140 million read-through, and set a company quarterly record. The upside versus the expected range was modest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Logistics segment (DKL) posted its best quarterly results in company history at approximately $144 million in adjusted EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Read-through is a Q2 logistics contribution around $130–140M.”

surprises.description: Management was strongly optimistic about pending 2025 SRE petitions and cited a $468.4 million 2025 RVO obligation at roughly $1 per gallon RIN pricing. The preview expected no sizing of the August exemption and treated further relief as uncertain; the call offered more concrete context, though it did not give a dollar value for the exemption itself.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Krotz Springs was recently awarded a small refinery exemption after a prior denial,” and management expressed “strong optimism about pending 2025 SRE petitions,” citing “the total 2025 RVO obligation at $468.4 million at roughly $1 per gallon RIN pricing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “SRE deferred to Q3 with no sizing”; the preview also said the market wanted “a dollar figure and a share count” for the exemption.

surprises.description: Management introduced a mid-cycle free-cash-flow outlook of $650–700 million, equivalent to a roughly 15–20% yield at current prices. The preview discussed the balance sheet and buybacks but gave no comparable FCF forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management projects mid-cycle free cash flow of $650 million to $700 million including DKL distributions, representing a roughly 15% to 20% free cash flow yield at current prices.”

surprises.description: DK did repurchase shares, but Q2 buybacks were about $20 million—some activity after almost none in Q1, but not evidence of the large-scale step-up the preview identified as a possible catalyst. The reported 10% cumulative repurchase since early 2025 adds context but does not make the quarter’s buyback amount large.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Returned capital during the quarter via ~$16 million in dividends and ~$20 million in buybacks,” and “repurchased approximately 10% of the company since the beginning of 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the absence of a buyback step-up would be conspicuous” and listed “evidence of meaningful Q2/July repurchase” as a catalyst.

surprises.description: The company reduced its term loan by $70 million and stand-alone net debt by $72 million in the quarter, an additional balance-sheet improvement not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Refinanced its term loan, reducing it from $920 million to $850 million,” while “stand-alone Delek net debt (excluding DKL) declined by $72 million in the quarter.”

surprises.description: Q3 guidance included no planned turnarounds for the rest of the year and throughput of 296,000–316,000 barrels per day. The preview flagged Q3 guidance as important but did not anticipate a no-turnaround schedule or provide a Q3 throughput range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for total system throughput of 296,000 to 316,000 barrels per day with no planned turnarounds for the rest of the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Q3 guidance — throughput, turnaround calendar” as a key item to watch.

surprises.description: Management said the sharp easing in crude backwardation—from $6–7+ in Q2 to about $1.50 in Q3—should improve refining margin capture roughly one-for-one. This was a favorable Q3 margin-capture signal not specified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Crude backwardation eased sharply from $6-$7+ in Q2 to a roughly flat curve (~$1.50) in Q3,” and management said it “should translate roughly one-to-one into improved refining margin capture.”

in_line: DKL reaffirmed its 2026 EBITDA guidance of $520–560 million and its expectation that third-party EBITDA will exceed 80% pro forma, as previewed.
EOP contributed about $60 million in Q2 and retained its at-least-$220-million annual run-rate target, consistent with the preview; no quantified increase to the target was reported.

surprises.description: Kadant reported adjusted EPS of $3.42, far above the $2.94 consensus and $0.44 above the high end of its prior guidance. The call attributed the beat to lower operating expenses and stronger acquisition performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS reached a record $3.42, up 26% year-over-year, exceeding the high end of guidance by $0.44 due to lower operating expenses and stronger acquisition performance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS | Consensus | $2.94”; company guidance was “$2.88–$2.98.”

surprises.description: Revenue of $313 million exceeded the $299.17 million consensus by about 4.6%. The reported 23% total growth included 8% organic growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue rose 23% to a record $313 million, with organic revenue up 8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Consensus | $299.17 million.”

surprises.description: The full-year revenue range rose to $1.19B–$1.21B, and the adjusted EPS floor increased from $12.33 to $12.43 while the ceiling stayed at $12.68. This modest improvement contrasts with the preview’s focus on whether the prior EPS guidance cut would persist.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $1.19B-$1.21B and narrowed adjusted EPS guidance to $12.43-$12.68, up from $12.33-$12.68.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 full-year guidance” was “Revenue: $1.178B–$1.203B” and “Adjusted EPS: $12.33–$12.68”; the preview said to watch “for any update to the $12.33–$12.68 FY adjusted-EPS range.”

surprises.description: Despite the strong Q2 beat and higher full-year guidance, Q3 guidance was $297M–$307M in revenue and $2.90–$3.00 in adjusted EPS, with management cautious about capital-project timing. The preview highlighted guidance sensitivity and bookings momentum but did not anticipate this specific near-term outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for revenue of $297M-$307M and adjusted EPS of $2.90-$3.00, implying no upside from the Q2 beat as management remains cautious on capital project timing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Forward commentary — especially any update to the $12.33–$12.68 FY adjusted-EPS range — is likely to matter more for the share-price reaction than the Q2 beat/miss itself.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded to 21.8% from 20.5%, even as gross margin fell and the aftermarket mix declined. The preview expected aftermarket mix to support margin resilience, but did not anticipate this degree of EBITDA margin expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA hit a record $68.1 million, up 30%, with margin expanding to 21.8% from 20.5% a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Continuation of this mix supports margin resilience.”

surprises.description: Organic capital revenue surged 23%, reaching the company’s second-best Q2 capital-equipment revenue in its history despite a prolonged capital-investment downturn. That strength was not anticipated in the preview’s discussion of demand and bookings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Organic capital revenue surged 23%, representing the second-best Q2 capital equipment revenue in company history despite a prolonged capital investment downturn.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q1 bookings and backlog as “a positive underlying demand signal to reconcile against cautious guidance,” but did not flag a capital-revenue surge.

surprises.description: Gross margin declined 210 basis points to 43.8% as aftermarket parts fell to 68% of revenue from 71%. This runs counter to the preview’s expectation that continued aftermarket mix would support margin resilience.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin declined 210 basis points to 43.8% as higher-margin aftermarket parts fell to 68% of revenue from 71%, reflecting a higher capital mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Aftermarket parts revenue has been a recurring highlight”; “continuation of this mix supports margin resilience.”

surprises.description: Bookings rose 16%, but the preview had pointed to Q1’s record bookings and backlog as a positive demand signal; Q2 bookings were lower than that Q1 record, and large capital-project orders were delayed. The reported total was supported by acquisitions and aftermarket parts rather than broad capital-project momentum.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bookings increased 16% to $312 million, driven by recent acquisitions and strong aftermarket parts demand, even as large capital project orders were delayed.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 2026 bookings were a record $320.8M (+25.2%, +10% organic) with backlog of $326M” and were described as “a positive underlying demand signal to reconcile against cautious guidance.”

surprises.description: Net debt rose $129 million sequentially after acquisition borrowing, and leverage increased to 1.72 from 1.27. The preview discussed acquisition-related EPS dilution but did not flag this increase in borrowing or leverage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt rose $129 million sequentially to $373 million after borrowing $181.8 million for acquisitions, lifting the leverage ratio to 1.72 from 1.27.”

surprises.description: Capital expenditures more than doubled to $10.9 million, partly because Kadant purchased a facility it had previously leased. This facility purchase and higher capex were not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Capital expenditures more than doubled to $10.9 million partly due to purchasing a previously leased facility.”

surprises.description: IPAR held full-year guidance at about $1.48 billion in sales and $4.85 EPS, rather than raising it toward the preview’s higher consensus estimates of $1.50 billion and $4.88. The preview said a reaffirmation would be a mild negative because the Street was leaning toward a raise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year guidance was maintained at approximately $1.48 billion in sales and $4.85 diluted EPS.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 consensus: $1.50B / $4.88”; “consensus already assumes a modest raise”; “a simple reaffirm is a mild negative.”

surprises.description: The company now expects full-year gross margin to improve about 150 basis points, rather than stay flat as management had previously targeted and the preview expected. Tariff refunds are expected to contribute 110 basis points, with mix and cost efficiencies providing the rest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year gross margin is expected to improve roughly 150 basis points, with 110 basis points from tariff refunds and the balance from mix and cost efficiencies.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had a “flat full-year GM target” and listed “anything above that” as a genuine positive surprise.

surprises.description: IPAR recognized $6.9 million of IEEPA tariff refunds in Q2, with the remaining refunds expected to benefit Q3 and Q4. The preview identified the roughly $17 million refund as a major uncertainty and described its base case as the refund remaining excluded, so the reported recognition and timing are favorable relative to that case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received $17.6 million in IEEPA tariff refunds ($6.9 million recognized in Q2) that will benefit Q3 and Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the refunds were “explicitly excluded from guidance” and that the base case assumed “refund still excluded”; it also called whether any refund would be recognized or deferred the largest EPS swing factor.

surprises.description: IPAR authorized a share repurchase program for both Interparfums, Inc. and Interparfums SA shares, backed by a new credit line of up to $250 million. The preview did not anticipate this capital-allocation announcement; the buyback is favorable, while the credit-line funding makes the development mixed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Board authorized a share repurchase program (for both Interparfums, Inc. and Interparfums SA shares) backed by a new line of credit of up to $250 million.”

surprises.description: First-half operating cash flow rose to $46 million from $5 million, alongside a 12% inventory reduction. The preview did not flag cash generation or this working-capital improvement as an earnings debate, making the stronger cash flow an unanticipated positive.
surprises.fact_evidence: “H1 operating cash flow surged to $46 million (49% of net income) from $5 million (5%) prior year, aided by a 12% inventory reduction to $376 million and the tariff refunds.”

surprises.description: Asia Pacific grew 14% and South America 15%, while the Middle East and Africa fell 24% due to the war. The preview focused on the Middle East headwind and U.S./European performance, but did not anticipate these strong results in other regions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Middle East and Africa region fell 24% due to the ongoing war, while Asia Pacific rose 14% and South America grew 15%, demonstrating geographic diversification benefits.”

surprises.description: Lacoste’s reported decline was 16%, somewhat less severe than the preview’s Q2 expectation of a 19% decline. The improvement was limited, and the preview had already noted a 16% first-half decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lacoste declined 16% against a 44% prior-year comparison.”

in_line: Q2 net sales were already pre-announced at $341 million, up 2%, matching the preview’s estimate; the reported 4% organic growth excluding Middle East war-related headwinds also matched the preview’s +4% figure.
U.S.-based operations grew 18% in Q2 while European-based operations declined 4%, in line with the preview’s pre-released segment figures.
Ferragamo grew 41% and Jimmy Choo 23% in Q2, matching the brand figures the preview had already reported.
Maintained guidance implies an approximately 3% second-half sales decline, consistent with the preview’s implied H2 sales decline of about 3%.
The first-half operating-margin compression and higher SG&A/A&P investment were consistent with the preview’s expectation of margin pressure from A&P phasing and its estimated operating margin range.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EPS was $0.82, well above the preview’s $0.65 consensus estimate and its $0.63–$0.66 base-case range. The preview also cautioned that like-for-like adjusted growth was likely materially below the headline growth math, whereas the call reported adjusted EPS up 52%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EPS rose 52% to $0.82”; results were supported by “roughly $16 million of new revenue from new rates plus greater-than-anticipated Texas HB 4384 benefits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 2026 EPS $0.65”; base case: “EPS $0.63–$0.66.” The preview said “true like-for-like YoY growth is likely materially below 22.6%.”

surprises.description: Management moved the full-year outlook from an affirmed range to the upper half, narrowing adjusted EPS guidance to $4.89–$4.95 and adjusted net income to $310–$314 million. The new EPS range retains the old high end but raises the low end from $4.83.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management now expects full-year results in the upper half of guidance, narrowing to adjusted net income of $310-314 million and adjusted EPS of $4.89-4.95.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said guidance was “affirmed, not raised” and listed adjusted net income of “$305.9–314.0M” and adjusted EPS of “$4.83–$4.95.”

surprises.description: Texas HB 4384 contributed more than anticipated, with management now expecting about $0.42 per share for the full year and roughly $0.28–$0.29 already realized in the first half. The preview discussed Texas GRIP as a July/Q3 benefit but did not anticipate this separate HB 4384 contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Texas House Bill 4384 is now expected to contribute approximately $0.42 to full-year adjusted EPS, with about $0.28-0.29 already realized in the first half”; Q2 included “greater-than-anticipated Texas HB 4384 benefits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Texas GRIP’s “~$36.9–37M revenue increase” would be effective with July bills, “Q3, not Q2”; it did not mention HB 4384.

surprises.description: O&M growth eased to 6.6% in Q2 from above 8% in Q1, better than the preview’s concern about a second consecutive high-single-digit increase. Management also expects back-half sequential growth to fall meaningfully below its 3–4% long-term rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 O&M expenses rose 6.6% year-over-year (down from 8%+ in Q1)”; management expects sequential growth to fall “meaningfully below the 3-4% long-term rate in the back half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called “a second consecutive high-single-digit O&M print” the most likely source of a miss and asked about the path back to the “3–4% CAGR target.”

surprises.description: The large-load pipeline had advanced beyond the preview’s one identified signed agreement: management reported three high-volume projects under contract, representing about $15 million of annual revenue and $175 million of capital, alongside five late-stage and 17 early-stage opportunities.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Three high-volume large-load projects under contract represent roughly $15 million of incremental annual revenue and $175 million of associated capital”; there are “5 late-stage large-load prospects plus 17 additional early-stage opportunities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “six late-stage large-load projects” and “one signed Oklahoma data-center agreement.”

surprises.description: Kansas capacity-release revenue was already $2.8 million year-to-date, with another $1.2 million opportunity remaining this injection season. That is stronger and earlier progress than the preview’s description of a benefit of only “a couple million dollars” that was back-half weighted.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company has realized $2.8 million in Kansas capacity release revenues year-to-date (shared 50-50 with customers), with an incremental $1.2 million opportunity remaining this injection season.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had sized the Kansas capacity-release benefit at “a couple million dollars,” “explicitly back-half weighted.”

in_line: The quarterly dividend remained $0.68 per share, as listed in the preview.

surprises.description: Adjusted continuing-operations EPS was $0.45, below the $0.47 consensus and the preview’s $0.50–$0.54 base-case range. That is a modest headline shortfall despite growth from the clean prior-year comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EPS from continuing operations rose to $0.45”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS (cont. ops) | Q2 2026 consensus | $0.47”; preview base case: “EPS $0.50–0.54.”

surprises.description: The California deferred-margin benefit was recognized in Q2 as expected, but the reported $9.7 million net-income benefit was below the preview’s estimated full-H1 catch-up of about $0.21 per share. The preview’s estimate was stated on a pre-tax basis, so the comparison is approximate rather than exact.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The California rate case decision…provided approximately $40 million of incremental annual revenue, with a $9.7 million net income benefit recognized in Q2 from deferred margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A full H1 true-up = ~$20M pre-tax ≈ $0.21/sh recognized in Q2.”

surprises.description: The Great Basin project’s capital estimate rose by $600 million to approximately $2.3 billion after the company switched to a 48-inch pipeline—an unflagged cost increase, though the expanded project is expected to generate $270–$300 million of incremental annual margin once complete.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Great Basin 2028 Expansion Project capital estimate increased to approximately $2.3 billion (a $600 million rise) after switching to a 48-inch pipeline, expected to generate $270-$300 million of incremental annual margin upon completion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for capex quantification and whether design capacity is upsized above 1.0 Bcf/d.”

surprises.description: Nevada intervenors converged on a 9.3% ROE and recommended an average revenue increase just under $40 million, well below the company’s approximately $74 million request. The preview identified the case and its timing but did not anticipate this materially lower intervenor recommendation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In Nevada's general rate case, intervenor parties converged on a 9.3% ROE and recommended an average revenue increase just under $40 million versus the company's ~$74 million request, targeting an October 2026 effective date.”

surprises.description: The utility’s trailing ROE was 8.1%, below the preview’s cited 8.5% level; adjusted ROE was 8.0%, matching the preview. The reported overall return therefore showed less improvement than the earlier trailing figure suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The utility delivered a 12-month trailing ROE of 8.1% (8% adjusted), still below its weighted average authorized return of 9.89%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Utility ROE trajectory | 8.5% trailing / 8.0% adjusted at 3/31/26.”

in_line: Management reaffirmed 2026 and long-term guidance, including the 9.5%–11.5% rate-base CAGR target through 2030, as the preview expected.

The California case provided approximately $40 million of annual incremental revenue and deferred-margin revenue was recognized in Q2, matching the preview’s expected decision economics and timing; the quantified Q2 benefit was lower than the preview estimate.

The Great Basin project had approximately 1 Bcf/day contracted for 2028, consistent with the preview’s expectation around the project’s 1.0 Bcf/day design and signed agreements; the preview had also cited substantial additional market interest.
The company expected no equity issuance in 2026 beyond its dividend reinvestment plan, in line with the preview’s financing expectation.

surprises.description: Management now expects 2026 EPS to land in the top half of the $2.95–$3.15 range, improving on the preview’s base case of an unchanged outlook. The range itself was not narrowed.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management raised its expectation to deliver 2026 EPS in the top half of its $2.95 to $3.15 guidance range, citing strong year-to-date performance and improved second-half visibility.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base” scenario: “guidance reaffirmed unchanged at $2.95–$3.15”; the preview also called a move to the upper half “the single most bullish outcome available.”

surprises.description: Q2 EPS was $0.01, above the preview’s near-zero adjusted estimate and the consensus range for a GAAP loss. This was a positive headline surprise despite weaker-than-modeled contributions from SiEnergy and Water.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total EPS was $0.01, flat year-over-year but above expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GAAP EPS” consensus: “$(0.05) – $(0.082)” (midpoint about “$(0.06)”); “Adjusted EPS” estimate: “~$0.00.”

surprises.description: Northwest Natural Gas EPS was $0.09, well above the preview’s $0.01 estimate, even though the preview expected higher costs to weigh on the segment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Northwest Natural Gas EPS declining to $0.09 from $0.12.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated NWN Gas Utility EPS at “$0.01” and said “depreciation, O&M and interest keep climbing.”

surprises.description: SiEnergy EPS was $0.05, below the preview’s $0.07 estimate, despite customer growth and backlog broadly meeting the preview’s operating expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SiEnergy rising to $0.05 from $0.03.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated SiEnergy EPS at “$0.07” and cited “16% organic meter growth” and a “250k+ meter backlog.”

surprises.description: Water EPS was $0.05, below the preview’s $0.07 estimate; management also said first-half Water results were modestly below plan. The segment earnings result was weaker than expected even though customer growth was stronger than the preview’s estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Water falling to $0.05 from $0.07”; Water customer growth was 3.4%, “though first-half results were modestly below plan.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Water EPS at “$0.07” and “2.2% organic growth.”

surprises.description: Water customer growth was 3.4% over the 12 months ended June, above the preview’s 2.2% organic-growth estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Water customer growth was 3.4% for the 12 months ended June 30, 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Water estimate cited “2.2% organic growth.”

surprises.description: MX3 was described as fully contracted with 25-year agreements, a more de-risked project status than the preview’s focus on EPC and permit progress. The expected end-2027 Notice to Proceed and conditional growth-target increase remained on the preview’s timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The $300 million FERC-regulated MX3 storage expansion is fully contracted with 25-year agreements at a 12.5% ROE and 50% equity structure”; Notice to Proceed is “expected end of 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “MX3 (4–5 Bcf, ~$300M) EPC/permit progress” and whether NTP stayed “by late 2027”; it described the 5%–7% growth target as conditional on NTP.

surprises.description: Quarter-end liquidity was about $628 million, above the preview’s stated $590 million, a modestly better funding position than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company reported “liquidity of about $628 million at quarter end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “$590M liquidity.”

surprises.description: The company completed an inaugural $75 million Water bond issuance after receiving an A- investment-grade rating, a financing development the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed its inaugural $75 million Water bond issuance after receiving an A- investment-grade rating.”

in_line: SiEnergy organic customer growth was over 15% and its future-meter backlog was over 260,000, broadly consistent with the preview’s 16% growth estimate, 15%–20% target, and 250k+ backlog.
Washington’s new rates took effect August 1, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the revenue increase would be effective in August.
Oregon’s alternative rate mechanism had rates expected October 31, 2026, consistent with the preview’s expected October 31 timing.
The 2026 capital expenditure plan of $500 million to $550 million and $40 million to $50 million of ATM equity matched the preview’s expectations.

surprises.description: Mosaic lowered Q3 phosphate volume guidance to 1.1–1.4 million tonnes; the range puts a sub-1.3 million-tonne quarter within reach, beyond the preview’s general expectation of H2 volume cuts and into its downside scenario. This leaves a more pronounced near-term volume risk than the preview’s base case implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance lowered to a range of 1.1 to 1.4 million tonnes, signaling potential volume downside.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base” scenario: “H2 volumes cut but offset by a higher DAP price guide”; “Bear” scenario: “Q3 phosphate guided <1.3 Mt.”

surprises.description: Management described a much deeper fertilizer application downturn than the preview quantified: North American application is forecast down about 20% after last year’s roughly 15% decline, with a similar 30% decline in Brazil. The resulting large nutrient shortfall is a near-term demand concern, though management expects it eventually to support yields and pent-up fertilizer demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “North American phosphate application is forecast down ~20% this year on top of last year's ~15% decline, cumulatively over 30% below normal, with a similar ~30% decline expected in Brazil”; cumulative under-application is estimated at 1.4 million tonnes of DAP-equivalent nutrient in the U.S. and up to 1.3 million tonnes in Brazil, which management expects to “eventually pressure crop yields and drive pent-up fertilizer demand.”

surprises.description: The preview anticipated weak free cash flow, but the call quantified a substantial full-year funding gap: year-to-date operating cash flow of about $270 million versus roughly $1.5 billion in capex and dividends leaves Mosaic about $500 million short for the year. Debt is expected to remain stable in Q3 before declining in Q4, rather than falling sooner.
surprises.fact_evidence: “With year-to-date operating cash flow of ~$270 million against ~$1.5 billion in CapEx and dividends, the company expects to be roughly $500 million short for the year, keeping debt stable in Q3 before declining in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Dividend is ~$280M/yr against a quarter that may generate little FCF — 16 consecutive years of payments makes a cut unlikely but the coverage commentary matters.”

surprises.description: Despite sequential margin pressure, phosphate stripping margins are expected to remain well above historical averages. That is more resilient than the preview’s discussion of margins below $300 per tonne and negative in some geographies suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company expects phosphate stripping margins to decline sequentially in Q3 due to higher sulfur/ammonia costs and reduced fixed cost absorption, but still remain well above historical averages.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Stripping margins compressed below $300/t vs. >$600 peaks, negative in some geographies.”

surprises.description: Q3 sulfur costs are set to rise sharply from Q2, despite the preview’s note of a July sulfur price decline. However, Mosaic says its new contract and Gulf Coast refiner relationships keep costs well below unsustainably high spot prices, partially cushioning the supply shock the preview emphasized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 sulfur costs are guided to $700-$710 per tonne (up from $522 in Q2) after settling a new contract at $705, though this remains well below unsustainably high spot prices due to Gulf Coast refiner relationships.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “First relief signal: sulfur −7.03% month-over-month as of July 13”; “Mosaic is structurally short sulfur”; “Until the sulfur lane reopens, higher DAP prices do not translate into higher phosphate earnings.”

surprises.description: Mosaic cut full-year capex again, to $1.2 billion from the preview’s stated $1.25 billion level. The additional reduction supports expected sequential free-cash-flow improvement in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reduced full-year CapEx guidance to $1.2 billion (from $1.25 billion and an original $1.5 billion), supporting expectations of sequentially improving free cash flow in Q3 and Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Is $1.25B capex holding or getting cut again?”

surprises.description: Fertilizantes’ Q2 EBITDA was $60 million, but management expects it to decline in Q3 as curtailed Brazilian commodity production limits sales. That conflicts with the preview’s base case that Brazil would peak in Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fertilizantes Q2 EBITDA of $60 million is expected to decline in Q3 as curtailed Brazilian commodity production limits sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base scenario: “Fertilizantes ~$50–80M (shoulder quarter; Brazil peaks in Q3).”

surprises.description: Potash netbacks face pressure from higher export freight rates and a Canpotex-weighted channel mix, a headwind not reflected in the preview’s picture of potash as the earnings floor amid a firm market backdrop.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Potash netbacks face pressure from higher export freight rates and a Canpotex-weighted channel mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Potash — the entire earnings floor”; “Market backdrop is genuinely firm”; “Reaffirmation of 9.0 Mt FY production matters as much as the price.”

surprises.description: Management still expects a $400 million working-capital release, but says it will be weighted toward Q4 collections from Brazil while customer prepayments there have fallen to near zero. The release could support cash generation, but its timing and dependence on collections add execution risk not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A $400 million working capital release (range $300-$500 million) is still expected, weighted roughly one-third in Q3 and two-thirds in Q4 as Brazil collections arrive, though customer prepayments in Brazil fell to near zero.”

surprises.description: SG&A was already down 20% year over year, with further second-half declines expected and management characterizing the savings as permanent. The preview identified a cost program but did not describe savings of this size as already realized or permanent.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A costs were cut 20% year-over-year and are expected to decline further in the second half, with management characterizing these savings as permanent.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cost program: >$150M annual ($100M value capture + $50M overhead).”

in_line: Q2 phosphate production and sales of 1.4 million tonnes came in at the bottom of the preview’s 1.4–1.7 million-tonne guidance range.
Q2 Fertilizantes EBITDA of $60 million was within the preview’s $50–80 million base-case estimate.

surprises.description: Prudential reported adjusted operating EPS of $4.08, well above the preview’s $3.35–$3.42 consensus band and even its $3.45–$3.50 effective-whisper estimate. Instead of the expected year-over-year decline, EPS was up 14%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 after-tax adjusted operating income was $1.4 billion, or $4.08 per share, up 14% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. operating EPS: $3.42”; alternate consensus “$3.35”; effective whisper “closer to $3.45–3.50”; consensus YoY “–4.4%.”

surprises.description: The Japan suspension hit was materially lighter than the preview’s estimated $140–$160 million for the first full suspended quarter: Prudential reported $105 million, also below Q1’s $130 million. This was a favorable difference even though management retained the full-year range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Prudential of Japan sales suspension impact was $105 million in the quarter (below expectations, down from $130 million in Q1).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate: $140–160M pretax”; the preview also noted Q1’s “$130M” impact.

surprises.description: Prudential announced a much broader footprint reduction than the preview’s general expectation of further portfolio pruning: it plans to exit 6–7 emerging markets and cut its retirement and insurance footprint roughly in half. The exits are expected to free substantial capital, but also mean a significant pullback from those markets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Plans to cut its retirement and insurance footprint by roughly half, exiting 6-7 emerging markets (primarily via sales rather than shutdowns) to free up well north of $3 billion of capital over roughly a 5-year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview anticipated “further portfolio pruning” and noted prior exits, but did not forecast this scale of retrenchment.

surprises.description: The strategy update set a larger PGIM ambition than the preview’s stated 25–30% long-term margin target: PGIM is to reach about 25% of PFI adjusted operating income versus roughly 12% currently, with margins targeted above 30%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “PGIM growing to about 25% of PFI's adjusted operating income, more than double its current ~12% contribution, and aims to expand PGIM margins above its 30% multiyear target.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “25–30% long-term margin” and described PGIM as the “re-rating engine”; it did not give a target for PGIM’s share of PFI income.

surprises.description: Prudential raised its structural-efficiency ambition far beyond the small PGIM savings figure in the preview: the company now targets about $750 million of pretax run-rate benefits by year-end 2028, versus an original $150 million target for 2027. It also plans a further 150-basis-point expense-ratio improvement over three years.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its structural efficiency target to approximately $750 million in pretax run-rate benefits by year-end 2028 (full benefit in 2029), up from the original $150 million target for 2027”; it also “expects to improve its adjusted operating expense ratio by an additional 150 basis points over the next 3 years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview mentioned PGIM’s “~$100M run-rate savings” but did not anticipate this company-wide target increase or the additional expense-ratio goal.

surprises.description: PGIM’s private-capital deployment accelerated more than the preview’s expectation of continued deployment: it rose nearly 60% sequentially to almost $21 billion, including about $7 billion in asset-backed finance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “PGIM private capital deployment grew nearly 60% sequentially to nearly $21 billion (including ~$7 billion of asset-backed finance).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 private-asset deployment of “$13B” and expected confirmation of PGIM’s margin trajectory, but did not forecast a further acceleration of this size.

surprises.description: Group Insurance produced record earnings of $155 million, a much stronger outcome than the preview’s concern about whether the weak Q1 disability experience would stabilize. The preview highlighted Q1 AOI of only $38 million and warned that another weak print would be concerning.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Group Insurance delivered record earnings of $155 million (up 24%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called stabilization the key question after “Q1 AOI collapsed to $38M from $89M” and said two consecutive weak prints would reframe the issue as structural.

surprises.description: Individual Life earnings did not show the mean-reversion weakness the preview warned could follow Q1’s favorable mortality: earnings were $176 million and more than doubled year over year. That is a favorable result against the preview’s concern that reversion could reduce the U.S. contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Individual Life earnings of $176 million more than doubled year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q1’s “$139M vs $52M” as driven by favorable mortality and warned that “a reversion here quietly eats $50–80M of the U.S. beat.”

in_line: Prudential maintained the Japan full-year 2026 impact guidance of $525–$575 million and targeted sales resumption by November 5–6, consistent with the preview’s base case of reaffirmed guidance and a firm Nov. 6 restart.
PGIM remained on track for more than 200 basis points of margin expansion in 2026, as the preview expected.

Management did not provide a specific numerical EPS growth target, but described a top-quartile, around-high-single-digit goal. The preview’s base case anticipated directional strategy without hard numeric targets, though its catalyst checklist said investors wanted a number.
PGIM continued to record positive third-party net flows despite equity outflows, consistent with the preview’s expectation of positive flows despite continued active-equity outflows.

surprises.description: The preview treated the full FY2026 guidance range of $925M–$1.0B as still live in its base case. USANA instead lowered its full-year outlook, citing weaker expected HIYA second-half sales and reduced near-term Rise Wellness sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “USANA lowered its full-year fiscal 2026 outlook,” citing “a more expensive direct-to-consumer digital marketing environment hurting HIYA's second-half sales and reduced near-term Rise Wellness sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base = a verbatim reaffirmation of the full wide range with no phasing detail”; the preview identified whether the FY26 guide was “still live” as the central question.

surprises.description: The preview expected Rise Wellness to ramp, forecasting about $17M for Q2 and a $65M–$80M full-year range, with retailer rollouts underway. A packaging issue instead reduced its top-line guidance by roughly $30M–$40M and is expected to pressure margins by about $4M–$5M.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Rise Wellness packaging issue lowered its top-line guidance range by roughly $30 million to $40 million and created about $4 million to $5 million of margin pressure.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Rise Wellness ~$17M” in Q2 and “$65–80M” for FY2026; the preview also said “nine new Rise retailers rolling out in Q2/Q3.”

surprises.description: The preview flagged HIYA's Meta-related acquisition-cost problem but looked for CAC to normalize and subscribers to stabilize or rise. The call instead described continuing Meta algorithm challenges and a strategic pivot toward TikTok, retail, and international markets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “HIYA has faced rising customer acquisition costs due to Meta algorithm challenges, prompting a strategic shift toward TikTok, retail expansion, and international markets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Need subs flat-to-up sequentially plus commentary that CAC has normalized — otherwise the H2 Hiya reacceleration story loses credibility.”

surprises.description: The preview anticipated HIYA weakness and risk to its outlook, but did not anticipate a large impairment. USANA reported a preliminary $29M non-cash goodwill charge tied to HIYA after weaker performance and lower near-term forecasts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “USANA recorded an estimated preliminary non-cash goodwill impairment charge of $29 million tied to the HIYA reporting unit, reflecting weaker-than-expected performance and reduced near-term forecasts.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag an unusual tax burden. USANA recorded $9M of tax expense despite a $19M pre-tax loss and said the elevated tax rate should persist through the year, well above the second-quarter catch-up level.
