surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reported $9 million in income tax expense on a pre-tax loss of $19 million,” due to “a structural misalignment between where revenue is generated and where costs are incurred.” Management expects “an elevated tax rate to persist through the full year.”

surprises.description: The preview's segment build anticipated a modest decline in Core Nutritional, but the call highlighted a much sharper 20% drop in North Asia, mainly tied to prolonged softness in Korea after a leadership transition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “North Asia direct revenue declined 20%, driven mainly by prolonged softness in Korea following a leadership transition at the start of the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's segment build forecast Core Nutritional at about $194M, down 2.6%, without forecasting a 20% North Asia decline.

surprises.description: USANA ended with more cash and no debt, compared with the preview's $163M cash and $14M debt. It also generated $20M of free cash flow, which the preview had not projected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “USANA ended the quarter with $169 million in cash, zero debt, and generated $20 million of free cash flow aided by improved working capital management.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “$163M cash, $14M debt” and noted “zero repurchased in Q1.”

surprises.description: The preview expected Rise Wellness growth and retailer rollouts, but the call gave a stronger scale update: it had already surpassed its full prior-year sales year-to-date and expects to be in more than 4,000 retail doors by year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rise Wellness has already exceeded its full prior-year sales year-to-date and expects to be selling in over 4,000 retail doors by year-end despite being less than a year old as a national brand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview forecast Rise Wellness at “~$17M” in Q2 and described a Costco/Walmart ramp and “nine new Rise retailers rolling out in Q2/Q3.”

in_line: Greater China showed renewed sales growth, consistent with the preview's focus on whether the Q1 momentum would hold into Q2; the call noted that some of the growth reflected a lingering tail from the Q1 incentive and product-launch program.

surprises.description: WTRG said it had finalized rate cases and surcharges representing $56.6 million in annualized revenue year to date, well above the $15.1 million already completed as of Q1 cited in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Year-to-date the company finalized rate cases and surcharges representing $56.6 million in annualized revenue, with ~78% from water and wastewater.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “$15.1M annualized already completed in 2026” as of Q1.

surprises.description: Management disclosed that full-year effective tax rates are expected to be below 5%, along with a one-time benefit later this year. The preview noted that prior-year favorable tax items would not repeat, so this is a more favorable tax outlook than it led investors to expect.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects “low single-digit (under 5%) effective tax rates for the full year plus a one-time benefit later this year disclosed in the S-4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q1 as having “no repeat of prior-year favorable tax items” and did not identify a later 2026 one-time benefit.

surprises.description: WTRG identified a broader municipal acquisition pipeline of about 400,000 customers, an opportunity not mentioned in the preview, which focused on Greenville and the pending DELCORA deal.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company cited “a broader municipal pipeline of ~400,000 customers.”

surprises.description: The company maintained its Q1 2027 merger-close expectation, but added that Pennsylvania’s ALJ recommendation could shift the date and that Illinois’ statutory timeline runs through November 2026. The preview flagged both states as pending but did not describe these specific timing risks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The merger with American Water is expected to close in Q1 2027”; “Illinois is the last state with a statutory merger timeline, finishing by November 2026,” and Pennsylvania’s ALJ “has up to 90 days to issue a recommendation that could shift the close date.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the close was targeted “by end of Q1 2027” and identified Pennsylvania and Illinois as still pending approvals.

in_line: Q2 non-GAAP EPS was $0.38, matching the preview’s $0.38 consensus; GAAP EPS was $0.37 after about $0.01 of merger costs.
The company reaffirmed 5%–7% multiyear EPS growth through 2027, consistent with the preview’s stated guidance.
The Q1 2027 merger-close target remained in place, and the approval and Texas settlement updates were broadly consistent with the preview’s merger discussion.
WTRG remained on track for $1.7 billion of 2026 infrastructure investment, consistent with the preview’s capex target.
The 5.25% dividend increase matched the increase already reported in the preview.
The pending Pennsylvania natural gas rate request remained $163.2 million, matching the preview’s stated request.

surprises.description: Diluted EPS was $1.39, well below the preview’s $1.83 estimate, even though earnings from operations rose to $17 million from $3.9 million. The preview’s reported-EPS estimate was therefore materially too high despite expecting a large refund benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS surged to $1.39 from $0.24”; “earnings from operations to $17 million from $3.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Reported diluted EPS” Q2’26E: “~$1.83.”

surprises.description: Reported gross margin reached 70.4%, far above the preview’s 44.0% estimate, as $15.3 million of tariff refunds was recorded as a reduction to cost of sales. The reported margin is not representative of the ongoing business: management said wholesale margin would be materially lower excluding the refund.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated gross margin jumped to 70.4%” from 43.3%, “largely inflated by $15.3 million in one-time IEPA tariff refunds recognized as a reduction to cost of sales”; “Excluding the $14.3 million tariff refund, wholesale gross margin would be materially lower.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin” Q2’26E: “44.0%.”

surprises.description: The post-July tariff rate was higher than the 10% rate the preview described as scheduled to sunset: an incremental 12.5% tariff on imports from China and Vietnam took effect July 24. That adds near-term second-half margin uncertainty rather than resolving the sourcing-cost question.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The administration raised the incremental tariff on imports from China and Vietnam to 12.5% effective July 24, 2026, creating near-term gross margin uncertainty for the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Section 122’s 10% across-the-board rate was scheduled to sunset ~July 24, 2026,” with Section 301 actions “widely expected as the replacement.”

surprises.description: Wholesale selling and administrative expenses were a much heavier burden relative to sales than the preview’s modest increase in consolidated SG&A suggested. The 37% wholesale expense ratio, up from 29%, pressured underlying operating margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Wholesale selling and administrative expenses climbed to 37% of net sales from 29% a year ago, driven by higher employee costs, pressuring underlying operating margins.”

surprises.description: Sales modestly exceeded the preview model, rising 7% to $62.2 million versus its $61.5 million estimate and projected 5.7% growth. Wholesale sales also came in above the preview’s estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales rose 7% year-over-year to $62.2 million”; “Wholesale net sales grew 7% to $48.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales” Q2’26E: “$61.5M” and “+5.7%”; segment estimate: “N.A. Wholesale $48.3M (+6%).”

surprises.description: Several wholesale brands performed better than the preview’s recent-trend discussion implied: Florsheim accelerated, Stacey Adams returned to growth, and Bogs grew despite being described as seasonally immaterial in Q2. Nunn-Busch, however, declined rather than holding flat, making the brand picture mixed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Florsheim (+12%), Stacey Adams (+4%), and Bogs (+10%), while Nunn-Busch declined 3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 trends of “Florsheim +5%, Nunn Bush flat, Stacy Adams –9%, BOGS –11%” and said “BOGS is seasonally immaterial in Q2.”

in_line: The refund benefit was broadly in line with the preview’s $18.6 million base case: $15.3 million was recognized as a reduction to cost of sales and another $3.3 million reduced inventory. The preview had identified both cost-of-sales and inventory credits as possible treatments.
Management’s year-end inventory plan of roughly $70 million was at the upper end of the preview’s stated $60–70 million normalization target.

surprises.description: Revenue was $396 million, well above the preview’s dispersed $374–380 million consensus range and its roughly $371 million segment-guidance estimate. The result exceeded even the preview’s bull-case revenue threshold of $385 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue grew 8% sequentially to $396 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Published consensus for this print is dispersed across vendors ($374M vs. $380M revenue)” and the segment build implied “$366–377M (mid ~$371M).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $93 million, substantially above the company’s $77–80 million Q2 guidance range. The preview identified that range as the primary beat/miss measure, so the result was a much larger beat than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA of $93 million significantly exceeded the company's guidance range of $77 million to $80 million, driven by outperformance across all three segments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA vs. $77–80M” was the “cleanest beat/miss read”; the preview also listed $77–80 million as company guidance.

surprises.description: Water Infrastructure revenue was $102 million, above the preview’s expected roughly $96–99 million and even its bull-case threshold of more than $100 million. Its 58% gross margin also topped the preview’s base-case expectation of about 55–56%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Water Infrastructure segment posted record revenue of $102 million (up 26% year-over-year) with strong 58% gross margins before D&A.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The segment build estimated “$96–99M”; the bull case called for “Infra >$100M at ≥56% margin,” while the base case anticipated “Infra $97–100M at ~55–56%.”

surprises.description: Chemical Technologies revenue reached $96 million, above the preview’s $86–90 million estimate based on 10–15% sequential growth. Gross profit grew 35% sequentially despite rising oil-based raw material costs, indicating stronger segment performance than the preview’s guidance-based expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Chemical Technologies segment posted record revenue of $96 million, up 23% sequentially, with 35% sequential gross profit growth to $19.4 million despite rising oil-based raw material costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Chemical Technologies was guided to “+10–15% sequential” and estimated Q2 revenue of “$86–90M.”

surprises.description: Select signed a new seven-year agreement backed by a 128 million barrel MVC and the conveyance of 14 strategic SWDs. The preview highlighted MVC and dedication additions as an important backlog debate but did not anticipate a contract of this scale or duration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company executed a new 7-year agreement with a large public operator supported by a 128 million barrel MVC contract, which included the conveyance of 14 strategic SWDs across Eddy and Lea County, New Mexico.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “Watch the MVC/dedication count specifically” and listed prior-quarter additions, but gave no expectation of a new seven-year, 128 million barrel MVC agreement.

surprises.description: The company raised the 2026 net capex ceiling to $290 million, $40 million above the preview’s already-raised $250 million high end. The preview framed another increase as a downside risk, though the call tied the additional spending to new infrastructure awards.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its 2026 net capital expenditure guidance to $250 million to $290 million, up from the prior $250 million high end, to support new infrastructure contract awards.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited FY capex of “$200–250M” and identified “capex raised again” as a bear-case risk.

surprises.description: Management went beyond simply reaffirming the 25–30% 2026 Water Infrastructure growth range: it said the segment should reach the high end and projected double-digit revenue growth continuing into 2027, with improved free-cash-flow potential. The preview expected a reaffirmation to be table stakes and specifically looked for evidence of a 2027 cash-flow inflection.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects Water Infrastructure to hit the high end of its 25% to 30% full-year growth guidance and projects double-digit segment revenue growth continuing into 2027 with improved free cash flow potential.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called a reaffirmation of “25–30%” “table stakes” and said the buy side wanted “a credible 2027 FCF inflection.”

surprises.description: Surfactant demand was up 50% year over year, but management said surfactants remain a small share of chemicals revenue and are used on fewer than 10% of new well completions. That detail suggests adoption is still limited despite the rapid growth, a constraint the preview did not quantify.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Surfactant demand is growing rapidly (up 50% year-over-year) but remains a small portion of chemicals revenue, with less than 10% of new well completions currently using surfactants.”

in_line: Management kept the 2026 Water Infrastructure growth range at 25–30% rather than raising the formal range; the preview said reaffirming that range was table stakes, although the call’s high-end confidence and 2027 commentary were incremental.

surprises.description: PACS reported Q2 adjusted EPS of $0.63, above the preview’s $0.54 consensus estimate by about 17%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS rose 34% to $0.63 from $0.47 a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 EPS | $0.54 | Zacks consensus, published May 11, 2026”

surprises.description: Management raised FY2026 adjusted EBITDAR guidance to $640–$660 million, up $35 million from the preview’s previously reported $605–$625 million adjusted EBITDA range. The new midpoint is about 6% above the old midpoint, although the guidance metrics are labeled differently in the two sources.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year 2026 … adjusted EBITDAR guidance by $35 million to $640-$660 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “At Q1 (May 11, 2026) management raised FY2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to $605–625M from $555–575M”; “a further raise is a live possibility.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $1.43 billion modestly exceeded the preview’s $1.41 billion consensus estimate, a beat of about 1.4%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue rose 9.1% year-over-year to $1.43 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 revenue | $1.41B (~8% y/y) | Zacks consensus, published May 11, 2026”

surprises.description: PACS disclosed a 20-facility Texas acquisition cohort, larger than the preview’s stated pace of roughly five underperforming-facility acquisitions per quarter. The first 20 began operating August 1, while 14 more facilities remain pending; the first group is only modestly included in guidance and has substantial occupancy ramp potential.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Acquired the operations of the first 20 of 34 Eduro Healthcare facilities in Texas on August 1,” with “only a modest contribution included in guidance” and “the remaining 14 facilities excluded pending third/fourth quarter closings.” The 20 facilities “currently run at mid-60% occupancy and 10-11% skilled mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management targets roughly five underperforming-facility acquisitions per quarter.”

surprises.description: Management identified additional possible reimbursement upside not included in guidance: anticipated Ohio quality incentive payments and at least one more California WQIP supplemental payment in 2026. The preview did not flag these potential payments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Potential upside not reflected in guidance includes anticipated Ohio quality incentive payments and at least one more California WQIP supplemental payment in 2026, neither of which has been accrued.”

surprises.description: FY2026 revenue guidance was raised by $100 million to $5.75–$5.85 billion. Its $5.80 billion midpoint is modestly above the preview’s cited full-year revenue estimates of $5.71 billion and $5.75 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance by $100 million to $5.75-$5.85 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 revenue | $5.71B (Zacks, May 11, 2026); $5.75B (StockAnalysis consensus, July 8, 2026)”

in_line: Net leverage remained at 0.1x, consistent with the preview’s Q1 figure of 0.1x and its description of ample acquisition capacity.

surprises.description: Revenue reached $260 million, above the preview’s modeled $250–253 million and 6.5–7.8% growth range; year-over-year growth was 11%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY2027 revenue reached $260 million,” up 11% year-over-year.

surprises.description: The preview expected Patient Management to remain a low-single-digit grower, but it contributed roughly $12.5 million of the quarter’s revenue growth—about half the total increase—alongside Network Solutions. That points to a stronger-than-expected Patient Management contribution, although the call facts do not give its exact growth rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Patient Management and Network Solutions each contributed roughly $12.5 million of revenue growth,” with enterprise claims TPA driving Patient Management.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “PM (case management, clinical) grew low single digits in Q4 and is the drag”; the base case expected “PM low-single.”

surprises.description: EPS of $0.63 exceeded the preview’s modeled $0.58–$0.60, but roughly $0.07 came from one-time CERIS items, primarily a legacy receivables settlement. That leaves roughly $0.56 after subtracting the one-time benefit, below the preview’s clean-EPS threshold, though net income excluding one-time items still grew 18%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Earnings per share rose 22% to $0.63”; “roughly $0.07 came from one-time CERIS items primarily tied to a legacy accounts receivable settlement.” Excluding one-time items, “total net income increased 18% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled “Diluted EPS ~ $0.58–0.60” and set a catalyst of “EPS ≥ $0.58 on a clean basis.” It also said the prior quarter’s “$0.02 of timing-related post-payment recoveries” did not recur.

surprises.description: The call disclosed a sharp increase in new customer sales—over 60% year over year, with nearly half of the increase in June—and 40% growth in trailing 12-month new sales. The preview discussed Q4 bookings and asked when they would convert to revenue, but did not anticipate or quantify this current-period sales acceleration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New customer sales improved over 60% year-over-year, with nearly half of that growth occurring in the single month of June”; trailing 12-month new sales “rose 40%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “+56% bookings and +20% RFPs are backlog, not revenue. The question for the call: when does it hit the P&L?”

in_line: Network Solutions/CERIS was a major source of growth, consistent with the preview’s expectation that Network Solutions/CERIS would lead.
The CEO transition was anticipated: the preview identified Sarah Scott as CEO and described this as her first call in the role.
Buybacks continued at a slightly higher dollar pace than in Q4 ($21.8 million versus $20.1 million), broadly consistent with the preview’s watch for a step-up in capital returns.

surprises.description: AGL reported Q2 adjusted EBITDA of $70 million against a $20 million guidance midpoint—about $50 million higher than expected. The preview treated the $20 million guide as the benchmark and highlighted a much lower threshold as a key risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA was $70 million” and “exceeded the guidance midpoint by approximately $50 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA **$20M**” for Q2; the preview also called for monitoring whether the result reached “≥$75M” for full-year guidance.

surprises.description: Q2 medical margin was $197 million, about $74 million above the $123 million guide midpoint. That substantially exceeded even the preview’s stated $135–145 million whisper range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 medical margin was $197 million” and “beating the guidance midpoint by roughly $74 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Medical margin **$123M**”; the preview also said the “whisper” was “closer to $135–145M.”

surprises.description: AGL raised full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to an $85 million midpoint, far above the prior $10–40 million range and the preview’s key $75 million threshold. The new $485 million medical-margin midpoint also greatly exceeds the prior $350–400 million range, while revenue guidance moved only modestly to about $5.8 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 guidance to approximately $5.8 billion revenue, $485 million medical margin, and $85 million adjusted EBITDA at the midpoints.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance … Revenue $5.68–5.81B · Medical margin $350–400M · Adjusted EBITDA $10–40M”; the preview identified “FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance ≥ $75M” as a catalyst.

surprises.description: Management doubled its 2026 net risk-adjustment estimate to about 3%, rather than holding at the preview’s stated 1.5% estimate. That is a materially more favorable risk-adjustment outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 2026 year-over-year risk adjustment estimate was raised to approximately 3% net of the V28 impact, double the prior 1.5% estimate given at Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 risk score uplift was revised up to **+1.5%** (from +0.4%).”

surprises.description: The underlying cost-trend picture improved: the full-year 2025 estimate fell to 5.8% from 6.2%, and Q1 2026 developed favorably into the low 6% range. This was more favorable than the preview’s discussion of Q1’s recorded 7.4% trend, although management kept its roughly 7% assumption for the rest of 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The full-year 2025 cost trend estimate improved to 5.8% from the 6.2% estimated at Q1, while Q1 2026 trends developed favorably into the low 6% range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 recorded **7.4%**”; the preview also noted favorable late-2025 development but said the company’s FY26 guide assumed **7.0%**.

surprises.description: Management said it expects ACO REACH to contribute $25–30 million of EBITDA in 2026, alongside reporting $229 million of gross savings and a 96% average quality score for the 2024 results. The preview described Q1 ACO REACH outperformance as non-recurring, so the stated full-year contribution is a more concrete positive outlook than it provided.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 2024 ACO REACH results delivered $229 million in gross savings with a 96% average quality score across eight ACOs,” and management “expects the raise to be a positive contributor with $25-30 million ACO REACH EBITDA in 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ACO REACH's Q1 outperformance (+$27M adj. EBITDA, ~$5M above plan, helped by CMS removing fraudulent claims) is non-recurring.”

surprises.description: AGL said it will record Part D net in revenue to limit seasonality effects. The preview discussed Part D exposure and delayed reconciliation but did not anticipate this revenue presentation approach.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Part D exposure now sits at less than 15% of the book, and management intends to reduce it further while recording Part D net in revenue to limit seasonality effects.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Exposure is <15% of business” and “reconciliation data doesn't arrive until Q3 2026.”

in_line: Management kept its approximate 7% cost-trend assumption for the remainder of 2026; the preview expected the 7.0% assumption to hold.
Part D exposure remains below 15% and management intends to reduce it further, consistent with the preview’s description of the exposure and its watch for further reduction.
Membership remains lower year over year under a deliberate profitability-focused contracting approach, consistent with the preview’s expectation of continued deliberate shrinkage.

surprises.description: SmartRent reported $40 million of total revenue, slightly above the $39.62 million consensus, while core revenue grew 14% to $38 million. That core growth was stronger than the preview’s implied 11–12% pace needed to reach consensus, although the $40 million headline was only a small beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Core revenue grew 14% to $38 million” and “total revenue rose 4% to $40 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $39.62M”; the preview also said core revenue “would need to grow roughly +11–12% YoY” to reach that total.

surprises.description: ARR reached $65 million, above the preview’s estimated $62–63 million range and meaningfully ahead of the preview’s base-case range of $61.5–62.5 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Annual recurring revenue (ARR) increased from $57 million to $65 million year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ARR ~$62–63M (est., no formal consensus)” and base-case “ARR $61.5–62.5M.”

surprises.description: Bookings were much stronger than the preview’s expectation of flat to down 5% bookings: trailing 12-month units booked accelerated 40%, and quarterly bookings were 48,000. The quarter’s bookings mix leaned more toward lower-ARPU IoT solutions, tempering the quality of the acceleration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trailing 12-month units booked accelerated 40% to over 112,000 units,” while “quarterly bookings of 48,000 were more weighted toward lower-ARPU IoT solutions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “bookings flat to -5%” in its base case and highlighted Q1 bookings of “16,592, -9% YoY.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was positive for a third straight quarter, as expected, but at $0.7 million it came in below the preview’s estimated $1–2 million range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company posted its third consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA at $700,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$1–2M (est., no formal consensus).”

surprises.description: Professional services margin improved well beyond the preview’s recent breakeven reference, reaching positive 21% versus negative 44% a year earlier; total gross margin also expanded to 41%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total gross margin expanded 760 basis points to 41%, with professional services margin swinging dramatically to positive 21% from negative 44% a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said professional services had swung “from a -$3.4M loss to breakeven” in Q1 and noted that total gross margin had expanded to 39.1%.

surprises.description: SaaS revenue grew 13% and exceeded 40% of total revenue, while SaaS gross margin expanded to 75% from 70%. The preview did not set expectations for SaaS revenue mix or SaaS margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SaaS revenue grew 13% to $16 million and now represents more than 40% of total revenue, with SaaS gross margin expanding to 75% from 70%.”

surprises.description: Management described building a new data and analytics practice anchored by Databricks and Hexaware partnerships, a more concrete practice-building initiative than the preview’s discussion of those partnerships as strategic moves to monitor.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management is “building a new data and analytics practice (anchored by Databricks and Hexaware partnerships) to expand its addressable market and drive ARPU growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “the Hexaware AI-native customer-ops partnership” and “the Databricks analytics partnership,” and said to watch for “monetization commentary on recent strategic moves.”

in_line: Installed IoT footprint reached nearly 930,000 units, within the preview’s estimate of roughly 925,000–935,000; the expectation to reach 1 million units around Q1–Q2 FY2027 was also consistent with management’s target to surpass 1 million in the first half of next year.
Management’s expectation that second-half revenue, profitability, and cash flow will exceed the first half matched the preview’s expectation of an H2 recovery and stronger H2 than H1.
Renewal renegotiations are expected to add about $0.05 per unit per month, consistent with the preview’s cited renewal uplift of roughly $0.05 per unit per month.

surprises.description: A10 raised FY26 revenue growth guidance to 12%–14% from 10%–12% and EPS growth guidance to 14%–16% from 12%–14%. That exceeded the preview’s required revenue floor lift and its hoped-for move above 14% EPS growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management raised full-year 2026 revenue growth guidance to 12%-14% (from 10%-12%) and EPS growth guidance to 14%-16% (from 12%-14%).
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The market now needs the FY revenue growth floor lifted (to ~12%+) or the EPS growth range taken above 14%.”

surprises.description: A10 announced a significant multi-year expansion of its Microsoft relationship with mutual performance commitments and no prebuy requirements. The preview identified Microsoft as central to the AI opportunity and said investors needed evidence of a multi-year, repeat-deployment relationship, so this provided more concrete evidence than it had anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company announced a significant multi-year expansion of its Microsoft relationship with mutual performance commitments, but no prebuy requirements.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Listen for whether AI-related revenue is recurring deployment or a lumpy project”; the bull-case checklist called for “evidence the Microsoft work is a repeating deployment cadence” and specifically cited “multi-year.”

surprises.description: Product revenue reached $49 million, up approximately 25%, above the preview’s $44–46 million estimate and its roughly 14%+ growth threshold. The result was stronger than the preview’s expected product growth range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Product revenue grew approximately 25% year-over-year in Q2, reaching $49 million (61% of total), driven by security-led revenue and AI-related traffic demand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Product revenue: ~$44–46M (57–59% mix)” and “needs ~$45M+ / +14%+ to sustain the growth-reacceleration narrative.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $80.1 million, about 4% above the preview’s derived consensus of approximately $77 million. It was also around the preview’s estimated $79–80 million whisper range, so the beat was less striking against that higher bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A10 delivered Q2 2026 revenue of $80.1 million, up 15.5% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue **~$77M** (derived)” and “assume the functional whisper sits ~2–4% above the derived consensus (~$79–80M).”

surprises.description: Reported diluted EPS was $0.25, above the preview’s estimated GAAP EPS range of $0.15–$0.17. The preview separately estimated non-GAAP EPS at $0.24, so the comparison depends on the reported diluted figure being on the GAAP basis implied by its presentation alongside net income.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 diluted EPS was $0.25 (net income of $18.7 million), up from $0.21 in the year-ago period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GAAP EPS: ~$0.15–0.17”; the preview separately listed “Non-GAAP EPS: $0.24.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA margin was 30.5%, slightly above the preview’s expected 28%–30% range. This was a modest positive margin result even though gross margin landed within its expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA of $25.4 million (30.5% of revenue).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA margin: 28–30%” and “FY26 company target range.”

surprises.description: Enterprise customers made up 60% of Q2 revenue and about half of trailing-12-month revenue, indicating a broader customer mix than the preview’s highlighted concern about dependence on a few large AI infrastructure buildouts. The preview did not provide an expected enterprise share.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Enterprise customers represented 60% of Q2 revenue and about half of trailing-12-month revenue, reflecting balanced growth versus service providers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bear case explicitly cites ‘heavy dependence on a few large AI infrastructure buildouts.’”

in_line: Non-GAAP gross margin was 80.3%, within the preview’s 79%–81% expected range.
EMEA and Japan continued to face geopolitical and macroeconomic pressures, consistent with the preview’s expectation of continued regional weakness.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $8.3B, above the preview’s $7.8–8.0B whisper and even the $8.2B upper end of its bull case. The preview warned that a result merely near the guidance midpoint could disappoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 FY2026 revenue reached a record $8.3 billion, up 48% year-over-year and 17% sequentially, exceeding the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “the buy-side whisper is almost certainly above the $7.60B guidance ceiling — call it $7.8–8.0B revenue”; bull case: “$7.9–8.2B.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $2.28 exceeded the preview’s $1.90–2.00 whisper and the $2.15 upper end of its bull case. That was a substantially stronger result than the preview’s already elevated expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS hit a record $2.28” and “beat[] the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “the buy-side whisper is almost certainly above the $7.60B guidance ceiling — call it $7.8–8.0B revenue and $1.90–2.00 EPS”; bull case: “$2.00–2.15.”

surprises.description: Q1 FY2027 guidance was far above the preview’s expected range: revenue of $9.0–9.3B versus a bull-case threshold of $8.2B, and EPS of $2.80–2.90 versus the preview’s $2.10 upper-end bull-case threshold. Management also suggested December could exceed seasonal norms.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY2027 guidance projects revenue of $9.0-9.3 billion (implying ~10% sequential growth) and EPS of $2.80-2.90, with management indicating December could exceed seasonal norms.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 FY27 guided ≥$2.10 / ≥$8.2B” in the bull case; base case: “Q1 FY27 guided $1.90–2.10.”

surprises.description: Electronic Components margin reached 4.1%, well above the preview’s 3.6–3.7% base-case expectation and its 3.8% bull-case threshold. All three regions also grew by double digits both sequentially and year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Electronic Components operating margin reached 4.1% (a two-year high) with all three regions growing double digits both year-over-year and sequentially, led by 55% Americas growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base case: “EC margin 3.6–3.7%”; bull case: “EC op margin ≥3.8%.”

surprises.description: Farnell’s operating margin jumped to 9%, a much stronger improvement than the preview’s prior-quarter reference of 5.2% suggested, while the double-digit margin goal remains on track. The preview’s stated timing for that goal was 2H CY2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Farnell operating margin jumped nearly 400 basis points to 9%, a three-year high, and remains on track to reach double-digit margins before the end of 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Farnell $455M (+24% y/y), op margin 5.2% (3-yr high, 6th straight quarter of expansion; targeting double-digit by 2H CY2027).”

surprises.description: Working-capital efficiency was stronger than the preview’s expectation of pressure from rising component prices: inventory days fell to 71, below the cited sub-80 target, and return on working capital reached 19%, above the 16% near-term target stated on the call.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inventory days improved to 71 (lowest in nearly four years) and return on working capital reached 19%, exceeding the near-term 16% target.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Rising component prices mechanically inflate inventory dollars; expect FCF pressure”; the preview also noted inventory at “77 days (below the sub-80 target).”

surprises.description: Memory pricing accounted for a smaller share of sequential growth than the preview’s Q3 reference—about one-third versus about one-half—making the sequential growth mix less pricing-dependent. However, its share of year-over-year growth was higher than the preview’s Q3 reference of about one-quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately one-third of both sequential and year-over-year sales growth came from memory pricing increases.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Memory pricing drove ~half of sequential growth and ~one-quarter of y/y growth.”

in_line: Book-to-bill remained above 1 across all regions, consistent with the preview’s reference to book-to-bill above parity in all regions; management also described backlog as extending and providing FY2027 visibility.
Farnell remained on track for double-digit margins by the end of 2027, consistent with the preview’s stated 2H CY2027 target.

surprises.description: Blue Bird reported $517 million of Q3 revenue, above the preview’s $498.7 million consensus and its $505 million base case. The beat was notable even against the preview’s higher $505–515 million estimate of the effective buy-side bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 revenue of $517 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales: $498.7M”; “My estimates (base case): Revenue $505M”; and “assume the effective buy-side bar sits modestly above published consensus — call it $505–515M revenue.”

surprises.description: Q3 adjusted EBITDA of $71 million exceeded the preview’s $66–68 million derived range, including its $68 million base case. This was a meaningful quarterly beat, though the preview had anticipated a raise in full-year guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record Q3 adjusted EBITDA of $71 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA: ~$66–68M (derived*)”; “My estimates (base case): ... adj. EBITDA $68M.”

surprises.description: Unit sales fell 7% year over year, sharply below the preview’s estimate of 26–34% growth including Micro Bird. The company attributed the decline to GSA and fleet units held in finished goods inventory, with revenue recognition deferred to Q4 and fiscal 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Blue Bird's unit sales fell 7% year-over-year due to a large number of GSA and fleet units held in finished goods inventory that will be revenue-recognized in Q4 and fiscal 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Units sold: ~3,100–3,300 incl. Micro Bird (est.)”; “Implied YoY: +26–34%.” The preview noted that unit estimates were uncertain and Micro Bird’s mix could swing them.

surprises.description: Legacy Blue Bird’s margin was stronger than the preview’s expectation: the preview looked for core margins around 15%, while the reported ex-Micro Bird adjusted EBITDA margin was a record 16.1%. Consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin was 13.8%, also slightly above the preview’s estimated 13.3–13.6% range despite Micro Bird’s dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “[Micro Bird] compressing EBITDA margin to 13.8% from an ex-Micro Bird record of 16.1%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Core (ex-Micro Bird) Blue Bird margins held ~15%”; “Adj. EBITDA margin: ~13.3–13.6% (derived*).”

surprises.description: The combined backlog was about 4,900 units, above the preview’s expected Q3 range of roughly 3,400–3,700. However, about 1,300 units were Micro Bird backlog, so the reported total does not by itself establish a comparable increase in legacy Blue Bird demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Combined backlog stood at ~4,900 units (including ~1,300 Micro Bird and ~800 EVs).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base [scenario]: ... backlog ~3,400–3,700”; the preview also cited an exiting-Q2 backlog “just under 3,600 units.”

surprises.description: Micro Bird contributed about $123 million of revenue, above the preview’s rough assumption of about $100 million for the first consolidated quarter, but contributed $8 million of adjusted EBITDA and reduced reported gross margin by 180 basis points. The larger revenue contribution was a positive surprise, while the reported contribution also shows meaningful margin dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Micro Bird was consolidated for the first time, contributing ~$123 million in revenue and $8 million in adjusted EBITDA, but reducing reported gross margin by 180 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “That mechanically adds roughly $100M of quarterly revenue but only the incremental 50% of Micro Bird's EBITDA.”

surprises.description: Blue Bird announced an unanticipated Ford chassis business that expands its addressable market and carries substantial long-term targets. It will require about $90 million of investment in 2027, but the company said there would be no equity dilution and projected more than $100 million of longer-term adjusted EBITDA.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Expanded collaboration with Ford to design, manufacture and sell next-generation F-53/F-59 Class 5-6 commercial strip chassis, running through 2033 with extension potential to 2036”; “Detroit Chassis asset acquisition costs only $7 million, with total chassis market entry requiring a ~$90 million investment in 2027 (of which $50 million is CapEx), and no equity dilution”; “expands ... total addressable market by $1.4 billion, targeting ~10,000 units by 2030 and generating longer-term adjusted EBITDA of $100 million-plus at 14-15% margins.”

surprises.description: Adjusted free cash flow guidance rose to $125–135 million, above the preview’s $100–125 million full-year target. The preview had highlighted cash generation and capital allocation as watch items but did not anticipate this higher range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “[Full-year guidance] ... with adjusted free cash flow of $125-135 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Full-year FY2026 guidance ... adjusted FCF $100–125M.”

in_line: Full-year revenue guidance remained centered around $1.75 billion, consistent with the preview’s expected range; the company reported $1.74–1.76 billion versus the preview’s $1.725–1.775 billion.
The company raised full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to $245–250 million, a $247.5 million midpoint, broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of a modest raise toward $250 million.

Tariff management remained margin-neutral, as the preview expected: the reported roughly $10,000 year-over-year increase in average bus revenue per unit was attributed mainly to price increases, tariff recovery, and EV mix.

surprises.description: Vir recognized $238.9 million in license and collaboration revenue, well above the $135.88 million consensus and the preview’s $130–155 million base case. That was closer to the preview’s full-upfront-recognition bull scenario, although below its $255–265 million bull revenue range.
surprises.fact_evidence: Vir reported “$238.9 million in recognized license and collaboration revenue” and “net income of $80.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed consensus revenue of “$135.88M,” a base scenario of “$130–155M,” and a bull scenario of “$255–265M” if the full $240M was recognized point-in-time.

surprises.description: R&D expense came in substantially above the preview’s roughly $108 million estimate. The preview did not anticipate the $48 million Sanofi milestone or the specific hepatitis delta manufacturing costs driving the increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “R&D expense rose to $135.3 million from $97.5 million a year prior,” largely due to “a $48 million milestone payment to Sanofi” and hepatitis delta manufacturing costs.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “R&D ~$108M” and said the discipline test was “R&D holding ~$108M.”

surprises.description: The SOLSTICE update added favorable comparative results that the preview did not discuss: combination therapy substantially outperformed tobevibart monotherapy on undetectable virus and hepatitis B surface antigen levels, with ALT normalization despite many patients having cirrhosis. The preview already cited an 88% Week-96 subset result, so that figure itself was not new relative to the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: At 96 weeks, “88% of intention-to-treat patients on the Elapseron/Tobevibart combination achieved undetectable virus” versus “53% on tobevibart monotherapy”; roughly “90%” of combination patients had hepatitis B surface antigen below 10 IU/ml versus “only 25%” on antibody monotherapy, with “an ALT normalization rate of 53% despite ~50% of patients having cirrhosis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “77% HDV RNA target-not-detected at Week 72 (88% in the Week-96 subset),” but did not set expectations for these combination-versus-monotherapy or additional liver-marker results.

surprises.description: Vir reported that drug-substance PPQ manufacturing was complete for both lead hepatitis delta drugs and that the major manufacturing expenses were behind it. The preview anticipated substantial ongoing R&D spending but did not flag this manufacturing-cost milestone or the resulting forward cost relief.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Drug substance PPQ manufacturing is now complete for both Elapseron and Tobevibart,” drug-product PPQ batches are progressing, and “the major manufacturing expenses [are] now behind the company.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled “R&D ~$108M” and described three Phase 3 ECLIPSE trials plus oncology expansion as the “discipline test.”

surprises.description: The call described active searches for both a new CFO and a new CMO, broadening the leadership transition beyond the CFO vacancy the preview highlighted. The preview sought a permanent CFO-hire timeline, but the reported facts provide no hiring timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management was “actively interviewing for both a new CMO and CFO” during a CEO-cited management transition.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged the “Permanent CFO search” and asked for the “timeline for a permanent hire.”

surprises.description: Vir described VIR5500 as being dosed across monotherapy and several combination cohorts, with an ambition to start Phase 3 registration trials next year. The preview discussed the Astellas collaboration but did not mention this clinical expansion or a Phase 3 ambition.
surprises.fact_evidence: Vir is dosing VIR5500 patients across “three monotherapy and multiple combination cohorts (enzalutamide, docetaxel, darolutamide)” and has an “ambition to start Phase 3 registration trials next year.”

in_line: Cash and investments were approximately $1.01 billion, within the preview’s ~$1.00–1.02 billion estimate, and the projected runway into the second half of 2028 matched the preview’s expected runway language.
ECLIPSE 1 top-line data remained expected in Q4 2026, with ECLIPSE 2 and 3 readouts in Q1 2027, matching the preview’s flagged timeline.

surprises.description: Revenue was $105.4 billion, above the $104.25 billion consensus and the preview’s base-case range of $103–105 billion. That ran against the preview’s expectation that McKesson would probably miss revenue again.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY27 revenue grew 8% to $105.4 billion” and exceeded company expectations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $104.25B”; the preview also said McKesson would “probably miss on revenue again” and gave a base case of “$103–105B.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $9.93 exceeded the preview’s $9.46 Zacks and $9.59 broader-street estimates, and was above its $9.50–9.80 base case. The preview anticipated an EPS beat, but this result was closer to its bull-case threshold of $9.90 or more.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS rose 20% to $9.93,” exceeding company expectations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS $9.46 (Zacks) / $9.59 (broader street)”; base case “$9.50–9.80”; bull case “≥$9.90.”

surprises.description: Oncology and Multispecialty operating profit reached $405 million, well above the preview’s own $300–330 million model. The headline growth was partly acquisition-related: profit grew about 15% excluding Core Ventures, in line with the preview’s cited 13–16% long-term target for organic growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: Revenue rose 33% to $14.2 billion and operating profit rose 41% to $405 million; excluding Core Ventures, growth was about 24% for revenue and 15% for operating profit.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s modeled Q1 operating profit was “~$300–330M” and it flagged “organic vs. acquired split” as a key issue, citing a “13–16% long-term target.”

surprises.description: Medical-Surgical operating profit fell to $195 million, below the preview’s $230–250 million model and the $244 million prior-year figure the preview highlighted. The 20% decline was a sharper setback than the preview’s modeled level and its warning about a possible second consecutive decline suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: Medical-Surgical operating profit “decline[d] 20% to $195 million” on product mix and one-time costs.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled “~$230–250M,” noted Q1 FY26 operating profit of “$244M,” and warned that “a second consecutive profit decline” would undercut the separation narrative.

surprises.description: North American Pharmaceutical operating profit grew 19% and the full-year growth outlook moved to the high end of the 5.5–9.5% range, stronger than the preview’s concern that GLP-1 mix could dilute profitability. However, the reported $894 million was below the preview’s own $1.00–1.08 billion Q1 model, making the comparison mixed.
surprises.fact_evidence: Operating profit grew 19% to $894 million on 5% revenue growth, and full-year operating profit growth was guided to the high end of 5.5–9.5%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled Q1 operating profit of “~$1.00–1.08B” and asked whether “GLP-1 volumes (high-revenue, thin-margin) are diluting mix.”

surprises.description: GLP-1 distribution revenue reached $15 billion, up 24% year over year and 13% sequentially. That was a strong realized increase despite the preview’s warning about quarterly variability and potential headwinds, though the preview gave no numerical expectation to compare against.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GLP-1 medication distribution revenue reached $15 billion in the quarter, up approximately $3 billion or 24% year-over-year and 13% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “GLP-1 quarterly variability” and said management had identified GLP-1 quarterly variability as an FY27 headwind.

surprises.description: The quarter benefited from generics favorability and new-product launches arriving earlier than expected, with management saying those benefits would come at the expense of later quarters. This qualifies the strong Q1 result with an unanticipated pull-forward of benefit into the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management said Q1 benefited from “earlier-than-expected generics favorability and new product launch timing that will come at the expense of later quarters.”

surprises.description: McKesson said it would accelerate second-half investment in growth and AI, with returns expected to begin only in 2028. The preview did not flag this near-term investment timing or delayed return profile.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management flagged “accelerated second-half investments in growth and AI expected to yield returns starting in 2028.”

surprises.description: McKesson repurchased $2.5 billion of shares in Q1, including a $2.25 billion accelerated repurchase, and plans about $5 billion of buybacks for FY27. The preview flagged repurchase cadence as important but gave no expectation for a Q1 ASR of this size or a FY27 total.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company repurchased “$2.5 billion of shares in Q1 (including a $2.25 billion ASR at roughly $755 per share)” and plans “about $5 billion in total buybacks for FY27.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified “Free cash flow and buyback pace” as a key metric and noted FY26 repurchases of $4.8 billion, but did not project FY27 buybacks.

surprises.description: The Board approved a 15% dividend increase, the company’s tenth consecutive annual raise. The preview did not identify a dividend increase as an expected event.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Board approved a 15% dividend increase marking the tenth consecutive annual raise.”

in_line: McKesson raised FY27 adjusted EPS guidance to $44.20–45.00, matching the preview’s stated bull-case range of approximately $44.20–45.00.

Q1 free cash flow was negative, as the preview cautioned was normal for the seasonally weakest quarter; the reported negative $372 million was also better than roughly negative $1 billion a year earlier.
Total adjusted operating profit of $1.7 billion was within the preview’s modeled $1.69–1.75 billion range.
Oncology and Multispecialty operating profit growth excluding Core Ventures was about 15%, within the 13–16% long-term organic-growth range cited in the preview.

surprises.description: The Apple renewal completed alignment with all major DSP partners on contractual per-subscriber minimum increases, covering 88% of subscription streaming revenue; the preview focused on premium-tier opportunities but did not anticipate this contract-floor coverage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The renewed Apple deal completes alignment across all major DSP partners on contractual per-subscriber-minimum increases, now covering 88% of subscription streaming revenue versus 0% two years ago.”

surprises.description: Management said Q3 ad-supported streaming growth got a boost from non-recurring World Cup advertising and is expected to normalize to mid-single-digit growth in Q4. The preview highlighted Q3 ad-supported growth but did not flag this one-off driver or give a Q4 growth expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ad-supported streaming grew 10% on an adjusted basis, boosted by non-recurring World Cup ad spending, and is expected to normalize to mid-single-digit growth in Q4.”

surprises.description: Management described a path to mid-20s margins in the short term and high-20s in the long term, adding a longer-range margin outlook beyond the preview’s focus on the FY26 expansion target and the cost program.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 2025 restructuring plan is on track to deliver $200 million in savings this year and $300 million on an annualized basis in 2027, supporting a path toward mid-20s margins short-term and high-20s long-term.”

surprises.description: The call reported 100 basis points of Q3 margin expansion, slightly below the preview’s 110-basis-point figure calculated from the preliminary margin estimates. The difference is small and may reflect rounding.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted OIBDA rising 15% and delivering 100 basis points of margin expansion in Q3 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. OIBDA margin: 23.2% (vs. 22.1% LY) | +110bps.”

in_line: The headline results largely confirmed the pre-release: revenue growth was 9% on the basis cited in the call versus 9% constant-currency growth in the preview, and adjusted OIBDA growth was 15% versus the preview’s 15% constant-currency figure.

Recorded music subscription streaming growth was broadly in line with the preview’s reported growth rate: the call cited 12% adjusted growth, while the preview cited 11% constant-currency growth. Management’s FY27 timing for material AI-licensing contributions also matched the preview’s expectation; the call added that Suno is to transition to a license model later this year, without quantifying the contribution.

Management reaffirmed the FY26 targets and the high end of the 150–200-basis-point margin-expansion target, as the preview was watching for. It also said operating cash flow conversion was 55% over nine months, within the preview’s stated 50–60% target range.

The CFO succession update was consistent with the preview: Lou Dickler is acting CFO during the search, and Tom Corson takes the COO role. The preview had already described Zerza’s departure and Corson’s transition to COO.

The restructuring savings plan was reported on track, consistent with the preview’s description of the $300 million cost program. The Beethoven JV’s $650 million of deployed capacity and target returns of roughly 20% also fit the preview’s expectation of continued catalog acquisitions and its focus on capital allocation.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was positive at $0.5 million, well above the preview’s near-breakeven-to-$0.5 million loss consensus and the buy-side bar of breakeven or better. That is a stronger result than expected, even though the preview noted the company had pre-announced results at or above its earlier guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA of $0.5 million exceeded expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: ~breakeven to -$0.5M”; the “Effective buy-side bar” was “Adjusted EBITDA at breakeven or better.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin came in above the preview’s 47–48% estimate, rather than merely holding around that range despite aluminum and fuel pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin was 48.9% in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin: ~47–48% (est.).”

surprises.description: The new CEO identified singles as a substantial untapped opportunity: Zevia has essentially no share in singles despite 20% share in multi-pack soda. The preview anticipated strategic commentary but did not flag this specific opportunity or quantify it.
surprises.fact_evidence: The CEO called singles the “top priority,” estimating an “~$80 million opportunity” given Zevia’s 20% multi-pack share and essentially zero singles share.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for Ruberti’s “route-to-market/DSD changes, SKU rationalization, marketing model, and any FY27 framing,” but did not identify a singles opportunity.

surprises.description: Management quantified an additional $3–5 million of cost savings beginning in Q1 2027, beyond the $20 million already removed. The preview raised the possibility of restructuring or a strategic reset but did not anticipate this specific savings target and timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management is “on track to achieve $3-5 million in additional cost savings,” primarily in COGS and selling expenses, “beginning in Q1 2027,” on top of $20 million already removed.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted elevated odds of “a guidance reset, restructuring, or spending-reinvestment announcement” and said to watch for FY27 framing; it gave no quantified savings expectation.

surprises.description: Management reaffirmed the full-year sales and EBITDA ranges instead of raising them, despite the preview’s view that a sales increase was the highest-probability bullish catalyst after strong first-half growth. The unchanged guide was also the preview’s base case, so the shortfall is relative to the anticipated upside case rather than a clear miss against the stated range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company maintained full-year 2026 net sales guidance of $170-175 million” and adjusted EBITDA guidance of “negative $2 million to negative $4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A raise is the highest-probability bullish catalyst”; “a failure to raise after a pre-announced strong Q2 will read as caution on H2 velocity.”

surprises.description: The outlook put Q3 gross margin at approximately 46%, below the preview’s 46.5% concern threshold and weaker than its expectation of only “slight pressure” in the back half. Management attributed the decline to aluminum costs, deeper promotions, and higher marketing spend.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin was 48.9% in Q2 but is expected to fall to approximately 46% in Q3,” with full-year results absorbing about $11 million in fuel and aluminum cost pressures.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “slight pressure” in the back half and said “Below ~46.5%” would be concerning for the EBITDA path.

surprises.description: Management announced a Cardi B co-developed signature product for early January 2027 as part of a full-funnel marketing strategy. The preview asked whether the campaign was converting to sales but did not anticipate this specific product launch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to launch a new Cardi B co-developed signature product in early January 2027 as part of a full-funnel marketing strategy.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked for a read on “the Cardi B campaign converting to sales rather than impressions,” but did not mention a co-developed product launch.

in_line: Q2 net sales were $45 million at the high end of the previously announced range, consistent with the preview’s roughly $45 million expectation.
First-half sales growth of 10.4% and $91.1 million in sales matched the preview’s first-half estimate.
The roughly $11 million combined fuel and aluminum cost pressure was already embedded in the preview’s description of the full-year outlook.

The Q3 adjusted EBITDA loss guidance of $3 million to $3.5 million was consistent with the preview’s implied $2.4 million to $4.4 million second-half EBITDA loss and its expectation that promotions and marketing spending would weigh on Q3.
Management’s expectation of no further price increases this year was consistent with the preview’s statement that no additional price increases were planned.

surprises.description: Alto reported adjusted EBITDA of $23.7 million, above the preview’s derived $17–18 million bar by roughly $6–7 million. The preview expected a seasonal improvement, but the reported result was a substantially larger step-up than its central estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA improved by $23.9 million year-over-year to $23.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA (my derived bar): ~$17–18M”; the base case was “$16–18M.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $246 million, above the preview’s roughly $233 million consensus midpoint by about $13 million. The preview’s bull case was $245 million, but its base case was materially lower.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated net sales rose $27 million to $246 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales: $231.2M – $235.9M (~$233M mid)”; the scenario table’s bull case was $245M.

surprises.description: GAAP EPS came in at $0.15, well above the $0.08 consensus estimate. The preview cautioned that EPS was a wide-band estimate, but the reported result still exceeded its point estimate by $0.07.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net income attributable to common stockholders was $11.4 million ($0.15 per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (GAAP): $0.08”; the preview said to “treat the EPS point estimate as a wide band, not a line in the sand.”

surprises.description: The preview expected roughly $3.5–4.5 million of Q2 45Z recognition, while the call attributed $5.1 million of Q2 adjusted EBITDA improvement to 45Z tax credit earnings. That is above the preview’s expected quarterly range, even though the annual framework itself was not raised.
surprises.fact_evidence: Adjusted EBITDA improvement was driven partly by “$5.1 million in 45Z tax credit earnings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “~$3.5–4.5M recognized in Q2.”

surprises.description: Export volumes declined, whereas the preview’s base case assumed export premiums held and its bottom-line framing pointed to healthy export demand. Alto said freight disruptions and Brazil’s stronger competitiveness into Europe contributed to the decline; it redirected production toward higher-margin domestic fuel-grade ethanol.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Renewable fuel export volumes declined due to Middle East geopolitical disruptions raising freight costs and boosting Brazil's competitiveness into Europe,” with production redirected toward “higher-margin domestic fuel-grade ethanol.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “healthy export demand” and its base case assumed “export premiums held”; it did flag Brazilian competition as a risk to watch.

surprises.description: Alto established a new $50 million at-the-market equity program, a potential source of shareholder dilution that the preview did not mention. The facts do not state that shares have already been sold under the program.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company established a new $50 million at-the-market equity program.”

surprises.description: The company reported $28.5 million of operating cash flow and ended with $24 million of cash and $106 million of borrowing availability—better liquidity figures than the preview’s reference points of cash above $20 million and $94 million of availability.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company generated $28.5 million in operating cash flow during Q2 and ended with a $24 million cash balance and $106 million in total borrowing availability.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “cash $20M, $94M availability” and flagged cash “above $20M” as a balance-sheet checkpoint.

surprises.description: Alto disclosed that it is executing more than $10 million of high-return capital projects with average paybacks of just over one year. The preview expected the FY26 capex budget to track to plan but did not anticipate these project-return details.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ... is executing over $10 million of high-return capital projects with average paybacks of just over one year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview anticipated “the $25M FY26 capex budget tracking on plan.”

in_line: The 45Z annual framework remained broadly as expected: Alto was still on track to qualify 90 million or more gallons and expected at least $15–16 million of net income after monetization costs; the preview expected about 90 million gallons and roughly $15 million annually.

The Pekin debottlenecking project’s roughly 8% (5 million gallon) capacity increase, with full benefit expected in Q4 2026, matched the preview’s expectation of a Q4 benefit from the completed project.
The preview expected continued deleveraging and a term-loan balance below $38.4 million; Alto reported an $8.5 million Q2 paydown and $29.9 million of outstanding term debt.

surprises.description: BBSI reported $0.52 per diluted share, below the preview’s $0.56 consensus and its own roughly $0.53 estimate. The shortfall was small, and the lower year-over-year result was largely anticipated because favorable workers’ comp adjustments were much smaller than a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net income fell to $0.52 per diluted share,” with favorable workers’ comp adjustments of “$2 million versus $8.8 million in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS Consensus $0.56”; “I model ~3c below consensus”; “Diluted EPS ~$0.53.”

surprises.description: Gross billings grew 2.6%, below the preview’s modeled 3.5% growth and $2.31 billion. The gap was modest, but the quarter’s billings growth came in weaker than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross billings rose 2.6% year-over-year to $2.29 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross billings … $2.31B (+3.5%).”

surprises.description: Staffing revenue fell 18%, rather than improving to the 14% decline the preview modeled. Although staffing is a small part of the business, the decline was worse than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Staffing revenue declined 18% to $14 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “PEO / Staffing … ~$305M / ~$15M”; “Staffing −14% (improving from −21%).”

surprises.description: Total PEO worksite-employee growth was only 1%, below the preview’s roughly 1.5% estimate, as client workforce reductions resumed. That is a weaker hiring trend than the preview’s expectation that client hiring reluctance would moderate in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total PEO worksite employees grew only 1% as strong controllable growth of ~4,500 net new client WSEs was offset by client workforce reductions that resumed in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Avg WSEs … ~141,000 (+1.5%)”; “Management said client hiring reluctance should moderate in 2H.”

surprises.description: Management cut the full-year ranges instead of reaffirming them: billings growth, average WSE growth, and gross margin all have lower upper bounds. This is a broader and more cautious outlook than the preview’s base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management narrowed full-year guidance, cutting gross billings growth to 3%-4% (from 3%-5%), average WSE growth to 2%-3% (from 2%-4%), and gross margin to 2.7%-2.75% (from 2.7%-2.85%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management FY2026 guidance (reaffirmed at Q1)”; the preview’s base case was “guide reaffirmed unchanged.”

surprises.description: Workers’ comp pricing momentum had continued longer than the preview reported: eight consecutive months of price increases rather than the five months cited before the release. Management also said the increases are more than offsetting rising claim costs, strengthening the favorable pricing picture.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Eight consecutive months of workers’ comp price increases—its first in a decade—which are more than offsetting rising claim costs,” supported by an “8.7% 2025 rate increase” and a “6.6% increase effective September 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Five consecutive months of rate increases”; “Commissioner Lara adopted a +6.6% CA pure premium rate … effective Sept 1, 2026.”

in_line: The smaller favorable workers’ comp reserve adjustments explain much of the year-over-year EPS decline, as the preview had emphasized that Q2 2025 included $8.8 million of favorable development and that the headline comparison would be optical.

Management’s view that 2026 is the gross-margin low point, with improvement expected in 2027 as California rate increases compound, is consistent with the preview’s expectation that the pricing benefit would land mainly in 2027.
The East Coast’s continued double-digit growth was consistent with the preview’s report of 20 consecutive quarters of double-digit growth in Q1.

Benefits retention remained at 97%, consistent with the preview’s 97% renewal figure, and the expected medical-cost pressure remained present: the preview had flagged health-premium inflation and benefits economics as a key debate.

New-client acquisition and asset-light market growth remained strong, consistent with the preview’s solid-sales-execution base case and its asset-light growth thesis; the preview also anticipated three additional branch conversions in 2026.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $83.3 million, about 7% above the preview's $77.83 million consensus, and organic growth of 6.7% exceeded the roughly 4.3% implied expectation. The reported year-over-year decline was also milder than the preview's implied 16.8% decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 reported revenue was $83.3 million, down 10.9% year-over-year due to strategic exits and diaper declines, but organic revenue grew 6.7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $77.83M”; “Revenue (organic basis) ... ~+4.3% organic.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was far above the preview's estimated $5.5–6.5 million, reaching $14.5 million including one-time items. The call also reported an all-time-high underlying adjusted EBITDA margin of 9.8%, so the result was not only a one-off headline comparison, though the full $14.5 million includes one-time items.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was $14.5 million (17.3% margin including one-time items)”; “all-time-high underlying adjusted EBITDA margin of 9.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$5.5–6.5M (no published consensus).”

surprises.description: Management raised the full-year adjusted EBITDA range to $23–25 million from $20–23 million, whereas the preview's base case expected the existing range to be reaffirmed and identified a possible trim as a risk. The new range is a clear upgrade rather than the uncertain back-half ramp the preview focused on.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year guidance: ... adjusted EBITDA to $23-25 million (from $20-23 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance treatment. Reaffirm at $20–23M, narrow, or trim?”

surprises.description: Underlying adjusted gross margin reached 43.8%, above the preview's 42–43% estimate and above its 43% catalyst threshold. That improvement came despite the call's disclosure that apparel liquidation diluted reported gross margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Underlying adjusted gross margin of 43.8% (up ~340 bps).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. gross margin ~42–43% (no formal consensus)”; “Adjusted gross margin ≥ 43%.”

surprises.description: The company raised its full-year organic revenue growth outlook to 5–7% from 4–6%, rather than merely reaffirming the prior range as the preview's base case anticipated. The upgrade moves the low end above the old low end and the high end above the old high end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year guidance: organic revenue growth to 5-7% (from 4-6%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base ... FY guidance reaffirmed unchanged”; the preview identified raising the low end as a bull-case outcome.

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted gross margin guidance rose to the mid-40s from the low-40s, an upgrade beyond the preview's expectation that management would reaffirm guidance and its concern that the full-year guide implied sequential margin decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year guidance: ... adjusted gross margin to mid-40s (from low-40s).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY guide is only ‘low 40%s’”; the base scenario expected “FY guidance reaffirmed unchanged.”

surprises.description: Reported gross margin was 48.4%, with an unexpected $6.6 million tariff refund contributing to the result; the preview discussed tariffs beginning to lap but did not anticipate a refund. Management said it plans to aggressively reinvest the refund into growth, while the underlying adjusted margin was 43.8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reported gross margin of 48.4% included a one-time $6.6 million tariff refund and dilution from apparel liquidation, which management plans to aggressively reinvest into growth.”

surprises.description: The call reported $35.3 million of free cash flow and $105.9 million of cash, while the preview cited $90.4 million of cash at Q1 but did not provide a Q2 cash-flow expectation. The strong cash generation and higher cash balance were therefore not part of the preview's quantified setup.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Generated $35.3 million in free cash flow (versus negative $3.8 million prior year)”; “ended the quarter with $105.9 million in cash and zero debt.”

surprises.description: Nearly two-thirds of the quarter's household-penetration growth came from households with no children, a source of demand the preview did not identify. This adds evidence that household expansion is not limited to families with children.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Overall household penetration reached 8.1%, up 100 basis points year-over-year, with nearly two-thirds of that growth coming from households with no children.”

in_line: Total wipes consumption grew 26%, broadly in line with the preview's +25% expectation; flushable wipes were up over 200%, close to the preview's +208% figure.
Household penetration was 8.1%, matching the preview's cited Q1 level of 8.1%.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue totaled about $31.4 million, above the preview’s roughly $30.7 million consensus; both ClearanceJobs revenue ($15.6 million) and Dice revenue ($15.8 million) were slightly above their respective estimates. The overall beat was modest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ClearanceJobs revenue grew 14% to $15.6 million” and “Dice revenue declined 14% year-over-year to $15.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue” consensus “~$30.7M”; ClearanceJobs consensus “~$15.5M” and Dice consensus “~$15.5M.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS was $0.09, above the preview’s $0.05 published consensus and also above its estimated effective bar of $0.07–$0.08. That is a clearer beat than the revenue result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS rose to $0.09 from $0.07.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview lists Q2 consensus EPS of “$0.05” and says the effective bar is “roughly $0.07–0.08 non-GAAP EPS.”

surprises.description: Management said Dice bookings are not expected to return to growth in 2026, pushing against the preview’s late-2026 Dice inflection thesis and its scenario in which revenue growth resumes in Q4. The Q2 bookings decline itself was within the preview’s base-case range, but the full-year timing commentary was more cautious.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management does not anticipate Dice bookings returning to growth in 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview describes a “late-2026 inflection” and its bull case says management would expect “Dice revenue growth to resume in Q4.”

surprises.description: ClearanceJobs’ retention rate rose to 110%, better than the preview’s expected 105%, although its 87% renewal rate was slightly below the preview’s 88%. The overall retention result was stronger than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CJ's revenue retention rate reached 110% (renewal rate 87%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “CJ revenue renewal rate fell to 88% from 92%, CJ retention to 105% from 106%.”

surprises.description: Dice’s retention and renewal measures weakened more than the preview anticipated: retention was 98% versus an expected 100%, and renewal was 66% versus an expected 71%. The reported churn was concentrated among smaller customers.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Dice's retention rate was 98% with a weaker 66% renewal rate due to churn among smaller customers”; sub-$15,000 accounts represented “80% of the customer count churn.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Dice improved (renewal 71% vs 70%; retention 100% vs 92%).”

surprises.description: ClearanceJobs’ new-business sales rose about 75% year over year and its pipeline reached a more-than-five-year high, stronger forward indicators than the preview had identified. The preview discussed CJ bookings growth, but did not anticipate these sales and pipeline figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New business sales at ClearanceJobs increased approximately 75% versus the prior-year quarter, with the sales pipeline reaching its highest level in over 5 years.”

surprises.description: ClearanceJobs’ margin came in at 39%, below the preview’s 40% FY guide and the level it highlighted as the key benchmark. The company attributed some of the compression to PSG labor costs.
