surprises.expectation_evidence: “$104M of the $110M target already realized; integration ‘substantially complete.’”

surprises.description: International AUM through the Amundi partnership was $62.6 billion, above the preview’s cited $55 billion scale, and management said the partnership was trending above its initial financial expectations. The preview already noted that the partnership had been net-flow positive since the Pioneer close.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International AUM reached $62.6 billion across 61 countries via the Amundi partnership, which management said is trending above initial financial expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The Amundi distribution partnership, now $55B AUM across 60 countries and net-flow positive since close.”

surprises.description: A Term Loan B repricing cut annual interest expense by about $2.5 million, a modest financing benefit not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A Term Loan B repricing that cut annual interest expense by ~$2.5 million.”

in_line: The normalized forward fee-rate range of 46–47 basis points matched the long-term range the preview said management had guided to, even though the Q2 realized rate was higher.
Management said Amundi-related flows had been cumulatively net-flow positive since the Pioneer close, consistent with the preview’s description of the partnership as net-flow positive since close.

Management continued to emphasize inorganic growth and described an active acquisition opportunity set, consistent with the preview’s expectation of an extensive pipeline and its focus on post-Janus M&A commentary; no specific deal was reported.
Quarter-end client assets of about $346 billion were broadly in line with the preview’s already-disclosed June figure of $346.1 billion.

surprises.description: The preview expected linear advertising to decline about 21%, with the NBA lapse accounting for roughly a 20% drag. WBD reported a decline of nearly 30%, and management said international ad markets weakened further in Q2 versus Q1 amid consumer caution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Linear advertising revenue declined nearly 30%, driven largely by the loss of the NBA, with international ad markets weakening further in Q2 versus Q1 amid consumer caution.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “total ad revenue forecast down ~21%”; “The NBA rights lapse is now a ~20% drag on advertising.”

surprises.description: The preview anticipated that the related-party distribution deal would make streaming distribution growth harder to read in Q2, with the full benefit landing in Q3. Management said growth excluding that deal would have been in the low teens and guided to teens-level growth for the rest of the year, indicating a stronger underlying and forward trend than that framing suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding a previously disclosed related-party deal, streaming distribution revenue growth would have been in the low teens, with management guiding to teens-level growth for the remainder of the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “laps related-party distribution deal (full benefit lands Q3)”

surprises.description: The preview expected a weak Studios quarter because of the tough comparison and slate miss, but management said the film business underperformed expectations this year. The call facts do not give a result or quantify how far it fell short of the preview’s $300–400 million Studios EBITDA estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The studio segment underperformed expectations in the film business this year against a tough Q2 2025 comp.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Studios” Q2’26E EBITDA “$300–400M”; “Brutal comp; slate miss.”

surprises.description: Management said the studio segment had fallen short of its over-$3 billion adjusted EBITDA goal even in a strong 2025, a negative qualification to the long-term target that the preview did not report. Management nevertheless maintained the goal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management maintained its long-term goal of over $3 billion in adjusted EBITDA for the studio segment, acknowledging it fell short of that target even in a strong 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The $3B annual Studios EBITDA target reaffirmed on the Q1 call is now the pressure point.”

surprises.description: Management offered a more upbeat streaming retention outlook, expecting 2026 to be its best year ever for retention and lowest for churn, supported by expanding bundles including Disney in the U.S. The preview focused on subscriber growth and the year-end target but did not flag this retention outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects 2026 to be its best year ever for streaming retention and lowest churn, driven by expanding distributor and programmer bundles such as the Disney partnership in the U.S.”

surprises.description: Management described a substantial planned increase in film production—from 14 films this year to 19 in 2027—and named a richer slate of tentpole IP. The preview focused on the current-year slate miss and did not anticipate this production ramp or slate detail.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Film production is ramping from 14 films this year to 19 films in 2027, with a richer slate of tentpole IP including Lord of the Rings, Batman, Superman, and Minecraft II.”

surprises.description: Management highlighted the scale and durability of library and licensing revenue: roughly $5 billion annually with healthy demand even for decade-old shows. The preview noted that large licensing deals had helped the prior-year comparison, but did not describe this recurring business or its continued demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The library and content licensing business generates roughly $5 billion in high-margin revenue annually, with healthy demand even for decade-old shows.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2’25 delivered … large content licensing deals.”

in_line: Streaming revenue exceeded $3 billion, within the preview’s $3.00–$3.10 billion estimate; streaming adjusted EBITDA of $512 million was within its $450–$550 million estimate.
Management declined to take questions on the Paramount Skydance transaction, matching the preview’s expectation that it would maintain the same disclosure posture as on the Q1 call.

surprises.description: The preview set a bar of at least 8% growth for digital advertising, with programmatic growth above 20%; Q2 growth came in at 11% and programmatic accelerated to 27%. Management also expects Q3 digital advertising growth to exceed Q2's 11%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Digital Advertising revenue grew 11% year-over-year in Q2, accelerating from 6.8% in Q1, with programmatic (now ~70% of digital ad revenue) up 27%; management expects Q3 digital advertising growth to be even stronger than 11%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bar: ≥8% Y/Y”; Q1 programmatic was “+21%” and management said Q2 growth would be “higher than Q1's,” with programmatic “over 20%.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag a material FCC license impairment; the company recorded $26.6 million of non-cash charges in Q2, contributing to a $41.8 million net loss. The reported adjusted EPS was positive, but the impairment created a much larger GAAP loss than the preview's adjusted-EPS framing addressed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-cash FCC license impairment charges of $26.6 million in Q2 ($35.2 million year-to-date), driving a Q2 net loss of $41.8 million ($2.36 per diluted share).”

surprises.description: The preview did not identify a media-partnership revenue ramp of this scale. Management now expects revenue to more than double from about $6 million in 2025 to over $12 million in 2026, with a four-year target of $50 million in revenue and a 20% profit margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The media partnership business expects revenue to more than double from ~$6 million in 2025 to over $12 million in 2026, targeting $50 million in revenue at a 20% profit margin ($10 million profit) within four years.”

surprises.description: Townsquare reported its first technology licensing deal, a new recurring-revenue opportunity that the preview did not discuss. SummitMedia is adopting the in-house Blueprint CRM, which management says also deepens partner integration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Townsquare completed its first technology licensing deal, with SummitMedia adopting its in-house 'Blueprint' CRM, creating a new recurring revenue stream and deeper partner integration.”

surprises.description: The preview said Interactive's margin staying above 33% mattered less than the revenue trajectory; instead, the margin reached a record 37.6%, up from about 33% a year earlier. That was a stronger margin outcome than the preview's stated benchmark.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Townsquare Interactive segment profit margin rose to a record 37.6% (up from ~33% in Q2 2025).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Margin holding above 33% matters less than the trajectory.”

surprises.description: The preview expected adjusted EPS of $0.19, while adjusted EPS was $0.21. This was a modest beat of the limited analyst consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was $0.21 versus $0.22 a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (adjusted) — $0.19.”

surprises.description: The preview's base case expected broadcast revenue to decline about 6% excluding political, whereas the reported ex-political decline was 7.2%. Although that was an improvement on 2025's roughly 8% declines, it was weaker than the preview's near-term expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Broadcast revenue declined 5.5% (7.2% ex-political), an improvement from the consistent 8% ex-political declines throughout 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “broadcast ~–6% ex-political.”

surprises.description: The preview looked for Townsquare Interactive's margin recovery into the mid-to-high 20s from Q1's seasonal level; Q2 segment margins were 30%, above that range. Management expects margins to moderate to the high 20s for the rest of the year, broadly matching the preview's forward expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Segment margins of 30% expected to moderate to high-20s for the remainder of the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch whether segment margin “recovered to the promised mid-to-high 20s from Q1's seasonal ~19%.”

surprises.description: The preview noted that Interactive's sales force was about 40% below peak but did not specify that it would take until 2027 to rebuild to target levels. That timeline adds a constraint on how quickly the business can scale its recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The sales force remains 40% below peak and won't be rebuilt to target levels until 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that “Sales headcount is still ~40% below peak” and said to listen for hiring pace, but gave no timeline for rebuilding to target.

surprises.description: The preview did not discuss the company's tax-loss carryforwards or expected cash-tax timing. Management said Townsquare does not expect to be a material cash taxpayer until roughly the end of 2028, which is favorable for near-term cash retention.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company does not expect to be a material cash taxpayer until roughly end of 2028 given ~$121 million of federal NOLs.”

in_line: Q2 net revenue of $115.4 million and adjusted EBITDA of $24.8 million were within the $114–116 million and $24–25 million guidance ranges, respectively; both were above their range midpoints.

Interactive revenue of $17.2 million was consistent with the preview's expected roughly $17.1–17.2 million and approximately 2% sequential decline. Management's expectation of month-over-month growth by year-end, potentially as early as Q3, broadly matched the preview's anticipated Q3 inflection.
Net leverage of 5.44x was close to the preview's estimate of leverage rising toward approximately 5.4x.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $235.5M, below the preview’s $237.9M consensus and at the low end of company guidance. The company attributed the late-quarter softness to the final two weeks of June, which had been unexpectedly weak.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $235.5 million,” landing “at the low end after unexpected softness in the final two weeks of June.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net revenue: $237.9M” consensus; the preview also said revenue consensus sat “at the very top of company guidance.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA of $32.9M was well above the preview’s roughly $28–29M expectation, but the reported result included an $11.8M tariff-refund benefit. That benefit more than explains the headline gap, while roughly $6M of incremental pre-launch investment partly offset it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $32.9 million (14% margin),” including “an $11.8 million tariff refund benefit that offset roughly $6 million of incremental pre-launch investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: ~$28–29M (implied)” and “Adj. EBITDA margin: ~12.0%.”

surprises.description: Active-customer growth was weaker than the preview’s demand-watch threshold: trailing-12-month growth was 4.1%, with management citing soft traffic. Management pointed to a Q4 rebound, but the reported growth rate confirms the near-term customer-acquisition weakness the preview identified as a bear case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trailing-12-month active customer growth was only 4.1%” and management “flag[ged] soft traffic,” while “pointing to a Q4 rebound in active customer growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Anything with a 4-handle or below on growth confirms the market's core bear case”; the preview also said to watch for “2.72–2.76M” active customers.

surprises.description: The company disclosed that it will reinvest all $14.4M of tariff refunds recognized this year rather than allow the proceeds to flow through to the bottom line. The preview discussed tariff-related margin relief but did not anticipate this specific use of the refund proceeds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is recognizing a total $14.4 million tariff refund this year and plans to reinvest all proceeds back into the business rather than let it flow to the bottom line.”

surprises.description: Warby Parker said about half of its existing customers are still unaware it offers eye exams, a potential awareness barrier not raised in the preview. Exams already account for about 7% of revenue and management sees 15–20% long-term potential, so the disclosure also highlights room to grow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Eye exams grew over 30% year-over-year to ~7% of revenue,” with “long-term potential of 15-20%,” though “roughly 50% of existing customers are still unaware Warby Parker offers exams.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “eye exams +30% Y/Y” and insurance penetration as an “ARPC engine,” but did not mention customer awareness.

surprises.description: Insurance-related reach and usage included a new milestone: covered lives rose to more than 35 million, and out-of-network claim-submission penetration surpassed in-network penetration. The preview noted the chain-wide out-of-network tool, but not that its penetration had overtaken in-network.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In-network insurance lives grew to over 35 million (up from 32M last quarter) with penetration reaching ~8%, while out-of-network claim submission penetration has now surpassed in-network, both driving higher average order values.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “an out-of-network submission tool rolled out chain-wide in March” and described insured customers as carrying “higher AOV and frequency.”

in_line: Full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance was reaffirmed, matching the preview’s stated base case and published guidance ranges.
Eye-exam growth was over 30% year over year, consistent with the preview’s expectation of about 30% growth.

Intelligent Eyewear remains scheduled for a fall launch with holiday-season deliveries on track, and its revenue remains excluded from full-year guidance, consistent with the preview’s fall-launch and no-revenue-in-guidance setup.

surprises.description: Axcelis raised its FY2026 outlook from approximately flat revenue to mid-single-digit year-over-year growth, a stronger outlook than the preview’s flat-revenue framing and roughly flat consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management raised full-year 2026 guidance to approximately mid-single-digit year-over-year revenue growth, up from the prior expectation of flat revenue versus 2025.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management has explicitly guided FY26 “approximately flat vs. 2025”; FY26 revenue consensus was $843.9M (+0.6%).

surprises.description: Q3 revenue guidance of approximately $230 million is well above the preview’s $215 million threshold and above the $220 million level it said would validate the H2 ramp. Q3 EPS guidance of about $1.11 is close to the preview’s implied H2 quarterly pace of roughly $1.10.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q3 2026 guidance calls for revenue of approximately $230 million and EPS of approximately $1.11.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q3 revenue “needs to be ≥$215M”; “$220M+ validates it outright.” The preview’s implied H2 EPS was “~$1.10/qtr.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue and EPS both beat the preview’s consensus estimates: revenue was about 5% above the $203.4–$205.0 million range, while EPS was about 19% above the $0.89–$0.894 range.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 2026 revenue was $215 million with EPS of $1.06, both exceeding company expectations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus revenue was “$203.4M – $205.0M” and non-GAAP EPS was “$0.89 – $0.894.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin came in slightly below the approximately 43% outlook rather than meeting it, with management attributing the shortfall to CS&I mix and higher-than-anticipated services costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 gross margin was 42.7%, slightly below the 43% outlook, due to unfavorable CS&I mix and higher-than-anticipated services costs.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 guided to “~43%”; the preview said “Delivering 43%+ is table stakes.”

surprises.description: Bookings were $131 million, well below the preview’s $180 million level it said was realistically needed to support the H2 ramp. However, the reported book-to-bill of approximately 1x meets the preview’s stated 0.9 threshold, and backlog was nearly unchanged from $453 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: Bookings were $131 million with a book-to-bill ratio of approximately 1x, and total backlog exited the quarter at $452 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 bookings realistically need to be $180M+ (book-to-bill ≥0.9).” The preview also flagged a second sub-0.7 quarter and backlog eroding toward ~$400M as a concern.

surprises.description: China’s share of revenue rose to 46%, up from 40% in the prior quarter and above the preview’s 40% reference point, increasing the company’s already elevated geographic concentration.
surprises.fact_evidence: China revenue rose to 46% of total (up from 40% prior quarter).
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed China at “40% of Q1 revenue” and flagged the elevated mix as an export-control overhang to watch.

surprises.description: Silicon carbide bookings showed concrete strength: first-half bookings exceeded the average levels of the past two years, with two new China customers and orders for high-energy channeling superjunction applications. That is stronger evidence of an inflection than the preview’s cautious framing of SiC as a segment that still needed to convert.
surprises.fact_evidence: Silicon carbide bookings in the first half exceeded the average levels of the past two years, with two new China customers added and orders secured for high-energy channeling superjunction applications.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said H2 depended on SiC “converting” and called for “concrete” evidence; its bull case required power/SiC bookings to inflect.

in_line: CS&I revenue was $83 million, consistent with the preview’s expectation that it would trend back toward record territory after $73 million in Q1 and a prior record of $82 million.
The approximately 1x book-to-bill and $452 million ending backlog were broadly consistent with the preview’s stated credibility threshold of book-to-bill of at least 0.9 and a stable backlog.
Management said second-half 2026 memory revenue should be similar to the first half and remain lumpy; the preview had allowed that memory bookings might simply hold rather than grow sequentially.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $33.3 million, above the preview’s $29.8–$30.7 million consensus range and its inferred $27–$28 million whisper. The beat was substantial even against the published high-end estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue grew 50% year-over-year and 60% sequentially to $33.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $29.8M – $30.7M”; the preview also says “the practical whisper is closer to $27–28M.”

surprises.description: Space-based intelligence and AI services revenue reached $24.5 million, well above the preview’s $19–20 million sequential on-track range. The preview had identified this as the key metric, so the size of the step-up was a notable upside surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record space-based intelligence and AI services revenue of $24.5 million (up 50% from Q1).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$19–20M is on-track”; Q1 was “$16.5M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was positive $4.7 million rather than merely around breakeven or slightly positive, as the preview expected. That is a meaningful profitability upside against the preview’s implied Q2 threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $4.7 million (a 14.2% margin), a $7.5 million improvement over the prior-year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA … ~breakeven to slightly positive implied by FY guide”; the preview says “Q2 essentially has to reach breakeven-or-better.”

surprises.description: Year-to-date bookings were reported at up to $200 million, above the preview’s roughly $160 million of year-to-date contract awards. This improves the bookings picture against the preview’s concern about the gap between signed business and the full-year revenue target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured up to $200 million in year-to-date bookings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bookings support the story — ~$160M of YTD contract awards.”

surprises.description: BlackSky disclosed an 8-figure NRO contract to accelerate AROS development, a specific contract win not anticipated in the preview. It adds a new award and supports development toward the stated 2028 launch target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Won an 8-figure NRO contract to accelerate AROS development toward a targeted 2028 launch.”

surprises.description: International space-based intelligence subscriptions grew 150% year over year, and multi-year international contracts now make up over 80% of funded backlog. The preview discussed backlog conversion risk but did not anticipate this level of international growth or the resulting concentration of funded backlog in multi-year contracts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International space-based intelligence subscription revenue grew 150% year-over-year, and multi-year international contracts now comprise over 80% of total funded backlog.”

surprises.description: Management said Gen 3 products and services account for 90% of growth and provide 35-centimeter imagery at about one-fifth the cost of legacy platforms. The preview focused on satellite deployment cadence, not this degree of growth contribution or the stated cost advantage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gen 3-related products and services are driving 90% of the company's growth, delivering 35-centimeter imagery at roughly one-fifth the cost of legacy platforms.”

surprises.description: The preview’s base case assumed no launch slippage, but management reported launch-related delays. However, it still plans to have eight Gen 3 satellites on orbit by year-end and said no additional satellites are needed to meet 2026 revenue targets, partly limiting the concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to have 8 Gen 3 satellites on orbit by year-end despite launch-related delays”; “no additional satellites [are] needed to hit 2026 revenue targets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario specified “no launch slippage”; the preview also noted “four more launches in roughly seven months.”

surprises.description: BlackSky raised $150 million through ATM offerings, confirming substantial issuance and adding significant liquidity. The preview had flagged possible meaningful ATM issuance, so the existence of issuance was anticipated, but the reported $150 million amount and resulting cash increase make its scale concrete.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised $150 million through ATM offerings, boosting cash to $244.1 million … and total liquidity above $325 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “meaningful ATM issuance” and asked investors to watch “ATM usage to date, share count, and whether $50–60M capex is funded without further dilution.”

in_line: Full-year 2026 revenue, adjusted EBITDA, and CapEx guidance was reaffirmed at the ranges already in the preview: $130–150 million revenue, $12–24 million adjusted EBITDA, and $50–60 million CapEx.

The company reached the approximately $100 million annualized run rate for imagery and AI subscription services, consistent with the preview’s stated target of a roughly $100 million annualized run rate.

Management’s warning that large, lumpy Mission Solutions deals will cause quarter-to-quarter revenue variability is consistent with the preview’s warning that total revenue can be affected by lumpy program revenue and backlog-conversion timing.

surprises.description: Arhaus reported Q2 revenue of $385 million, beating both the $365.7 million consensus and the $370 million high end of guidance. The result was stronger than the preview’s already high-end revenue bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record net revenue of $385 million in Q2 2026,” “above the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 consensus net revenue of “$365.7M” and guidance of “$350–370M.”

surprises.description: Comparable written sales rose 12.5%, far exceeding the preview’s concern that they needed to be at least flat-to-positive to validate the recovery. The result also followed a negative Q1 written-sales comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable written sales surged 12.5% in Q2,” lifting year-to-date comparable written sales “to positive 2.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called written comps “the single most important number” and said they needed to be “at least flat-to-positive.”

surprises.description: Comparable delivered sales increased 4%, compared with Q2 guidance of -5% to flat. Deliveries were therefore materially better than the preview’s already cautious range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable delivered sales rose 4%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 comparable delivered guidance as “−5% to flat.”

surprises.description: Arhaus had already requested $37.8 million of tariff refunds, and the full amount had been received in cash; $23.8 million was recognized as a cost-of-goods-sold benefit. The preview expected a quantified but uncollected refund disclosure, so actual cash receipt was a substantial positive difference.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total refunds requested were $37.8 million and have since been fully received in cash”; the company recognized “a one-time $23.8 million benefit in cost of goods sold.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “expect a sized-but-uncollected disclosure” and noted that refunds “aren’t automatic.”

surprises.description: Even excluding the one-time tariff benefit, adjusted EBITDA would have been $55 million—above the preview’s $49 million high end of guidance and roughly $44–46 million consensus. This underlying result was stronger than expected despite year-over-year declines.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding the tariff benefit, gross margin was 40.7%” and “adjusted EBITDA would have been $55 million, down 8.9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed adjusted EBITDA guidance of “$40–49M” and consensus of “~$44–46M.”

surprises.description: Management raised full-year net income and adjusted EBITDA guidance, rather than simply reaffirming the outlook assumed in the preview’s base case. Adjusted EBITDA guidance moved to $160–171 million from the preview’s cited $150–161 million range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year net income guidance to $71–80 million and adjusted EBITDA to $160–171 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case said “FY reaffirmed unchanged”; it said a raised FY guide was required for its bull case. It cited FY adjusted EBITDA guidance of “$150–161M.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed about $10 million of higher shipping costs tied to Middle East disruption, an additional headwind beyond the tariff and fuel pressures discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company faces “roughly $10 million in higher shipping costs tied to Middle East disruption.”

surprises.description: SG&A rose 16.1%, lifting its share of revenue by 230 basis points to 30.6%. The preview flagged possible eCommerce investment changes but did not anticipate this scale of reported expense growth and increased burden.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A rose 16.1% to $118 million, increasing the SG&A load by 230 basis points to 30.6%,” including “roughly $3 million in strategic technology investments and $7.9 million higher selling expenses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch whether “eCommerce investment gets re-based,” but gave no expected SG&A increase.

surprises.description: Client deposits ended the quarter up 11.8% year over year, a strong forward-demand signal that corroborated the written-sales rebound highlighted in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Client deposits ended the quarter up 11.8% year-over-year at approximately $264 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified client deposits as “the cleanest corroboration of a written-demand recovery” and cited $233.1 million in Q2 2025.

surprises.description: A June delivery-fee increase is expected to generate $5–6 million in annual run-rate benefit, with virtually no customer pushback. The preview did not anticipate this pricing action or its expected contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: A June delivery fee increase, “the first in 3–4 years,” is expected to add “$5–6 million in annual run-rate benefit with virtually no customer pushback,” beginning to flow through in Q3.

in_line: Full-year net revenue guidance remained $1.43–1.47 billion, matching the preview’s base-case expectation of reaffirmed guidance.
The stated $30–40 million 2026 tariff impact was already identified in the preview; the unexpected tariff development was that refunds had been received in cash.
Underlying gross margin fell 70 basis points year over year, consistent with the preview’s warning about tariff and other margin pressure.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $5.8 million, far above the preview’s $0.5–2.0 million guidance range. That was a much stronger profit result than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA reached $5.8 million (a 5% margin), far outperforming guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA” Q2 FY26 guidance: “$0.5–2.0M.”

surprises.description: The company raised full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to $13–15 million, well above the roughly $9–11 million implied by the prior outlook. The preview had highlighted the risk of a softened outlook, not an increase of this size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Driving a raise in full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to $13-$15 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY26 adjusted EBITDA was described as “Profitable, slightly lower than 2025” and estimated at “~$9–11M”; the preview also said H2 EBITDA implied “~$12.4–14.4M.”

surprises.description: Q2 net sales of $115.1 million exceeded the expected $110–112 million range implied by guidance and the $111.4 million current consensus. The result was also above the high end of company guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales grew approximately 5.7% year-over-year to $115.1 million, exceeding the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview translated guidance into “~$110–112M” and cited consensus of “$111.4M” (while noting a stale estimate of $115.7M).

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 57.9%, above the preview’s implied 55–57% range, and improved about 360 basis points sequentially—more than the preview’s 150-basis-point threshold for confirming recovery from Q1. The year-over-year decline was limited to about 40 basis points.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin was 57.9%, down about 40 basis points year-over-year but up roughly 360 basis points sequentially from Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview put gross margin at “~55–57% (implied)” and said to watch for “sequential GM improvement ≥150bps.”

surprises.description: Adjusted operating expenses showed leverage across all three categories, with total adjusted OpEx improving 250 basis points as a share of sales. Marketing leverage was 130 basis points, more than the 90 basis points cited in the preview as the Q1 comparison point.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Year-over-year operating expense leverage across all three adjusted categories,” with “marketing down 130 bps to 22.8% of sales and total adjusted OpEx improving 250 bps to 53%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “23.6% of sales in Q1 with 90bps of leverage” and asked for a bridge to H2 EBITDA.

surprises.description: AOV rose about 8% to roughly $2,238, accelerating from the 3.3% growth reported in Q1. The preview expected AOV durability but did not anticipate this degree of sequentially stronger year-over-year growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Average order value rose about 8% year-over-year to roughly $2,238.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 AOV was “$2,131 (+3.3%)” and noted that AOV growth had been driven by “price increases and customer mix.”

surprises.description: Although total orders fell about 2%, orders excluding sub-$500 purchases rose 5%, and two-year stacked order growth was 16%. That indicates better underlying order momentum than the aggregate decline alone suggests, despite the preview’s concern that higher AOV could come with weakening unit demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total orders declined about 2% year-over-year, but excluding sub-$500 orders (a few percent of sales), orders rose 5%, and two-year stacked order growth was 16%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview warned: “A quarter where AOV is up but orders are flat-to-down means price increases are now destroying units.”

surprises.description: Cash ended the quarter at about $75 million, roughly $16 million higher sequentially, rather than the preview’s expectation that the balance would likely be below the prior $58.6 million level after H1 working-capital use.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with about $75 million in cash and no debt, a sequential increase of roughly $16 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that “H1 is a working-capital use of cash, so the Q2 balance is likely below $58.6M.”

surprises.description: Bookings from showroom walk-ins without appointments grew 47% year-over-year, an operating-channel result the preview did not flag. This suggests stronger walk-in showroom demand than investors had been led to expect from the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Showroom bookings from walk-in customers without appointments grew 47% year-over-year.”

surprises.description: The new Beverly Hills flagship generated over 40% higher bookings and about 10% higher AOVs than prior locations, a specific store-performance result not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The new Beverly Hills flagship delivered over 40% higher bookings and about 10% higher AOVs versus prior locations.”

in_line: Fine jewelry bookings grew about 32%, within the preview’s expected range of roughly 25–33% and close to the prior quarter’s 33% growth.

Q3 guidance for roughly flat year-over-year sales and $3–5 million of adjusted EBITDA matched the preview’s expectation that the quarter would be roughly flat year-over-year and faced a strong prior-year tariff-driven comparison.
Full-year net sales guidance of $459–462 million remained within the preview’s estimated range of roughly $455–462 million.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $29.1 million, about 9% above the preview’s $26.6 million consensus (and above its $28.5 million bull-case threshold).
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue reached $29.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 Consensus” revenue was “$26.6M”; the bull scenario called for “$28.5M+.”

surprises.description: Management raised FY26 revenue guidance to $104–108 million, exceeding the prior “at least $100M” guide and topping the preview’s $103.2 million consensus at the midpoint. The preview’s bull case anticipated a raise to $103–106 million, so the reported range was also somewhat higher than that scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $104-108 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited FY26 revenue consensus of “$103.2M” versus guide of “at least $100M”; its bull case expected “FY guide raised to $103–106M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin substantially outperformed the preview’s roughly 85% Q2 expectation, reaching 90%; management also raised FY26 gross-margin guidance above the preview’s stated range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin was 90% versus 86% a year ago, with full-year guidance raised to 86-89%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected Q2 gross margin of “~85% (guide 84–87%)” and noted FY26 guidance of “84–87%” as the operative range.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $7.6 million, well above the preview’s base-case expectation of approximately breakeven, and the company continued to expect positive adjusted EBITDA for FY26.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA” was “$7.6 million in Q2 2026”; the company “expects positive adjusted EBITDA for the full year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “adj. EBITDA ~breakeven,” while its bear case was “adj. EBITDA clearly negative”; it also flagged the FY26 positive-EBITDA commitment as a key test.

surprises.description: HEPZATO kit volume grew 30%, but revenue grew only 21% because 340B pricing reduced effective ASP from about $185,000 to $170,000–$173,000 per kit. The preview flagged volume versus price as something to watch but did not anticipate this specific pricing drag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “HEPZATO revenue grew 21% year-over-year but represented 30% volume growth,” with the gap “entire[ly] attributable to 340B pricing” that cut effective ASP from “~$185K to ~$170-173K per kit.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed that breast-cancer trial enrollment, like colorectal-cancer enrollment, is running below expectations because of training challenges. The preview already identified slow colorectal enrollment, but did not flag a similar enrollment problem in the breast trial.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management acknowledged “enrollment in both colorectal and breast cancer trials is running below expectations due to training challenges.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described colorectal enrollment as “slower than anticipated,” but said the breast-cancer Phase 2 had its “first patient dosed July 2026” and referenced “>20 sites.”

surprises.description: The company reported that it had already repurchased about $9 million of stock under its $25 million buyback program, a capital-allocation action the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $95.9 million in cash and investments, generated $5.7 million in operating cash flow, and has repurchased ~$9 million of stock under a $25 million buyback program.”

in_line: Delcath had 31 active treatment centers and remained on track for 37 by year-end, in line with the preview’s expectation of 31–32 centers at Q2 and its stated 37-center year-end target.

Colorectal-cancer trial progress remained slow: the call reported 13 active screening centers and a late-2027 interim readout, consistent with the preview’s warning that mCRC enrollment was already slower than anticipated.

surprises.description: Excelerate raised and narrowed its 2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook to $490–515 million, rather than simply reaffirming $480–510 million. Both ends of the range moved higher, although the new range still overlaps the preview’s base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised and narrowed full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $490 million to $515 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 Adj. EBITDA (company guide): $480–510M”; the base case expected the guide to be “reaffirmed $480–510M.”

surprises.description: The FSRU Express received a firm seven-year Colombia charter with a projected 35% increase in its annual EBITDA contribution beginning in early 2027. The preview looked for redeployment economics but did not anticipate these specific commercial terms or quantified uplift.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The FSRU Express was recontracted to Colombia under a seven-year charter… expected to boost the vessel's annual EBITDA contribution by roughly 35% starting in early 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Express redeployment at ‘improved economics’” and said firm commercial terms could shift the conversation past Iraq.

surprises.description: Excelerate gave a more specific Iraq startup target—early Q2 2027—and reported a five-year take-or-pay contract with minimum offtake of 250 million standard cubic feet per day. That is more concrete than the preview’s general 2027 expectation, though the preview’s requested construction restart date was not provided.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Iraq LNG terminal operations are now expected to commence early in Q2 2027 under a five-year take-or-pay contract with a minimum contracted offtake of 250 million standard cubic feet per day.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the terminal had slipped “to 2027” and that investors “need a restart date, not a startup date”; it also cited a “60-month contract clock starting at operational startup.”

surprises.description: The selected FSRU conversion vessel pushed expected conversion capex above the previously communicated roughly $200 million, even though management said returns should remain in line with prior guidance. This is an unanticipated increase in the project’s capital requirement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FSRU conversion capex is now expected to exceed the previously communicated ~$200 million due to the higher-capability vessel, though returns are expected to remain in line with prior guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “the FSRU conversion” as part of the 2027–2028 bridge but gave no expectation of higher conversion capex.

surprises.description: Excelerate named and agreed to buy a specific LNG carrier for about $79 million as its FSRU conversion candidate, advancing the conversion beyond the preview’s general discussion of the project. Deployment is expected in early 2028.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company agreed to purchase the LNG carrier Methane Patricia Camilla for approximately $79 million as its FSRU conversion candidate, with commercial deployment expected in early 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview referred to “the FSRU conversion” as a 2027–2028 bridge item but did not identify a vessel or purchase.

surprises.description: Quarter-end net debt and leverage were higher than the preview’s figures: $898 million and 1.9x trailing leverage versus $714 million and 1.5x. The company nevertheless said leverage remained below its target range and reported substantial cash and revolver availability.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with $342 million in cash, full $500 million revolver availability, net debt of $898 million, and trailing net leverage of 1.9 times, below its target range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Net debt was $714M at 1.5x trailing” and asked whether the dividend plus capex plan implied leverage drifting above 2x.

in_line: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $120 million, within the preview’s modeled range of approximately $118–125 million and close to its ~$120 million expectation.

The Accelerate Acadia was deployed to Jordan on a nine-month NEPCO charter and is expected to contribute about $20 million of 2026 EBITDA, consistent with the preview’s expected Jordan on-hire and ~$20 million contribution.
The quarterly dividend remained $0.09 per Class A share after a roughly 13% increase, matching the dividend raise already noted in the preview.
Q2 EBITDA growth was primarily attributed to the full-quarter Jamaica platform contribution, consistent with the preview’s expectation that Jamaica would support growth.

surprises.description: Revenue was $235.6 million, $4.1 million below the $239.7 million consensus, and fell 1.5% sequentially instead of the preview’s expected slight sequential increase. This was worse than the preview’s base range and crossed its ≤$236 million bear-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue declined 1.5% ($3.6 million) sequentially to $235.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus service revenue was “$239.7M”; the preview said Q2 was “the quarter where consolidated revenue should stop declining” and its base range was “$237.5–240M.”

surprises.description: The 2027 notes were not refinanced in the quarter; Cogent now plans to refinance them in Q3 with secured debt and indicated a cost near the 8.8%–8.9% yield on existing secured notes. That is less favorable than the preview’s upside case of a completed refinancing at 8% or less, although its base case allowed for a refinancing still in progress.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cogent is refinancing its $750 million 2027 unsecured notes (now current) with secured debt in Q3 2026” and management indicated “a higher cost of capital near the 8.8%-8.9% yield on existing secured notes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked whether refinancing “has been executed, and at what coupon?” Its bull case assumed “2027 notes refinanced at ≤8%”; its base case said “refi in progress.”

surprises.description: Management acknowledged that Cogent is not generating positive free cash flow without T-Mobile subsidy payments, which end in under two years. The preview highlighted the payments and their eventual run-off, but did not state that the business would remain free-cash-flow negative without them.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management acknowledged the business is not generating positive free cash flow excluding T-Mobile subsidy payments, which end in under two years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the “$25.0M/quarter T-Mobile IP transit payments” were “the entire gap” between unadjusted and adjusted EBITDA and that the payments “run off in late 2027.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $71.1 million, below the preview’s $72–74 million base range and the roughly $73 million implied estimate. Margin reached 30.2%, within the preview’s base-case range but well below the roughly 32% needed to stay on pace for more than 200 basis points of 2026 expansion; severance and integration wind-down costs weighed on the result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EBITDA as adjusted rose only $0.9 million sequentially to $71.1 million, with margin up 90 basis points to 30.2%, dampened by severance and integration wind-down costs including a 6% (113-employee) workforce reduction.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case was “$72–74M / 30.0–30.9%”; it said Q2 needed “roughly 32% (~$76–77M)” to average more than 200 basis points of margin expansion in 2026.

surprises.description: Wavelength revenue was $14.8 million, below the preview’s $15.0–15.5 million base case, though it landed at the preview’s stated $14.8 million threshold rather than below it. Connection growth, by contrast, was within the preview’s expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Wavelength revenue grew 63.8% year-over-year and 9.2% sequentially to $14.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case was “$15.0–15.5M”; it said “Below $14.8M” would confirm the bear thesis.

surprises.description: The Sprint Wireline revenue base had fallen further than the preview’s estimate, to $34 million per quarter versus roughly $39 million expected. Cogent Classic was slightly ahead of its expected run-rate at $200 million versus about $198 million, but had not offset the deeper Sprint decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The acquired Sprint Wireline revenue base has declined 71% since deal closing, from $118 million to $34 million per quarter, while Cogent Classic revenue grew 29% from $155 million to $200 million per quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said legacy Sprint was “down to ~$39M/quarter from $118M at close” and Cogent Classic’s run-rate was “$198M.”

surprises.description: Cogent repurchased $138.8 million of the principal on its 2032 secured notes below par, reducing the balance and realizing a gain. The preview expected deleveraging from the data-center sale proceeds but did not flag this specific debt repurchase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased $138.8 million par value of its 2032 secured notes at an average price of $90.348, realizing a cumulative $13.4 million gain, reducing the principal balance to $461.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the data-center sale proceeds would “accelerate deleveraging,” but did not mention repurchasing the 2032 notes.

surprises.description: Net leverage improved to 6.23x, below the preview’s 6.5x bull-case threshold after the data-center proceeds and T-Mobile payments. This was a better reported leverage outcome than the preview’s cited Q1 net-leverage figure suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net leverage as adjusted improved to 6.23x EBITDA from 6.79x last quarter and 6.61x in Q2 2025, aided by data center sale proceeds and T-Mobile payments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 exit net leverage of “7.41x” and included “leverage <6.5x post-proceeds” in its bull case.

surprises.description: Capital spending fell substantially from Q1, and management guided to further sequential declines, easing the preview’s concern that another capex overshoot could create a liquidity problem.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CapEx fell 16.7% sequentially and 31.4% year-over-year to $38.5 million, with capital lease principal payments down 27.7% to $9.7 million, and management guiding to further sequential declines.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview warned that “another overshoot against ~$14.8M of operating cash flow is a liquidity problem” and identified capex discipline as a key issue.

surprises.description: The data-center sale produced a $130.7 million GAAP gain, a positive one-off result whose size and direction were not specified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company sold 10 former Sprint data centers in June for $225 million cash … generating a GAAP gain of $130.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the sale closed during Q2 and that “any book gain/loss land[s] in this print,” but did not forecast the gain’s amount or direction.

in_line: Wavelength connections increased by 182 to 2,445, within the preview’s expected 180–220 additions and above its under-150 bear-case trigger.
The sale of 10 data centers for about $225 million and the roughly 14 remaining facilities were consistent with the preview’s stated expectations.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $107 million, below the preview’s $118–$126 million estimate range, and fell year over year because of restatement costs. Excluding those costs, EBITDA rose 3.4%, so the reported shortfall was concentrated in the expected-but-costly accounting work.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA fell $7.9 million to $107 million due to restatement costs (though excluding those costs EBITDA rose 3.4%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA ~$118–$126M (~23–24% margin) — author estimate”; the preview also cited “$15M+ in Q2” of restatement costs as guided.

surprises.description: Management kept the full-year guidance ranges, but indicated results would land near their low ends. The preview viewed a modest lift to the low end as the bullish outcome after Q1 and noted that an unchanged range could imply second-half risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reiterated full-year 2026 guidance … but signaled results will land near the low end of the range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Given Q1 came in ahead, a reiteration is the base case and a modest raise to the low end is the bull tell”; “Buy-side wants the low end lifted toward $440M+ after a Q1 beat.”

surprises.description: Restatement costs are tracking to the top end of the $35–$45 million annual range, and about $3 million shifted from Q2 into Q3. The annual total remains within the preview’s range, but the shift pushes some cost into Q3 despite the preview’s expectation of $15 million or more in Q2 and a lower run rate in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Restatement costs are now expected at the top end of the initial $35M–$45M range, with $20.9M incurred year-to-date and roughly $3M shifting from Q2 into Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Restatement costs (P&L drag): $15M+ in Q2 (guided); $35–45M FY”; the preview said “2H has to drop toward ~$5–8M/quarter.”

surprises.description: Take 5’s same-store sales growth was close to the preview’s mid-3% expectation, but its EBITDA margin declined about 70 basis points as inflation and store operating expenses rose. The preview flagged unit-margin risk from promotions, but did not anticipate this specific cost-driven margin decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Take 5 delivered its 24th consecutive quarter of same-store sales growth … but its EBITDA margin declined about 70 basis points due to inflation and store operating expenses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Take 5 SSS: ~+3.5% (management-guided ‘mid 3% range’)”; the preview also warned that promotional flexibility “hurts unit margin.”

surprises.description: The customer groups that had been softening were described as stabilized, while remaining cohorts showed resilience in average check, premium mix, and attachment rates. That is better than the preview’s concern about continued softening and its description of stabilization as a bullish outcome to watch for.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lower-income and newer customers continue to moderate but have stabilized, while remaining cohorts show resilience with rising average check, premium mix in the low 90s, and attachment rates in the high 50s.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “softening traffic and higher churn among newer and sub-$50K-income households” and said stabilization of the sub-$50K cohort would be a bull signal.

surprises.description: Management cited rising base-oil input costs tied to the Middle East conflict, made modest price increases at the end of Q2, and expects further pricing in the second half. The preview discussed inflation and price/mix generally but did not anticipate this specific input-cost shock and pricing response.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rising base oil input costs from Middle East conflict prompted modest price increases at the end of Q2, with the company managing to gross margin dollars in the short term and expecting further pricing in the back half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview referred to inflation as a factor in customer softness and discussed Take 5’s “price/mix,” but did not mention rising base-oil costs or planned price increases.

surprises.description: The board disclosed that it unanimously rejected activist ADW’s acquisition proposal, calling it highly conditional and significantly undervaluing the company. The preview did not anticipate an acquisition proposal or a board decision on one.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The board unanimously rejected activist ADW's acquisition proposal, calling it highly conditional and stating it significantly undervalued the company.”

in_line: Revenue of $507.4 million fell within the preview’s modeled $505–$525 million range.
Take 5 same-store sales growth of 3.6% was close to the preview’s approximately 3.5% expectation; consolidated same-store sales growth of 1.4% was within the preview’s 1%–2% estimate.
Franchise Brands’ 0.5% comp was consistent with the preview’s flat-to-slightly-positive expectation.

Management reiterated the stated full-year revenue, adjusted EBITDA, and adjusted EPS ranges, consistent with the preview’s base case of reiterated guidance; the near-low-end signal is the separate negative surprise above.
Net leverage of 3.1x matched the preview’s expectation of approximately 3.1x, and full-year free cash flow guidance of $125–$145 million remained unchanged.

surprises.description: Cognex gave a full-year outlook for the first time alongside Q2 and raised 2026 guidance to $1.13–$1.15 billion of revenue and $1.64–$1.68 of adjusted EPS. Management said visibility into the second half had improved, making this a substantial step-up from the prior target of exiting the year at a 25% EBITDA run rate, although it cautioned that visibility remains only 3–4 months.
surprises.fact_evidence: “raised full-year 2026 guidance to revenue of $1.13-$1.15 billion (~15% growth at midpoint) and adjusted EPS of $1.64-$1.68 (~63% growth), well ahead of its prior target of a 25% EBITDA run rate exit”; “issued full-year guidance alongside Q2 results for the first time,” citing improved second-half visibility while noting “only 3-4 months of visibility.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Q3 FY2026 revenue guidance — the single most important number” and framed the event around the Q3 guide; it did not anticipate a first-time full-year guide alongside Q2.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin reached 32.2%, far above the preview’s roughly 29.5% implied consensus and above the company’s 28–31% guidance band. That was a much stronger margin result than the preview’s base case of 29.5–30.5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 32.2%,” expanding 1,150 basis points year over year and “exceeding the guidance midpoint by more than 250 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Adj. EBITDA margin ~29.5% (implied)” and forecast a base scenario of “29.5–30.5%,” against company guidance of 28–31%.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $0.45 beat the preview’s $0.42 consensus estimate, though it was within the preview’s inferred $0.45–$0.46 whisper range. The result was also stronger year over year than the preview’s implied 68% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS grew 80% year-over-year to $0.45,” driven by roughly 100% revenue flow-through.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Adj. diluted EPS $0.42” consensus and inferred a “whisper at ~$0.45–$0.46”; it also showed “+68%” implied year-over-year growth.

surprises.description: The full-year growth outlook improved across nearly all end markets: logistics was forecast at high-single-digit growth, while packaging, electronics, and semiconductor were forecast at double-digit growth. The preview expected logistics to normalize to mid-to-high single digits and described electronics and semiconductor as high-single-to-double-digit opportunities, so the broader upgrades—especially packaging—were better than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year outlooks were raised across nearly all end markets: logistics to high single-digit, packaging to double-digit, electronics to double-digit, and semiconductor to double-digit growth, with automotive maintained at flat to low single-digit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said logistics was expected to “normalize to mid-to-high single digits” and described semiconductor and electronics outlooks as “high-single-to-double-digit.”

surprises.description: The Q3 memory-cost headwind was larger than the preview’s 50-basis-point estimate: management now expected roughly 75 basis points of gross-margin pressure in Q3, with some spillover into Q4. Management characterized it as a timing issue and expected pricing to fully offset it by 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rising memory prices are expected to create roughly 75 basis points of gross margin headwind in Q3 (with some spillover into Q4),” which management viewed as “a timing issue” it expects to “fully offset through pricing by 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had guided to “a 50bps gross-margin headwind in Q3 from memory-chip costs.”

surprises.description: China revenue grew 42% year over year in constant currency, a strong result in light of the preview’s concern that growth in China ex-automotive could decelerate. The comparison is not exact because the preview’s 36% figure was for China ex-auto in Q1, while the reported 42% was for China overall in Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “China was the fastest-growing region with revenue up 42% year-over-year in constant currency.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “Greater China ex-automotive (+36% in Q1)” and said “a deceleration there would validate the bear concern.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed data center supply-chain revenue as a rapidly growing, early-stage platform, with growth above 30% year over year. Its current scale is still limited, at a low-single-digit percentage of total revenue, but the comparison to logistics a decade ago introduced a growth opportunity the preview had not identified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Data center supply chain revenue represents a low single-digit percentage of total revenue but is growing more than 30% year-over-year,” and was described as “an early-stage growth platform similar to logistics a decade ago.”

surprises.description: Cognex reported adding roughly 9,000 customers in 2025 and another 4,500 year to date in 2026. The preview discussed product opportunities and monetization but did not flag customer additions as a metric to watch, so this was new evidence of customer acquisition momentum rather than a beat against a stated target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cognex added ~9,000 new customers in 2025 and ~4,500 year-to-date in 2026.”

in_line: Q2 revenue growth of 17% was broadly in line with the preview’s 17.7% consensus-implied growth rate, despite being slightly below it.
The cost-reduction target was consistent with the preview: management expected approximately $35 million of annualized net reductions by end-2026 versus the preview’s $35–40 million target.
Europe remained weak, as the preview had anticipated; the reported 15% decline was down only low single digits excluding the shift of electronics orders to Americas entities.
Logistics’ full-year outlook of high-single-digit growth matched the preview’s expectation of normalization to mid-to-high single digits.
The reported return of nearly 80% of trailing-12-month free cash flow to shareholders was consistent with the preview’s focus on continued substantial capital returns.

surprises.description: FA reported Q2 revenue of $449 million, up 15% year over year, versus the preview’s $415 million consensus and 6.3% implied growth. Even excluding the temporary customer initiatives, management estimated growth of 11%–12%, still well above the preview’s expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 15% year-over-year to $449 million”; excluding one-time customer initiative benefits, “Q2 total revenue growth was still 11% to 12%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $415.0M” and “Implied Y/Y | +6.3%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.35, substantially above the preview’s $0.29 consensus. The 30% year-over-year increase was also far stronger than the preview’s implied 5.6% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS rose 30% year-over-year to $0.35.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | $0.29” and “Implied Y/Y | +5.6%.”

surprises.description: The preview expected base revenue to be flat to down 2%, but it grew 6.7%. The quality of that upside was qualified: roughly half came from episodic customer initiatives expected to normalize by Q4, leaving underlying base growth at about 3.3%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Base revenue grew an exceptionally strong 6.7%, with roughly half attributed to episodic customer-driven volume initiatives expected to normalize by Q4,” implying “underlying base growth of about 3.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management's FY26 assumption is 0% to -2%” for base revenue; base revenue “turned flat in Q1.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was about 11% above the preview’s roughly $116 million estimate, and its 28.6% margin exceeded the approximately 28% expectation. The margin also improved 130 basis points sequentially, although the preview had highlighted a year-over-year comparison against 29.2%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA increased 13% to $128.5 million with a margin of 28.6%, up 130 basis points sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$116M (derived @ 28% mgmt-framed margin)” and “Adj. EBITDA margin | ~28.0%.”

surprises.description: FA raised the low end of its FY2026 revenue guidance by $45 million and lifted the ranges for EBITDA and EPS, rather than merely reaffirming or narrowly raising the outlook. The new revenue, EBITDA, and EPS ranges are $1.67–$1.71 billion, $472–$486 million, and $1.23–$1.29, respectively.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year 2026 guidance across all metrics,” to revenue of “$1.67-$1.71 billion,” adjusted EBITDA of “$472-$486 million,” and adjusted diluted EPS of “$1.23-$1.29,” with “the bottom end raised by $45 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a narrow-to-$1,650–$1,700 million revenue range and EPS floor “lifted to ~$1.20” as the realistic good outcome, while warning that a “flat reaffirm is a modest negative.” Prior guidance was revenue $1,625–$1,700 million, EBITDA $460–$485 million, and EPS $1.15–$1.25.

surprises.description: FA signed 20 enterprise bookings worth at least $500,000 in expected annual contract value each, up from 17 in Q1. That reached the preview’s 20-plus booking bull-case marker and showed further pipeline conversion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “20 enterprise bookings (each with expected annual contract value of at least $500,000) signed in Q2, up from 17 in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the bull case required “20+ enterprise bookings”; it also noted Q1 had delivered 17 and that the key question was pipeline conversion.

surprises.description: FA repaid debt faster than the preview’s stated cumulative total: it made a $25 million prepayment in Q2 and another $45 million this week, bringing cumulative voluntary repayments since the Sterling acquisition to more than $165.5 million. Net leverage fell to 3.7x from the preview’s 3.9x figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company made a $45 million voluntary debt prepayment this week on top of a $25 million prepayment in Q2,” bringing cumulative repayment “to over $165.5 million” and reducing net leverage to “3.7x.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$120.5M cumulative voluntary debt prepayment since the Sterling close” and net leverage of “3.9x.”

surprises.description: Synergy actions advanced beyond the preview’s Q1 snapshot, but management did not raise the $65–$80 million target the preview identified as a potential positive catalyst. $63 million had been actioned, while only $51 million had been realized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company actioned $63 million of its $65-$80 million Sterling synergy target (with only $51 million realized so far)” and remained on track to complete integration actions by December 31, 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited $58 million actioned and $47 million realized as of March 31, and said to “watch for another target raise” as a reliable positive catalyst.

surprises.description: Retention was 96%, one percentage point below the preview’s expectation that 97% retention would repeat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Customer retention held at 96%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario said “97% retention repeats.”

in_line: Combined upsell, cross-sell, and new-logo revenue grew 12.5%, broadly consistent with the preview’s note that this growth channel was already running at about 12%.

Management’s outlook for moderating growth in the second half was consistent with the preview’s expectation that H2 would remain derisked and that growth would slow against strong prior-year comparisons.

surprises.description: Fluence cut its FY2026 revenue guidance midpoint by about $400 million to $3.0 billion, below the previous $3.2–$3.6 billion range. The preview expected guidance to be reaffirmed or narrowed within that prior range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “lowered its fiscal 2026 revenue guidance midpoint by approximately $400 million to $3 billion”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue $3.2–3.6B”; the preview’s base case expected “FY revenue narrowed to $3.2–3.4B with EBITDA reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Q3 revenue was $650 million, well below the preview’s roughly $762–$801 million consensus range and its own ~$770 million bogey. The shortfall was attributed to production delays at two new contract manufacturing facilities.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 revenue of $650 million rose 8% year-over-year but came in roughly $90 million below prior expectations due to production delays at two new contract manufacturing facilities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $761.9M” consensus, with an alternative estimate of “~$801M”; the preview said, “I'd use ~$770M” as a bogey.

surprises.description: Fluence also cut its FY2026 adjusted EBITDA midpoint from $50 million to negative $10 million, sharply reversing the prior positive-profit outlook. The cut reflects lost margin as revenue moves into 2027 as well as an unanticipated battery-supply-agreement charge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “cut its adjusted EBITDA midpoint from $50 million to negative $10 million”; the cut was driven partly by “about $44 million of lost margin from shifting roughly $400 million of revenue into 2027 and a $15 million charge tied to a long-term battery supply agreement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited a FY2026 adjusted EBITDA guide of “$40–60M” and expected the base case to have “EBITDA reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Manufacturing problems were more consequential than the preview’s expected clean recovery implied: delays at two new contract manufacturers contributed to the revenue shortfall, and the Houston 15 GWh facility will not reach full production until fiscal Q1 2027 because of construction and automation issues.
surprises.fact_evidence: Revenue was “roughly $90 million below prior expectations due to production delays at two new contract manufacturing facilities”; the Houston facility “has been delayed by construction and automation issues and is now expected to reach full production in fiscal Q1 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the ~$80 million of Q2 revenue pushed into Q3 was “described as resolved,” and its bull scenario assumed “clean US factory throughput.”

surprises.description: Q3 order intake reached $1.44 billion, substantially above the preview’s indication that the quarter needed to clear roughly $1.0 billion to grow backlog. The record orders were nearly triple the year-ago quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fluence signed a record $1.44 billion of orders in Q3 2026, nearly triple the $509 million signed in the same quarter last year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “>$600M was signed in Q3 as of the call date” and said backlog grows only if “the full quarter clears ~$1.0B.”

surprises.description: Fluence announced $850 million of data-center orders and awards, including a $300 million behind-the-meter developer contract. That is a much larger disclosed opportunity than the preview’s anticipated first project order, although part of the total remains awards rather than purchase orders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fluence received its first data center orders and awards totaling $850 million, including a $300 million behind-the-meter developer contract and $550 million in awards from a hyperscaler.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a first data-center project order was expected “within the third quarter” and identified the hyperscaler order’s “Size” as something to watch.

surprises.description: Despite the substantial hyperscaler awards, the $550 million was not yet in purchase orders. The preview specifically treated a booked hyperscaler purchase order in Q3 as a key test, so the reported awards did not fully meet that expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: The “$550 million in awards from a hyperscaler” were “not yet purchase orders.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed the “First hyperscaler purchase order” as a key metric and asked whether it was “booked in the quarter, or slipped?”

surprises.description: Backlog reached $6.4 billion, above the preview’s expected $5.8–$6.1 billion base-case range and its $6.0 billion bull-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog reached a record $6.4 billion, up 14% sequentially and more than 30% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case anticipated “backlog $5.8–6.1B”; its bull case specified “backlog >$6.0B.”

surprises.description: Fluence said $2.2 billion of backlog is expected to convert to FY2027 revenue, providing a specific forward-conversion figure not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$2.2 billion expected to convert to fiscal 2027 revenue versus $1.5 billion of comparable coverage a year ago.”

surprises.description: Quarter-end liquidity was about $863 million, below the preview’s approximately $900 million expectation, with cash also below the preview’s cited range. Management nevertheless expects liquidity to return to $900 million by fiscal year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total liquidity ended the quarter at approximately $863 million (including $365 million in cash), with management expecting a return to $900 million by fiscal year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “~$900M total liquidity ($413–430M cash)” and flagged “Sub-$800M” as the level that would revive the balance-sheet bear case.

surprises.description: Management warned that supporting the record order intake may require $300–$500 million of additional working capital over the coming year, a much larger funding need than the preview’s planned Q3 inventory build suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management flagged that supporting record order intake may require “an additional $300 million to $500 million of working capital over the coming year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$220M inventory build in Q2, another ~$100M planned in Q3.”

surprises.description: Fluence disclosed a $15 million charge tied to a long-term battery supply agreement, an additional cost not identified in the preview’s outlook discussion.
surprises.fact_evidence: The EBITDA cut included “a $15 million charge tied to a long-term battery supply agreement.”

surprises.description: The company reorganized senior leadership, moving Roman Lewsen to lead supply chain and Peter Williams to focus on product, with both reporting directly to the CEO; the preview did not anticipate this management change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reorganized leadership, moving Roman Lewsen to head supply chain and Peter Williams to focus on product, both reporting directly to the CEO.”

in_line: Management reaffirmed the approximately $180 million FY2026 ARR target, consistent with the preview’s expectation of “ARR ~$180M exiting FY26.”

surprises.description: Shift4 cut its FY2026 non-GAAP EPS range to $5.15–$5.35 from the previewed $5.50–$5.70, while also lowering GRLNF guidance to $2.48–$2.53 billion from $2.50–$2.60 billion and adjusted EBITDA to $1.15–$1.18 billion from $1.165–$1.215 billion. Management said the GRLNF midpoint reduction was only 100 basis points on an FX-neutral basis, but the guidance still fell short of the expected reaffirmation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full year 2026 guidance calls for GRLNF of $2.48-$2.53 billion (up 25-28%), adjusted EBITDA of $1.15-$1.18 billion (up 19-22%), and non-GAAP EPS of $5.15-$5.35.” Management said the GRLNF midpoint was “reduced only 100 basis points on an FX-neutral basis” and cited a “~$20 million FX translation impact” and the “$25 million Q3 Middle East headwind” as most of the “$40 million guidance revision.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance (reaffirmed at Q1): ... GRLNF $2.50–2.60B · Adj. EBITDA $1.165–1.215B · Non-GAAP EPS $5.50–5.70.” The preview also said to watch for “FY26 EPS guide: reaffirm $5.50–5.70, raise, or trim.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the FY free-cash-flow range of $490–$510 million to be reiterated, but management specifically said higher net interest expense from the new term loan weighs on free-cash-flow guidance. The reported facts do not provide a revised FCF range, so the size of any change cannot be determined.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised an additional $1 billion Term Loan B on July 8 to prefund the August 2027 convertible note maturity, terming out its capital structure to 2031, which drives higher net interest expense weighing on free cash flow guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. FCF ... FY $490–510M reiteration” and the checklist expected “Adj. FCF ≥$10M + FY $490–510M reiterated.”

surprises.description: Management estimated a roughly $25 million Middle East travel-disruption headwind for Q3. The preview highlighted Q3 disruption sizing, but did not give a Q3 dollar estimate; the disclosed headwind is a meaningful added drag amid the expected back-half ramp.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Middle East conflict caused travel disruption that management estimates as a ~$25 million headwind for Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Travel/TFS disruption sizing for Q3 — did the $20M Q2 embed prove conservative or light?” The preview also identified “Q3 travel drag extends” as a bear-case risk.

surprises.description: Shift4 reported Q2 adjusted free cash flow of $21 million, more than twice the $10 million guidance. That was a substantially better quarter than the preview’s already-stretched $10 million expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted free cash flow of $21 million more than doubled the $10 million guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. FCF: ~$10M” for Q2, and the checklist called for “Adj. FCF ≥$10M.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross revenue reached $1.29 billion versus $1.17 billion of guidance, a sizable beat.
