surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed its ATM program raising ~$72 million in net proceeds at an average price over $35, ending the quarter with $123 million in cash and no debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash + investments ~$41.9M, no debt.”

surprises.description: Management reported that no customer accounted for more than 10% of first-half revenue and that enterprise computing averaged 29% of ACV plus royalties over the past four quarters. This provided new evidence of customer and business-line diversification, although the preview supplied no numerical expectation for either measure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “No single customer exceed[ed] 10% of revenue in the first half of 2026, while enterprise computing averaged 29% of ACV plus royalties over the past four quarters.”

in_line: Q2 ACV plus royalties of $99.5 million exceeded the $99 million guide high end, but was broadly in line with the preview’s $98–$100 million base case and its approximately $99 million functional bar.
Q2 revenue of $24.1 million was above the $24.0 million guide high end, but within the preview’s $23.9–$24.4 million base-case range.
The FY2026 revenue guidance increase to $95–$98 million was anticipated: the preview’s bull case expected that range, and its checklist called for a raise to at least a $94 million midpoint.
The CFO transition was already disclosed in the preview: Nick Hawkins was retiring and Saurabh Sinha was expected to take over effective September 8, 2026.
TTM royalty growth of 65% was broadly in line with the preview’s cited 67% growth expectation, notwithstanding the slight sequential dip noted above.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $125.8 million, about 4.8% above the preview’s $120 million consensus estimate and above the preview’s $123–126 million bull-case range at the top end. Constant-currency growth was 9%, stronger than the 6.2% growth implied by consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue was $125.8 million, up 9% year-over-year on a constant currency basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 2026 Consensus” revenue: “$119.99M”; implied Y/Y: “+6.2% reported.”

surprises.description: The full-year adjusted EBITDA outlook was reiterated at $92–99 million, below the preview’s stated $100–107 million guide. That is a lower outlook despite the Q2 adjusted EBITDA result exceeding the preview’s expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reiterated full-year 2026 guidance” of adjusted EBITDA “$92-$99 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EBITDA” guide: “$100–107M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $26.4 million, just above the preview’s estimated $24–26 million range. The beat was modest rather than a substantial overshoot.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA grew 7% from $24.8 million to $26.4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA” consensus: “~$24–26M (est.).”

surprises.description: Despite the adjusted EBITDA beat, adjusted EBITDA margin fell about 90 basis points to 21%, with management attributing the decline to higher R&D investment after the Endospan acquisition. This contrasts with the preview’s expectation of margin expansion implied by the annual guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin declined roughly 90 basis points to 21% due to increased R&D investments following the Endospan acquisition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the FY guide “implies 100bps expansion” and set an adjusted EBITDA bogey of “≥$25M, GM ≥65%.”

surprises.description: Stent graft growth accelerated to 12%, exceeding the preview’s minimum 10% bogey, even against a tougher comparison. This is a positive update on a metric the preview identified as important to the second-half growth outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Stent graft revenue accelerated to 12% growth (from 10% in Q1) against a tougher comp.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bogey was “≥+10% cc (matching Q1).”

surprises.description: ONIX grew 18%, ahead of the preview’s expectation of at least 15% growth. The reported growth was attributed to global market-share gains among patients under 65.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ONIX grew 18% on global market share gains in patients under 65.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s ON-X bogey was “≥+15% cc.”

surprises.description: Tissue processing grew about 1% rather than producing the negative print the preview said was expected on the hard comparison. However, management said roughly $2 million of tissue releases shifted from Q3 into Q2, making the result partly a timing benefit rather than evidence of stronger underlying demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tissue processing revenue was approximately $26 million (up 1%), aided by roughly $2 million of upside from tissue releases that shifted from Q3 into Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said preservation services faced “difficult comps in Q2 and Q3” and that “A negative print here is expected.”

surprises.description: Q2 free cash flow was negative $12 million, with $1.5 million of Endospan diligence costs and a $10.2 million contractually required transaction bonus booked as a post-acquisition expense. The preview flagged financing and integration costs but did not identify this bonus payment or forecast a cash outflow of this kind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow was negative $12 million in Q2,” impacted by “$1.5 million of Endospan diligence costs” and a “$10.2 million contractually required transaction bonus payment booked as a post-acquisition expense.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “no cost surprise” while flagging Endospan “integration cost, interest expense, contingent consideration.”

surprises.description: The acquisition financing left net leverage at 3.1x, excluding a $25 million AMDS milestone paid in July. The preview noted the borrowing but did not quantify this leverage level or the additional milestone payment, adding a financing burden beyond the details it highlighted.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Endospan/Nexus acquisition closed for “a $135 million purchase price funded by $150 million of borrowings, raising net leverage to 3.1x (excluding a $25 million AMDS milestone paid in July).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted a “$150M term loan draw” and flagged “Endospan financing drag,” including expected interest expense and any integration or contingent-consideration charges.

in_line: Management reaffirmed FY2026 revenue guidance of $480–496 million, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the company would reaffirm that range.

AMDS had received FDA PMA approval before the release, as the preview noted; the call’s expectation that approval would accelerate account conversion and second-half sales was prospective, not a report of quantified post-PMA placements.
The Nexus U.S. commercial launch remains planned for January 2027, with inconsequential 2026 revenue expected, matching the preview’s stated launch timing and minimal-2026-revenue expectation.

surprises.description: BARK’s underlying subscriber economics improved despite the expected sharp drop in DTC orders: retention rose more than 170 basis points year over year, average order value increased 45 cents per unit, and BarkBox lifetime value approached its highest level as a public company.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Subscriber retention rate improved by over 170 basis points year-over-year,” “average order value grew 45 cents per unit,” and subscriber lifetime value was “near its highest level as a public company.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the tell is in subscriber and DTC commentary” and called for “new-subscriber acquisition and retention commentary,” while anticipating DTC declines of about 28%.

surprises.description: Commerce revenue fell 11% to $12.1 million, rather than coming in around the preview’s implied $14 million and roughly flat year over year. Management expects meaningful increases heading into the holidays, but the reported decline deepens the weakness in a segment the preview said needed to scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Commerce revenue fell 11% year-over-year to $12.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q1 Commerce at “~$14M (implied)” and “~flat” year over year, and said “a second consecutive down quarter here breaks the diversification story.”

surprises.description: Reported gross margin reached 72.7%, but the figure was lifted by a one-time $7.4 million tariff recovery; normalized margin was 63.4%, slightly below the 63.8% a year earlier. The recovery’s effect was flagged as a possibility, but its scale produced much higher reported margin than the preview’s roughly 62% historical margin reference would suggest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reported gross margin was 72.7%, inflated by a one-time $7.4 million IEPA tariff recovery from FY26; normalized gross margin was 63.4% versus 63.8% a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited 62.3% consolidated gross margin for Q1 FY26 and said, “Watch how much landed in Q1, and where — a COGS credit would flatter gross margin and adjusted EBITDA.”

surprises.description: Bark Air reached $3.2 million of revenue, above the preview’s roughly $3 million estimate, and more than 90% of Q2 seats were already sold, offering a favorable demand indicator beyond the expected growth in the business.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bark Air revenue grew 37% year-over-year to $3.2 million, with over 90% of Q2 seats already sold.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q1 BARK Air revenue at “~$3M” and growth of “~+30%.”

surprises.description: BARK made share repurchases under its $40 million program, confirming that the authorization was being used, while cash declined from $19.3 million at fiscal year-end to $16.1 million. The preview had identified both buyback execution and ending cash as unresolved questions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter debt-free with $16.1 million in cash, down from $19.3 million at fiscal year-end due to working capital build and share repurchases under its $40 million buyback program.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said, “Any Q1 repurchases, and the ending cash balance ex-refund, tell you whether the buyback is real or ornamental,” and described the authorization as “funded by ongoing free cash flow” as “a stretch.”

surprises.description: Marketing spend was cut 37% year over year, a much larger reduction than the preview’s question about whether marketing would be redeployed suggested. The lower spend supports cost control but leaves less visible support for acquiring subscribers as DTC orders fall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Marketing spend was cut 37% ($5.6 million) year-over-year to $9.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified “whether marketing spend is being re-deployed” as something to watch alongside the DTC subscriber trajectory.

in_line: Q1 revenue of $78.8 million was within guidance and at its high end, as the preview expected revenue of $77–79 million and described the effective consensus as about $78 million.
Adjusted EBITDA of approximately $0.6 million was within the guided $0–1 million range, as the preview used that range as its anchor.
DTC orders declined about 28% year over year, consistent with the preview’s implied roughly 28% DTC decline.
Management reiterated full-year revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance, as the preview treated reaffirmation as the expected outcome to watch.

surprises.description: AerSale reported $70.9 million of revenue, $10.3 million below the preview’s $81.2 million consensus. There were no flight equipment sales, versus the preview’s base case of a couple of engine transactions; the preview had flagged a zero-sale quarter as a downside scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue fell to $70.9 million” and was driven primarily by “the absence of flight equipment sales versus $33.4 million (eight engines) in the prior-year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue ~$81.2M”; “Base requires: a couple of engine transactions”; “Zero units means revenue lands near $65–70M and EPS goes negative.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was a loss of $0.09 rather than the preview’s expected $0.11 profit, a 20-cent shortfall. The preview warned that consensus depended on high-margin whole-asset sales, but its base case still assumed some engine transactions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted loss per share of $0.09.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS ~$0.11”; the preview said clearing $0.11 required “a meaningful slug of high-margin whole-asset sales.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was only $2.2 million, far below even the preview’s bear-case range of $5–8 million. The result reflected both the missing high-margin equipment sales and lower gross margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA collapsed to $2.2 million (3.1% of revenue) from $18.3 million (17% of revenue) a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bear scenario projected “Adj. EBITDA $5–8M”; its base case projected “$9–12M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin fell to 22.9%, below the preview’s 28–30% base-case range and its 30% marker for the startup drag to have eased. The call attributed the decline to lost high-margin equipment sales as well as startup costs at Goodyear and Millington.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Overall gross margin fell to 22.9% from 32.9% due to lost high-margin equipment sales and startup costs at Goodyear and Millington.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case called for “GM 28–30%”; the preview said Q2 was when startup drag “should visibly abate” and flagged “Gross margin ≥30%” as the marker to watch.

surprises.description: Even excluding flight equipment sales, revenue declined 4.2% year over year: lower USM sales outweighed growth in leasing and MRO. That was weaker than the preview’s recurring-revenue thesis and expectation that TechOps would grind higher.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding flight equipment sales, overall revenue declined 4.2% year-over-year as lower USM sales offset growth in leasing and MRO.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called sustained growth in Asset Management Solutions ex-flight-equipment “the recurring-revenue thesis” and said the base case required “TechOps [to] grind higher.”

surprises.description: Liquidity was tighter than the preview’s already-cautious balance-sheet framing: available liquidity was $34 million, including just $2.2 million of cash, and revolver availability was $31.8 million. The preview identified availability below roughly $35 million with cash near zero as the point when liquidity could become the main issue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Year-to-date cash used in operating activities was $33.5 million,” leaving “available liquidity of just $34 million ($2.2 million cash plus $31.8 million revolver availability).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Below ~$35M with cash near zero” the conversation shifts from growth to the balance sheet; it cited Q1 “$2.1M cash” and “$41.8M total availability.”

surprises.description: Goodyear was operating at under 20% of available capacity, despite the preview’s expectation that the MRO network was filling and that startup drag should begin to abate. The landing gear shop was much busier at about 80% of single-shift capacity, a contrast that points to uneven utilization across the operation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Goodyear is operating at under 20% of available capacity with 84 stored ex-Spirit Airlines aircraft awaiting maintenance work, while the landing gear shop runs at about 80% single-shift capacity with plans to add a second shift.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the MRO network is filling” and that Q2 was when the “startup drag should visibly abate.”

surprises.description: Feedstock acquisitions dropped to $5.6 million from $27.1 million a year earlier. The preview anticipated disciplined purchasing but also highlighted the risk of continued feedstock deployment; the sharp pullback limits that buying, while reflecting a hyper-competitive market.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Feedstock acquisitions dropped sharply to $5.6 million in Q2 from $27.1 million a year ago due to pricing discipline in a hyper-competitive acquisition market.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the “disciplined-acquisition posture” but also warned of liquidity risk “if Q2 is another no-asset-sale quarter with continued feedstock purchases.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a specific $35 million 737 sale to the U.S. Marshal Service expected to close in late Q3 or early Q4, plus 17 engines in repair expected to exit over the coming months. This offers concrete future monetization and repair activity, though neither the aircraft sale nor the engine exits add to Q2 results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management secured a $35 million 737 aircraft sale to the U.S. Marshal Service plus several engine sales expected to close in late Q3 or early Q4, and has 17 engines in work expected to exit repair over the coming months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management might point to “Q4-weighted asset monetization” and warned that pipeline strength could be offered “rather than closed transactions.”

in_line: Leasing revenue grew about 50% to $12.4 million, consistent with the preview’s expectation of continued leasing growth; the company had 18 engines and three 757 freighters on lease.
TechOps revenue rose 8.7% to $33.8 million on the Millington CRJ ramp, broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation that TechOps would rise modestly.

surprises.description: The preview expected no likely update on the unresolved CSL arbitration, but CSL Seqirus instead terminated the collaboration. Arcturus regained global rights to CoStave and its broader infectious-disease portfolio, received a one-time $12 million payment, and was released from roughly $16 million in liabilities.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The CSL Seqirus collaboration was terminated, returning global rights to the CoStave COVID vaccine and the broader infectious disease portfolio (seasonal flu, pandemic flu, RSV, EBV) plus a one-time $12 million cash payment and release from roughly $16 million in liabilities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “CSL Seqirus arbitration (EU KOSTAIVE milestone) … No update likely.”

surprises.description: The preview expected ARCT-032 enrollment to be on track and wanted a specific data window, with data guided for H1 2027. Management instead centered guidance on a Q4 2026 go/no-go decision for Phase 3; that gives a dated decision point but does not provide the expected data window.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The pivotal go/no-go decision to advance the CF candidate ARCT-032 into Phase 3 is expected in Q4 2026”; management “reframed CF guidance to focus on the Q4 2026 Phase 3 decision rather than a data disclosure or enrollment completion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ARCT-032 12-week Ph2 enrollment + data guidance … Enrollment ‘on track’; data guided H1 2027”; investors wanted “a specific data window.”

surprises.description: Arcturus reported lower Q2 R&D spending than the preview’s $21–24 million estimate: $17.5 million. That is a notable reduction against the expected quarterly spend, though the facts do not explain the cause.
surprises.fact_evidence: “R&D expenses declined to $17.5 million (Q2) … from $29.6 million” a year earlier.

surprises.description: The preview expected the ARCT-810 end-of-Phase-2 meeting to be scheduled or reaffirmed for H2 2026. Instead, management said full Phase 2 data and the regulatory path, including a plan for the meeting, would be disclosed in Q3; the update gives a nearer data disclosure but does not report a scheduled meeting date.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Enrollment and study-drug dosing were completed for … ARCT-810, with full Phase 2 data (including FDA-requested supplementary Type C data) and the regulatory path forward, including an end-of-Phase 2 meeting plan, to be disclosed in Q3 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ARCT-810 End-of-Phase-2 meeting … Guided to H2 2026”; the preview also said a “scheduled date” would de-risk the pivotal design.

surprises.description: The preview did not anticipate the CF study’s expansion into Israel and Turkey. Management said those locations have a larger share of patients with eligible null mutations than the US group described in the call, which is intended to boost recruitment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The CF Phase 2 study was expanded to Israel and Turkey, where 30%-40% of CF patients carry null mutations eligible for enrollment versus up to 10% ineligible-for-modulator patients in the US, boosting recruitment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Up to 20 Class I CF patients, US + ex-US”; the preview expected enrollment to be “on track.”

surprises.description: The call gave more reassuring ARCT-032 dosing and safety detail than the preview provided: more than 50 participants had been dosed, including at the highest stated dose, without steroid pretreatment or clinic-based administration. The preview had focused on enrollment and the timing of data rather than these treatment details.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ARCT-032 has now been dosed in over 50 participants at up to 15 mg daily for 28 days without steroid pretreatment and with at-home self-administration,” and management said “no serious safety issues have required disclosure in the ongoing 12-week study.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “12-week Ph2 enrollment + data guidance” and expected enrollment to be “on track.”

surprises.description: Arcturus reported Q2 G&A expense of $11 million, above the preview’s $9–10 million estimate. The difference is modest compared with the larger-than-expected reduction in R&D.
surprises.fact_evidence: “G&A remained roughly flat at $11 million (Q2) … .”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag a change in the Japanese CoStave profit split. With CSL out, Arcturus’s profit share will be split two ways with Meiji instead of three ways, improving its share of the Japanese economics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In Japan, the loss of CSL means the CoStave profit share will now be split two ways with Meiji instead of three ways.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed the KOSTAIVE royalty stream and CSL arbitration, but did not anticipate a change to the Japanese profit split.

surprises.description: The preview did not mention progress on the pandemic-flu program ARCT-2304. The call reported that Phase 1 was complete, results were accepted by Nature Communications, and EMA scientific advice was planned for Q4 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The pandemic flu program ARCT-2304 completed Phase 1 with results accepted by Nature Communications and EMA scientific advice planned for Q4 2026.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $3 million, in line with the preview’s $2.5–3.5 million estimate and close to the $3.1 million consensus; the preview also anticipated a steep year-over-year decline as CSL collaboration revenue wound down.
First-half revenue of $5 million was close to the preview’s derived expectation of about $5.2 million.

Cash of $191.5 million was within the preview’s $190–195 million estimate. Management’s runway statement—over 2.5 years through year-end 2028—was broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of runway beyond Q2 2028.

The call’s description of Thermo Fisher contributions following a positive Phase 3 decision was consistent with the preview’s reference to Phase 3 capacity commitments under the Thermo Fisher/PPD arrangement.

surprises.description: The Q3 outlook calls for loan volume to fall to $1.375–$1.525 billion and revenue to $49–$52 million, rather than the preview’s base case of roughly flat volume and $56–$62 million revenue. Revenue guidance is also at or below the preview’s bear-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance implies a sequential decline, with loan volume of $1.375-$1.525 billion” and “net revenues of $49-$52 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “volume roughly flat QoQ” and “Q3 Revenue Guide” of “$56–62M”; its bear case was “$50–55M.”

surprises.description: Q3 adjusted EBITDA loss guidance of $15–$18 million is worse than the preview’s base-case loss of $10–$13 million and reaches below the preview’s bear-case threshold of a loss worse than $15 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance implies … an adjusted EBITDA loss of $15-$18 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “$(10)–(13)M”; its bear case was “Worse than $(15)M.” It also cited a “~$(10)M ‘on track’ whisper.”

surprises.description: Management said it will miss the previously guided September adjusted EBITDA break-even goal and did not provide a replacement target month. The preview’s base case anticipated a dated push to 1H27, so leaving the timing unanchored is less specific than that expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “will fall short of its previously guided goal of reaching adjusted EBITDA break-even by September,” and management “declined to re-anchor to a specific target month.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case said “Breakeven formally pushed to 1H27”; it also listed “withdraw” as a possible outcome and called breakeven language the “highest-variance sentence on the call.”

surprises.description: Q2 refinance volume rose sharply despite the preview’s concern that refinance demand was contracting in a high-rate environment. The growth is a positive contrast to that market setup, although management still described the business as rate-sensitive.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Refinance volume surged 239% year-over-year to $549 million,” though it “remains highly rate-sensitive amid an elevated rate environment management expects to persist over the medium term.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said refinance applications were “down 9% YoY” and noted that BETR’s growth was “disproportionately refi-levered into a market where refi demand is now contracting.”

surprises.description: Ending cash was about $102 million, plus $10 million restricted, versus the liquidity cushion implied by the preview’s Q1 cash balance and subsequent equity raise. The reported balance makes the liquidity position tighter than that context suggested, even as warehouse capacity remained substantial.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company ended Q2 with “~$102 million in cash plus $10 million restricted cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Q1 ended with ~$136M cash/equivalents/restricted, plus a $69M April equity raise” and highlighted “Q2 ending cash” as a key item to watch.

surprises.description: Management disclosed that signed HELOC partnerships, including Credit Karma, have not launched and are excluded from Q3 guidance, with meaningful contributions expected only from Q4. That means they will not support the near-term outlook, while also identifying a later-period growth contribution not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Signed HELOC partnerships—including Credit Karma—have not yet launched and are excluded from Q3 guidance, with meaningful contributions expected to begin in Q4 2026.”

in_line: Q2 loan volume and revenue were already pre-released and matched the preview’s stated figures; the preview described volume as within guidance and revenue as an approximately 3.5% consensus beat.

Q2 adjusted EBITDA of a $14 million loss, including the $6.5 million trade reserve release, was already known from the preliminary results; the preview had also highlighted the reserve benefit and estimated adjusted EBITDA excluding it at about a $20.5 million loss.
The founder’s transition, Daniel Lewis’s interim appointment, and the permanent CEO search were already disclosed or anticipated in the preview.

The annual cost-savings goal above $45 million was already stated in the preview. The projected decline in OPEX from about $75 million in Q2 to $67 million in Q3 is consistent with its expectation that cost reductions would continue, though Q3 EBITDA guidance was worse than expected.

The increase in HELOC mix and the expectation of further growth fit the preview’s focus on HELOC mix as a revenue lever. Continued pursuit of a Birmingham Bank sale and expanded warehouse capacity were also consistent with the preview’s discussion.

surprises.description: The preview expected cash to fall to roughly $95–105 million after the Q1 decline and April JV contribution. Instead, cash and short-term investments rose to $138 million, with less than $5 million left to contribute to the Maas JV.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and short-term investments grew to $138 million at quarter-end (up from $126 million in March), with less than $5 million remaining to be contributed to the Maas Energy Works dairy JV.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 could exit near ~$95–105M”; “Anything under ~$100M with no financing plan articulated reopens the dilution conversation.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the dairy RNG ramp to improve through the year, but the upstream business was already approaching EBITDA breakeven in Q2 as South Fork and East Valley ramped. That is a more concrete profitability milestone than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The RNG upstream business approached breakeven EBITDA in Q2 as South Fork (Texas) and East Valley (Idaho) ramped.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch South Fork (TX) and East Valley (Idaho, ~3.5M gal/yr, commissioned Q1) throughput”; management “explicitly promised improvement through the year.”

surprises.description: The preview described the company as still waiting for updated GREET guidance and said a quantified 45Z benefit could be upside. The call put a number and timing on it—up to $5 million of incremental EBITDA with guidance expected in Q4—but also said a delay into 2027 or minimal benefit could put EBITDA below the stated range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Finalized 45Z GREET model guidance—now expected in Q4—could add up to $5 million of incremental adjusted EBITDA, but a delay into 2027 or minimal benefit would push EBITDA below the $70-$75 million range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Quantified 45Z capture would be a clean upside surprise; continued ‘we’re waiting’ is neutral-to-negative.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the dairy RNG ramp to support volumes, but most of the reported total fuel-volume growth came from conventional natural gas rather than RNG. That makes the growth mix less driven by the RNG ramp than the preview's focus suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 fuel volumes rose 7% year-over-year to 81.8 million gallons, with about two-thirds of the growth coming from conventional natural gas rather than RNG.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Upstream dairy RNG production ramp”; “management explicitly promised improvement through the year.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed that X15N truck adoption remains slow, with a large prebuy of legacy diesel trucks contributing to the weakness. The preview did not flag this demand or adoption issue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “X15N truck adoption remains slow, hurt by a large prebuy of legacy diesel trucks amid uncertainty over final 2027 EPA emission standards.”

surprises.description: The company announced a $27 million contract for its largest hydrogen fueling station, using a cost-plus structure that avoids commodity and capital risk. The preview did not anticipate this contract.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured a $27 million contract with Orange County Transportation Authority for its largest hydrogen fueling station, using a low-capital cost-plus model that avoids commodity and capital risk.”

surprises.description: The company described a new off-pipeline power-generation opportunity using existing tube trailers and underutilized compression capacity across 600 stations, with little to no new investment. This opportunity was not raised in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Clean Energy is pursuing an off-pipeline power-generation market (data centers, fulfillment centers, EV charging) using existing tube trailers and underutilized compression capacity at 600 stations, requiring little to no new investment.”

in_line: Q2 revenue of $106.4 million, adjusted EBITDA of $16 million, and RNG sold of 63 million gallons were reported as in line with expectations; the preview's own estimates were about $108 million, $16 million, and 64 million gallons, respectively.
The company maintained its full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $70–75 million, as the preview's base case expected.

surprises.description: Blink cut its FY2026 revenue outlook from $105–115 million to $83–90 million, a substantial reduction from the guide the preview expected to be tested. The new range is roughly 21%–22% below the prior range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance” was cut “to $83-90 million from the prior $105-115 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Standing guidance ... FY26 revenue $105–115M”; the preview called whether the guide was “held, narrowed, or cut” the “single largest binary.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $21.7 million, well below the preview’s roughly $24.6 million consensus estimate. That is an approximately 12% miss, despite sequential growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 revenue fell to $21.7 million from $28.7 million year-over-year, though it rose 4.3% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | ~$24.6M (range $24.25M–$24.6M).”

surprises.description: Service revenue was $11.5 million, missing the preview’s roughly $14.5 million estimate and falling sequentially from Q1’s $13.3 million. This reversed the sequential uptrend the preview said was needed to support the recurring-revenue story.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Service revenue grew 6.2% to $11.5 million”; Q1 service revenue was listed in the preview as $13.3 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Service revenue (est.) ~$14.5M”; “service revenue needs to clear ~$14.7M to re-establish a sequential uptrend.”

surprises.description: Product revenue came in at $7.4 million, below the preview’s estimated $8–9 million. The shortfall was smaller than the service-revenue miss but added to the overall revenue disappointment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Product revenues dropped to $7.4 million from $14.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Product revenue (est.) ~$8–9M.”

surprises.description: Blink said the revenue-guidance reduction reflected its focus on revenue quality and the Envoy divestiture, rather than weak demand. That is more reassuring than the preview’s framing that a cut would indicate the turnaround was stalling.
surprises.fact_evidence: Blink cut guidance, “citing revenue-quality focus and the Envoy divestiture rather than weak demand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A cut converts BLNK from ‘turnaround executing’ to ‘turnaround stalling.’”

surprises.description: Q2 GAAP gross margin reached 38.9%, well above the preview’s roughly 33% base case and its 35% bull-case threshold. The reported margin improvement was stronger than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP gross margin expanded to 38.9% from 16.8% year-over-year”; adjusted gross margin was 47.9%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “GM ~33%,” and its bull case specified “GAAP GM ≥35%.”

surprises.description: Blink raised its FY2026 GAAP gross-margin outlook to approximately 38% from 35%, rather than merely maintaining the prior target. That is a meaningful upward revision to the full-year margin expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 GAAP gross margin outlook was raised to approximately 38% from 35% previously.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Standing guidance ... FY26 GAAP gross margin ~35%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to $2.2 million, substantially better than the preview’s expected loss of roughly $4–5 million. It also came close to the preview’s bull-case threshold of a loss no worse than $2 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to $2.2 million ... a 72% improvement and a multiyear low.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA (est.) ~−$4M to −$5M”; the bull case listed “adj. EBITDA ≥ −$2M.”

surprises.description: Management gave a concrete target to exit 2026 at approximately adjusted-EBITDA breakeven and said it expects positive adjusted EBITDA for full-year 2027. The preview had noted that management had previously declined to provide a 2026 breakeven target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management targets exiting 2026 at approximately breakeven adjusted EBITDA and a positive full-year adjusted EBITDA in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “has explicitly declined to provide a 2026 adjusted-EBITDA breakeven target.”

surprises.description: The disclosed 2026 DC build plan was 25 sites and 118 stalls, below the preview’s cited target of 27 sites and 136 stalls. The difference is modest but leaves the stated buildout smaller than the plan investors had been told to track.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Blink plans to build 25 DC fast charging sites (118 stalls) by end of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “27 sites / 136 stalls targeted” and said those were the Q1 targets.

in_line: Cash remained around the level implied by the preview’s burn scenario: the preview expected Q2 burn of $4–6 million from $38.0 million of Q1 cash and flagged cash below roughly $33 million as a concern; Blink reported roughly $34 million at quarter-end. The preview also stated the company had zero debt, consistent with the call’s no-debt report.
Blink reiterated the goal of recurring revenue reaching roughly 80% of total revenue by 2028, matching the preview’s stated service-revenue mix target.

surprises.description: Q3 sales guidance of about $13.5 million was below the preview’s $15 million-plus threshold for keeping the trucking ramp on track, and even below its $14–16 million base-case range. Management attributed the softer outlook to timing factors for EBITDA, but the sales guide itself is materially short of the preview’s expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for net sales of approximately $13.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 needs to guide to $15M+ with a line of sight to $17.5M”; the base case expected “Q3 guided $14–16M.”

surprises.description: Reported gross margin of 33.0% was well above the preview’s 22–25% expectation, but the margin included a $1.1 million tariff-refund benefit. Excluding that benefit, the margin would be about 24.7%, near the upper end of the expected range, so the headline outperformance was largely due to the refund.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded 470 basis points to 33.0%, though this included a $1.1 million benefit from tariff refund payments recognized in cost of sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “At $13.2M of revenue the fixed-cost absorption argument should deliver 22–25%.”

surprises.description: The company reported only $13.2 million of Q2 sales, $0.6 million below the $13.8 million consensus estimate, although it met its own $13.2 million guidance. The preview treated company guidance as the more reliable benchmark, making this a modest consensus shortfall rather than a miss against management’s guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales were $13.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | Company Guide (5/14/26) ~$13.2M | Consensus $13.8M”; the preview also says “the company’s own guidance is the more reliable benchmark.”

surprises.description: Lenders deferred senior leverage and fixed-charge coverage covenant compliance until September 2027, extending relief beyond the preview’s stated covenant-waiver period through December 2026. That is a more favorable financing runway than the preview described.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lenders ... deferred senior leverage and fixed charge coverage covenant compliance until September 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said covenants were “waived through 12/31/26.”

surprises.description: The Stevens Transport plan now involves a possible conversion of the customer’s full 2,500-truck fleet, with Werner and other carriers also advancing through the pipeline. The preview highlighted a Stevens order across about 500 trucks, so the broader fleet opportunity and additional carrier pipeline were incremental commercial upside, though not confirmed fleet-wide orders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Stevens Transport shipments have begun as the first phase of a plan to convert its full fleet of 2,500 trucks, with Werner Enterprises and additional carriers advancing through the pipeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Stevens Transport is a $3M+ order across ~500 trucks with deliveries starting Q2.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was a $1.6 million loss, $0.3 million better than the company’s guided $1.9 million loss and slightly better than the $2.7 million sequential improvement implied by guidance. This was a modestly better Q2 result despite continued losses.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was negative $1.6 million, a $0.6 million year-over-year improvement and a $3.0 million sequential improvement from Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | Company Guide (5/14/26) ~$(1.9)M”; the preview says this “implies $2.7M sequential improvement.”

in_line: Q2 sales met the company’s $13.2 million guide despite coming in below the preview’s $13.8 million consensus estimate.
DTC sales rose sequentially from the preview’s cited Q1 level of $3.7 million to $4.5 million; the preview specifically flagged sequential DTC growth as important.

The expected Dakota Lithium deal terms and Q4 contribution timing were broadly confirmed: the preview anticipated a $4 million purchase ($1 million cash and $3 million in stock) and Q4 accretion, and the call said the brand should become accretive to adjusted EBITDA in Q4.
The Q3 adjusted EBITDA guide of a $2.4 million loss falls within the preview’s base-case range of a $1.5–$2.5 million loss, even though the Q3 sales guide was below expectations.
The company reiterated the positive adjusted EBITDA target at an approximately $70 million annualized sales run rate; the preview had already identified that target as management’s breakeven marker.
The reduction in the minimum cash covenant and permission to pay the next two quarters of interest in kind were already anticipated in the preview.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was nearly $1 billion, up 20% year over year, versus preview estimates of $929–939 million and 12.6%–14% growth. That was a clear top-line beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue reached nearly $1 billion, representing 20% year-over-year growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | Q2 2026 Consensus | $929M ...; $939M”; the preview also described implied growth of “+13% to +14%.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS of $1.20 substantially exceeded the preview’s $0.92–$0.95 consensus range and the author’s $0.98 estimate, rather than landing near the expected level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP diluted EPS of $1.20.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP diluted EPS | $0.92 ...; $0.93–$0.95”; the preview’s “My estimates (base case)” were “non-GAAP EPS $0.98.”

surprises.description: VOXZOGO grew 14% against the preview’s forecast of about 5%, while patient growth and retention also held up despite the new competitor. Management said more than 20% more children were treated globally and approximately 90% of U.S. patients stayed on therapy.
surprises.fact_evidence: “VOXZOGO grew 14% year-over-year in Q2 with more than 20% growth in children treated globally, and approximately 90% of U.S. patients remained on therapy despite a U.S. competitor launch in February.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled VOXZOGO at “$232M (+5%)” and flagged the first competitor as “the entire bear case,” asking investors to watch treated-patient growth and any erosion.

surprises.description: Management quantified competitor switching at fewer than 100 patients over roughly six months, describing the impact as small relative to projected VOXZOGO revenue. The preview highlighted competitor entry as a major risk but had no quantified switching estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Competitor switching at approximately 10% of VOXZOGO patients, equating to fewer than 100 patient switches over roughly six months—a small impact on nearly $4 billion in projected revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called VOXZOGO’s first competitor “the entire bear case” and said “Competitor entry has been priced in as a fear, not yet as a number.”

surprises.description: BioMarin raised full-year revenue, VOXZOGO revenue, and non-GAAP EPS guidance, whereas the preview treated reaffirmation as the base case and said a raise would be a bull-case outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “BioMarin raised full-year 2026 guidance for total revenues, VOXZOGO revenue and non-GAAP diluted EPS.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case assumed FY26 guidance “reaffirmed at both revenue and EPS”; it said “FY26 revenue guide raised or narrowed to the top half” would characterize the bull scenario.

surprises.description: The disclosed $220 million annual synergy run rate by 2028 was above the preview’s bull-case threshold of at least $150 million. Management also specified that more than 70% would come from G&A, quantifying a substantial cost reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cost synergies of approximately $220 million annual run rate are expected by 2028, representing a ~50% reduction from Amicus’ 2025 non-GAAP operating expenses of $432 million, weighted over 70% toward G&A.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said synergy detail was due on the call and described “a named synergy number (≥$150M)” as part of its bull scenario.

surprises.description: Management put the combined peak-revenue potential at $2.6 billion, with Galafold at $1.4 billion and POMBILITI/OPFOLDA at $1.2 billion. The preview expected both assets could exceed Amicus’ prior roughly $1 billion-each framing, but did not anticipate these specific, higher figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Amicus acquisition adds combined peak revenue potential of $2.6 billion, with Galafold targeted at $1.4 billion ... and POMBILITI/OPFOLDA at $1.2 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had hinted “both assets can exceed Amicus’ prior $1B-each peak framing.”

surprises.description: The Amicus products showed sharply different growth rates: POMBILITI/OPFOLDA grew more than 65% pro forma while Galafold grew about 10%. The preview described Amicus revenue growth broadly as high-teens to low-20s, so the POMBILITI/OPFOLDA pace was much faster than that framing, while Galafold was slower.
surprises.fact_evidence: “On a pro forma basis Q2 Galafold grew ~10% and POMBILITI/OPFOLDA grew over 65% year-over-year, while total metabolic conditions revenue was $695 million, up 25%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Amicus’ FY25 revenue as “growing high-teens/low-20s.”

surprises.description: The deal was expected to be close to breakeven in 2026 and substantially accretive starting in 2027, with deleveraging pulled forward by about a year. The preview focused on debt and integration but did not provide an expected accretion or deleveraging timetable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Amicus deal is expected to be close to breakeven (modestly dilutive) in 2026 but substantially accretive to non-GAAP EPS beginning in 2027, with half or slightly more of synergies realized next year and deleveraging pulled forward by about one year.”

surprises.description: BioMarin submitted the VOXZOGO hypochondroplasia sNDA in 79 days from database lock, adding a roughly 14,000-patient global opportunity and targeting a 2027 launch. The preview anticipated a second-half 2026 submission but did not give this rapid filing timeline or market-size detail.
surprises.fact_evidence: “BioMarin submitted its sNDA for VOXZOGO in hypochondroplasia in just 79 days from database lock, targeting a ~14,000-patient global addressable market with anticipated launch in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said hypochondroplasia Phase 3 results supported a “2H’26 submission planned.”

surprises.description: BioMarin disclosed BMN 820, an oral CCR2 inhibitor for FSGS, with an estimated 30,000 U.S. addressable patients and Phase III data expected in 2028. The preview did not mention this asset or program.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New pipeline asset BMN 820 (oral CCR2 inhibitor for FSGS) targets an estimated 30,000 U.S. addressable patients with Phase III data expected in 2028.”

in_line: The preview estimated acquisition-debt interest at roughly $45–55 million per quarter; the call’s approximately $200 million annualized interest expense is broadly consistent with that run rate.
The preview expected a second-half 2026 hypochondroplasia submission; the sNDA was submitted in the second half of 2026, although the 79-day filing turnaround was new detail.

The preview expected both acquired Amicus products to have peak potential above the prior roughly $1 billion-per-product framing; the disclosed $1.4 billion Galafold and $1.2 billion POMBILITI/OPFOLDA targets are consistent with that direction.

surprises.description: Avalaya brought in $3.6 million in its first full commercial quarter, about 67% above the preview’s $2.15 million consensus estimate. The preview viewed the quarter’s revenue as a low-signal launch print, but the reported amount still materially exceeded that bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Avalaya (Ablea) generated $3.6 million in net product revenue in its first full commercial quarter for Hunter syndrome.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | Consensus | $2.15M”; the preview also described its estimate as “$2.0–2.5M.”

surprises.description: Management pushed DNL593 data from the preview’s expected year-end 2026 timing to the first half of 2027, a delay of at least several months. The stated reason was to allow longer observation of biomarkers.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DNL593 for FTD-granulin data was delayed from end of 2025 to first half of 2027 to allow longer observation of biomarkers like neurofilament light chain.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said DNL593 was guided “by end of 2026” and that the timing “must survive verbatim.”

surprises.description: Q3 product-revenue guidance of $10–12 million implies a fast sequential ramp, but is below the roughly $16 million per quarter H2 pace implied by the preview’s FY2026 revenue consensus. If Q3 lands within guidance, reaching that annual consensus would require a substantially higher Q4 quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided to Q3 net product revenue of $10-12 million, implying roughly 3x sequential growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY2026 revenue consensus of $33.97 million, less roughly $2.2 million expected in Q2, “leaves ~$31.8M for H2 — roughly $16M per quarter.”

surprises.description: Pro forma cash exceeded $1.15 billion, well above the preview’s estimate of $920–940 million exiting Q2. The comparison includes $195 million received in July from the voucher sale, so it is a pro forma figure rather than cash at June 30.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Pro forma cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities exceeded $1.15 billion, including $195 million received in July from the sale of a rare pediatric disease priority review voucher.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Cash + securities (6/30) … ~$920–940M.”

surprises.description: Denali reported concrete early access and engagement figures: policies covered more than half of lives, 14 state Medicaid programs listed coverage, and the company had engaged over 100 families. That is a positive launch signal against the preview’s uncertainty about payer access and patient metrics, though coverage was below the preview’s greater-than-70% bull-case marker.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Commercial policies covering more than 50% of lives have been established, with 14 state Medicaid programs publicly listing Ablea as covered in the first quarter of launch”; Denali “engaged more than 100 families, representing over one-quarter of eligible US patients.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “Payer coverage” and asked for “quantified launch metrics”; its bull case required “payer policy coverage above ~70% of covered lives.”

surprises.description: The DNL593 program also received FDA orphan drug designation, a favorable regulatory development the preview did not flag.
surprises.fact_evidence: DNL593 “recently received FDA orphan drug designation.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses were below the preview’s modeled level: Q2 R&D of $97 million and SG&A of $36.3 million total about $133 million, versus the preview’s roughly $141 million estimate. SG&A was also below the preview’s $40 million estimate and its $37 million marker for especially disciplined launch spending.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 R&D expenses were $97 million … while SG&A rose to $36.3 million … keeping overall OpEx roughly flat year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled “R&D expense … ~$101M” and “G&A expense … ~$40M”; it said “below ~$37M suggests disciplined, targeted deployment.”

in_line: Avalaya’s weight-based annual maintenance pricing—about $270,000 for a 10-kg patient to about $800,000 for a 30-kg patient—was broadly in line with the preview’s estimate of approximately $270,000 to $811,000.

The preview expected DNL921 clinical initiation and 2027 proof-of-concept work, and DNL628 Phase 1b data in 2027; the call reported that both programs had entered clinical development, with initial biomarker and proof-of-concept data expected in 2027.

surprises.description: MYQORZO product revenue was far above the preview’s implied $14–16M, reaching $25.3M; total revenue of $28.6M also exceeded the $17.6M consensus estimate. The strong product launch, rather than a recurring collaboration payment, drove the headline beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: MYQORZO generated $25.3 million in net product revenue ($23 million U.S., $2.3 million Europe); total Q2 revenue was $28.6 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus total revenue” of $17.6M; consensus “backs into roughly $14–16M of product sales.”

surprises.description: Acacia produced a better clinical result than the preview’s unresolved efficacy-and-safety debate implied: it met both primary endpoints and had no new safety signals. The preview had highlighted the LVEF signal and awaited the fuller data readout.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Phase III Acacia HCM trial in nonobstructive HCM met both dual primary endpoints (KCCQ Clinical Summary Score and peak VO2) with no new safety signals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for FDA feedback on “whether the agency has engaged on the LVEF signal” and said the later readout would show the “full efficacy-safety tradeoff,” including the 10% LVEF <50% rate.

surprises.description: The planned nHCM sNDA moved substantially earlier than the timing embedded in sell-side models: management plans to submit in Q4 2026 rather than the modeled H2 2027 filing window.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Acacia results support “a planned sNDA submission to the FDA in Q4 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said sell-side models “embed an H2 2027 filing” and clarified that this was a modeling assumption, not company guidance.

surprises.description: More than 80% of Q2 dispensed prescriptions were paid for, ahead of the preview’s expectation that paid conversion would hold above 70%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Over 80% of Q2 dispensed prescriptions” were paid for.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case assumed conversion “holds ~70%” and its checklist said investors wanted “>70% paid maintained.”

surprises.description: The reported 1,500 dispensed patients fell short of the preview’s 1,600–1,800 cumulative-patient in-line scenario, even as product revenue and paid conversion were stronger than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: MYQORZO “was dispensed to 1,500 patients by the end of Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario anticipated “in-line adds (~1,600–1,800 cumulative patients).”

surprises.description: The company raised its expense guidance instead of reaffirming the existing range, increasing the midpoint by $25M. Management attributed the increase to commercial readiness for a potential 2027 nHCM launch.
surprises.fact_evidence: FY2026 combined GAAP R&D and SG&A guidance rose to $860–890 million from $830–870 million, driven by commercial readiness investments for a potential 2027 nHCM launch.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Reaffirmation is expected”; it also noted a raise could reflect launch investment but would pressure runway.

surprises.description: The quarterly loss per share was narrower than expected: the company reported a $1.50 loss per share versus the preview’s $1.63 loss estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: Net loss was $198.8 million, or $1.50 per share.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 EPS estimate: “$(1.63).”

surprises.description: A public offering lifted cash and investments to about $1.7B, a significant financing outcome beyond the preview’s starting cash balance and discussion of a possible opportunistic raise. It improves liquidity, though the financing was an equity offering.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company ended Q2 with approximately $1.7 billion in cash and investments, up from $1.1 billion, largely from a May public offering generating roughly $760 million in net proceeds.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited cash and investments of “~$1.1B” and said “an opportunistic equity raise is a live risk.”

surprises.description: Management quantified a large potential treatment runway for obstructive HCM: it estimates only about one-fifth of eligible patients are treated today and that class penetration could eventually reach 60–70%. The preview did not provide these market-size or penetration estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management estimates 110,000–120,000 eligible oHCM patients, with about 20,000–25,000 treated (roughly 20% penetration), and projects peak class penetration of 60–70%.

in_line: The Maple HCM sNDA remained under review with the November 14, 2026 PDUFA date, as the preview expected to be confirmed.
Europe contributed $2.3M of MYQORZO revenue, consistent with the preview’s expectation of de minimis revenue from the first EU launch.

surprises.description: CTSO was expected to report revenue of about $9.3M–$9.39M and a year-over-year decline; it reported approximately $9.6M, flat year over year and up 9% sequentially. The result was modestly above the preview’s revenue estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was approximately $9.6 million, flat year-over-year but up 9% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $9.39M | My Estimate $9.3M”; the preview also modeled “Revenue YoY | –2% | –3%.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was expected to be about 69.5%; it came in at 73%, a sizeable beat. The company attributed the improvement to manufacturing optimization and cost management.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margins improved to 73%, up from 71% in the prior-year quarter and 69% in Q1 2026, driven by manufacturing optimization and cost management.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | … My Estimate 69.5%.”

surprises.description: The preview’s base case expected management to soften the H2 2026 operating-cash-flow break-even target to ‘exiting 2026.’ Instead, the company said it remained on track for break-even in the second half, with operating cash burn reduced to about $200,000 excluding restructuring costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash burn was reduced to approximately $200,000 excluding restructuring costs, keeping the company on track to reach operating cash flow break-even in the second half of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case anticipated “breakeven softened to ‘exiting 2026’” and warned to watch for a reframe from “H2 2026” to “exiting 2026” or “in 2027.”

surprises.description: Distributor and strategic partner revenue had been flat in Q1, and the preview treated a recovery as uncertain. It grew 16% year over year and 18% sequentially in Q2, a stronger channel result than the preview’s setup suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Distributor and strategic partner revenue grew 16% year-over-year and 18% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q1 distributors as “flat” and identified the revenue mix, including distributors, as a key metric to watch.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case expected Germany to stabilize, but Germany remained weak. That leaves the key sales-territory recovery unresolved despite the overall revenue beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Direct sales outside Germany rose 9%, offsetting continued weakness in Germany and the Middle East.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case assumed “Germany stabilizes but flat,” and called Germany’s return to growth the “single most important operating datapoint.”

surprises.description: The preview expected feedback on the DOAC pre-submission filed around June and cited a late-2026/early-2027 De Novo timeline. Instead, the company described two FDA pre-submission meetings still scheduled for later this month and said it would file a new De Novo after gathering more mechanistic and real-world evidence, leaving the submission path less settled than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to file a new de novo application for DrugSorb-ATR after gathering additional mechanistic and real-world evidence data, with two separate FDA pre-submission meetings scheduled later this month.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “FDA feedback on the DOAC … pre-submission filed ~June 2026” and described the De Novo timeline as “late 2026/early 2027.”

surprises.description: The upcoming DOAC pre-submission meeting covers a parallel indication and management framed the Eliquis/Xarelto market at about $20B. The preview discussed the DOAC pathway but described the combined opportunity as $500M–$1B, so the reported market framing is substantially larger, though it is not the same as an estimate of CTSO’s obtainable revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Two separate FDA pre-submission meetings [are] scheduled later this month, including one for a parallel DOAC-removal indication targeting the ~$20 billion Eliquis/Xarelto market.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed the DOAC indication and said the “Combined TAM [was] framed by management at $500M–$1B.”

surprises.description: The STAR-T CABG per-protocol analysis showed a statistically significant reduction in severe bleeding, an encouraging result not anticipated in the preview. However, the primary MITT endpoint was not statistically significant, tempering the positive signal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In the CABG per-protocol analysis of the STAR-T pivotal trial, DrugSorb-ATR achieved a statistically significant 58% risk reduction in severe bleeding or >1L blood loss (win ratio 1.59) with a number needed to treat of six, though the primary MITT endpoint was not statistically significant.”

surprises.description: The company plans to add three to five sales representatives through early 2027, mainly to restore German territory coverage. The preview discussed sales-team restructuring and Germany’s weakness, but did not anticipate this specific hiring plan; it could rebuild coverage while adding expense for a cash-constrained company.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Headcount has been reduced by roughly 23% since September 2025, and the company plans to selectively add three to five sales reps through early 2027, mainly to restore German territory coverage weakened by restructuring.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified Germany’s sales-team restructuring as a key issue but did not state that the company planned to rehire sales representatives.

surprises.description: Operating loss was $2.6M, slightly worse than the preview’s $2.4M estimate, even though it improved substantially year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating loss narrowed 27% to $2.6 million … versus the prior-year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Operating loss | … My Estimate $(2.4)M.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA loss was $1.6M, matching the preview’s estimate and falling within its $1.5M–$2.0M base-case range.

The GAAP net loss was largely an FX-driven result, as the preview cautioned that Q2 2025’s $1.9M net income was FX-related and that non-cash FX remeasurement could materially affect the comparison. The reported $0.07-per-share loss was close to the preview’s $0.06 GAAP estimate.

surprises.description: Full House's adjusted EBITDA grew 19.5%, well below the preview's implied expectation of roughly 35–45% growth. The gap is meaningful even though the preview cautioned that its EBITDA estimate was a back-solve rather than published consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated Q2 2026 revenues grew 5.6% while adjusted EBITDA rose 19.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: ... ~$15–16M implied”; the preview's back-solve described expected growth of “+35–45%.”

surprises.description: Revenue growth was slightly below the preview's 6.1% consensus-implied growth rate. The reported 5.6% increase points to a small shortfall, rather than the roughly 6.1% increase expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated Q2 2026 revenues grew 5.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview forecast Q2 revenue of “$78.4M” versus Q2 2025 actual revenue of “$73.9M,” implying “+6.1%.”

surprises.description: American Place grew faster than the preview's estimate: revenue reached $34.8 million, above the preview's $32.5–33.5 million range. It also reported its best quarter ever and a May monthly gaming revenue record, rather than the deceleration the preview was watching for.
surprises.fact_evidence: “American Place revenues increased 13.4% to $34.8 million”; it had “its best quarter ever” and “set a monthly gaming revenue record of $12.7 million in May 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated American Place revenue at “$32.5–33.5M” and flagged growth below roughly 5% as concerning, against a “+7.1% (Q1 26)” comparison.

surprises.description: Rising Star's results were hit by an unanticipated power outage: it moved from a $500,000 profit a year earlier to a $100,000 loss, with no insurance recovery expected. The preview did not flag this event.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rising Star lost $100,000 in the quarter due to a 42-hour power outage from a downed power line, versus a $500,000 profit a year earlier, with no business interruption insurance recovery expected.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed that Chamonix's win per position per day is only about half the Blackhawk average, indicating a substantial gap in current productivity. It also described sizeable potential if Chamonix reaches or exceeds that benchmark, an operational opportunity not quantified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Chamonix's win per position per day is only about $175, roughly half the Blackhawk average of $330,” with management targeting “roughly $30 million of annual EBITDA at the Blackhawk average and up to $40 million at a 15% premium.”

surprises.description: The city approved keeping the temporary Waukegan structure as an event center for five years after the permanent casino opens. The preview discussed the temporary casino's operating extension, but did not anticipate this additional use of the structure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gained city approval to retain the temporary structure as an event center for five years after the permanent casino opens.”

in_line: The preview expected West-segment EBITDA to be near breakeven in its base case; Chamonix's property EBITDA was approximately break-even, improving from a loss a year earlier. The reported figure is for Chamonix, not the full West segment, so it does not establish that the segment turned positive.

The refinancing remained in documentation, with management expecting a Q3 2026 close. That broadly matches the preview's base case of financing still “progressing / close” without signed terms; the preview had identified the financing as the central issue.
The temporary Waukegan operating extension to February 2029 was already reported as approved in the preview, and the call confirmed approval to operate until February 2029.
The roughly $302 million permanent Waukegan project budget and an opening around Q3 2028 were consistent with the preview's stated project budget and mid-2028 opening target.

surprises.description: Cash, equivalents and marketable securities were about $10 million, well above the preview’s $7.0–7.5 million estimate. Management also said it is targeting positive adjusted EBITDA using existing cash without a dilutive raise, rather than the preview’s base case of continued opportunistic ATM use.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash, equivalents and marketable securities declined to approximately $10 million as of June 30, 2026”; management is “targeting positive adjusted EBITDA by Q3 2027 using existing cash without a dilutive capital raise.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash & equiv. (6/30) … My estimate: $7.0–7.5M”; base case included “continued opportunistic ATM use.”

surprises.description: Management raised full-year revenue guidance to greater than 30% growth, whereas the preview expected roughly 30% growth to be reaffirmed. That is an upside change, although the call’s facts do not quantify how far above 30% the new outlook is.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to greater than 30% growth over 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 guidance of ~30% growth”; “FY ~30% reaffirmed” was the base case, and “a raise is the bull trigger.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to $1.8 million, but that was worse than the preview’s expected $1.3–1.6 million loss for the base case. The loss did improve sequentially and year over year, but it did not reach the preview’s expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed 26% year-over-year and 25% sequentially to $1.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base scenario: “Adj. EBITDA ($1.3M)–($1.6M)”; the preview also expected a clean quarter under the new cost base.

surprises.description: Revenue was flat sequentially at $9.5 million, below the preview author’s $10.0 million estimate and expected 4% sequential growth. It was essentially in line with published consensus, so the shortfall is against the preview’s higher estimate rather than consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $9.5 million, up approximately 28% year-over-year but flat sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate” was “$10.0M” and “+4% QoQ”; the preview also said revenue of at least $10.0M was a catalyst.

surprises.description: Prescription gammaCore growth was weaker than the recent momentum highlighted in the preview: revenue grew about 11% year over year and fell roughly 4% sequentially, compared with the preview’s cited Q1 gammaCore growth of 26%. The call did not provide total VA prescription revenue, so the preview’s $8.2 million VA base case cannot be directly tested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Prescription gammaCore revenue grew about 11% year-over-year but declined roughly 4% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “VA prescription revenue ($7.9M in Q1, +48% YoY; gammaCore +26%). … Base case ~$8.2M.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed that its top 15 VA accounts generated 54% of Q2 VA revenue, adding a concentration risk not quantified in the preview’s discussion of VA facility utilization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The top 15 VA accounts produced 54% of Q2 VA revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified VA prescription revenue and facility utilization as key metrics to watch, but gave no expectation for account concentration.

surprises.description: A staffing backlog at one facility pushed about $145,000 of revenue into Q3, an unanticipated timing delay that weighed on Q2 revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A staffing backlog at one facility pushed roughly $145,000 into Q3.”

surprises.description: Management named Q3 2027 as its target for positive adjusted EBITDA and gave specific expense-reduction levers, including lower sales incentives, a lower sales-and-marketing burden, and G&A savings from consolidating federal contracts. The preview said management had previously declined to name a breakeven quarter and expected a date only in its bull case.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management is “targeting positive adjusted EBITDA by Q3 2027”; it expects sales incentive expense to fall from about 35% to 27% of prescription revenue, total sales and marketing expense to reach roughly 54% by end of 2027, and contract consolidation to cut about 3% of G&A.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “explicitly declined to give” a breakeven quarter in Q1; a specific quarter was part of the bull-case signal.

surprises.description: The company added 17 sales representatives covering 29 VA medical centers and doubled its sales regions from three to six with minimal incremental cost. The preview sought a facility-depth update but did not anticipate this specific expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added 17 new 1099 sales reps covering 29 VA medical centers (about 20% of the network) and doubled sales regions from three to six with minimal incremental cost.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “watch for a facility-depth metric” tied to the goal of 75% of VA facilities at consistent utilization; it did not forecast this sales-force expansion.

in_line: Revenue of $9.5 million was essentially equal to the preview’s cited $9.494 million consensus, despite falling short of the preview author’s $10.0 million estimate.
Quell sales of $1.3 million cleared the preview’s $1.2 million-plus threshold for maintaining the implied ramp.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $40.9 million, far above the preview’s roughly $6 million estimate and the company’s $5–10 million guidance. Even excluding the $25 million tariff-related credit, EBITDA was $15 million, still above the guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA swung to $40.9 million from negative $16.5 million a year earlier, and even excluding the tariff benefit was $15 million, exceeding guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA ~$6M implied by EPS consensus”; company guidance was “$5–10M.”

surprises.description: Funko raised its full-year adjusted EBITDA outlook to $100–$110 million, well above the preview’s $70–$80 million company guidance and roughly $75 million consensus midpoint. The increase was driven mostly by the tariff credit, with another $5 million attributed to improved profitability.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year net sales guidance was reiterated at flat to up 3%, while adjusted EBITDA guidance was raised to $100-$110 million, driven by the $25 million tariff credit plus $5 million of improved profitability.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EBITDA” company guidance “$70–80M”; consensus “~$75M midpoint.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 56.6% as reported, boosted by the tariff credit, while normalized margin was 44.4%—above both the preview’s roughly 43% expectation and the top of the 42–44% guidance range. The normalized figure was also described as a record high.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin reached 56.6% versus 32.1% a year ago, but this included a $25 million tariff-related credit; normalized margin was 44.4%, still a record high and above the 42%-44% guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin ~43%”; company guidance “42–44%.”

surprises.description: Loungefly sales fell just 2% despite the roughly 50% SKU reduction, a much smaller decline than the preview’s expected high-single-digit contraction. This suggests the remaining assortment was far more productive than the preview’s base case implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Loungefly sales declined 2% but did so with roughly 50% fewer SKUs, signaling substantially improved SKU productivity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bull case needs the rate of decline to compress toward high single digits”; the base scenario expected Loungefly to be “still −15–20%.”

surprises.description: Sales growth was 7% year over year, above the preview’s roughly 3.5% consensus growth estimate and just above the company’s guided range of 1% to 6% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales rose 7% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus was “~$200M (StockStory, +3.5% y/y)” and company guidance implied “+1% to +6%.”

surprises.description: Wholesale sell-through was notably strong, with global point-of-sale units up 6% in Q2 and 9% year to date, and European POS growth above 20%. The preview discussed regional revenue and competitive pressure but did not anticipate or set an expectation for POS trends.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Wholesale point-of-sale trends were strong, with global POS up 6% in units in Q2 and 9% year-to-date, and European POS growth exceeding 20%.”

surprises.description: Funko used $15 million of the proceeds from selling its tariff claims to pay down debt, an additional concrete deleveraging step beyond the preview’s discussion of possible claim monetization. The preview highlighted the company’s leverage and liquidity constraints but did not anticipate this specific use of proceeds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company sold its IEEPA tariff claims for $19 million in proceeds and used funds to pay down $15 million of debt, continuing deleveraging.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Funko was “pursuing refunds and exploring monetizing the claims,” but did not specify a debt repayment.

surprises.description: Management identified potential freight and oil cost increases as downside risks to guidance, a cost-risk concern the preview had not specifically raised. Tariffs themselves were already a watched issue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management flagged tariffs (currently 10%-12%) and potential freight/oil cost increases as key downside risks to guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed tariff-refund optionality and said current tariff rates were “running below plan,” but did not mention freight or oil costs.

surprises.description: Management announced that Kristin Hamilton would become Chief Commercial Officer on August 24, a leadership change not anticipated in the preview. The provided facts do not establish the change’s likely business impact.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Announced a new Chief Commercial Officer, Kristin Hamilton, starting August 24.”

in_line: Full-year net sales guidance was reiterated at flat to up 3%, as the preview expected management to reiterate its sales outlook.
