surprises.description: CarGurus raised its full-year profitability outlook: instead of the previewed 1.5–2.5 points of adjusted EBITDA margin compression, it now expects only about 0.5–1.5 points of compression, citing AI-driven efficiency gains.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management now expects 2026 adjusted EBITDA margins to compress only ~50 to 150 basis points versus 2025, citing AI-driven efficiency gains.
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY2026 guide: adj. EBITDA margin down 1.5–2.5pts vs. 2025 (explicit “investment year”).

surprises.description: International revenue grew 28%, below the preview’s 30% threshold for avoiding a negative surprise and well below the 39% growth cited for Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: International revenue growing 28% year-over-year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Sub-30% growth would be a negative surprise.”

surprises.description: Management described dealer spending as softer than the preview’s stable-to-modestly-supportive market backdrop suggested, citing dealer margin pressure, fewer days on lot, and FTC pricing rules. It tempered that concern by calling the factors temporary and noting some improvement over the first half.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management attributes softer dealer spending to temporary factors—dealer margin pressure, fewer days on lot, and FTC all-in pricing rules—rather than structural issues, noting some improvement over the first half.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net: a stable-to-modestly-supportive dealer ad-spend environment.”

surprises.description: Q2 buybacks were only $29 million, a sharp reduction from the $175 million repurchased in Q1 and a realization of the preview’s concern that a much slower pace could remove an EPS tailwind. Year-to-date repurchases nevertheless reached $204 million of the $250 million program.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company repurchased $29 million in shares in Q2 (bringing year-to-date buybacks to $204 million of the $250 million 2026 program).
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A sharply reduced Q2 repurchase pace removes an EPS crutch and signals balance-sheet caution.”

surprises.description: Cash generation and liquidity improved more than the preview’s cash-focused setup implied: free cash flow was $88 million and cash ended the quarter at $122 million, up $50 million sequentially from the cited Q1 balance of $72 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company converted 103% of adjusted EBITDA into $88 million of free cash flow, ending the quarter with $122 million in cash, up $50 million sequentially.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$175M of buyback against $63.2M of FCF drew cash down to $72M.”

surprises.description: PriceVantage showed stronger reported traction than the preview’s adoption-versus-monetization debate alone anticipated: bookings grew more than 50% sequentially, and adopting dealers saw higher VDPs and leads per listing.
surprises.fact_evidence: PriceVantage bookings grew more than 50% sequentially, with adopting dealers seeing a median 15% lift in VDPs and 9% lift in leads per listing.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The question the buy side will press: how much of this is free/bundled trial versus incremental ARPU already inside QARSD?”

surprises.description: The reported call facts give PriceVantage adoption and dealer-performance measures but no quantification of incremental ARPU, leaving the preview’s central AI-monetization question unanswered.
surprises.fact_evidence: The reported PriceVantage figures were bookings growth and lifts in VDPs and leads per listing; no incremental ARPU figure is provided in the call facts.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any quantification of incremental ARPU from Shopper Signals / PriceVantage / Dealership Mode would be a narrative unlock; continued adoption-only stats will read as deflection.”

in_line: Q2 revenue of $251 million was near the roughly $249.85 million consensus and within the $247–252 million company range, consistent with the preview’s $250–251 million base case.
Adjusted EBITDA of $85 million landed at the high end of company guidance; the roughly 200-basis-point year-over-year margin decline was close to the preview’s roughly 210-basis-point estimate.
The company reiterated full-year revenue growth guidance of 10%–13%, as the preview expected.
Q3 revenue guidance of $253.5–258.5 million was broadly in line with the preview’s $253–257 million base-case range, and the deceleration from Q2 growth was anticipated.
U.S. dealer adds and QARSD were within the preview’s expected ranges: 673 net paying dealer adds versus a 500–800 base-case range, and 8% U.S. QARSD growth versus an expected 7%–8%.
Add-on product adoption remained the largest driver of QARSD growth, consistent with the preview’s expectation that product-led dealer re-acquisition would support the business.

surprises.description: Total operating revenue and other income was $744.3 million, above the preview’s $716.35 million consensus and its $690–720 million base case. That is a positive departure from the preview’s modal expectation of an optical revenue miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total operating revenue and other income increased 89% year-over-year to $744.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $716.35M”; the base case forecast was “$690–720M” and the bottom line said the modal outcome was “a revenue ‘miss’.”

surprises.description: Diluted EPS of $2.50 edged above the preview’s working consensus range of $2.41–$2.49, though it was within the preview’s broader base-case range of $2.35–$2.60. The beat versus the cited consensus band was narrow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income attributable to common shareholders was $47.4 million … or $2.50 per diluted share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat $2.41–$2.49 as the working consensus band.”

surprises.description: ROE reached 28.1%, above the preview’s recent mid-20s reference point and the company’s 20% long-term target. That was stronger than simply sustaining the mid-20s level the preview identified as a potential positive signal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Return on average equity reached 28.1%, materially exceeding the company's long-term target of 20%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ROE … 26.8%” in Q1; “Sustained mid-20s materially re-rates the multiple.”

surprises.description: Interest expense was essentially flat sequentially at about $123 million, even though the preview cited management’s expectation for quarterly interest expense to increase through 2026. The company also reported tighter spreads on term ABS and its first AAA bond ratings, favorable funding developments the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Interest expense more than doubled to $123 million from $54 million”; it reflected Mercury debt and growth financing, but “the company issued term ABS at tighter spreads and achieved its first AAA bond ratings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management explicitly guided to ‘increased quarterly interest expense throughout 2026.’”

surprises.description: Managed receivables reached $6.9 billion, slightly below the preview’s roughly $7.0 billion base-case expectation. Sequential growth was only 2.5%, a modest shortfall against that benchmark.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total managed receivables grew approximately 126% year-over-year to $6.9 billion, up 2.5% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “receivables ~$7.0B.”

surprises.description: Management said ROE should move back toward 20% as the company delevers, tempering the possibility of sustained mid-20s returns suggested by the preview’s ROE discussion. The strong quarter therefore came with a more modest outlook for maintaining that level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects ROE to revert toward 20% as the company delevers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Sustained mid-20s materially re-rates the multiple”; the base case anticipated “no change to the 20% ROE framing.”

surprises.description: Direct mail originations were behind plan and solicitation volumes above 50% year over year were raising acquisition costs. The preview had flagged lower mail response rates and higher marketing spend, but did not anticipate originations falling behind plan; digital originations running ahead of plan partly offset the issue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Direct mail solicitation volumes are up over 50% year-over-year, raising customer acquisition costs and leaving direct mail originations behind plan, though digital originations are running ahead of plan.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said mail response rates were “somewhat lower due to increased mail solicitation” and flagged “acquisition cost per account.”

surprises.description: The quarter still benefited from a $5.5 million favorable Mercury contingent-consideration adjustment. The preview emphasized that Q1 had received a much larger favorable earnout release and that the Q2 EPS hurdle required underlying improvement, so the additional favorable adjustment means the result was not entirely free of one-off support.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A $5.5 million favorable adjustment to Mercury-related contingent consideration boosted the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 included “~$13M of favorable contingent-consideration release” and that consensus required “underlying sequential improvement”; it also noted concern if a beat came from “another favorable mark.”

surprises.description: Management introduced the possibility of capital actions if ROE remains in the high 20s. The preview discussed the ROE target and returns but did not flag potential capital actions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Capital actions [are] possible if it stays in the high 20s.”

in_line: The combined principal net charge-off rate was up only modestly sequentially, with a slight further rise expected next quarter; this is consistent with the preview’s warning that Q1’s tax-season credit benefit would reverse and its focus on seasonal credit normalization.

Interest expense remained high year over year, consistent with the preview’s warning about rising funding costs; the surprise was that it was nearly flat sequentially and that funding access improved.

surprises.description: Century’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA guide of $325–345 million was well above the preview’s $270–300 million base-case expectation. The guide is especially strong given management’s stated summer energy and hedge-settlement headwinds.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management guided Q3 2026 adjusted EBITDA to a range of $325 million to $345 million, with headwinds including $10-15 million in summer energy costs and $20-25 million from realized hedge settlements.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected Q3 guided EBITDA of $270–300M; it said consensus math needed at least $300M.

surprises.description: Century’s Q2 net sales were $752 million, well below the preview’s $818.7 million consensus estimate, even though realized LME and regional premiums were higher and shipments increased sequentially.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 net sales rose $103 million sequentially to $752 million, driven by higher realized LME and regional premiums, plus a 6% shipment increase to ~131,000 tonnes.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2'26 consensus revenue of $818.7M.

surprises.description: Century shipped about 131,000 tonnes in Q2, below the preview’s expected recovery toward 135,000–145,000 tonnes. Shipments did rise 6% sequentially, but the quarter fell short of the anticipated range.
surprises.fact_evidence: Shipments increased 6% to ~131,000 tonnes.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q2 shipments should recover from 122,865t toward ~135–145kt.

surprises.description: Century’s adjusted EPS of $2.46 exceeded the preview’s $2.35 consensus estimate, despite the revenue shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 adjusted net income was $257 million ($2.46/share).
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2'26 consensus adjusted EPS of $2.35.

surprises.description: Century’s realized LME price was $3,250 per tonne, $75 above the $3,175-per-tonne assumption in its Q2 guide. The preview considered that assumption conservative-to-fair, so the realized price was a modest favorable variance.
surprises.fact_evidence: Realized LME was up $350 to $3,250/tonne.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2'26 guided realized LME at $3,175/t and said the assumption looked “conservative-to-fair.”

surprises.description: Century reduced net debt to $98 million, substantially below the preview’s cited $220 million level, and reported that cash exceeded total debt by the end of July. The preview had noted that capital returns might become possible after credits and recoveries cleared, but did not anticipate this degree of debt reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: Net debt reduced to $98 million with $66 million in debt repayments, and cash on hand exceeded total debt as of end of July after receiving a $94 million 45X tax credit and ~$20 million in insurance recoveries.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited net debt of $220M and said returns were possible once project spend, insurance recoveries and 45X credits cleared.

surprises.description: A new executive order lets Century import up to 300,000 metric tons annually from 2027 at a 25% tariff rather than 50%, creating a potential earnings and cash-flow benefit that the preview did not flag.
surprises.fact_evidence: A new July 20 executive order will let Century import up to 300,000 metric tons annually at a reduced 25% tariff (versus 50%) starting in 2027, a potentially material EBITDA and cash flow benefit to help fund the Oklahoma project.

surprises.description: Century’s retained 6.8% Hawesville stake gained a potential monetization catalyst after partner TeraWulf signed Anthropic to a 20-year lease expected to generate about $19 billion in total lease revenue. The preview did not anticipate this data-center development.
surprises.fact_evidence: Century's retained 6.8% stake in the Hawesville data center gained value as partner TeraWulf signed Anthropic to a 20-year lease expected to generate ~$19 billion in total lease revenue, with monetization possible beginning one year after 2027 energization.

surprises.description: Management described a persistent global aluminum deficit of about 1 million tonnes and inventory days approaching all-time lows, supporting elevated prices. That outlook contrasts with the preview’s emphasis on falling LME prices and a potential H2 price reset.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects a persistent global aluminum deficit of ~1 million tonnes in 2026 continuing into 2027, with global inventory days of consumption approaching all-time lows, supporting elevated prices.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described LME aluminum’s slide from ~$3,790–3,855/t to ~$3,170/t in late July and said the market had pre-traded the H2 price reset.

surprises.description: Century expects the new Jamalco turbine to enable fully self-generated energy from August and save roughly $20 per tonne, an operational cost benefit the preview did not specify. Lower-quality bauxite remains a modest offsetting headwind for a couple more quarters.
surprises.fact_evidence: The new TG4 power turbine at Jamalco enables full self-generated energy starting August, delivering roughly $20/tonne in cost savings, though lower-quality bauxite remains a modest headwind for a couple more quarters.

in_line: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $327 million, within the preview’s cited company-guidance range of $315–335 million and its $320–335 million base-case range.
The Oklahoma JV remained on track for FID and groundbreaking by year-end, consistent with the preview’s expectation; the preview also cited the secured $500 million DOE grant.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $1.4 million, far below the preview’s $11.33 million consensus estimate. The preview expected ratable Regeneron revenue, but the $37 million payment is to be recognized over several years, while the BMS and Astellas collaborations that had contributed revenue have concluded.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue fell to $1.4 million from $18.7 million in Q2 2025, primarily due to the conclusion of the BMS and Astellas collaborations”; the July Regeneron payment is “to be recognized over several years as work progresses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Q2 2026E | $11.33M”; the preview says consensus “clearly assumes ratable” recognition of the Regeneron payment.

surprises.description: Cash at quarter-end was $330.3 million, below the preview’s expectation of about $365 million because the additional $37 million Regeneron payment arrived in July rather than during Q2. After that payment, pro forma cash was approximately $367 million, close to the preview’s expected level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CytomX ended Q2 2026 with $330.3 million in cash”; it “received an additional $37 million payment from Regeneron in July,” bringing pro forma cash to “approximately $367 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 should be up sequentially: ~$18M burn offset by the $37M Regeneron cash receipt → ~$365M expected.”

surprises.description: R&D spending came in below the preview’s estimate: $17.6 million versus an estimated $20–22 million. Total operating expenses were $25.2 million, below the preview build’s implied total of roughly $30.5–32.5 million using its R&D and G&A estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses rose to $25.2 million” and “R&D [was] up $4.3 million to $17.6 million, driven by Varseta-M manufacturing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My build … R&D ~$20–22M … G&A ~$10.5M”; the preview also said a “jump to $24M+ signals commitment.”

in_line: The Regeneron payment was recognized over time rather than as a point-in-time revenue boost, consistent with the preview’s expectation of ratable recognition; its eventual receipt also brought pro forma cash close to the preview’s estimate.
Cash runway was projected to last at least through the second half of 2028, as the preview expected.
The comprehensive Varseta-M Phase I data update remained on track for 2026: the call said it is expected by year-end, within the preview’s expected second-half 2026 window.
The planned first Varseta-M registrational monotherapy study remained targeted for the first half of 2027, as expected.
Preliminary PFS of 6.8–7.1 months at the top two doses was consistent with the 6.8–7.1-month PFS already cited in the preview.
The 10% Grade 3 diarrhea rate was consistent with the 10% rate referenced in the preview’s discussion of dose-optimization cohorts.
The company described non-CRC Varseta-M expansion cohorts, as the preview anticipated; it named gastric/GEJ, pancreatic, and biliary tract cancers.
The bevacizumab, 5-FU, and leucovorin combination study was set to launch in Q4 2026, within the preview’s anticipated second-half 2026 start window.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $49 million, below the preview’s estimated $50–51 million buy-side bar, even though it exceeded the published $48.21 million consensus. The preview had specifically warned that a $48–49 million print would miss the market’s positioning.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue reached $49 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat the buy-side whisper as ~$50–51M, not $48.2M”; “A print of $48–49M … would be a miss versus how the stock is positioned.”

surprises.description: Cryoport reaffirmed its $192–196 million FY26 revenue range instead of raising it as the preview expected after a Q2 beat. Management cited geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty, and the preview characterized a reaffirmation as signaling caution about the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cryoport affirmed its full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $192 to $196 million, citing geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty as reason for conservatism despite ~$97 million first-half revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A repeat implies $194–198M. Simply reaffirming $192–196M after another mid-single-digit beat would signal H2 caution”; “FY26 guidance raised to ≥$194M at the low end.”

surprises.description: Commercial cell and gene therapy revenue reached $9.4 million, below the preview’s expected threshold of more than $10 million, and growth was 9% versus 26% in Q1. The services portion grew 26%, but that did not prevent the total commercial CGT line from falling short of the preview’s bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Commercial cell and gene therapy revenue grew 9% to $9.4 million, but the services portion grew 26% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch: does the count move 21 → 22/23, and does commercial CGT clear $10M?”; “Commercial CGT ≥$10M.”

surprises.description: Life Science Services grew 15%, below the preview’s expectation that it would sustain roughly its Q1 growth trend of 17–18%. At 57% of $49 million in total revenue, the segment was about $27.9 million, just below the preview’s $28 million threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Life Science Services growing 15% year-over-year and representing 57% of total revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Life Sciences Services at Q1’s +18% trend”; “Life Sciences Services ≥ $28M”; base case: “Services does the work (+17–18%).”

surprises.description: Management’s outlook for new therapy approvals was lower than the preview’s stated expectation: up to five new therapy approvals, plus one label or geographic expansion, rather than up to eight new approvals. The preview’s expected number of BLA/MAA filings was exceeded, but the lower approval outlook is a separate disappointment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For the balance of 2026, up to 11 possible BLA/MAA filings, five new therapy approvals, and one label/geographic expansion approval among clients.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided to up to 8 new approvals in the remainder of 2026, 10 BLA/MAA filings, and 5 therapies with set PDUFA dates.”

surprises.description: First-half operating cash flow improved by $17 million year over year to approximately $5 million, a favorable cash-generation result not forecast in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half 2026 net cash from operating activities was approximately $5 million, a $17 million improvement over the first half of 2025.”

surprises.description: The company raised its expected number of possible client BLA/MAA filings for the balance of 2026 to as many as 11, above the preview’s figure of 10.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For the balance of 2026, up to 11 possible BLA/MAA filings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided to … 10 BLA/MAA filings.”

surprises.description: Cryoport began producing cryogenic freezers domestically in China to avoid tariffs and improve competitiveness, a specific operational response not anticipated in the preview. The stated exposure is limited because China represents only 2–3% of revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “China represents only 2-3% of total revenue, and the company began producing cryogenic freezers domestically in China to avoid tariffs and improve competitiveness.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA was positive at $0.4 million, meeting the preview’s key threshold of at least breakeven and falling within its base-case range of negative $0.5 million to positive $1.0 million.
Cryoport supported 22 commercial therapies, in line with the preview’s expectation that the count would move from 21 to 22 or 23.

Clinical trials supported increased to 779, including 94 in Phase III, broadly continuing the growth and commercialization-funnel trend the preview highlighted from Q1’s 766 trials and 91 in Phase III.

surprises.description: Q2 GTV was $10.35 billion, up 14%, versus the preview's $10.2 billion consensus and $10.23 billion base case. That also exceeded the prior company-guidance ceiling of $10.25 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 GTV reached $10.35 billion, up 14% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus ~$10.2B” and “My base case: $10,230M”; company guide was “$10,100–10,250M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $313 million, ahead of the preview's $298 million consensus and $305 million base case, as well as the top of the company's $290–300 million guide. At about 3.0% of GTV, it also cleared the preview's 3.0% margin marker.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 19% to $313 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus ~$298M,” “My base case: $305M,” and company guide “$290–300M”; the preview also highlighted “Printing ≥3.0%” as a margin milestone.

surprises.description: Advertising and other revenue grew 16% to $297 million, above the preview's $289–290 million expectations and the company's 11–14% growth guide. This extended the faster-growth trend the preview was watching.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Advertising and other revenue grew 16% year-over-year to $297 million,” lifting the investment rate to “2.9% from 2.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “~$289M” consensus and “$290M” base case, against a company growth guide of “+11–14%”; it said “≥15% sustains the ‘ads reaccelerating’ narrative.”

surprises.description: Cash generation reversed the weak conversion trend highlighted in the preview: operating cash flow rose 143% and free cash flow rose 156%. The improvement was substantially driven by collecting a large receivables balance, so the surge was not solely evidence of a durable change in cash conversion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow surged 143% to $493 million and free cash flow jumped 156% to $480 million, largely driven by a large accounts receivable balance collected in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted Q1 “OCF $268M (-10% YoY), FCF $253M (-10%)” and called out “FCF conversion and buyback pace” as a key metric to watch.

surprises.description: Management said it would widen guidance ranges beginning in Q3 and now expects to land at the midpoint, rather than continuing the historical pattern of beating the high end. That is a more cautious framework than the preview's expectation that the company would likely clear the high end of guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management changed its guidance philosophy starting Q3 2026, widening ranges and stating it now expects to land within the range at the midpoint, rather than beating the high end as it had done historically.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the company has cleared the high end of GTV guidance recently” and described the usual pattern as “GTV at/just above the high end, EBITDA a few million over.”

surprises.description: AOV rose 4% to $115, above the preview's $113.2 base case and roughly $113 consensus. The stronger basket size helped GTV grow faster than orders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Average order value rose 4% to an industry-leading $115, with GTV outpacing order growth driven by deepening engagement and strong club retailer performance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed consensus AOV of “~$113” and a base case of “$113.2 (+3.1%).”

surprises.description: New-customer activation reached its fastest year-over-year growth rate since 2022, a positive demand signal not specifically anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Instacart activated net new customers at its fastest year-over-year growth rate since 2022.”

surprises.description: Found rate and perfect order fill rate both improved for a 16th consecutive quarter, an ongoing service-quality improvement the preview did not specifically forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Improved both found rate and perfect order fill rate for the 16th consecutive quarter.”

surprises.description: GAAP net income fell 4% even as adjusted EBITDA rose, whereas the preview cited consensus for GAAP diluted EPS growth. The call attributed the decline primarily to higher stock-based compensation after annual equity grants' first vesting date shifted from August to May; no EPS result was provided in the facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net income fell 4% to $111 million, primarily due to higher stock-based compensation from shifting the first vesting date of annual equity grants from August to May.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “GAAP diluted EPS” consensus of “$0.55 (+34%),” while cautioning that vendor definitions were inconsistent.

in_line: Total revenue of $1.04 billion was close to the preview's $1.03 billion consensus and $1.035 billion base case.
Orders grew 9% to 90.3 million, broadly matching the preview's estimate of about 90 million and 9.3% growth.

Gross profit was 7.3% of GTV, up from 7.2% in Q1. That avoided the further sequential decline the preview flagged as a concern and was consistent with its base case of roughly flat gross profit as a share of GTV.

Q3 guidance included 14% GTV growth and 19% adjusted EBITDA growth at the midpoint, with advertising growth guided at 15–18%. The GTV midpoint of $10.425 billion was just above the preview's bull-case marker of $10.4 billion, and the advertising range met its threshold of at least 15% growth.

The company repurchased $325 million of shares and reiterated that it remains on track to return the majority of free cash flow through repurchases, consistent with the preview's stated capital-return commitment.

surprises.description: Q1 revenue was $157 million, well above the preview’s $151.7 million consensus and the $151–152 million company guide. The 3% beat over the guide’s high end and return to 7% growth were stronger than the preview’s base case of a small beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY27 revenue reached $157 million, up 7% year-over-year, beating the high end of guidance by 3% and reaccelerating growth after prior slower quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | Consensus $151.7M | Company Guide $151–152M”; the base case anticipated “Small beat on a sandbagged guide.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $75 million, materially above the preview’s $68.5–69.5 million guide. That is a much larger beat than the preview’s expectation that margins would be in line.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was $75 million (48% margin), exceeding the high end of guidance by 8%, driven by flow-through of incremental revenue growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$69M | $68.5–69.5M”; the base case expected “margins in line.”

surprises.description: Doximity raised FY27 revenue guidance by $6 million, rather than reaffirming the prior range, and the new midpoint is above the $670.3 million consensus. The raise was positive but did not reach the preview’s bull-case threshold of at least $680 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year FY27 revenue guidance by $6 million to a range of $671-681 million (5% growth at midpoint).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “reaffirms FY27” was the base case and described a raise to “≥$680M” as bull-case; consensus was “$670.3M.”

surprises.description: Despite raising revenue guidance, Doximity lowered its full-year adjusted EBITDA margin outlook to about 47% from 49%, citing increased AI investment. This is a clear deterioration from the preview’s stated margin guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “[It] lowered the full-year adjusted EBITDA margin to ~47% due to increased AI investment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 adj. EBITDA | ~$329M | $323–335M | 49% margin.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue guidance of $170–171 million falls below the preview’s derived $173–176 million Street range. The midpoint implies only 1% year-over-year growth, weaker than the preview’s expected Q2 bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 FY27 revenue guidance of $170-171 million implies only 1% year-over-year growth at midpoint, reflecting a tough comparison against last year's 23% growth and minimal AI search revenue in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Derived Q2 FY27 bar (not directly sourced): ... roughly $173–176M for the September quarter.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP gross margin fell to 88% from 89% in the prior quarter, and management expects mid-to-high-80s gross margins for the year. That indicates the AI compute pressure continued rather than stabilizing at the prior-quarter level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin declined to 88% (non-GAAP) from 91% a year ago due to higher AI compute spend, with management guiding gross margins to the mid-to-high 80% range for the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Non-GAAP gross margin (89% in Q4)” and said to watch whether “AI compute drag stabilizes or keeps stepping down”; its base case assumed “margins in line.”

surprises.description: The count of customers generating over $500,000 in annual subscription revenue was 127, below the preview’s estimate of 129. The shortfall is modest, although these customers still accounted for 83% of revenue, as the preview had indicated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “127 customers generating over $500,000 in annual subscription revenue, contributing 83% of total revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Customers >$500K TTM sub rev | 129 | ... (125 in Q4).”

surprises.description: AI engagement indicators included a 25% quarter-over-quarter increase in prompt volume and a tenfold year-over-year increase in AI scribe users in July. The preview described growing AI usage, but did not anticipate these specific adoption rates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI prompt volume rose over 25% quarter-over-quarter, and AI scribe users grew 10x in July versus prior year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that “AI Search + Scribe users tripled in nine months” and that “~half used AI tools,” but gave no expectation for prompt-volume or scribe-user growth at these rates.

surprises.description: The company reported 165 signed health system AI clients, providing a fresh indication of commercial reach that the preview did not quantify. The preview had cited 140 health systems live previously, but did not give a directly comparable forecast for signed AI clients.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company now has 165 signed health system AI clients (including Northwestern, Penn Medicine and University of Michigan).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “140 health systems live” and described first pharma AI Search deals, but did not forecast a count of signed health system AI clients.

surprises.description: Doximity repurchased $92 million of shares in Q1 and reported that diluted shares were down 5%. The preview identified the buyback pace as a watch item and said an aggressive Q1 repurchase would be a positive signal, but provided no expected dollar amount.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Doximity repurchased $92 million of shares in Q1 (with ~$400 million remaining in the program) ... and reduced diluted shares 5% to 191 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked to watch “Buyback pace” and said “Aggressive Q1 repurchase at $18–22 is a strong management signal”; it noted “$493M authorization remaining.”

in_line: AI Search generated no revenue in Q1, consistent with the preview’s warning of “minimal AI revenue contribution in the first half”; the preview expected material revenue beginning in Q3, and the call said the majority of contracted AI Search revenue is expected to be recognized in Q3.
Quarterly active workflow prescribers grew over 30% year-over-year, consistent with the preview’s cited prior trend of “800K+ quarterly active prescribers, +30% YoY.”

The No Harm study’s favorable results for Doximity’s Ask product were not a new directional surprise: the preview already said Doximity had cited an independent Stanford–Harvard study in which it “outranked OpenEvidence and frontier models.”
Large customers continued to contribute 83% of revenue, matching the preview’s cited figure that “large accounts = 83% of revenue.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $138 million, above the preview’s $131.4 million consensus and its $135 million base case. The beat was about 5% versus consensus, though closer to the preview’s own estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 33% year-over-year to $138 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 Consensus” revenue: “$131.4M”; “My Base Case” total revenue: “$135M.”

surprises.description: Grindr’s new 2026 revenue guidance of approximately $540 million was below the preview’s $542–545 million buy-side expectation and slightly below the cited $541.4 million FY consensus, despite being raised from $535 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Grindr raised full-year 2026 guidance to approximately $540 million in revenue (up from $535 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Buy-side expects ≥$542M revenue”; the preview’s base case anticipated a guide “nudged to ≥$542–545M.” FY2026 revenue consensus was “~$541.4M.”

surprises.description: The adjusted EBITDA margin was 42%, below the preview’s roughly 43% expectation and its stated threshold of holding at least 43%. Adjusted EBITDA dollars, however, were within the preview’s expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA of $58 million at a 42% margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “$58M (43.0% margin),” cited consensus of “~43%,” and said to watch whether the margin “holds ≥43%.”

surprises.description: The Edge AI-enabled premium tier showed better-than-expected retention, and some non-paying users converted directly, an outcome management said differed from its initial assumptions. The preview identified Edge as important but did not anticipate these specific conversion and retention signals.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retention exceeding expectations and some non-paying users converting directly, contrary to initial assumptions.”

surprises.description: Management reported a large AI-related productivity gain: engineering output rose about 2.5 times with roughly the same team, avoiding an estimated 200 additional engineers and about $60 million in annual cost. The preview did not flag this specific productivity or cost-avoidance result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Engineering output increased approximately 2.5x from July 2025 to April 2026 with roughly the same team size, avoiding the need for an estimated 200 additional engineers and about $60 million in annual cost.”

surprises.description: App-based revenue reached $113 million, growing 30%, above the preview’s estimate of about $111 million and 27% growth. This added to the overall revenue beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “App-based revenue grew 30% year-over-year to $113 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case estimated “App/direct revenue” of “~$111M (+27%).”

surprises.description: Advertising revenue was $25 million and grew 44%, ahead of the preview’s approximately $24 million estimate and its watchpoint of whether growth would remain above about 35%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Advertising revenue grew 44% to $25 million, driven by programmatic strength and a year-long direct brand campaign.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Advertising/indirect” at “~$24M (+41%)” and asked whether Q2 ad growth would “hold above ~35%.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA of $58 million was within the preview’s expected $56–58 million range, even though the reported margin was below the preview’s 43% expectation.
The company raised its full-year guidance rather than merely reaffirming it, as the preview expected a raise; the revenue level was below the preview’s buy-side and base-case expectations.

Management expects growth to decelerate in Q3 and Q4 as pricing changes anniversary and stronger 2025 comparisons are lapped, consistent with the preview’s warning that second-half growth would moderate.
Advertising’s expected 2026 mid-to-high-teens share of revenue and normalization toward 15% in 2027 were already described in the preview.
Another accelerated share repurchase was consistent with the preview’s expectation of continued aggressive buybacks.

surprises.description: ESCO’s 8% organic sales growth came in below the preview’s roughly 10–12% underlying-growth expectation, while reported sales growth of 14% was also slightly below the 15.3% consensus growth implied by the preview. The $23 million of incremental Maritime revenue explains part of the reported growth but does not close the organic-growth gap.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reported sales rose 14% (8% organic), with the balance from $23 million of incremental Maritime acquisition revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Organic revenue growth ex-Maritime” was ranked highest importance; the preview cited “~10–12% expectation” and said consensus growth of 15.3% was “now essentially an all-organic number.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $2.20 exceeded the $2.12 consensus and the $2.15 upper end of the company’s prior guide, though it landed within the preview’s $2.18–$2.25 buy-side whisper range and its base-case range. The beat was therefore positive but modest against the preview’s more demanding framing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS grew 37.5% to $2.20.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave “Adjusted EPS … Consensus $2.12,” a company guide of “$2.05–$2.15,” and said the buy-side whisper was “$2.18–$2.25.”

surprises.description: ESCO raised FY26 adjusted EPS guidance to $8.30–$8.40, above its prior $8.00–$8.25 range and above the preview’s base-case expectation of roughly $8.15–$8.35. The new range also reaches the preview’s anticipated third-raise level of about $8.35 at its midpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ESCO raised full-year FY26 adjusted EPS guidance to $8.30–$8.40, representing 38%–39% growth versus FY25.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a third raise to “~$8.35+” was the base-case expectation and modeled a nudge to “~$8.15–$8.35.”

surprises.description: Book-to-bill reached 1.21 and backlog rose to a record $1.54 billion, stronger than the preview’s base case of roughly 0.95–1.10 book-to-bill and $1.45–$1.50 billion backlog. It also cleared the preview’s “all clear” threshold of at least 1.0 book-to-bill and $1.45 billion backlog.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated book-to-bill reached 1.21 in Q3, with all three segments above 100%, lifting backlog to a record $1.54 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case was “b:b ~0.95–1.10x” and backlog “roughly flat ~$1.45–1.50B”; it called “≥1.0x with backlog holding ≥$1.45B” the “all clear.”

surprises.description: Aerospace & Defense adjusted EBIT margin reached 30%, above the preview’s expected 28–29% range and its base-case durability assumption. Sales grew 23%, but only 9% organically, so the stronger reported segment growth did not indicate a comparable acceleration in underlying growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Aerospace & Defense delivered 30% adjusted EBIT margins (up 120 bps) on 23% sales growth (9% organic).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch whether A&D margin remained around “~28–29%” and described that level as its base-case expectation.

surprises.description: Utility Solutions margins declined 130 basis points, with NRG margins falling to the low double digits, rather than holding near the preview’s expected 24%–24.7% level for the segment. Doble’s growth was not enough to offset NRG deterioration amid soft renewables demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Utility Solutions adjusted EBIT margins declined 130 basis points, as modest Doble margin gains were more than offset by NRG margin deterioration to low double digits amid soft renewables demand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch whether Doble could “hold USG margin near 24.7%” and described “USG holding ~24%+ despite NRG” weakness as the expected margin story.

surprises.description: Doble’s orders grew 30%, including a 67% surge in condition-monitoring orders, signaling stronger order momentum than the preview’s general expectation of Doble strength. Doble sales growth of 17% was also above its Q2 growth rate cited in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Doble drove Utility Solutions strength with 30% order growth and 17% sales growth, including a 67% surge in condition monitoring orders.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called Doble “the structural winner” and highlighted its Q2 “+11.3%” sales growth, but did not forecast the Q3 order or condition-monitoring growth rates.

surprises.description: Test orders increased 42%, a substantial order surge not forecast in the preview, although sales grew only 5%. The sales-to-orders gap suggests the order strength had not yet translated into current-quarter revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Test orders grew 42%, driven by industrial shielding projects and EMI filters for data centers, though sales rose only 5%.”

surprises.description: Operating cash flow more than doubled to over $193 million, driven by advanced Navy contract payments; the preview discussed strong YTD cash generation and capital deployment but did not anticipate this quarter’s scale or the payment timing. The advance payments may make the cash-flow strength less indicative of recurring operating performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow more than doubled to over $193 million (from $88 million) driven by advanced Navy contract payments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited YTD operating cash flow of “$134.6M (+$88M y/y)” and flagged free cash flow and capital deployment, but gave no Q3 cash-flow expectation.

surprises.description: The call disclosed a specific Megger deal closing timeline and anticipated debt cost, details not identified in the preview’s general expectation for possible M&A commentary. The approximately 6% cost of debt is a financing consideration, but the supplied facts do not establish the deal’s overall financial impact.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Megger deal [is] expected to close in Q1 fiscal 2027 at an anticipated ~6% cost of debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “any M&A commentary is a live catalyst” but did not mention Megger or a deal timeline or financing cost.

surprises.description: The Navy awarded its largest shipbuilding contract in history, covering nine Block VI Virginia-class and five Columbia-class submarines. This was not specifically anticipated in the preview, although ESCO said the relevant content was already under contract, limiting evidence of incremental business from the award itself.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Navy awarded the largest shipbuilding contract in its history for 9 Block VI Virginia-class and 5 Columbia-class submarines, content for which ESCO is already under contract.”

in_line: Test adjusted EBIT margin was 16.4%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the segment would sustain margins above 15%; the preview’s bull case had specified at least 16.5%.
Doble’s 17% sales growth was consistent with the preview’s expectation that Doble would remain a source of strength, even as its order growth was stronger than anticipated.
Aerospace & Defense sales grew across commercial, defense, and Navy, consistent with the preview’s expectation that those end markets would hold up.

surprises.description: Expensify raised its full-year 2026 free-cash-flow outlook to $12–14 million from $6–9 million, after Q2 free cash flow reached $6.4 million. That is a substantial increase above the preview’s stated guidance and its identified upside trigger.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow reached $6.4 million, up 2% year-over-year and up 162% sequentially, prompting management to raise full-year 2026 FCF guidance from $6-9 million to $12-14 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company guidance ... FY2026 free cash flow of $6.0M–$9.0M”; “any raise to the FCF guide is the cleanest bullish catalyst available.”

surprises.description: New Expensify showed substantial adoption and net-new business momentum: it had nearly 12,000 net-new customers, more than $10 million in net-new ARR growing over 250% year-over-year, and 56% of users were on the platform. The preview discussed migration and new-platform conversion but did not anticipate these reported scale and growth figures; the business still accounts for less than 10% of total business.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net new revenue from customers who signed up on New Expensify ... grew over 250% year-over-year to more than $10 million in ARR”; “New Expensify now serves nearly 12,000 net-new customers”; “56% of users are now on New Expensify”; “virtually all incremental revenue” came from it, though it “still represents less than 10% of the total business.”

surprises.description: July paid members fell to 634,000, below the preview’s 635,000 threshold for the inflection narrative, even though the Q2 average was 640,000. Management attributed the dip to seasonal summer travel patterns.
surprises.fact_evidence: “July 2026 paid members dipped to 634,000 due to seasonal summer travel patterns.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Below 635K kills the inflection narrative outright.”

surprises.description: Beyond the already-known tender, Expensify also bought 712,000 shares in the open market at an average price of $1.63. The preview described the tender repurchase as already known, but did not anticipate these additional open-market purchases.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased approximately 6.8 million Class A shares ... including 6.1 million via a substantially undersubscribed Dutch auction tender at $1.20 and 712,000 in the open market at an average of $1.63.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The $25M Dutch auction tender ... came in substantially undersubscribed — only 6.14M Class A shares at $1.20.”

surprises.description: The call named Consolidated Travel Billing, usage-based AI pricing, and bill pay as additional monetization avenues, but said they were still being developed and had not been announced. These possible revenue streams were not identified in the preview, and the call provided no launch timing or quantified contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New monetization avenues including Consolidated Travel Billing, usage-based AI pricing, and bill pay are being developed but not yet announced.”

in_line: Revenue was $33.9 million, close to the preview’s $33.70 million consensus and within its $33.5–34.0 million base range.
Average paid members were 640,000, within the preview’s expected range of roughly 640,000–645,000 for a sequential increase.
Adjusted EBITDA was $6.6 million, within the preview’s $6–7 million base-case range.
Card interchange grew 12% year-over-year, in line with the preview’s key test of whether double-digit growth would hold.
Management gave no clear timing for New Expensify growth to offset Classic churn; the preview’s base case anticipated no date for a return to growth.

surprises.description: HCAT cut FY2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to $18–18.5 million from the prior $30–33 million range. The reduction is much sharper than the revenue reset and leaves profitability well below the prior outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full year 2026 guidance was cut to total revenue of $246 million to $249 million and adjusted EBITDA of $18 million to $18.5 million, primarily reflecting the removal of 5 months of Vitalware revenue and EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guide (as issued May 11, pre-Vitalware): revenue $260–265M, adj. EBITDA $30–33M.”

surprises.description: The Q3 outlook was markedly weaker than the preview’s implied second-half pace: revenue is guided to $55–56 million, versus roughly $60–63 million per quarter implied by the prior FY outlook. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to be only breakeven to $500,000.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for total revenue of just $55 million to $56 million and adjusted EBITDA of only breakeven to $500,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 guide of $260–265M implies a sharp 2H step-down to ~$60–63M/quarter from ~$69M in Q2.”

surprises.description: HCAT’s full-year revenue outlook of $246–249 million is above the preview’s illustrative estimate of a $225–230 million ex-Vitalware reset, even though it is below the previous $260–265 million guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full year 2026 guidance was cut to total revenue of $246 million to $249 million,” primarily due to removing five months of Vitalware revenue.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If management rebases FY26 to ~$225–230M ex-Vitalware, that is mechanical, not a cut.”

surprises.description: The full-year adjusted gross margin outlook is now below 50%, under the preview’s 50–52% estimate. Management cited client migrations and HIE data-loading costs as pressures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full year adjusted gross margin is now expected to fall below 50%,” pressured by “client migrations and HIE data loading costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s estimate was “Adj. gross margin” of “50–52%.”

surprises.description: Management said some DOS-to-Ignite churn has pulled forward into the second half and that migration headwinds will persist through the end of 2027. The preview identified the at-risk ARR and expected retention floor, but did not anticipate this pull-forward.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DOS-to-Ignite migration churn continues to show significant pressure with $12.5 million of notified ARR down-sell/churn plus $52 million of at-risk ARR (only $22 million expected to be retained), and some churn has pulled forward into the second half; headwinds expected to persist through end of 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “≥$22M is now expected to be retained” from $52M at risk, with “the remaining $30M hitting ~$20M in 2026 and ~$10M in 2027.”

surprises.description: HCAT disclosed that Vitalware was a higher-margin contributor, with $11.4 million of first-half adjusted EBITDA, while saying that level was not sustainable without significant investment to grow. That makes the business removed in the divestiture more consequential to profitability than the preview detailed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Vitalware was a higher-margin business contributing $11.4 million in first half adjusted EBITDA, a level management said was not sustainable and would have required significant investment to grow.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $0.04 exceeded the preview’s $0.02 consensus and its $0.02–0.03 estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net income per share was $0.04 on a 74 million weighted average share count.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 adjusted EPS consensus of “$0.02” and its estimate as “$0.02–0.03.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue reached $70.5 million, above the $68–70 million guide and the preview’s $69.0 million consensus and $69.4 million estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $70.5 million, exceeding the high end of the guided $68 million to $70 million range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave Q2 revenue guidance of “$68–70M,” consensus of “$69.0M,” and its estimate of “$69.4M.”

in_line: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $9.9 million, within the preview’s $9–10 million guidance range and close to its $9.5 million consensus and $10.0 million estimate.
The Vitalware sale and debt repayment delivered the debt-free outcome the preview expected: it said proceeds plus cash would fully repay the term loan and leave the company roughly debt-free.
Professional Services is expected to exit 2026 at about $55 million annually, within the preview’s $55–65 million expected range, albeit at its lower end.
The FY2026 bookings target of $22–26 million was maintained, consistent with the preview’s expectation that bookings would remain on track.

surprises.description: Good Times same-store sales were only +0.6% for the quarter, below the preview’s +2.5% estimate and its roughly +2% bar for the promotion to show traction. The positive result is better than a decline, but it fell short of the expected quarter-wide lift.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Good Times same-store sales turned positive at +0.6% for Q3 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Good Times: ... SSS ~+2.5%”; “Anything below +2% means the promotion failed to move traffic”; “Good Times SSS vs. the ~+2% bar I'd set.”

surprises.description: Bad Daddy’s same-store sales fell 2.3%, rather than the preview’s expected +0.5%, and did not cross zero as the preview identified as a key test of the improvement trend.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bad Daddy's same-store sales declined 2.3% for the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bad Daddy's: ... SSS ~+0.5%”; “The trend is –1.4% → –1.2% → –0.8%”; “A positive print would be the first in roughly two years.”

surprises.description: Net income was $1.9 million, or $0.18 per share, well above the preview’s $0.09 EPS estimate. The preview cautioned that the prior-year $0.14 included a tax benefit and estimated core EPS at about $0.10, so the reported result also exceeded that underlying comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income to common shareholders rose to $1.9 million, or $0.18 per share, versus $1.5 million, or $0.14 per share, in the prior-year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted) ... My estimate: $0.09”; “Ex the $0.4M tax benefit, Q3 FY25 core EPS was ~$0.10.”

surprises.description: Despite the modest quarter-wide Good Times comp, the Bambinos promotion produced mid-single-digit same-store sales growth in June, and management is considering keeping it beyond summer. The preview flagged an extension as a bullish tell, but the strong June result contrasted with the weaker quarter-wide comp.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The $2 Bambinos slider promotion drove mid-single-digit same-store sales growth at Good Times during fiscal June, and management is considering extending it beyond its planned summer end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bull — ... Bambinos extended past summer”; “+5% or better is the surprise.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $2.5 million, above the preview’s $2.3 million estimate and last year’s $2.2 million, indicating more improvement than the preview’s base case of flat-to-slightly-up EBITDA.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA increased to $2.5 million from $2.1 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ... My estimate: $2.3M”; “Base ... EBITDA flat-to-slightly-up YoY”; “Adjusted EBITDA ≥ $2.2M.”

surprises.description: The balance sheet ended the quarter stronger than the preview’s Q2 snapshot: management paid down the revolving facility, leaving $3.6 million of cash and only about $0.3 million of seller-finance long-term debt, compared with the preview’s $2.7 million cash and $1.0 million debt figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company paid down its revolving credit facility and ended the quarter with $3.6 million in cash and only about $0.3 million in seller-finance long-term debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Debt was $1.0M at Q2 with $2.7M cash”; management’s stated goal was “a debt-free balance sheet.”

surprises.description: Total revenue was $35.2 million, slightly below the preview’s $35.4 million estimate. Bad Daddy’s sales were also below the preview’s $25.5 million estimate, while Good Times sales matched its $10.1 million estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total company revenues decreased to $35.2 million”; Bad Daddy's sales were “$24.9 million” and Good Times sales “$10.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total ≈ $35.4M”; Bad Daddy's “≈ $25.5M”; Good Times “≈ $10.1M.”

surprises.description: Management said Good Times would have no further price increases for the rest of the year because of market competitiveness. The preview anticipated low pricing and a traffic-led comp, but did not flag this specific limit on future pricing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management does not plan further Good Times price increases for the rest of the year due to market competitiveness.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted Q2 pricing of “~1% at Good Times” and emphasized “Traffic vs. price mix.”

surprises.description: Bad Daddy’s announced core menu additions for Q1 FY2027, including its first-ever sampler platter and an ahi tuna Power Bowl. The preview did not anticipate these planned menu changes, so their effect on results is not yet clear.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bad Daddy's plans core menu additions in Q1 fiscal 2027, including its first-ever sampler platter and a new ahi tuna Power Bowl, absent from the core menu since 2019.”

in_line: Good Times sales of $10.1 million matched the preview’s estimate.
Good Times restaurant-level operating margin improved to 13%, consistent with the preview’s expectation of margin expansion; Bad Daddy’s margin held at 14.4%, matching the prior-year comparison.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $64 million, about $1.5 million above the $62.49 million consensus estimate and $2 million above the guidance midpoint. This was a modest headline beat against the preview’s expected $62–64 million outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $64 million” and was “$2 million above the guidance midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus **$62.49M**”; the preview’s base scenario expected “**$62–64M** (in line to modest beat).”

surprises.description: The Q3 revenue guide was stronger than the preview’s base case: the $67–73 million range has a $70 million midpoint, above the preview’s $64–68 million base-case range. But it still falls short of the roughly $75 million quarterly pace the preview said FY consensus implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for revenue of $67-73 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base” scenario: “**Q3 guided $64–68M**”; the preview also said FY consensus implied “**~$75M/quarter in 2H**.”

surprises.description: Q3 core-business guidance of about $40 million is below the preview’s desired $42 million-plus level, even though the total-company guide is better than its base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q3 guidance includes “core business at ~$40 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said core needed to “guide toward **$42M+** to keep the 2H story intact.”

surprises.description: Q2 core revenue was about $36 million, slightly below the preview’s roughly $37 million expectation and its forecast of 8% sequential growth; reported sequential growth was 5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Core business revenue of ~$36 million (up 5% sequentially).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Core business: **~$37M (+8% q/q, +20% y/y)**.”

surprises.description: Wuxi contributed $28 million in Q2, above the preview’s roughly $25 million expectation. That stronger Wuxi contribution helped lift consolidated revenue despite core revenue coming in below its preview estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Wuxi subsidiary contributing $28 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Wuxi indie Micro: **~$25M**.”

surprises.description: Cash including restricted cash fell by $35.7 million sequentially to $149 million. The preview highlighted cash burn as a key risk, but this balance decline was larger than the roughly $22 million Q1 operating cash outflow it cited; the reported decline was attributed to losses, inventory, receivables, and CapEx.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and equivalents (including restricted cash) fell $35.7 million sequentially to $149 million,” driven by “operating losses, inventory build,” rising receivables, and CapEx.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Operating cash flow **($22.1M)** in Q1”; the preview warned that “Two more like it before the Wuxi cash lands would change the financing conversation.”

surprises.description: The ams OSRAM image-sensor acquisition is now expected to close by Q4 or year-end, later than the preview’s Q3 2026 expectation. It remains under regulatory review.
surprises.fact_evidence: The acquisition “remain[s] under regulatory review” and is “expected to close by Q4/year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The acquisition was “expected to close **Q3 2026**.”

surprises.description: indie disclosed a new radar design win with a Tier 1 supplier serving Volvo, adding a named opportunity beyond the previously disclosed $25 million radar production order. The preview focused on timing for that existing order and did not anticipate this additional win.
surprises.fact_evidence: “indie secured a radar design win with a Tier 1 supplier serving Volvo,” described as “a high-penetration, luxury-volume opportunity,” following the “previously disclosed initial $25 million radar production order.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged the “**$25M radar order — recognition schedule**” and said quantified timing would de-risk the ramp.

surprises.description: Management described a larger long-term radar opportunity than the preview quantified, saying most vehicles average 4–5 radars and citing a projection of up to five standard radar configurations per vehicle by 2030. This adds a favorable market-demand case beyond the preview’s focus on timing for the existing order.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects radar to be a “major growth driver through 2026-2029,” with “most vehicles averaging 4-5 radars” and Yole projecting “up to 5 radar configurations per vehicle standard by 2030.”

surprises.description: Management reported that surging DRAM prices are speeding adoption of the DRAMless iND880, with design wins converting within weeks to a quarter across dozens of models and in automotive and physical AI. The preview identified the iND880 pipeline as a key issue but did not anticipate this specific demand catalyst or accelerated conversion pace.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Surging DRAM prices are accelerating adoption” of the iND880, “converting design wins within weeks to a quarter across dozens of models” in automotive and physical AI.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the iND880 pipeline needed “a named ramp, not another design-win list.”

surprises.description: The call named new iND880 wins with leading Chinese OEMs, Cadillac, and North American Tier 1s, providing specific customer detail beyond the preview’s request for a named ramp. The preview had already noted management’s expectation that the processor could exceed radar revenue in 2026, so that comparison itself is not a surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The iND880 secured new design wins with leading Chinese OEMs plus Cadillac and North American Tier 1s”; management reiterated it could generate more 2026 revenue than radar.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the CEO believed iND880 “could ‘**exceed radar this year**’.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed physical-AI wins with humanoid-robot makers Unitree and Agibot and potential content of about $100 per high-end robot. The preview did not anticipate these wins or the robot opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Physical AI wins include humanoid robot makers Unitree and Agibot” and potential content is “easily $100 per high-end robot”; each maker shipped over 5,000 robots in 2025.

in_line: Non-GAAP loss per share was $0.05, matching company guidance and the preview’s central consensus estimate.

The Wuxi divestiture remains under regulatory review and is still expected to close in 2026; the preview already described it as pending review and expected “later this year.” The call’s description of Wuxi as a gross-margin drag also aligns with the preview’s expectation that its exit should improve gross-margin mix.

surprises.description: Inogen cut its FY2026 revenue range to $355–361 million from $366–373 million, lowering midpoint growth from about 6% to roughly 3%. The preview’s base case expected the range to be reaffirmed; the cut also undercuts the expected second-half acceleration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company lowered full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $355-361 million (down from $366-373 million), representing roughly 3% growth at the midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance (reaffirmed 5/7/26): Revenue $366–373M (~6% growth at midpoint)” and the base scenario expected “FY $366–373M reaffirmed unchanged.”

surprises.description: Despite lowering its revenue outlook, Inogen raised FY2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to approximately $4 million. The preview only anticipated continued improvement, without a specific annual target, so the stated figure is a stronger profitability outlook than it had led investors to expect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance was raised to approximately $4 million, representing 48% growth over the $2.7 million reported for 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance … continued adjusted EBITDA improvement.”

surprises.description: U.S. rental revenue declined 12%, worsening from the 8% decline reported in Q1. The preview already described structural pressure, but highlighted whether the decline would stabilize or accelerate; the reported pace shows acceleration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. rental revenue fell 12% year-over-year to $11.6 million due to structural channel shift as HMEs increasingly prescribe POCs from day one instead of oxygen tanks.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Rental trajectory. Down 8% and structurally pressured … is the decline stabilizing or accelerating?”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin reached 45.6%, improving 65 basis points despite unfavorable channel mix. That is comfortably above the preview’s 44% downside warning level and shows cost and warranty improvements more than offsetting the mix pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin improved 65 basis points to 45.6%, driven by cost improvements and lower warranty expenses despite the unfavorable channel mix shift.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “44.7% in Q1 (+30bps). Mix shift toward B2B and international tenders is dilutive; cost improvements have been offsetting. Sub-44% would signal pricing pressure.”

surprises.description: The company repurchased over $7.5 million of shares in the first half, a faster pace than the $1.9 million executed in Q1 alone. That is more active buyback execution than the preview’s concern about a slow start suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Repurchased over 1.1 million shares for $7.5 million in the first half of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Only ~298K shares / $1.9M executed in Q1 against a $30M authorization.”

surprises.description: Inogen reported strong U.S. unit growth even though U.S. revenue declined: POC unit volume grew over 12% and total U.S. segment unit volume rose at a high-single-digit rate. The preview focused on U.S. revenue inflection and channel mix, but did not anticipate this evidence of underlying volume demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “POC unit volume grew over 12% and total U.S. segment unit volume rose high single digits, suggesting demand strength despite revenue mix pressures.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “U.S. sales returning to flat/positive is the highest-quality possible surprise.”

surprises.description: The call supplied product traction indicators—Voxy had shipped over 5,000 units and Aurora more than doubled its customer count sequentially—and expanded the estimated addressable market to over $3.4 billion. The preview sought quantified Aurora contribution; it got customer-count growth but no Aurora revenue figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Expanded its estimated total addressable market to over $3.4 billion across oxygen, sleep, airway clearance, and digital health (up from $400 million a year ago), with Voxy shipping over 5,000 units and Aurora more than doubling its customer count sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Aurora CPAP mask revenue disclosure. … First hard dollar figure — or continued refusal to give one — is the single biggest narrative swing factor.” The preview also said investors wanted “a dollar figure or at minimum units/reorder rate.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $95.1 million, essentially in line with the preview’s $95.23 million consensus and $94–97 million company guide.
International sales grew 15% and remained in double digits, consistent with the preview’s expectation that international growth would continue to carry the quarter.
U.S. sales remained soft, declining 2%; the preview’s base case anticipated continued U.S. weakness, even as the decline narrowed from Q1’s 4.8%.

surprises.description: Lyft’s gross bookings reached $5.5 billion, above the preview’s $5.31–$5.37 billion consensus range and the company’s $5.30–$5.43 billion guide. The 23% year-over-year growth was also faster than the roughly 19% growth implied by consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross bookings grew 23% year-over-year to $5.5 billion,” with management noting “accelerating top-line growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross Bookings: $5.31–5.37B” consensus; company guide “$5.30–5.43B (+18–21%).”

surprises.description: The bookings beat came with a wider bookings-versus-rides growth gap than the preview’s estimates implied: bookings grew 23% while rides grew about 11.6% (262 million versus 234.8 million a year earlier). That suggests a somewhat larger contribution from mix than the preview’s estimate that roughly half of bookings growth would come from price or mix, although management cited both lower-bookings bike rides and higher-value Freenow rides.
surprises.fact_evidence: “There was an 11% gap between gross bookings growth and rides growth,” driven partly by “mix shifts toward bikes (lower bookings per ride) and higher-value Freenow rides.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus implies gross bookings per ride of ~$20.72 vs. $19.12 in Q2'25 (+8.4%), i.e. roughly half of the 19% bookings growth is price/mix, not incremental trips.”

surprises.description: Rides modestly exceeded the preview’s consensus, rather than coming in below the roughly 259 million level that the preview identified as the key volume test. The beat was small: 262 million rides is about 1% above consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Completed 262 million rides in Q2 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Rides: 259.2M” consensus.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA growth implies a result above the preview’s roughly $169 million consensus and $170 million guide midpoint: 37% growth from the prior-year $129.4 million is approximately $177 million. This is a modest beat, rather than an in-line result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA grew 37% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: ~$169M” consensus; the guide was “$160–180M” with a “$170M” midpoint.

surprises.description: Lyft reported that nearly one in three North American rideshare rides is now linked to a partner, a new high, and said these rides tend to be higher-value. The preview discussed partnerships and mix but did not anticipate this scale of partner-linked rides.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately 30% (nearly 1 in 3) of North American rideshare rides are now linked to a partner, a new all-time high,” and these “tend to skew toward higher-value rides.”

surprises.description: Management offered evidence against the preview’s concern that autonomous-vehicle entry could threaten Lyft’s rides: San Francisco rides grew 20%, which management said showed AV entry expanding the market rather than cannibalizing traditional rideshare. This is a favorable but localized data point, not a broad AV economics update.
surprises.fact_evidence: “San Francisco showed 20% rides growth,” cited as evidence that “AV entry expands the total addressable market rather than cannibalizing traditional rideshare.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “robotaxi disruption risk” and asked whether AV deployment would become a monetized opportunity, but did not forecast this San Francisco rides result.

surprises.description: The call highlighted unusually strong driver-side indicators that the preview had not identified as expected: supply near record highs alongside higher driver earnings and tipping, plus a claimed sizable driver preference advantage over the main competitor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Driver supply is near record highs with driver earnings per ride up 8% year-over-year and tipping up 10%,” and Lyft claims “a roughly 30-point driver preference gap over its main competitor.”

in_line: The Waymo/Nashville milestones were consistent with the preview: the 80,000-square-foot depot is expected around October and Lyft-app supply sharing is on track before year-end, matching the preview’s fall 2026 depot and H2 2026 matching expectations.
Baidu’s London deployment remains small with a de minimis near-term P&L impact, consistent with the preview’s description of the testing as financially immaterial to Q2.
Lyft said it was on track to exceed 1 billion rides in 2026, broadly consistent with the preview’s approximately 1.01 billion FY26 rides expectation.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $202,000 versus the preview’s $183,000 consensus, a modest beat of about 10%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $202,000”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY26 Consensus” revenue: “$0.183M”

surprises.description: AEye’s GAAP loss was worse than expected: EPS was $0.22 loss versus the preview’s $0.173 loss estimate. The call attributed the higher expenses partly to non-cash stock-based compensation and partly to non-recurring production ramp costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss widened to $10 million ($0.22 per share)” and “GAAP operating expenses rose to $10.6 million from $8.9 million in Q1, with over half the increase from non-cash stock-based compensation and the rest from non-recurring production ramp costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (GAAP) Consensus” of “$(0.173)”

surprises.description: The quarter produced AEye’s first commercial win from its pipeline in a new market category: Alive3D selected it as its preferred LiDAR vendor for sports analytics. The preview identified a named customer as a possible bullish signal, but did not flag this customer or market.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AEye was selected as the preferred LiDAR vendor by sports analytics provider Alive3D, marking entry into an entirely new market category and its first commercial win from the sales pipeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “a named customer” was listed as a possible bull-case signal.

surprises.description: Defense activity showed concrete commercial progress not specified in the preview: engagements doubled quarter over quarter, and the lead defense customer placed a third consecutive paid order that was growing in size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Defense is the largest and fastest-growing vertical, with engagements doubling quarter over quarter and the lead defense customer placing its third consecutive paid order with growing size.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “a defense/ITS order with delivery dates” as a possible bull-case signal.

surprises.description: AEye reported a new $30,000 contract-development revenue stream from customer-funded engineering work, which management expects to become a more meaningful recurring contributor. The preview did not anticipate this source of revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The quarter included a new $30,000 contract development revenue stream from customer-funded engineering work, which management expects to become a more meaningful, recurring contributor over time.”

surprises.description: Quarter-end cash and marketable securities were about $71.5 million, above the preview’s $68–69 million estimate. The facts do not specify what drove the difference.
