surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with approximately $71.5 million in cash and marketable securities (down from $77.2 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “Q2-exit cash of ~$68–69M” absent ATM issuance.

surprises.description: Reported engagement growth was about 25%, below the preview’s stated expectation of roughly 40% quarter over quarter. Quote activity did grow about 40%, so the shortfall was limited to engagements.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Engagements [were] up ~25% and quote activity up ~40% quarter over quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “quotes/engagements +40% q/q.”

surprises.description: AEye described a production line capable of up to 60,000 Apollo units annually. The preview focused on whether Apollo evaluations would convert to volume but did not mention this production capacity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AEye is ramping production through its LightOn line, which is capable of up to 60,000 Apollo units annually.”

in_line: Proof-of-concept programs from revenue-generating customers reached 25, within the preview’s expected base-case range of 23–25.
Quote activity grew about 40% quarter over quarter, matching the preview’s stated expectation for quotes/engagements growth.
AEye reaffirmed its full-year 2026 cash-use guidance of $30–35 million, as the preview expected.
Apollo’s validation on NVIDIA’s Drive AGX Thor platform was already noted in the preview as announced before the release.

surprises.description: Revenue was $92.1 million, 7% above the preview’s $86.3 million published consensus and slightly above Q1’s $90.1 million. However, it landed near the bottom of the preview’s assumed $92–100 million buy-side range rather than delivering a large upside beat against that higher bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached a record $92.1 million” and “beating analyst consensus by $5.8 million (7%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Published Q2 consensus of $86.3M”; the preview also said to “assume a real buy-side bar in the $92–100M range, not $86M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin reached 49%, above the preview’s 45–47% base-case range and 2 points above Q1. The preview expected a similar benefit from the higher-margin dataset mix, so the surprise was the additional improvement rather than the direction of the margin trend.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin hit 49%, up 2 points sequentially,” driven by “higher-margin pretraining programs and IP-retained off-the-shelf datasets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “45–47%” adjusted gross margin and said “Q2 should see a similar benefit” to Q1.

surprises.description: Management kept FY26 revenue-growth guidance at 40% or more instead of raising it toward the 45% level the preview viewed as the likely base case. The preview had identified an unchanged guide as a possible outcome, but it was below the expected base-case improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reiterated full-year guidance of 40% or more year-over-year revenue growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected the guide to be “Raised modestly to 45%”; it said the buy-side wanted “45%+ minimum.”

surprises.description: Management added a near-term caution that revenue could fall sequentially in Q3 or Q4 depending on project mix. The preview discussed model-training timing risk, but its base case assumed sequential growth resumed, so this explicit warning was more cautious than that scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management cautioned that revenues could decline sequentially in Q3 or Q4 depending on project mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case called for “sequential growth resumes,” while describing a flat-to-down quarter as defensible because training phases do not always align.

surprises.description: The CEO announced a transition to Executive Chairman, with President/CRO Rahul Singhal taking over as CEO on September 30. The preview did not flag a leadership transition, making this an unanticipated governance and management change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CEO Jack Abuhoff will transition to Executive Chairman effective September 30, with President/CRO Rahul Singhal becoming President and CEO and joining the Board.”

surprises.description: Innodata established an at-the-market equity program despite the preview discussing a strong cash position, no debt, and an expanded credit facility without anticipating an equity program. The program provides optional growth capital but also creates potential dilution if shares are sold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Innodata is filing a prospectus supplement establishing an at-the-market equity program with Goldman Sachs as lead agent,” providing “optional supplemental capital for growth and strategic opportunities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “cash ($117.4M at Q1, +$35.1M Q/Q, no debt against an expanded $50M Wells Fargo facility)” but did not mention an ATM program.

surprises.description: The quarter’s effective tax rate was about 18% because of recognized tax benefits, below the company’s 23–25% long-term target range. The preview flagged tax-rate uncertainty, but did not anticipate these specific benefits or an 18% rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The effective tax rate was approximately 18% this quarter due to recognized tax benefits,” below the “long-term target range of 23% to 25%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the effective tax rate was “genuinely lumpy” and identified “a sharp tax/opex normalization” as a way its EPS bridge could break.

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA of $25.4 million was modestly above the preview’s estimated $21–24 million range, though the preview also anticipated strong profitability after Q1.
Diluted EPS of $0.41 nearly doubled the published $0.21 consensus, but was close to the preview’s own estimate of roughly $0.39–$0.40 and within its $0.33–$0.42 base-case range.

Customer concentration improved in the expected direction: the preview noted that the largest customer’s share had already fallen in Q1 and expected the new Big Tech engagement to become the second-largest customer. The reported largest-customer share fell to 37%, while the Big Tech customer rose to 34%.

Cash and liquidity were broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of continued cash growth and no debt: cash and short-term investments were $250.4 million including customer prepayments, or about $134 million excluding them, up $37 million sequentially; the Wells Fargo facility remained undrawn.

The reiterated guide excluded large likely-win opportunities that were not yet fully booked, consistent with the preview’s observation that management had flagged large programs not yet included in its forecast.
The possibility of sequential revenue softness from project timing was already identified in the preview as a risk, even though the call made the Q3/Q4 downside possibility explicit.

surprises.description: NATR reported Q2 sales of $117 million, well below the preview’s roughly $125 million consensus and its expected 7–10% growth range. Sales grew only 2% year over year, or 4% in constant currency.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales rose 2% year-over-year (4% in constant currency) to a record $117 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | ~$125M” and “Implied YoY | +9%”; the base model expected “revenue $124.3M (+8.3%).”

surprises.description: Instead of raising or reiterating its full-year outlook, NATR cut both sales and EBITDA guidance. The new sales range is below the preview’s already-above-guidance consensus, and the EBITDA range is also below the preview’s expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company lowered its full-year 2026 net sales guidance to $490-500 million from $500-515 million, and cut EBITDA guidance to $48-52 million from $50-54 million, citing FX changes and a China slowdown.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said consensus was “sales $517.4M” and that a raise was the key debate; its base case expected the “guide reiterated at $500–515M / $50–54M,” while the bear case described a trim to the low end.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $11.3 million, below the preview’s $12.5–13.0 million model estimate and its expectation of 11–15% year-over-year growth. At about 9.7% of sales, it also fell short of the preview’s 10.3% margin reference.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose nearly 1% to $11.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave “Adj. EBITDA | model est. $12.5–13.0M” and “Implied YoY | +11–15%,” and said the buy-side anchors on “margin vs. 10.3%.”

surprises.description: SG&A was substantially higher as a share of sales than the preview’s base case, leaving little of the expected operating leverage. The company also described investment spending ramping toward a $45–47 million quarterly run rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A increased to $44.9 million (38.4% of sales) as growth investments ramp toward a $45-47 million quarterly run rate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base model assumed “SG&A 36.0%,” and said “Anything near 36% delivers ~200 bps of YoY leverage.”

surprises.description: China sales fell 20%, rather than merely slowing after the prior quarter’s exceptional growth. The preview had flagged a China air-pocket as a risk, but its central discussion focused on growth not repeating rather than a sharp decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “China sales fell 20% due to operational issues, reversing a prior trend of over 30% growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said China’s Q1 “+40% quarter ‘is unlikely to be repeated’” and described the bear case as “a China air-pocket.”

surprises.description: North American digital growth was 26%, below the preview’s roughly 30% threshold for sustaining the digital-growth thesis, even though digital sales remain on track for $50 million by year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “North American digital sales grew 26% year-over-year and are on track to reach $50 million by year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Deceleration below ~30% digital growth would undercut the re-rating thesis.”

surprises.description: Japan grew 50%, a notably stronger result than the preview’s expectation that Japan and Korea maintain double-digit growth to offset weakness elsewhere in Asia.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Japan grew 50%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Japan and Korea double-digit growth needs to hold to offset.”

surprises.description: Social commerce revenue surged 177%, and subscription autoship customers were reported to have more than three times the lifetime value of other customers. The preview did not flag either metric.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Social commerce revenue within digital surged 177%, with subscription autoship customers carrying a lifetime value more than 3x higher than other customers.”

surprises.description: Management introduced a long-term vision to double sales to $1 billion and raise EBITDA margin to 15%, beyond the preview’s discussion of near-term guidance and margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company set long-term ‘vision for growth’ targets to double sales to $1 billion and lift EBITDA margin to 15% from just above 10%.”

surprises.description: Cash was $82.5 million, below the preview’s approximately $88 million figure, and operating activities used cash rather than providing it as in the year-earlier quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The balance sheet held $82.5 million in cash with zero debt, though operating activities used $1.1 million of cash versus $6.9 million provided a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the company as having “~$88M cash, zero debt.”

in_line: Gross margin exceeded the preview’s roughly 73.0% expectation at 73.7%; management’s low-to-mid 73% outlook for the rest of 2026 is consistent with its expected roughly 73% full-year trajectory.
The company remained debt-free, as the preview described.

surprises.description: Navient reported core EPS of $0.29 versus the preview’s $0.19 consensus, though $0.04 came from net one-time benefits; adjusted core EPS was $0.25. The underlying result still beat consensus, but by less than the headline figure suggests.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 core EPS was $0.29,” but excluding “a net $0.04 benefit from one-time items, adjusted core EPS was $0.25.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Core EPS | $0.19” consensus.

surprises.description: Despite private charge-offs improving to 1.8%, Navient built a $23 million reserve on the remaining private portfolio because credit improvement moderated during the quarter. The preview identified a reserve build as a key downside risk and described its base case as stable credit with no reserve build.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recorded $26 million in total provisions, including a $23 million reserve build on the remaining private portfolio because credit improvement moderated as the quarter progressed.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case assumed “stable credit”; the bear case flagged an “incremental reserve build,” and the preview said “any sequential deterioration or reserve build is the bear trigger.”

surprises.description: Beginning in Q3, new in-school loans will be accounted for at fair value without a CECL allowance or provision, removing near-term provision expense that otherwise would have affected 2026 earnings. That differs from the preview’s framing of day-one CECL provisioning as part of the expected 2026 investment drag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Beginning Q3 2026, newly originated in-school loans will be accounted for at fair value with no CECL allowance or provision, removing near-term provision expense that would have otherwise hit 2026 earnings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The FY26 EPS guide was described as “net of a $0.35–$0.40/sh drag from day-one CECL provisioning + opex” tied to origination growth.

surprises.description: Navient classified $528 million of its legacy private loan portfolio as held for sale and released $19 million of associated allowance, while signaling that additional reclassifications may follow. The preview did not anticipate this portfolio classification or its allowance release.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Navient classified $528 million (just under 10%) of its ~$5.4 billion legacy private loan portfolio as held for sale, releasing $19 million of associated allowance and signaling potential future reclassifications.”

surprises.description: Shareholder returns fell to $17 million in Q2, below the $38 million returned in Q1, with most of the $100 million buyback authorization still unused. Management attributed the slower repurchases to 10b5-1 plan mechanics and capital needs for growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Navient returned only $17 million to shareholders via dividends and buybacks in Q2, with ~$75-76 million remaining on its $100 million buyback authorization,” citing “10b5-1 plan mechanics and capital needs for growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “buyback cadence” and asked investors to watch “repurchase pace vs. Q1's $23M” in buybacks, alongside $15M in Q1 dividends.

surprises.description: The preview’s bull scenario called for Q2 originations above $1.3 billion, but Navient reported $815 million. Originations nevertheless grew more than 60% year over year, so the shortfall is relative to the preview’s bull-case level rather than a stated consensus estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Combined originations grew more than 60% year-over-year to $815 million,” including $735 million of refinance and $80 million of in-school originations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bull scenario specified “originations >$1.3B”; the base scenario expected originations “tracking to ~$4B” for the year.

in_line: Operating expenses were $85 million, keeping Navient on pace for the previewed $350 million full-year outlook; the preview had flagged a Q2 result materially above roughly $85–88 million as a risk.
Full-year in-school originations guidance of roughly $600 million, or 50% growth, was broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of more than 50% growth in in-school originations.
Private charge-offs improved to 1.8%, just below the preview’s 1.90% bull-case threshold, although the $23 million reserve build meant legacy private-credit commentary was not wholly clean.

surprises.description: TriLink grew 12%, well above the preview’s 5–8% estimate and management’s previously guided low-to-mid-single-digit pace. That was stronger than expected for the business excluding the anticipated COVID-related contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “TriLink growing 12%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “TriLink / Nucleic Acid Prod. … Q2’26E … $32.5–33.5M (+5–8%)”; management had guided base growth “low-to-mid single digits” Q2–Q4.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $51.4 million exceeded the preview’s roughly $50 million estimate and the $48.7–48.8 million consensus range. The beat was modest against the preview’s own estimate, but larger against consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $51.4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue … Q2’26E … ~$50M”; consensus was “$48.7–48.8M.”

surprises.description: The company raised full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance, as the preview expected, but the new $33–35 million range was below the preview’s $34–36 million base-case expectation and its highlighted $36 million-plus bar. The raise is positive versus the prior guide, but smaller than the preview’s more bullish expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised adjusted EBITDA guidance to $33-35 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the buy-side wanted “a full-year guidance raise”; its base case expected EBITDA “nudged to ~$34–36M,” and its catalyst checklist highlighted “a raise to ≥$36M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $8.7 million, above the preview’s $6–8 million estimate, though slightly short of its $9–11 million bull case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA improved by $19.1 million to $8.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Adj. EBITDA … $6–8M”; its bull scenario was “$9–11M.”

surprises.description: Cygnus grew 3%, below the preview’s 4–7% estimate and its expectation that China distributor timing would recover. However, it remained in growth for a fifth consecutive quarter, rather than showing a decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cygnus growing 3% (its 5th consecutive quarter of growth).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Cygnus at “$17.0–17.5M (+4–7%)” and said “China distributor timing from Q1 should recover.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was a loss of $0.02, better than the preview’s cited consensus loss of $0.04–$0.05, although it matched the preview’s own estimate range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS improving to a loss of $0.02.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus was “−$0.04 to −$0.05”; the preview’s own estimate was “−$0.02 to $0.00.”

surprises.description: The company now expects full-year gross-margin improvement of more than 1,400 basis points, above the preview’s cited company outlook of more than 1,300 basis points.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin now expected to improve by more than 1,400 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the company gave “only a directional ‘>1,300bps FY expansion.’”

surprises.description: Discovery mRNA customer additions and GMP customer transitions showed strong traction not quantified in the preview: the company added a record 67 discovery customers and completed six of its targeted nine GMP transitions for 2026 by Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Added a record 67 new discovery mRNA customers in Q2” and “converted 6 of a targeted 9 GMP customer transitions for 2026 (4 added in Q2).”

surprises.description: ModTill adoption advanced to more than 125 active customers, substantially above the 70-plus customers noted in the preview. That customer uptake is stronger than the preview’s stated baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ModTill adoption exceeded 125 active customers within one year of launch (up from over 70 in Q1).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “ModTail is at 70+ customers with repeat orders.”

surprises.description: Despite the planned second-half 2026 ModTill launch, GMP-grade ModTill orders are not expected until 2027, delaying revenue from the product relative to the preview’s H2 2026 launch schedule.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GMP-grade ModTill orders are not expected until 2027 despite a planned launch in the second half of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “GMP-grade enzymes and ModTail launches were slated for H2’26” and warned that “slippage here is a 2027 revenue problem.”

surprises.description: Management said commercial launches from the non-COVID pipeline are not expected until around 2028–2029, indicating a longer wait for commercial revenue than the preview had flagged.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Commercial launches from the non-COVID pipeline not expected until around 2028-2029.”

in_line: Full-year 2026 revenue guidance remained at $205–215 million, as the preview expected.
No COVID GMP-related revenue was reported in Q2, consistent with the preview’s statement that the Q1 CleanCap order was not expected to repeat.
The refinancing and debt level were broadly in line with the preview, which noted the June refinancing and debt of about $150 million.

surprises.description: Cloudflare reported $696.1 million of Q2 revenue, above the preview’s $675–685 million functional whisper and even the $682–692 million bull-case range. Growth was 36%, rather than the roughly 33–35% the preview framed as a strong result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $696.1 million, up 36% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat ~$675–685M as the functional whisper”; bull case revenue “$682–692M (+33–35%).”

surprises.description: The Q3 outlook implies 31% revenue growth, a deceleration from Q2’s 36%, rather than the mid-30s exit-rate trajectory the preview wanted the guide to support. This is a weaker growth trajectory than the high-bar setup called for.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 revenue guidance of $736-737 million implies 31% year-over-year growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the Q3 guide should “mathematically support mid-30s exit-rate growth” and wanted “revenue growth toward the mid-30s percentage range by year-end.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow was only 8% of revenue, well below the preview’s 13% margin hurdle. The 69% year-over-year increase did not meet the preview’s expectation for a high FCF margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow was $56.4 million (8% of revenue), up 69% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s FCF target was “≥13% margin; FCF guide intact.”

surprises.description: The full-year revenue guide rose to $2.864–2.870 billion, clearing the preview’s $2.85 billion threshold and its roughly $2.83 billion base-case expectation. However, the implied 32% growth still does not represent the mid-30s trajectory investors were looking for.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance of $2.864-2.870 billion implies 32% growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “>$2.85B” was the desired guide and its base case was a raise to “~$2.83B”; it also said investors wanted a guide supporting mid-30s exit-rate growth.

surprises.description: Large-customer additions accelerated beyond the preview’s expectation of sustained momentum: Cloudflare added a record 986 customers above $100,000 annually, and growth accelerated to 27% from 25% last quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added a record 986 net new large customers (over $100,000 annually) year-over-year, ending with 4,698 such customers, up 27% and an acceleration from 25% growth last quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “Sustained $1M+/$5M+ cohort momentum.”

surprises.description: Cloudflare added more than 80,000 paying customers in the quarter, producing 74% year-over-year paying-customer growth—an adoption measure the preview did not identify as a specific expected result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cloudflare added over 80,000 paying customers in the quarter—as many as it had in total at its 2019 IPO—driving 74% year-over-year paying customer growth.”

surprises.description: Workers developer adoption accelerated sharply: the platform added nearly 2 million developers in Q2, more than the 1.5 million added in all of 2025. The preview noted the existing developer base but did not anticipate this pace of additions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Workers platform grew to over 7.4 million developers, adding nearly 2 million in Q2 alone, surpassing the 1.5 million added in all of 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “5.5M developers (+1M in Q1)” and said it was watching for the developer base to convert into paid seats.

surprises.description: Gross margin rose to 73.1%, above the preview’s 72% floor, and improved sequentially for the first time in eight quarters. That was a positive change from the recent compression the preview highlighted, although the margin remained down year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin was 73.1%, improving 30 basis points sequentially for the first time in eight quarters but down 320 basis points year-over-year due to network cost allocation shifts.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s expectation was “≥72%, held” and it noted “Two quarters of compression.”

surprises.description: Operating margin reached 13.8%, just below the preview’s 14% minimum and short of the operating leverage it wanted to see from restructuring. Sequential improvement was strong, but the margin was still down 30 basis points year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating margin of 13.8% expanded 240 basis points sequentially but declined 30 basis points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview wanted “≥14%, with credible restructuring flow-through.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP diluted EPS was $0.29, above the published $0.27 consensus, though it was within the preview’s base-case range and below its bull-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net income was $107.8 million ($0.29 diluted EPS).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed non-GAAP EPS consensus at “$0.27”; its base case was “$0.28–0.29.”

surprises.description: The call described non-human traffic as already exceeding half of network traffic and introduced products such as cloudflare.pay, revealing a larger agentic-traffic opportunity than the preview had quantified. But the facts provided do not report the first pay-per-crawl revenue the preview wanted as proof of monetization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For the first time, over 50% of network traffic was non-human in Q2,” and management said it “could reach 1,000x human traffic within five years,” underpinning products “like cloudflare.pay.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “First pay-per-crawl revenue” and said a disclosed dollar figure would validate the agentic-internet opportunity.

surprises.description: Restructuring charges were slightly above the preview’s expected Q2 range, and the full-year charge estimate is now up to $165 million. That adds more one-off cost than the preview’s $140–150 million estimate suggested, although the Q2 difference alone is small.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Results excluded $151 million in severance and restructuring charges, with full-year charges now expected up to $165 million versus initial estimates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “$140–150M of restructuring charges” would land “mostly in Q2.”

in_line: Dollar-based net retention reached 120%, within the preview’s stated target of 119–120% or higher.

surprises.description: The preview put the functional revenue whisper at $44–45 million and described $43 million as a deceleration-confirming result. Nerdy reported $43.3 million: slightly above the $43 million consensus and within its $42–44 million guide, but below the preview’s higher whisper range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $43.3 million, down 4% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The functional whisper is $44–45M, not $43M.”

surprises.description: Nerdy cut its FY2026 revenue outlook to $168–175 million, below the preview’s $180–190 million range and below the $180 million level the preview said a cut would break. The company attributed the reduction entirely to exiting Varsity Tutors for Schools and First Tutors.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nerdy cut its full-year revenue guidance to $168-175 million from $180-190 million, attributing the reduction entirely to exiting Varsity Tutors for Schools and First Tutors.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 revenue guidance: reiterate, narrow, or cut?” The preview said “a cut below $180M breaks the story.”

surprises.description: Rather than seeking a recovery in Varsity Tutors for Schools bookings, Nerdy is winding down that profitable business and exiting First Tutors. The preview treated school bookings as a key leading indicator and said a recovery toward $4 million was needed to support the second-half outlook; the exits instead reduce fixed costs by about $11 million annually and bring $2–4 million of exit costs, mostly in Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is winding down Varsity Tutors for Schools (a profitable, low single-digit revenue business) and exiting First Tutors, lowering annual fixed cost run rate by approximately $11 million but incurring $2-4 million in exit costs mostly in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bookings need to recover toward $4M+ to validate management’s ‘more stable institutional funding environment in the second half’ assumption.”

surprises.description: Year-end cash guidance fell to $30–32 million from $40–45 million, and Q2 ended with $38.4 million—below the preview’s roughly $40 million watch level. The company linked the reduction to lost prepaid collections from Varsity Tutors for Schools and wind-down costs, rather than weaker consumer economics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Year-end cash guidance was lowered to $30-32 million from $40-45 million, driven by lost VT4S prepaid annual collections and wind-down costs rather than changes in consumer economics”; “the company ended Q2 with $38.4 million cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Cash balance vs. ~$40M” and said to watch for cash “below ~$38–40M”; it listed FY year-end cash guidance of “$40–45M.”

surprises.description: The call gave Q3 adjusted EBITDA guidance of a $6–9 million loss, excluding exit costs. That is a notably weak quarter against the preview’s roughly breakeven FY2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook, particularly after the preview’s Q2 expectation of a $2 million loss to breakeven; the preview did not give a specific Q3 estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 adjusted EBITDA is guided to negative $9 million to negative $6 million excluding exit costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance as “~breakeven” and Q2 adjusted EBITDA guidance as “−$2M to breakeven.”

surprises.description: Nerdy reported a steeper year-over-year headcount reduction than the preview’s cited 20% Q1 reduction, while AI-related expenses rose sharply to $2 million. The preview described the cost reset as AI-driven and noted an AI product roadmap, but did not anticipate this increase in AI spending alongside the workforce reductions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total headcount fell 34% year-over-year and the engineering team shrank 30%, while AI-related expenses rose to $2 million (up from $0.7 million in Q1 and $0.4 million a year ago).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “headcount −20% YoY” and a “genuine cost-structure reset,” and said “the AI-driven cost reset is real.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA loss was $0.9 million, close to the preview’s approximately $1 million expectation and within the guided range; the call said it beat the guidance midpoint.
Active Learning Memberships declined 5% year-over-year, within the preview’s expected roughly 4–6% decline, and management reiterated its expectation of positive member growth by year-end 2026.
ARPUM rose 5% year-over-year, in line with the preview’s expectation that growth would compress to mid-single digits as the February 2025 price increases began lapping.
Gross margin was 64.7%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that it would hold above roughly 64% in the weaker revenue quarter.

surprises.description: REAL’s Q2 GMV came in above the preview’s roughly $595–600 million expectation, reaching $617 million. That was a meaningful upside to the expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 GMV reached an all-time high of $617 million, up 22% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GMV | ~$595–600M (guide-anchored)”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue exceeded both the $187.8 million consensus estimate and the top of the company’s $186–189 million guide. The preview framed an in-line quarter as roughly $188–190 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue grew 17% to $193 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $187.8M” consensus and “$186–189M” company guide.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $13.5 million, above the preview’s $11–12 million guide and its $12.0–12.5 million base-case range; the 7% margin also topped the roughly 6.1–6.2% expectation. The result beat prior guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $13.5 million (7% of revenue), expanding 290 basis points year-over-year and beating prior guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$11.5–12.0M” consensus; company guide “$11.0–12.0M”; margin “~6.2%” consensus and “~6.1% (midpoint).”

surprises.description: REAL raised its full-year outlook rather than merely reiterating the existing ranges, contrary to the preview’s base case of maintained guidance. The new GMV, revenue, and EBITDA ranges are all above the previous ranges, including a higher EBITDA midpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year guidance to GMV of $2.535–$2.565 billion (19–20% growth), revenue of $788–$797 million (14–15% growth), and adjusted EBITDA of $66–$69 million (8.5% margin midpoint).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the key question was whether guidance would be “reiterate vs. raise vs. trim” and described its base case as “FY revenue and EBITDA ranges reiterated.” It listed the existing FY26 guide as GMV “$2.42–2.47B,” revenue “$770–784M,” and adjusted EBITDA “$59–67M.”

surprises.description: Active-buyer growth accelerated instead of decelerating: TTM active buyers grew 11% to more than 1.1 million, versus 10% growth and 1.083 million in the prior quarter. This was better than the preview’s stated bear-case concern about growth falling below roughly 8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trailing 12-month active buyers grew 11% year-over-year, surpassing 1.1 million, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of acceleration.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “TTM active buyers 1.083M (+10%)”; the preview identified “active buyer growth decelerating below ~8%” as a bear-case trigger.

surprises.description: The buyer-to-consignor flywheel strengthened slightly beyond the preview’s 43% reference point: 44% of new consignors came from active buyers. The company also said the share had risen from 40% two quarters earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “44% of new consignors came from the active buyer base in Q2, up from 40% two quarters ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “43% of new consignors came from the active buyer base (‘flywheelers’).”

surprises.description: The reported cash balance was $134 million, above the $124 million cited in the preview, despite the preview warning that Q2 was guided to be another weak cash quarter. The call also noted more than $80 million of debt reduction over two years, though it did not provide Q2 free-cash-flow figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $134 million in cash and has reduced total debt by over $80 million in the past two years, with continued deleveraging as a priority.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash / Total debt | $124.0M / $464.5M”; the preview also said “Q2 was guided to be another weak cash quarter.”

in_line: Take-rate pressure continued as expected: the preview highlighted the mix shift toward higher-value, lower-commission items, and REAL reported a 200-basis-point year-over-year decline to 35.9%.
AOV continued to rise, as the preview anticipated, reaching $659; the reported 13% growth was slower than the prior quarter’s 15% growth, but the preview did not set a specific Q2 growth expectation.
Athena remained on track for nearly 50% of items processed by year-end, consistent with the preview’s cited target of about 50% from 35%.

surprises.description: ORGO reported Q2 revenue of $42.8 million, well below the preview’s $53.7–59.3 million guidance-implied range and $54.27 million consensus. The preview implied roughly 49% sequential growth, while net product revenue grew only 18% quarter over quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue declined 58% year-over-year in Q2 2026 to $42.8 million”; “Net product revenue increased 18% quarter-over-quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Implied Q2 2026” revenue of “$53.7M” to “$59.3M”; Q2 net product revenue consensus of “$54.27M” and implied Q/Q growth of “+49%.”

surprises.description: Management cut full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $179–215 million, substantially below the preview’s already-reduced $270–310 million range. The new outlook implies a 62–68% decline rather than the previously guided 45–52% decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Slashed its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $179-215 million (a 62-68% decline), down sharply from prior guidance of a 45-52% decline, due to a slower-than-expected recovery.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 revenue” guide of “$270–310M”; the preview’s base case anticipated “Reaffirmed $270–310M,” while its bear case described a cut below $270M.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA loss was $34.4 million, worse than the preview’s base-case estimate of a $20–28 million loss and below its expected burn range. Management still expects positive adjusted EBITDA in Q4, so the preview’s concern about abandoning the second-half target was not borne out.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA loss widened to $34.4 million”; “management expects positive adjusted EBITDA in Q4 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base case: adjusted EBITDA of “$(20)–(28)M”; the preview also identified withdrawal of the “H2 positive-adjusted-EBITDA target” as a bear trigger.

surprises.description: The company disclosed a new agreement allowing it to sell up to $75 million of common stock. The preview flagged financing risk if cash fell, but did not anticipate an ATM equity-sale facility, which creates potential dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company entered an ATM agreement to sell up to $75 million of common stock, signaling potential shareholder dilution to fund operations and strategic initiatives.”

surprises.description: GAAP net loss reached $96.3 million and included roughly $30 million of non-cash tax expense from a full valuation allowance on deferred tax assets. The preview’s GAAP EPS consensus was a loss of $0.35 and did not flag this valuation-allowance charge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss was $96.3 million versus $9.4 million last year, including roughly $30 million of non-cash tax expense from recording a full valuation allowance on deferred tax assets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (GAAP)” consensus: “$(0.35).”

surprises.description: ORGO reported 30% sequential growth in wound care unit volume and said the improvement indicated market-share gains as the market resets. That is a positive operating signal against the preview’s open question of whether its Q1 share gains would hold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Advanced wound care sales up 23% sequentially and wound care unit volume up 30% versus Q1, indicating market share gains as the market resets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked, “Does [Q1’s share gain] hold?” and said, “Share gain in a collapsing category is the only bull case with legs.”

surprises.description: The two 2026 restructurings are expected to save more than $32 million annually in combined operating expenses, materially more than the preview’s cited roughly $14 million annualized savings from the March restructuring alone. The preview had not described the additional June workforce reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Two 2026 restructurings, including a June workforce reduction of 138 employees, are expected to cut annual operating expenses by more than $32 million combined.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the March restructuring “yields ~$14M annualized” and noted a “−25% FY target.”

in_line: Non-GAAP gross margin was 49%, within the preview’s expected 48–52% range.
Cash was $46.8 million at quarter end, close to the preview’s expectation of cash near $50 million after a $35–45 million burn.
Management expects positive adjusted EBITDA in Q4 2026, consistent with the preview’s focus on maintaining a positive-adjusted-EBITDA target in the second half.
The MNUVIX BLA acceptance and April 24, 2027 PDUFA target date had already been reported in the preview.

surprises.description: QuidelOrtho cut its 2026 revenue outlook to $2.52–2.60 billion from $2.70–2.75 billion, adjusted EBITDA to $540–560 million from $615–630 million, and adjusted EPS to $0.65–0.90 from $1.80–2.00. These cuts were substantially deeper than the preview’s base case of a trim to the low end or a widened EPS range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was revised down to $2.52-2.60 billion, with adjusted EBITDA of $540-560 million and adjusted EPS lowered to $0.65-0.90.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base (~45%): ... guide trimmed to low end ($2.70B rev, $1.80 EPS) or FY EPS range widened”; the preview’s updated guide was revenue “$2.70–2.75B,” EBITDA “$615–630M,” and EPS “$1.80–2.00.”

surprises.description: The company withdrew its 2026 free-cash-flow guidance instead of maintaining the $100–120 million target. Q2 free cash flow was negative $136 million, including a $25 million payment to Grifols, contrary to the preview’s expectation that cash flow would inflect positive in Q2/Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company withdrew its free cash flow guidance for 2026 due to uncertainty around China, respiratory demand, and related working capital impacts”; “Q2 free cash flow was negative $136 million ... including a $25 million payment to Grifols for terminating the joint business arrangement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The updated FY guide included “FCF | $100–120M”; the preview said “FCF must inflect positive in Q2/Q3 to hit the $100–120M guide.”

surprises.description: China revenue fell 23% year over year as customers cut inventories faster than anticipated amid uncertainty about proposed IVD pricing guidelines. The preview discussed an estimated 2026 impact of about $30 million with implementation slipping to mid-2027, so the reported near-term deterioration was worse and earlier than that framing suggested; it also pressured gross margin through geographic mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “China revenue declined 23% year-over-year as uncertainty around proposed IVD pricing guidelines drove customers to reduce inventories more quickly than anticipated”; adjusted gross margin “fell 130 basis points year-over-year to 44.4%, pressured by unfavorable geographic mix from lower China volumes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company models ~$30M 2026 impact with implementation slipping to mid-2027.”

surprises.description: Management modeled second-half respiratory revenue at the lower end of historical seasons rather than assuming a typical seasonal uptick. That is more cautious than the preview’s implied second-half revenue growth and its expectation that respiratory demand would support the back-half bridge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is modeling second-half respiratory revenue at the lower end of historical seasons rather than assuming a typical uptick, citing lower US positivity rates and weak southern hemisphere data.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s H2 revenue bridge implied “+3% to +6.5% Y/Y” and said the bridge needed to be defended through, among other things, “respiratory” demand.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $129 million, well above the preview’s $100–110 million estimate, and the 20% margin exceeded the preview’s roughly 17% expectation. This was a strong quarter-level result despite the sharply reduced full-year outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 21% to $129 million with EBITDA margin expanding 310 basis points to 20% of revenue during the seasonally weakest quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was expected at “~$100–110M (~17%).”

surprises.description: Revenue was $631 million, above the preview’s $613–619 million consensus range, and grew 2% on a constant-currency basis rather than being flat year over year. The beat was modest, but it exceeded the company’s previously described roughly flat sequential steer as well as consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue grew 2% on a constant currency basis to $631 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 revenue consensus was “~$613–619M (‘flat Y/Y’)”; management had steered to revenue “roughly flat with Q1” sequentially with year-over-year growth.

surprises.description: Core business outside China was stronger than the preview’s mid-single-digit Labs recovery expectation: Labs outside China and triage each grew 9% in Q2, while the company said its core labs and immunohematology businesses outside China were expected to grow 3–5% in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Labs outside China up 9% and triage up 9% in Q2”; the core labs and immunohematology businesses outside China “represent about 75% of the company and are expected to grow 3-5% in the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Labs return toward mid-single digits” as a key metric to watch.

surprises.description: Net debt leverage rose to 4.3x adjusted EBITDA, above the 4.1x Q1 level cited in the preview, while cash was only $123 million against $250 million drawn on the revolving facility. This moved leverage in the wrong direction from the preview’s deleveraging expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt leverage stood at 4.3 times adjusted EBITDA, with only $123 million in cash against $250 million outstanding under the revolving credit facility.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “4.1x net debt/adj. EBITDA at Q1” and said management targeted “3.25–3.5x by YE26.”

surprises.description: NETGEAR reported $168.6 million of Q2 revenue, above both the $165 million high end of its guidance and the roughly $157.8 million consensus estimate. The beat was about 6.9% versus consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $168.6 million…coming in above the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 revenue guidance of “$150M – $165M” and consensus revenue of “$157.8M.”

surprises.description: Profitability was substantially better than expected: NETGEAR posted a 2.4% non-GAAP operating margin, above the guidance range’s 2.0% ceiling, and $0.16 non-GAAP EPS versus roughly $0.01 consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company swung to a non-GAAP operating profit of $4 million (2.4% margin)…delivering non-GAAP EPS of $0.16.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s Q2 non-GAAP operating-margin guide was “(1.0)% – 2.0%,” and non-GAAP EPS consensus was “~$0.01.”

surprises.description: Enterprise revenue and margins exceeded the preview’s proof-point thresholds: revenue was $89 million, while gross margin reached 54.1% and contribution margin 25.9%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Enterprise segment revenue grew 7.7% year-over-year to $89 million”; enterprise gross margin was “54.1%” and contribution margin “25.9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for enterprise revenue “>$85M with GM held ≥52%” as the proof point, with a bull case of enterprise “>$88M with GM ≥53%.”

surprises.description: Consumer gross margin deteriorated rather than improving: it fell 210 basis points year over year to 27.3%, below the 29.4% Q1 level the preview pointed to as an improvement to judge against.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consumer segment revenue fell 9.4% year-over-year to $79.6 million and gross margin declined 210 basis points to 27.3% amid rising memory costs and aggressive competitor pricing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Consumer GM improved to 29.4%” and advised judging the segment on gross margin; its bear case flagged consumer GM “below 29%.”

surprises.description: The Q3 outlook was weaker than the preview’s expected range and consensus: the $165–175 million revenue guide has a $170 million midpoint versus roughly $176.1 million consensus, and the company guided to a negative-to-zero non-GAAP operating margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided Q3 2026 revenue to $165-175 million with non-GAAP operating margin of negative 3% to 0%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave Q3 revenue consensus of “~$176.1M” and described a base-case Q3 guide of “$170–178M”; it also cited Q3 EPS consensus of “$0.07.”

surprises.description: The memory supply outlook extended beyond the preview’s stated coverage: NETGEAR secured supply through the first half of 2027, whereas the preview said its pre-buy covered virtually all 2026 production and identified 2027 as the real exposure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured memory supply through the first half of 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said NETGEAR had “secured DDR4 supply for virtually all 2026 production” and that “2027 [was] the real risk.”

surprises.description: Enterprise results masked a pronounced regional weakness: APAC enterprise revenue fell 16% year over year, prompting a go-to-market restructuring and new regional leadership, while the Americas and EMEA grew.
surprises.fact_evidence: “APAC enterprise revenue declined 16% year-over-year, contrasting with 15% growth in the Americas and 9% in EMEA, prompting a go-to-market restructuring and new regional leadership.”

surprises.description: Recurring revenue improved more than the preview’s stated ARR reference, but subscriber count fell short of the preview’s build expectation: ARR reached $41.6 million and grew 15%, while subscribers were 558,000 versus the preview’s approximately 575,000-plus watchpoint and 559,000 at Q1 end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total annual recurring revenue grew 15% year-over-year to $41.6 million, with the company exiting Q2 with 558,000 recurring subscribers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$39.7M ARR, +12% YoY, 559K paid subscribers at Q1 end” and flagged “ARR crossing ~$41M and subscribers above ~575K.”

surprises.description: The Q2 enterprise price action appears more limited than the preview’s expectation of broad increases: the company implemented a small increase and was still evaluating additional actions for the second half, rather than reporting broad 5–6% increases as established across the portfolio.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company…implemented a small enterprise price increase in Q2, with additional pricing actions being evaluated for the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “pushed 5–6% price increases broadly across the enterprise portfolio” and called Q2 the first clean read on whether they stuck.

in_line: Management kept the total second-half memory headwind at roughly the expected 200 basis points rather than raising it to the preview’s 300–400 basis-point bear-case range, though it said the impact would be skewed toward Q3.

NETGEAR continued to repurchase shares in Q2, buying back 560,000 shares for $12.9 million and ending with about $75 million of authorization remaining; the preview flagged buyback pace but did not specify an expected Q2 amount.

surprises.description: Sweetgreen’s Q2 comparable sales fell 6.2%, about 2.2 percentage points worse than the roughly 4% decline implied by consensus. Revenue was also slightly below the $194.4 million consensus estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $192.7 million” and “comparable restaurant sales declined 6.2%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue: $194.4M”; same-store sales were “~–4% implied by revenue.”

surprises.description: Restaurant-level margin was 13.1%, well below the preview’s estimated 16–17% range and below the level the preview said would make the existing full-year margin guide unreachable. The preview anticipated a possible guide cut, but the reported Q2 margin was substantially weaker than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Restaurant-level profit margin fell to 13.1% from 18.9% a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Restaurant-level margin: ~16–17% (buy-side)” and “anything below ~15.5% makes the FY margin guide unreachable and forces a cut.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was a $0.2 million loss rather than the preview’s estimated $5–8 million profit, a much weaker result than the buy-side expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA swung to a loss of $0.2 million versus a $6.4 million profit in the prior year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA: ~$5–8M (buy-side).”

surprises.description: The full-year comparable-sales outlook was reset to an 8%–7% decline, materially worse than the preview’s base-case expectation of roughly a 6%–4% decline after a likely guide cut. The cut itself was anticipated; its depth was worse than that expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance was lowered to comparable sales decline of 8% to 7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected the “FY comp guide trimmed to ~–6%/–4%”; the preview also said to “Assume a meaningful probability the FY comp … ranges get cut or re-based tonight.”

surprises.description: The revised full-year margin outlook fell to 10.5%–11%, a steep reset from the prior 14.2%–14.7% guide. The preview warned that a cut was needed if Q2 margin came in below about 15.5%, but did not anticipate a revised range this low.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance was lowered to … restaurant-level margin of 10.5% to 11%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed the reiterated FY margin guide as “14.2%–14.7%” and said “anything below ~15.5% makes the FY margin guide unreachable and forces a cut.”

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance moved to a $23–27 million loss, far worse than the preview’s base case of a cut to the low end of the old positive $1–6 million range. The preview identified negative full-year EBITDA as a tail risk, but not as its base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance was lowered to … adjusted EBITDA loss of $27 million to $23 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed the prior FY guide as “$1M–$6M” and its base case expected “EBITDA to the low end”; it described a cut “to negative FY EBITDA” as a tail risk.

surprises.description: The outbreak’s sales impact was severe: it reduced July comparable sales by about 600 basis points, and guidance assumes another 600–700 basis points of comp impact in Q3. The preview flagged the outbreak as a key uncertainty and sought quantification, but the reported scale points to a sustained, substantial hit.
surprises.fact_evidence: The outbreak “cut July comparable sales by about 600 basis points”; guidance assumes “continued 600-700 bps comp impact in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q3 commentary and “cyclospora quantification” were key, and asked whether management would size the July/August traffic hit and whether it had recovered. It did not specify an expected impact of this size.

surprises.description: Transactions improved sharply late in the quarter, reaching roughly flat in June from down 11.2% in Q1, with positive comps and transactions in the first 10 days of July before the outbreak. That late-period momentum was stronger than the preview’s implied Q2 traffic decline of about 2%, although the outbreak then reversed it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable transactions improved sequentially from down 11.2% in Q1 to roughly flat in June,” with “positive comps and transactions in the first 10 days of July before the cyclospora outbreak disrupted momentum.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a “–4% comp built on –2% traffic is a turnaround” and described monthly positive June comps as a bull-case signal.

surprises.description: Wraps had a measurable transaction and repeat-visit contribution, but their lower entry price created meaningful check and mix drag. The preview flagged both incrementality and mix-down risk; the concrete 500-basis-point transaction improvement and repeat-purchase rate provide a stronger quantified contribution than it had projected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Wraps achieved roughly 20% incidence and drove about 500 basis points of transaction improvement,” and “more than half of wrap buyers” returned within 30 days, but “their lower entry price created meaningful check/mix drag.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “wraps performance” for “incrementality … and effect on average check,” noting that wraps’ lower price posed “a mix-down risk.”

in_line: A downward revision to full-year guidance was anticipated: the preview said to assume a meaningful probability of a cut or re-basing, and its base case included a cut blamed on July.
The preview anticipated that wraps could dilute average check because they were priced below the salad core; the reported check/mix drag is consistent with that concern.

surprises.description: Serve cut 2026 revenue guidance from about $26 million to $9–10 million, far below the preview’s expectation built around the $26 million outlook. Management attributed the reduction mainly to removing an assumed second-half ramp in Uber delivery volume.
surprises.fact_evidence: Serve “slashed its full-year 2026 revenue guidance from $26 million to a range of $9-10 million,” primarily because it removed an assumed second-half ramp in Uber delivery volume.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue ~$26M”; consensus was “$26.01M.”

surprises.description: Serve said it does not currently expect to renew its Uber agreement when it expires in early 2027 unless the operating model improves meaningfully. That is a sharper break from the prior growth pattern than the preview anticipated: Uber delivery volume had grown for 17 consecutive quarters before reversing in Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: Serve “does not currently expect to renew its Uber agreement when it expires in early 2027 unless the operating model meaningfully improves”; Uber delivery volume had grown “for 17 consecutive quarters before reversing in Q2.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $3.2 million, below both the $3.49 million consensus and the preview’s $3.8–4.1 million whisper range. The reported 9% sequential increase versus Q1’s reported figure did not meet the preview’s higher expectation for sequential growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue was $3.2 million, up 9% sequentially from Q1 and over 400% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 consensus was “$3.49M”; the preview said, “Assume a whisper of ~$3.8–4.1M, i.e. 10–18% real sequential growth.”

surprises.description: Cash and marketable securities ended Q2 above $240 million, well above the preview’s estimated $150–165 million. That leaves Serve with substantially more funding for its strategic pivot than the preview expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with more than $240 million in cash and marketable securities, providing runway to fund its strategic pivot.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “~$150–165M expected at 6/30/26.”

surprises.description: Gross margin improved from Q1’s negative 302% to negative 271%, but remained well short of the preview’s cited marker of moving toward negative 200% or better. The gross loss was still approximately $8.8 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross loss of approximately $8.8 million and gross margin of negative 271%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said, “Any narrowing toward (200)% or better is the strongest possible evidence that scale is converting to leverage.”

surprises.description: DoorDash delivery volume grew rapidly, providing a potential alternative as Uber weakened: it rose nearly 50% sequentially and then another 50% from June to July. The preview did not identify this specific platform as a growing offset.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DoorDash delivery volume grew nearly 50% sequentially last quarter and grew another 50% between June and July, positioning it as a growing alternative to Uber.”

surprises.description: Serve lowered its non-GAAP operating expense outlook to about $140–150 million rather than holding the prior $160–170 million guidance, and also reduced planned 2026 capital expenditures to $15–17 million from about $25 million. The lower spending supports cash preservation, though it also comes alongside the much weaker revenue outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: Serve “reduced planned 2026 capital expenditures from about $25 million to $15-17 million and cut non-GAAP operating expense guidance from $160-170 million to approximately $140-150 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 non-GAAP opex guidance of “$160–170M” and its base case expected the “opex guide held.”

surprises.description: The loss-per-share results differed depending on the measure: GAAP loss of $0.80 per share was worse than the preview’s $0.69 loss consensus, while the non-GAAP loss of $0.59 was better than the preview’s scenario range of $0.65–0.72. The two measures therefore gave contrasting signals.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss was $64 million (-$0.80 per share) and non-GAAP net loss was $47.1 million (-$0.59 per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview showed Q2 EPS consensus of “$(0.69)” and a base-case non-GAAP EPS range of “$(0.65)–$(0.72).”

surprises.description: Serve disclosed that advertising made up nearly half of robotic food delivery revenue and that recurring revenue exceeded half of total revenue. The preview did not anticipate this advertising contribution; the software revenue figure itself was broadly consistent with the prior-quarter level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recurring revenue exceeded 50% of total revenue, with advertising accounting for nearly 50% of robotic food delivery revenues and software revenue again reaching nearly $1 million.”

surprises.description: Management set an August 17 announcement covering a new delivery marketplace partner, the Beacon countertop integration device, new market launches, and autonomy advances. The preview sought named H2 catalysts but had not anticipated this announced package or date.
surprises.fact_evidence: Serve “plans an August 17 summer announcement covering a new delivery marketplace partner, its Beacon countertop integration device, new market launches, and autonomy advances.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to look for a “specific H2 bridge” with “named platforms/cities/hospitals.”

in_line: Software revenue was again nearly $1 million, broadly matching the preview’s Q1 baseline of $1.026 million.
Serve continued to operate about 2,000 robots, consistent with the preview’s report of an approximately 2,000-robot deployed fleet.

surprises.description: Revenue was $612 million, about 4.5% above the $585.4 million consensus and $585 million company frame, exceeding even the preview’s $598–608 million bull-case range. Leasing and services revenue grew 6%, while delivery and installation revenue surged more than 25%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue was $612 million… beating the company's own guidance of approximately $585 million, driven by 6% leasing and services revenue growth”; “Delivery and installation revenue surged over 25% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus revenue ($585.4M) sits exactly on the number management framed… (~$585M)”; bull case revenue was “$598–608M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA beat the $223 million outlook by $5 million, but the margin was 37.2%—below the preview’s roughly 38.1% expectation and its 38.2% “good” threshold. The margin decline was about 500 basis points year over year, worse than the preview’s expected 420-basis-point decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $228 million (beating the $223 million outlook), but adjusted EBITDA margin fell to 37.2%, a roughly 500 basis point year-over-year decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Adj. EBITDA margin ~38.1%” and said “≥38.2%” would look good; it expected “−420 bps” year over year.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.28, above the $0.246 consensus and the preview’s $0.24–0.26 base case, rather than declining about 9% year over year as consensus implied. Reported diluted EPS was flat at $0.26 year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS was flat year-over-year at $0.26 (adjusted EPS $0.28).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus adjusted EPS was “$0.246” versus $0.27 a year earlier, a “−9%” estimate; the base case was “$0.24–0.26.”

surprises.description: Management raised 2026 revenue guidance by $50 million to about $2.3 billion and lifted adjusted EBITDA guidance to about $920 million, rather than merely reiterating the prior $2.25 billion and $915 million outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance by $50 million to approximately $2.3 billion… and increased adjusted EBITDA guidance to approximately $920 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY2026 guidance as “Revenue ~$2.25B” and “Adj. EBITDA ~$915M” and said the base case was that the guide would be reiterated.

surprises.description: Net CapEx guidance rose to about $375 million, $50 million above the preview’s $325 million estimate. Adjusted free cash flow was consequently just $55 million, well below the preview’s $120–135 million expectation, as the company directed more capital to fleet.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net CapEx guidance was raised to approximately $375 million”; “Q2 adjusted free cash flow [fell] to $55 million as the company reinvests over half its capital generation into demand-driven fleet.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Net capex ~$325M” and estimated “Adj. FCF ~$120–135M”; its bull-case commentary expected “net capex held at $325M.”

surprises.description: Management gave a more specific path for margin recovery, calling for 200–300 basis points of sequential expansion in Q3 and another 300–500 basis points in Q4, with flat-to-positive year-over-year EBITDA margin comparisons possible by Q4. This addressed the preview’s concern about the required second-half margin ramp with quantified quarterly targets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided to sequential margin expansion of 200-300 basis points in Q3… and 300-500 basis points in Q4, potentially reaching flat-to-positive year-over-year EBITDA margin comparisons by Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for “a credible H2 margin bridge” and said management needed to attribute the ramp “specifically… with quantification”; it identified the implied “~43.1% margin” in H2 as the key risk.

in_line: The preview looked for a third consecutive quarter of modular activation growth; management reported that activations rose 16% and that this was the third consecutive quarter of growth.

The preview flagged quantifying the World Cup contribution as important and expected the event to be concentrated in Q2. Management reported about 2,000 units, $13 million of Q2 revenue, about 750 modular units on rent year over year, and roughly $5 million of dismantle-related D&I revenue remaining in Q3.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $292.9 million, above the preview’s roughly $272 million working consensus and its roughly $280 million whisper. The result cleared both expectations by a substantial amount.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $292.9 million, up 36% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Working consensus used here: Rev ~$272M”; “A reasonable whisper was ~$280M revenue.”

surprises.description: Shipments were $281.5 million, below revenue, despite the preview’s emphasis that shipments should continue to outpace revenue. Shipment growth also slowed to 36% from 54% in Q1, weakening the forward-demand signal the preview highlighted.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Shipments of $281.5 million, also up 36%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management explicitly guided shipments to keep outpacing revenue”; “Any print where shipments come in below revenue breaks that commitment.”

surprises.description: First-half purchase orders rose 105% year-over-year, with more emphasis on newer products across all categories. The preview focused on shipments as a bookings proxy and on possible shipment deceleration, but did not anticipate this reported order growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half 2026 orders (POs) increased 105% year-over-year, with a heavier emphasis on newer products across all categories.”

surprises.description: Single-wafer cleaning, Tahoe and semi-critical cleaning revenue fell 14.2%, a much steeper decline than the 5.5% decline cited for Q1. The preview flagged stabilization versus a steepening decline as a key debate, and the reported result showed the decline had steepened.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Single-wafer cleaning, Tahoe and semi-critical cleaning revenue fell 14.2% to $133.0 million”; the decline was “reflecting minimal contribution from newer SPM products.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “SWC is the legacy franchise and it shrank 5.5% YoY in Q1”; “If SWC declines are steepening rather than stabilizing, the growth story becomes a single-product (ECP) story with concentration risk.”

surprises.description: Management flagged tightening component supply and lead times that could extend from four to six months, creating a potential constraint on second-half shipments. The preview highlighted shipment trends but did not anticipate this specific supply risk; the company said key suppliers had not raised prices so far.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tightening component supply and longer lead times (extending from 4 months to potentially 6 months) as a potential constraint on second-half shipments, though without price increases from key suppliers so far.”

surprises.description: ACM reported orders for its panel-level horizontal plating tool, including a production order from an advanced-packaging customer in Mainland China and an evaluation system for a new customer in Asia. The preview identified international customer wins as a proof point to watch but did not anticipate these specific tool orders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received orders for its panel-level horizontal plating tool from advanced packaging customers, including a production order in Mainland China and an evaluation system for a new customer in Asia.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Tools installed outside mainland China, Oregon on-schedule commentary, and named international customers are the metrics that would break” the China-domestic-substitution framing.

surprises.description: Customer concentration improved sharply: only one customer accounted for more than 10% of first-half revenue, versus three such customers accounting for 49.9% a year earlier. The preview did not set an expectation for this change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Only one 10%+ customer at 12.7% of first-half revenue versus three 10%+ customers representing 49.9% in first-half 2025.”

in_line: Gross margin was 46.0%, matching the preview’s key threshold of at least 46% and its base-case expectation of roughly 45–46%, although it remained below the year-earlier level.

ECP, furnace and other technologies grew 167.7%, and advanced packaging revenue excluding ECP grew 153.3%. These results met the preview’s stated bull-case operating assumptions of ECP growth above 150% and continued triple-digit advanced-packaging growth.

The revenue-guidance floor rose from $1.08 billion to $1.125 billion while the $1.175 billion ceiling stayed unchanged. This was consistent with the preview’s base case of an upward move with the ceiling unchanged, though it fell short of the upside case in which the ceiling would rise.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $715 million, about $37 million below the $751.6 million consensus, and fell 3% year over year instead of growing about 8%. The call also said it was well below the company’s own expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $715 million, up just 3% year-over-year ... well below the company's historical ~34% CAGR and its own expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $751.6M” consensus; “Implied Y/Y +8.3%.”

surprises.description: Q3 guidance was dramatically below the preview’s derived $800–810 million estimate: the company guided to at least $650 million, implying about a 12% year-over-year decline. Management also said it is allowing time for its substantially overhauled leadership team to ramp up.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for revenue of at least $650 million, implying roughly a 12% year-over-year decline”; guidance assumptions “allow time for these new leaders to ramp up.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Derived Q3 setup ... Q3'26 consensus ≈ $800–810M”; the preview called for attention to whether guidance was below “~$790M.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $241 million versus roughly $260 million expected, and the 34% margin was also below the preview’s roughly 34.6% estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $241 million (34% margin).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$260M”; “Adj. EBITDA margin ~34.6%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.34, below the preview’s $0.40–$0.41 non-GAAP EPS estimate. GAAP net income was $64 million, while adjusted net income was $158 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net income was $158 million ($0.34 per diluted share)” and “GAAP net income was only $64 million ($0.14 per diluted share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS $0.41 (Zacks); $0.40 per StockStory.”

surprises.description: Management attributed the weakness not only to macro pressure on large customers but also to its own execution shortfalls. The preview emphasized macro and agency-spend risks, but did not anticipate management acknowledging execution problems.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management attributed underperformance to both macro headwinds affecting a handful of large customers and its own execution shortfalls,” while characterizing the issues as “cyclical rather than systemic.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview anticipated “macro caveats” and identified “agency spend still impaired” as a bear-case driver.

surprises.description: Despite the weak overall quarter and concerns about CTV competition, the company reported more than 50% year-over-year CTV growth in both EMEA and APAC, with those regions each growing nearly 30% year to date and China above 100%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EMEA and APAC each growing nearly 30% year-to-date, China growing over 100% year-to-date, and CTV growing over 50% year-over-year in both EMEA and APAC.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “CTV / biddable CTV and Amazon share” as a key watch item and said to watch for “any quantified CTV growth rate” amid intensified competition.

surprises.description: Revenue associated with joint business plans grew six times faster than overall revenue, offering a bright spot for agency relationships even as total growth slowed sharply.
surprises.fact_evidence: “217 joint business plans (JBPs) as of Q2, up 38% year-over-year, with revenue under JBPs growing at 6x the overall revenue growth rate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called JBP growth “the cleanest tell on agency trust” and highlighted Publicis-related agency concerns.

in_line: The company reported significant macro pressure in CPG and auto, consistent with the preview’s expectation that macro caveats around consumer categories, auto, and tariffs would remain relevant.

surprises.description: SUI Group reported $1.2 million of Q2 revenue, well above the preview’s $0.55–$0.65 million model. The increase was aided by new staking and digital-lending interest income.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue rose to $1.2 million in Q2 2026 from $948,000 a year earlier, aided by new SUI staking and digital lending interest income.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue: ~$0.55–0.65M.”

surprises.description: The reported net loss of $18.9 million, or $0.23 per diluted share, was materially smaller than the preview’s modeled $26–$30 million loss and $0.34–$0.39 loss per share.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net loss of $18.9 million ($0.23 per diluted share).”

surprises.description: The quarter included a large, unexpected loss tied to the Bluefin loan and another loss on returned SUI tokens from Galaxy Digital. The preview modeled Bluefin lending income and allowed only $0–$3 million for other investment marks, rather than these specific losses.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately $16.6 million of non-cash losses on digital assets and receivables, driven largely by a $14 million loss tied to the additional Bluefin loan and a $2.4 million loss on returned SUI tokens from Galaxy Digital.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Digital lending interest: ~$0.15–0.25M”; “Other investment marks: −$0M to −$3M.”

surprises.description: Cash and cash equivalents were only $3.1 million at quarter-end, far below the preview’s roughly $11 million modeled cash-and-stablecoin balance. Management nevertheless said the company has over two years of operating runway excluding treasury assets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents fell to $3.1 million as of June 30, 2026 from $21.9 million at year-end 2025, though management claims over two years of operating runway excluding treasury assets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash + stablecoins” were modeled at “~$11–12M” at 6/30; the base case expected “cash ~$11M.”

surprises.description: The company made $6 million of new investments in AI and agentic-finance companies, a capital-allocation move not anticipated in the preview’s discussion of buybacks versus the equity line. That is notable alongside the much lower-than-modeled cash balance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New agentic-finance investments of $3 million in AI firm N of 1 (via a SAFE) and $3 million in Recursive Superintelligence.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Buyback vs. equity line” was flagged as a key issue; the preview described the choice as resuming buybacks or drawing the equity line.
