surprises.description: Cash use was higher than the normalized level because GCT prepaid for wafer capacity, with management guiding to quarterly burn of $9–$9.5 million versus a normalized $8–$8.5 million. The prepayment also secured production capacity through Q1 2027 in anticipation of a relatively large ramp, making the development costly near term but supportive of future supply.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GCT prepaid for wafer capacity through the end of 2026, which inflated Q2 cash burn by $7 million to $7.5 million,” and “has secured production capacity through Q1 2027 in anticipation of a relatively large ramp.” Management guided “quarterly cash burn of $9 million to $9.5 million” versus a “normalized baseline of $8 million to $8.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted the cash balance and debt maturities but did not anticipate a wafer-capacity prepayment or give a quarterly cash-burn expectation.

surprises.description: After the quarter, GCT signed a customer in UAV/defense connectivity, adding a new customer opportunity that the preview had not identified.
surprises.fact_evidence: GCT “signed a new post-quarter customer in the UAV/defense connectivity space.”

in_line: GCT shipped more than 5,100 chipsets, above the preview’s 5,000-unit concern threshold and within its 5,000–7,000-unit base-case range.
Quarter-end cash of $30.2 million was broadly within the preview’s expected $20–30 million range.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $13.6 million, materially above the preview’s roughly $10.2 million back-solve and its $10.5–11.5 million base case. That is a sizable beat even though EBITDA was down 2% year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA fell 2% to $13.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA (not published; my back-solve) ~$10.2M”; base case: “$10.5–11.5M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS came in at $0.12, twice the preview’s $0.06 adjusted consensus. Adjusted net income was essentially flat year over year, so the EPS beat did not reflect year-over-year growth in adjusted earnings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net income of $6.4 million and adjusted EPS of $0.12 were both essentially flat versus the prior-year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The published $0.06 consensus”; the preview says to treat it as “an adjusted EPS consensus.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 17%, above the preview’s 16.3–16.6% estimate despite falling from 17.5% a year earlier. Incremental tariffs pressured the result, but IEEPA tariff refunds partly offset them.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit was essentially flat at $55 million with gross margin declining to 17% from 17.5%, pressured by incremental tariffs but partially offset by IEEPA tariff refunds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin (my est. of consensus) ~16.3–16.6%”; base case: “GM ~16.4%.”

surprises.description: Revenue exceeded the $320.5 million consensus and the preview’s +1–2% base case, rising 2.8%. The preview anticipated seafood deflation as a revenue headwind, whereas the reported quarter was driven primarily by seafood volume growth and improved pricing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue rose 2.8% year-over-year to a record $323.8 million, driven primarily by seafood volume growth and improved pricing, partially offset by price declines in meat and poultry.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net revenue $320.5M”; base case: “+1–2% revenue.” The preview also cited “Seafood deflation … is a revenue headwind.”

surprises.description: HF Foods’ net income more than doubled, but the increase was substantially supported by credits, a tariff refund, and a favorable swap valuation change. The preview had warned that the prior quarter’s GAAP profit relied on one-offs, but gave no Q2 GAAP earnings estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income attributable to HF Foods more than doubled to $2.6 million (EPS of $0.05 vs. $0.02), boosted by a $1.8 million employee retention credit, a ~$1.1 million tariff refund, and a $1.4 million favorable swap fair-value change.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 GAAP profitability “leaned on a $1.4M gain on a Utah property sale and a favorable interest-rate-swap mark.”

surprises.description: DSNA expense rose 2.4%, contrary to the preview’s expectation that it would be roughly flat as cost actions offset fuel. Higher fuel costs were the main driver, alongside insurance and professional services.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DSNA expense rose 2.4% to $52.2 million, driven largely by approximately $1.4 million in higher year-over-year fuel costs plus higher insurance and professional service expenses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base case: “DS&A roughly flat as cost actions offset fuel.”

surprises.description: Sea Ray’s reported mid-teens EBITDA margins and gross margins above 20%, together with management’s expectation that the deal is accretive to margins and EPS from close, add a margin-accretion rationale beyond the preview’s focus on the roughly 5x purchase multiple.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sea Ray operates at mid-teens EBITDA margins and gross margins north of 20%, making the deal accretive to both margins and EPS from close and supporting the 4.5%-5%+ consolidated EBITDA margin target.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Sea Ray as “bought at ~5x its ~C$9.6M 2025 EBITDA, which is accretive on multiple but adds debt.”

surprises.description: The company reported a post-quarter refinancing and larger credit commitments, adding $15 million to revolving commitments and expanding term loans from about $95 million to $125 million. This provides more committed financing capacity than the preview’s funding discussion addressed, although the facts do not say how the Sea Ray purchase will be funded.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company refinanced and upsized its credit facility after quarter end, increasing revolving commitments from $125 million to $140 million and expanding term loans from ~$95 million to $125 million, extending maturities to 2031 and 2036.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the Sea Ray cash portion “nearly exhausts revolver headroom” and described “Revolver-funded = manageable” versus “Any ATM usage … is a hard sell signal.”

in_line: The Sea Ray transaction’s approximate purchase price and valuation were broadly in line with the preview: it cited C$47.9 million and about 5x EBITDA, and the call reported a C$47.9 million base price against approximately C$9.6 million of adjusted EBITDA.

surprises.description: Revenue was $8.1 million, about $1.0 million above the preview’s $7.10 million consensus estimate. On a pro forma basis excluding the divested MRI assets, revenue grew 16.6%, rather than the zero core growth implied by the preview’s estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue rose 6% year-over-year to $8.1 million, and up 16.6% on a pro forma basis” excluding the prior-year MRI contribution.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $7.10M”; the preview says this was “almost exactly Q2 2025 ex-MRI” and that “the Street models core organic growth at zero.”

surprises.description: Adjusted profitability substantially exceeded the preview’s functional $0.15-per-share bar: adjusted EPS was $0.23, with adjusted EBITDA of $4.6 million versus the preview’s $3.5 million bull-case level. GAAP net income also more than doubled, while SG&A fell to $4.0 million from $5.9 million, reflecting both the absence of prior-year legal fees and restored economies of scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net income rose to $3.2 million ($0.23 per diluted share)” and “adjusted EBITDA increased to $4.6 million”; net income was $2.7 million versus $1.1 million, and “SG&A fell to $4.0 million from $5.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says the functional bar is “closer to $0.15 adj. EPS”; its bull case has “$3.5M” adjusted EBITDA, while its base case assumes “adjusted profitability roughly flat Y/Y.”

surprises.description: Systemwide sales showed core growth rather than the modest growth or decline contemplated in the preview: sales were $117.8 million, up 6.9% pro forma for the divested MRI assets. That exceeded the preview’s base-case estimate of about 2% ex-MRI growth and its stated $113 million threshold for a clearer positive signal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Systemwide sales declined to $117.8 million from $125.9 million, but grew 6.9% pro forma” after adjusting for divested MRI assets.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case was “~$112M” and “+2% ex-MRI”; it said “Anything above ~$113M signals the on-demand cycle has genuinely turned.”

surprises.description: Franchise royalties grew faster than systemwide sales on a comparable basis, a stronger result than the preview’s concern about royalty-rate leakage suggested. Pro forma royalty growth of 13.8% compared with 6.9% pro forma systemwide-sales growth indicates a more favorable royalty yield or mix than the preview’s recent trend implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Franchise royalties, the primary revenue source, grew 4.1% to $7.6 million, or up 13.8% pro forma for the MRI divestiture.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that “Q1 core royalties fell ~6% while ex-MRI SWS was ~flat” and said the “mix/rate gap hasn’t been fully explained”; it warned that if it persisted, “SWS growth won’t translate to revenue.”

surprises.description: The improvement was not limited to the reported quarter: year-over-year revenue growth accelerated during Q2 and continued into Q3. The preview’s base case anticipated only flat-to-slightly-up on-demand conditions and management repeating a general favorable-trends message, not this reported acceleration and persistence.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Year-over-year revenue growth accelerated within the quarter from roughly 2%-4% early on to as much as 12%-13% in some later weeks, and that momentum has held six weeks into Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case described “on-demand flat-to-slightly-up” and management repeating Q1’s “consistent decent results” and “trends more favorable” language “without a hard number.”

in_line: The company remained debt-free and had about $41 million of credit-facility availability, broadly in line with the preview’s report of no debt and $40.3 million undrawn.

surprises.description: Plug’s gross margin was nearly breakeven at negative 0.9%, substantially better than the preview’s base-case range of negative 10% to negative 15%. That is a much stronger step toward the Q4 positive EBITDAS target than the preview’s expected trajectory.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved to approximately breakeven (negative 0.9%)” and was “up from negative 13% last quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “GM ‑10% to ‑15%”; it said the company plausibly needed GM near breakeven by Q3 to hit positive Q4 EBITDAS.

surprises.description: Plug raised its full-year revenue growth outlook to 15%–16% from 13%–15%, rather than merely reaffirming the prior range. This is a positive revision against a preview that framed reaffirmation as the base case and highlighted the difficult H2 revenue step-up.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year revenue growth guidance to 15%-16% from the prior 13%-15%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the company’s framework as “+13–15% growth” and its base case as FY guidance being “reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Net cash usage fell to $61 million, down about 58% sequentially from Q1. The preview identified sequential cash-burn reduction as the key balance-sheet test, so this is a stronger improvement than simply maintaining the preliminary unrestricted-cash figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net cash usage improved to $61 million, down approximately 58% sequentially from Q1 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the market needs to see burn step down sequentially, not just a promise that it will,” and cited Q1 operating cash burn of “$(150)M.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $178.3 million exceeded the $167.7 million consensus estimate by about 6%. It was also within, rather than above, the preview’s $175–185 million functional whisper range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $178.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 revenue consensus of “$167.7M” and a functional whisper of “$175–185M.”

surprises.description: Service revenue reached $29.8 million, about 23% above the $24.2 million estimate, while service margin was 27%. The preview expected service revenue growth of 47.9% year over year, versus the reported 82%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Service revenue up 82% year-over-year to $29.8 million at a 27% service margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Services (fuel cell systems)” revenue at “$24.2M” and “+47.9%” year over year.

surprises.description: Fuel revenue was $39.5 million, roughly 18% above the $33.4 million estimate, and grew about 15% year over year instead of the expected 3% decline. Fuel gross margin, however, was negative 48%, essentially in line with the preview’s expectation that fuel margins were worse than negative 47%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fuel revenue grew approximately 15% year-over-year to $39.5 million, with fuel gross margin improving to negative 48%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated fuel revenue of “$33.4M” and “‑3%” year over year; it said fuel and PPA segments were “both running worse than ‑47% margin.”

surprises.description: PPA loss rates improved to roughly negative 30%, much better than the preview’s expectation that PPA margins were worse than negative 47%. This indicates a sharper improvement in that loss rate than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “PPA loss rates improved to roughly negative 30% from negative 92%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said fuel and PPA segments “were both running worse than ‑47% margin.”

surprises.description: Two of Plug’s largest material-handling customers plan to refresh more than 20,000 GenDrive units over three years, with roughly 2,000 expected in 2026. The preview discussed the need for H2 project and backlog detail but did not flag this specific refresh program.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Two of the largest Material Handling customers plan to refresh more than 20,000 GenDrive units over three years, with roughly 2,000 units expected to be refreshed in 2026.”

surprises.description: Plug deployed 1,666 GenDrive units, more than double the 739 deployed a year earlier. The preview did not provide a deployment expectation, so this is a favorable operational disclosure not anticipated there.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company deployed 1,666 GenDrive units in Q2, more than double the 739 units deployed a year ago.”

surprises.description: The reported 50% year-over-year operating-expense decline included $39.7 million of recoveries, principally a $37 million customer-contract dispute settlement gain; management put the normalized quarterly run rate near $75 million. The headline reduction therefore overstates the recurring cost improvement, and the one-off recovery was not flagged in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses fell approximately 50% year-over-year to $62 million, though this included $39.7 million of recoveries (principally a $37 million gain from a settled customer contract dispute), with a normalized run rate expected near $75 million per quarter.”

surprises.description: Only about $155 million of restricted cash is scheduled to release over the next 12 months, below the preview’s stated expectation of roughly $50 million per quarter, or about $200 million over a year. The release pace implied by the reported schedule is therefore slower than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Roughly $155 million of restricted cash [is] scheduled to release over the next 12 months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said restricted cash “was guided to release ~$50M/quarter; confirm that's tracking.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS loss of $0.07 was a small beat versus the preview’s $0.08 loss estimate. The gap was modest, while the much larger noncash GAAP charge was in line with the preview’s warning about mark-to-market effects.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS loss narrowed to $0.07 from $0.18.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Adj. EPS” at “$(0.08).”

in_line: Unrestricted cash ended Q2 at $161.9 million, essentially matching the preview’s preliminary estimate of approximately $162 million.
Management reaffirmed the target of positive EBITDAS in Q4 2026, consistent with the preview’s base and bull cases.
GAAP EPS included about $104 million of noncash mark-to-market charges; the preview explicitly warned that GAAP EPS would differ materially from adjusted EPS because of mark-to-market charges.
Fuel gross margin was negative 48%, broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation that fuel margins were worse than negative 47%.

surprises.description: The preview said Riot had only 50 MW contracted at Rockdale and framed a second tenant as a possible upside; Riot instead signed a 20-year lease with a frontier AI lab for 191 MW. The contract is expected to generate about $9.1 billion in revenue, with $365–411 million in average annual NOI, although it requires an illustrative $2.1–2.3 billion of CapEx.
surprises.fact_evidence: Riot executed a “20-year data center lease” for “191 megawatts” at Rockdale, expected to generate “approximately $9.1 billion in total contract revenue”; average annual NOI is projected at “$365-411 million,” with illustrative CapEx of “$2.1-2.3 billion total.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “AMD has 50 MW contracted at Rockdale”; the bull scenario said “Corsicana LOI or second AMD-style tenant announced.”

surprises.description: The preview said Corsicana had no tenant or LOI. Riot now has a nonbinding LOI for a single tenant to take the entire site, with potential annual rent exceeding $1 billion at full deployment—substantial progress, though not yet a signed lease.
surprises.fact_evidence: Riot “entered a nonbinding LOI with a single tenant for the entire Corsicana site” for up to 756 MW, which “could generate in excess of $1 billion in annual rent upon full deployment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “No Corsicana tenant, no LOI as of the last update.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $174 million, about 17% above the $148.7 million consensus estimate, a larger result than the preview’s base-case range of $140–152 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue rose 14% year-over-year to $174 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus revenue was “$148.7M”; the base scenario anticipated “$140–152M.”

surprises.description: The GAAP loss was substantially worse than expected: Riot reported a $0.68 per-share loss versus consensus of $0.39. The call attributed the loss in part to over $240 million of noncash items, including a $75 million Bitcoin mark-to-market loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: Riot reported a “GAAP net loss of $237 million ($0.68 per diluted share)” and “over $240 million in noncash items including a $75 million Bitcoin mark-to-market loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus GAAP EPS was “−$0.39”; the preview’s base scenario expected “−$0.35 to −$0.50.”

surprises.description: Engineering revenue was far above the $21.2 million consensus estimate, reaching $37.3 million. Its gross margin also expanded to over 27%, though the preview had not provided a margin estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Engineering segment tripled revenue year-over-year to $37.3 million with gross margin expanding from ~7% to over 27%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus Engineering revenue was “$21.2M.”

surprises.description: Data center segment revenue was $23.2 million, well above the preview’s implied estimate of about $8 million. The preview cautioned that the line could be dominated by fit-out work, so the recurring lease result is a separate and more informative comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The data center segment generated $23.2 million revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Data Center rev (implied residual) ~ $8.0M.”

surprises.description: Recurring data center lease revenue reached $4.9 million, above the preview’s expected $1–3 million range. That is a stronger recurring run rate than the preview anticipated, rather than merely a higher total driven by fit-out services.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recurring operating lease revenue of $4.9 million (up over 400% from Q1).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “recurring lease still ~$1–3M”; the preview said to judge the line by “recurring lease revenue.”

surprises.description: Bitcoin production exceeded the 1,527 BTC consensus estimate by 60 BTC, or about 4%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bitcoin mining produced 1,587 BTC.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus estimate: “Bitcoin mined 1,527 BTC.”

surprises.description: Riot secured a $573 million interim facility backed by the tenant’s credit while an investment-grade backstop is finalized. The preview was watching for project-level financing to close, but did not anticipate this specific interim facility or its tenant-credit security.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Riot secured a $573 million interim financing facility from Morgan Stanley to fund near-term development CapEx” and it is “fully secured by the tenant’s credit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged whether “project-level nonrecourse financing actually closed” and said the bull case included “nonrecourse project debt closed.”

surprises.description: The AMD financing is expected to provide nearly twice Riot’s initial equity and about $90 million in net new capital to recycle into the frontier AI lab build-out, reducing the net equity needed for that build to as little as $30–280 million. This financing-and-recycling benefit was not laid out in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The AMD financing is expected to close before end of Q3 with debt proceeds nearly double Riot's initial equity, generating ~$90 million in net new capital” to fund the build-out and reduce net equity required “to as little as $30-280 million.”

surprises.description: Riot ended the quarter with $1.2 billion of liquidity, including $549 million in cash, and issued no common equity. That is a stronger near-term liquidity position than the preview’s concern about tighter funding capacity and its expectation that further Bitcoin sales might be needed.
surprises.fact_evidence: Riot ended Q2 with “$1.2 billion in total liquidity,” including “$666 million in Bitcoin (11,380 BTC) and $549 million in cash,” and “did not issue any common equity during the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said funding capacity was “materially tighter than at Q1” and the base scenario anticipated “further BTC sales to fund capex”; it also described the strategy as “explicitly avoiding equity issuance.”

surprises.description: Mining cost was $49,912 per Bitcoin, above the Q1 baseline of $44,629, while the preview had highlighted summer curtailment credits as a tailwind. The reported $10 million of credits was also below Q1’s $21 million, so the expected tailwind did not prevent higher direct mining costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: Riot reported a “direct cost to mine of $49,912 per Bitcoin” and “$10 million in power curtailment credits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported Q1 cost to mine of “$44,629/BTC” and said “ERCOT summer curtailment credits should be a Q2 tailwind — quantify them.”

in_line: Mining revenue appears to have come in modestly below the $119.5 million consensus, broadly matching the preview’s anticipated shortfall: total revenue of $174 million less the reported $23.2 million data center and $37.3 million Engineering revenue implies about $113.5 million for mining, versus the preview’s $119.5 million estimate.

surprises.description: Revenue was $60.1 million, below the preview’s $60.87 million consensus, and core organic growth was only 0.4%, short of the preview’s 2%–3% base-case expectation. The positive core result avoided another negative quarter, but the underlying growth was weaker than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q1 revenue was $60.1 million, up just 1% year-over-year, with core organic revenue growth of only 0.4%”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $60.87M”; the base case expected “core organic +2–3%.”

surprises.description: SDC fell 3.6% organically to $24.5 million, worse than the preview’s base case of flat-to-slightly-up performance. Past-due backlog also rose about $1 million from its year-end low, indicating the Q4 backlog reduction did not provide a durable fix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SDC…posted a 3.6% organic decline to $24.5 million due to delivery reliability issues”; “SDC past-due backlog rose about $1 million from its year-end low.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “SDC flat-to-slightly-up on tough comp”; the preview said to “watch backlog commentary specifically.”

surprises.description: Adjusted operating income was $15.4 million at a 25.6% margin, above the preview’s implied roughly $14.6 million and 24% margin. That exceeded the preview’s threshold for evidence that margin gains were durable, although management cautioned against annualizing the seasonally light quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating income excluding unusual items grew 19.5% to $15.4 million (25.6% of revenue vs. 21.7% prior year), nearly 390 basis points of margin expansion,” with management warning “against annualizing this seasonally light quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus implied AOI “roughly $14.6M, or ~24.0% margin”; the preview said “anything at or above 25% suggests the FY26 expansion is durable.”

surprises.description: Clinical Genomics was essentially flat rather than showing the stabilization the preview expected; China was still down 7%. Non-China growth of 0.6% limited the overall decline but did not deliver the anticipated clearer improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Clinical Genomics was essentially flat at -0.1% ($10.3 million), with China down 7% but non-China up 0.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “CG China stabilization” was a key metric and that the drag “should mathematically fade”; it noted CG was “+5.8% organic in 4Q26.”

surprises.description: The preview anticipated GAAP/non-GAAP divergence largely because of acquisition-related amortization, but the reported GAAP net-income decline was driven by a $2.7 million swing in non-operating expense from unrealized FX losses on an intercompany loan. This left GAAP net income down sharply despite stronger operating income.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net income fell 40.3% to $2.8 million ($0.49 per diluted share) driven by a $2.7 million non-operating expense swing from unrealized FX losses on an intercompany loan, not operations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cautioned that “similar GAAP/non-GAAP divergence” could persist “given acquisition-related intangible amortization”; it did not identify an FX-driven expense swing.

surprises.description: Management gave a specific net-leverage target of 1.5x–1.75x by fiscal year-end and explicitly deprioritized acquisitions, providing a clearer and more debt-focused capital-allocation signal than the preview’s base case of qualitative strategy framing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repaid $8.7 million of debt, lowering net leverage to 1.85x… with a target of 1.5x-1.75x by fiscal year-end and an explicit de-prioritization of acquisitions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case anticipated “qualitative strategy framing only”; the preview said the first call was a “natural venue to define a target” and signal whether capital would go to debt, buybacks, or M&A.

surprises.description: Operating cash flow increased substantially, reaching $14.7 million, a positive cash-generation result the preview did not specifically anticipate for the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow rose $12.8 million to $14.7 million.”

surprises.description: The company installed a new general manager for BPD, an operational leadership change not specifically identified in the preview’s possible strategic announcements.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A new general manager was installed for BPD.”

surprises.description: Mesa said it had accelerated the next-generation Gyrolab platform launch to fiscal 2028, its first new platform since 2018. The preview did not flag this product-timing announcement, and no revenue contribution was provided.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The next-generation Gyrolab platform launch was accelerated to fiscal 2028 (its first new platform since 2018), though no revenue was attached to it.”

in_line: BPD returned to positive organic growth at 5%, broadly matching the preview’s expectation of a return to positive growth after the prior-quarter decline. Management attributed much of the rebound to easier comparisons and catch-up of export-control-deferred orders, so it did not establish that the turnaround was complete.
The company did not provide full-year guidance in this release; the preview expected guidance to be deferred until November.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was only just over $5 million, versus the preview’s $11–13 million base case and its roughly $12.5 million estimate. The 9.3% margin was also far below the expected 19–21%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA exceeded $5 million” and the “adjusted EBITDA margin [was] 9.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA / margin” estimated at “~$12.5M / ~20%”; base case “$11–13M (19–21%).”

surprises.description: Revenue reached $58 million, below both the $61.8 million consensus and the preview’s approximately $61 million build, despite recurring fees coming in near the expected level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue reached $58 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus revenue was “$61.8M”; the preview’s revenue build estimated “~$61.0M.”

surprises.description: AlTi recorded a nearly $19 million unrealized loss on its external Asian Credit and Special Situations fund stake after the manager unexpectedly decided to unwind the fund. The call also said net loss from continuing operations widened to $31 million, versus the preview’s positive $0.06 EPS consensus, with $20 million of other expense affecting the result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An unrealized investment loss of nearly $19 million” followed the manager’s decision to unwind the fund; “net loss from continuing operations widened to $31 million versus $26 million a year earlier, impacted by $20 million of other expense.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “EPS $0.06” consensus, while noting EPS was a “low-signal metric for ALTI.”

surprises.description: The fund unwind also creates a forward revenue headwind not anticipated in the preview: the fund had contributed recurring management fees and incentive distributions that will now diminish.
surprises.fact_evidence: The fund had contributed “about 75 basis points of recurring management fees and about 650 basis points of the incentive portion of distributions year-to-date, which will now diminish.”

surprises.description: Client flows were much stronger than the preview’s base case: wealth management had about $700 million of net inflows, and the company said overall AUM growth was driven partly by net positive client inflows.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Wealth management generated gross client inflows of nearly $800 million and net flows of about $700 million”; AUM growth was driven by “net positive client inflows.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected flows “~flat to −$0.3B”; the preview described positive net flows as part of the bull case.

surprises.description: The expected cost improvement appears pushed further out: the preview looked for expense normalization in the second half of 2026, while management said the benefits of zero-based budgeting and vendor rationalization would accelerate into 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects cost-reduction benefits “to accelerate into 2027,” with further reductions targeted in both compensation and non-compensation expenses.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management guided to “normalization in 2H26” and flagged that if normalized opex was not below about $56 million, “the cost story slips a quarter.”

in_line: Recurring management and advisory fees were $54 million, close to the preview’s $54.5 million estimate and its $54 million threshold for validating the fee base.
AUM reached $51 billion, above the Q1 level of $49 billion, consistent with the preview’s expectation that AUM would rise above Q1.
The strategic review remained ongoing with nothing further to report, matching the preview’s expected repeat of “nothing further to report.”

surprises.description: AAON reported Q2 net sales of $627 million, far above the preview’s $501–515 million consensus range. The result exceeded the top of that range by about 22%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales hit a record $627 million,” up 101% year-over-year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Revenue consensus band: “~$501–515M.”

surprises.description: AAON raised its 2026 sales-growth outlook to 55%–60%, above the prior 40%–45% guide and the preview’s base-case expectation that the guide would be reaffirmed. The scale of the increase was a substantial upgrade.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 sales growth guidance to 55%-60%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Prior guidance was “40–45%”; the preview’s base case expected the “FY guide [to be] reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.69, above the preview’s $0.51–$0.52 diluted-EPS consensus range. The reported figure is adjusted, while the preview labels its consensus diluted EPS without specifying an adjusted basis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS grew 213.6% to $0.69.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Diluted EPS consensus band: “~$0.51–0.52.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin fell to 24.3%, well below the preview’s base-case expectation of roughly 26%–27%. Memphis ramp costs, outsourcing, and price-cost timing weighed on the result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin declined to 24.3% from 26.6%,” pressured by “Memphis ramp-up costs, increased outsourcing, and inflationary price/cost timing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “GM ~26–27%,” and its bull case expected “GM holds ≥27%.”

surprises.description: AAON cut its full-year gross-margin guide by about 200 basis points, from 27%–28% to 25%–26%. The reduction was driven largely by lower-margin Memphis volume mix, against a preview base case that expected the guide to be reaffirmed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cut gross margin guidance by roughly 200 basis points to 25%-26%, driven largely by lower-margin Memphis volume mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Prior gross-margin guidance was “27–28%”; the preview’s base case expected the “FY guide [to be] reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: The preview flagged the sequential backlog decline and sub-1 book-to-bill as a risk and asked whether it reflected order softening. Management said BASX bookings were below recent elevated levels because of lumpy large-project timing, not cancellations or a change in market opportunity, offering reassurance on the cause even though bookings softened.
surprises.fact_evidence: “BASX bookings fell below recent elevated levels,” which management attributed to “lumpiness in large-project timing rather than any specific order cancellation or a change in market opportunity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called backlog “SOFT,” noted it was “down from $2.13B at Q1,” and asked whether the decline was “a timing artifact” or “genuine order softening.”

in_line: The preview flagged margin recovery as a key issue and expected sequential improvement in the second half; management still guided to improvement, though described Q3 gains as modest and Q4 as the year’s high watermark.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $19.3 million, about 3.5% below the roughly $20.0 million consensus and the company’s own Q2 expectation. The shortfall was worse than the preview’s base-case range of $19.8–20.3 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $19.3 million” and was “below company expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Consensus / Guide | $20.01M”; “The company's own words on the May 12 call were ‘approximately $20.0 million’”; base case: “Q2 Revenue | $19.8–20.3M.”

surprises.description: OviTex PRS deteriorated much more sharply than the preview’s discussion of US mix and pricing suggested: revenue fell to $5.5 million from $7.3 million, with units down 23%. A failed dedicated-rep pilot and losses concentrated among fewer than 10 sites and several surgeons on leave were unexpected explanations for the weakness.
surprises.fact_evidence: “OviTex PRS revenue fell to $5.5 million from $7.3 million,” with a “23% unit volume decline”; the decline was attributed to “a failed dedicated-rep pilot” and customer concentration, including surgeons out on leave.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview focused on US demand shifting toward “smaller, cheaper units” and said the concern was “a pricing problem,” while its base case called for an “in-line quarter.”

surprises.description: Gross margin came in well above the preview’s 66–67% expectation, at 72%. The improvement was helped by a tariff refund and lower inventory charges, so some of the upside came from favorable items rather than only underlying operations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved to 72% from 70%, aided by a refund of previously paid tariffs and lower excess/obsolete inventory charges.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~66–67% (no formal guide)” and the preview asked whether inventory charges would “keep gross margin below 67%.”

surprises.description: OviTex global revenue growth was 6.6%, better than the preview’s low-single-digit revenue-growth scenario, even though unit growth was 12%. The shift toward smaller, lower-priced robotic hernia units still meant revenue lagged volume.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Global OviTex unit volume grew 12% year-over-year to 5,776 units, outpacing its 6.6% dollar revenue growth due to a shift toward smaller, lower-priced robotic hernia units.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If Q2 repeats ‘units up double digits, revenue up low single digits’...”

surprises.description: Interest expense was higher than the preview’s estimated quarterly loan cost, contributing to a wider net loss. The preview estimated roughly $1.8 million per quarter in facility interest, while the reported amount was $2.1 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $11.3 million from $9.9 million,” largely due to interest expense of “$2.1 million” versus “$1.2 million previously.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated the facility would cost “~$1.8M/quarter.”

surprises.description: Liquifix grew 39%, an additional product-line bright spot that the preview did not identify while focusing on the revenue and US hernia risks. The preview provided no specific growth expectation for Liquifix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Liquifix revenue grew 39%, remaining [a] bright spot[] against domestic weakness.”

in_line: The company withdrew its full-year revenue guidance, consistent with the preview’s base case that guidance would be withdrawn or cut.
Cash ended Q2 at $30.4 million, within the preview’s estimated $29–31 million range.
Heather Goetz’s appointment as CEO was already known and explicitly discussed in the preview.
Management’s cost-reduction posture was broadly anticipated; the preview expected a turnaround-focused opening, while the call announced planned reductions without finalized specifics.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $5 million, far above the preview’s roughly $1.9 million estimate, which assumed Hawthorne Airport operations would be the main revenue source. The reported figure was more than twice the estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue grew to $5 million, a 213% increase over the prior quarter, driven by growth in operations at Hawthorne Airport in LA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $1.95M”; the preview’s estimate was “$1.9M” and noted “Hawthorne Airport FBO ops only.”

surprises.description: Management said the acquisitions would not structurally increase Archer’s cash burn and targeted relatively flat burn after closing. That is better than the preview’s concern that the burn curve could steepen ahead of deal synergies.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The acquisitions will not structurally increase overall cash burn, targeting relatively flat cash burn post-close through synergies across Midnight, Halo/Thunder, and ZEE platforms.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Standalone Q3 guide of >-$200M signals the burn curve steepening ahead of any Boeing-deal synergies.”

surprises.description: Archer held Q3 adjusted EBITDA loss guidance at $170 million to $200 million rather than moving toward the higher losses the preview considered possible. The preview’s base case was $190 million to $215 million, with a loss above $200 million flagged as a risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance held in the same range” as the $170 million to $200 million Q2 range.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 guide -$190M to -$215M” in the base case; “Standalone Q3 guide of >-$200M signals the burn curve steepening.”

surprises.description: The adjusted EBITDA loss was $177 million, modestly better than the preview’s $186 million estimate, although still within the company’s expected guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA loss was $177 million, at the lower (better) end of the $170 million to $200 million guidance range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Adj. EBITDA: -$186M” and cited company guidance of “-$170M to -$200M.”

surprises.description: Archer added a near-term profitability outlook for its AI businesses: ZEE and SkyGrid could generate revenue and become profitable as early as next year, with a potential significant ramp in the second half of 2027 and beyond. The preview discussed the acquisitions but did not anticipate this timing or profitability target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Archer targets its AI solutions (ZEE and SkyGrid) to be revenue-generating and profitable as early as next year, with potential for a significant ramp in the back half of 2027 and beyond.”

surprises.description: The call described Boeing’s consideration as locked-up Archer stock and said the warrants have exercise prices far above Archer’s current share price. That provides more detail and appears less immediately dilutive than the preview’s unresolved concern about the deal’s dilution and warrant math.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Boeing took all stock with a lockup and committed future equity investments, plus warrants with exercise prices far in excess of Archer's current share price.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the deal was being priced as “strategically positive but dilutive and un-quantified” and flagged the “four-year warrant strip” and post-Boeing share count.

surprises.description: Archer reported that Midnight is already in the FAA’s fourth and final type-certification phase and cited more than 150 piloted test flights, including intercity flights over 50 miles. The preview knew Phase 3 had closed and focused on TIA event counts and upcoming transition testing, but had not anticipated these reported flight-volume details or the stated final-phase status.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Archer reports being the only industry OEM in the fourth and final phase of the FAA type certification process for Midnight, having flown over 150 piloted test flights, up to 5 times a day, including intercity flights over 50 miles.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Archer closed FAA Phase 3 in April 2026”; the preview focused on “~10 discrete TIA events” and whether piloted transition testing remained slated for 2H26.

in_line: Insitu’s over $200 million in annual revenue and existing profitability were already disclosed and highlighted in the preview; the call’s expectation of positive free cash flow and self-funding operation is consistent with that anticipated cash-generating role.
Q2 adjusted EBITDA remained within the $170 million to $200 million company guidance range.
Ending liquidity of $1.6 billion was close to the preview’s estimate of approximately $1.57 billion to $1.59 billion.

surprises.description: APEI’s adjusted EBITDA was $20.7 million, well above the $18 million top of its Q2 guidance and above the preview’s $17.5–18.5 million base-case range. The 275-basis-point margin expansion to 12% made this a stronger operating result than the preview’s expected moderation implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA grew 36.8% to $20.7 million with margin expanding 275 basis points to 12%, exceeding the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA $16.5–18.0M” and the base scenario anticipated “$17.5–18.5M”; the preview also said the marketing step-up “moderates” Military+ margin toward long-range targets.

surprises.description: Diluted EPS of $0.52 exceeded both the $0.36 consensus and the preview’s estimated $0.42–0.48 functional whisper. Net income of $9.8 million also came in above the company’s $6.5–7.5 million guidance range, making the earnings result stronger than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income available to common stockholders was $9.8 million or $0.52 per diluted share, reversing a prior-year loss of $0.02 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS” guidance was “$0.34–0.39” and consensus was “$0.36”; the preview described the “functional whisper” as “$0.42–0.48.” Net income guidance was “$6.5–7.5M.”

surprises.description: Military Plus registrations were about 98,300, at the bottom of the expected range and below the preview’s 99,000–100,000 base-case level. The reported 2% growth and deployment pressure were anticipated, but the count landed at the low end of the outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Military Plus revenue grew 4.7% to $85.5 million on 2% net course registration growth to ~98,300,” with active-duty registrations “pressured by Middle East deployments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario anticipated “registrations ~99–100K”; the stated guidance range was “98,300–100,300.”

surprises.description: The combination removed the 2021 Department of Education growth restriction on Rasmussen’s total enrollment, an enrollment-growth opportunity the preview did not identify. The preview anticipated the combination and approvals, but not this specific consequence.
surprises.fact_evidence: The combination “united all units under a single HLC accreditation and lift[ed] the 2021 Department of Education growth restriction on Rasmussen's total enrollment.”

surprises.description: APEI introduced Q3 guidance of $164.5–167 million in revenue and $14–17 million in adjusted EBITDA, with about $6 million of revenue and $4 million of EBITDA shifted into Q4. The preview had no Q3 forecast; management attributed the softer quarterly profile to the September 7 Military Plus start date and nonrecurring marketing optimization costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance (revenue $164.5-167 million, adjusted EBITDA $14-17 million) reflects a ~$6 million revenue and ~$4 million EBITDA timing shift into Q4 due to a September 7 Military Plus start date plus nonrecurring marketing optimization costs.”

surprises.description: The company lowered its full-year capex outlook to $25–28 million from $28–32 million. The preview listed the prior capex range but did not anticipate a reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: APEI raised full-year guidance while “lowering capex to $25-28 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Capex $28–32M.”

surprises.description: APEI discussed a potential tuition-assistance increase under a pending NDAA provision, which could let it raise active-duty tuition while preserving its zero out-of-pocket commitment. This potential pricing opportunity was not raised in the preview and remains contingent on the provision.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A pending NDAA provision could raise military tuition assistance 40% (from $250 to $350 per credit hour), potentially allowing APEI to reprice active-duty tuition while maintaining its 23-year zero out-of-pocket commitment.”

in_line: Q2 revenue of $171.7 million was within guidance and at its high end, consistent with the preview’s expectation of a result near the $170.79 million consensus.
HealthPlus enrollment of about 19,600 matched the preview’s target; its 11% revenue growth and enrollment growth were consistent with the expected trajectory.

The company raised full-year revenue, adjusted EBITDA, and EPS guidance, as the preview expected a raise rather than a reaffirmation. The new ranges were modestly above the prior guidance, not the preview’s bull-case thresholds.

Cash and debt were broadly in line with the preview’s cited balance-sheet figures: $222.8 million in cash and investments versus about $221 million noted there, and $88.9 million in debt versus about $88 million.

The preview expected Middle East deployments to pressure active-duty registrations and military-family/veteran growth to help offset the pressure; the reported segment commentary was consistent with that outlook.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $319.7 million, far above the preview’s $196.97 million consensus estimate. The preview expected a beat to be likely, but the reported figure was much higher than that already-low forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue surged 130% year-over-year to $319.7 million, exceeding both company and consensus expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $196.97M” and “A revenue beat is the higher-probability outcome.”

surprises.description: B&W raised the 2026 adjusted EBITDA range to $80–$105 million rather than keeping the preview’s $80–$100 million range. The increase was partly due to Base Electron revenue being recognized ahead of schedule, indicating faster-than-expected progress on that project.
surprises.fact_evidence: “B&W raised its full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA target range to $80 million to $105 million, driven partly by ahead-of-schedule Base Electron revenue recognition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 core adj. EBITDA guidance | $80M–$100M” and “guidance reaffirmed at $80–$100M.”

surprises.description: Skilled-labor shortages increased direct costs on a construction project during Q2, requiring incentives, rehires, and delayed retirements to address staffing. The preview did not flag this project-cost pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Skilled labor shortages raised direct costs on a specific construction project during Q2, prompting incentives, rehires, and delayed retirements.”

surprises.description: B&W secured reservation rights for an additional 1 gigawatt of Siemens Energy steam turbines, with first deliveries expected in 12 to 14 months. This additional capacity was not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “B&W secured reservation rights from Siemens Energy for an additional 1 gigawatt (20 50-megawatt steam turbines) with first deliveries in 12 to 14 months.”

in_line: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $21.8 million, within the preview’s estimated range of approximately $20–$22 million.
Backlog was $2.6 billion, within the preview’s expected range of roughly $2.6–$2.7 billion.
The company reported cash and restricted cash exceeding total debt, consistent with the preview’s expectation that B&W would have a net cash position.
The $50 million share repurchase authorization was already expected; the preview said it had been authorized and was expected to begin after the Q2 10-Q filing.

surprises.description: The preview said management had promised a comprehensive update on the restaurant strategic-alternatives process, but the call facts report restaurant closures and operating results without a sale, deal, or comprehensive process update. That leaves the central restaurant-monetization question unanswered.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call facts describe the restaurant group’s revenue decline, reduced traffic, and O’Charley’s store closures, but report no comprehensive update or transaction on the strategic-alternatives process.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management had promised a “comprehensive update this quarter”; the preview said “Silence = credibility hit.”

surprises.description: Cannae repurchased no stock in Q2, despite the preview’s expectation of continued repurchases, and it allocated about $45 million to investments during the quarter. The preview specifically raised the possibility that buybacks would slow as capital went to new sports assets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Repurchased no stock in Q2 due to recently announced transactions”; Cannae allocated “approximately $45 million to investments in Q2” and $54 million year-to-date through July.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview anticipated “~1–2M shares bought back” in its base case and flagged buybacks slowing as cash was redirected to “Exeter/new sports assets” as a bear-case signal.

surprises.description: The restaurant group recorded $45 million of non-cash impairments, a much heavier charge than the preview’s base-case expectation of a modest impairment. The charges accompanied reduced traffic and O’Charley’s store closures.
surprises.fact_evidence: The restaurant group “incurred $45 million of non-cash impairment charges (versus $1 million a year earlier) due to reduced traffic and O’Charley’s store closures.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case anticipated “another modest impairment”; further closures and impairments appeared in the bear case.

surprises.description: The SpaceX IPO produced an $83.4 million mark-to-market gain, an unanticipated boost to Q2 reported results. Management also warned that future earnings could vary with these marks, so the gain is not a stable operating improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: The IPO “triggered mark-to-market accounting, producing an $83.4 million gain in Q2 based on the June 30th trading price,” with management warning of “future earnings variability from these marks.”

surprises.description: Cannae disclosed an additional $45 million federal tax refund expected in 2026, a cash source not identified in the preview. It adds to the liquidity outlook, although the preview had already flagged the Watkins and Brasada proceeds.
surprises.fact_evidence: Cannae had “$124 million” of liquidity after the Watkins and Brasada transactions, “with an additional $45 million federal tax refund expected in 2026.”

surprises.description: Black Knight Football’s adjusted EBITDA excluding player trading was $34 million, versus $8 million a year earlier, while total EBITDA reached $80 million. The preview emphasized that player-trading profits were lumpy and highlighted recurring EBITDA quality as a key question, making the reported ex-trading result a favorable operating datapoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: Black Knight Football revenue rose 45% to $89 million and EBITDA was $80 million versus $8 million; “adjusted EBITDA excluding player trading was $34 million versus $8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that $113 million of LTM EBITDA came from player-trading profit, described it as “lumpy and non-recurring,” and said to watch “BKFC economics ex-player-trading.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $102 million, above the $99.65 million consensus estimate. The beat was modest, and revenue still declined from the prior year.
surprises.fact_evidence: Restaurant-group revenue was “$102 million from $110 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 2026 revenue estimate: “$99.65M.”

in_line: The restaurant revenue decline was broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of roughly 9.6% year-over-year contraction, though the reported $102 million was above consensus.
The Watkins sale’s roughly 1.2x multiple on invested capital was in line with the preview’s reference to Watkins proceeds and an approximately 1.2x MOIC.
The Brasada transaction freeing about $47 million of capital was in line with the preview’s expectation that Brasada would free at least $47 million.
Corporate holding-company operating expenses staying below $9 million was consistent with the preview’s focus on continued cost discipline after Q1 expenses of $8.9 million.
AFC Bournemouth’s sixth-place finish and first Europa League qualification were already known and flagged in the preview.

surprises.description: BODI reported $49.6 million of Q2 revenue, above the $48.5 million guidance midpoint but below the preview’s $51 million functional bar. That makes the result a modest shortfall against the preview’s high-end expectation, despite being within company guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $49.6 million, above the guidance midpoint”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue vs. the $51M guide ceiling — not vs. the $52.9M ‘consensus.’” The preview also says “landing inside the range is a de facto disappointment.”

surprises.description: Digital subscriptions ended at 760,000, below the preview’s roughly 780,000 reference point, with a 6.2% sequential decline. That is worse than the preview’s desired flattening of better than about 5%, though it remains within the preview’s stated 760,000–785,000 base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Digital subscriptions fell 6.2% sequentially and 19.1% year-over-year to 760,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Digital subs vs. ~780K” and “Sequential decline better than ~-5% = the erosion is flattening”; the base scenario gave “Subs 760–785K (-4% to -6% q/q).”

surprises.description: Q3 revenue guidance of $44 million to $48 million came in below the preview’s $46 million to $51 million base-case range and its bull-case stabilization level near $48 million to $50 million. The lower end signals a steeper step-down than that base expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance projects revenue of $44 million to $48 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario put Q3 guidance at “$46–51M”; it said “anything implying stabilization near $48–50M is the bull’s evidence” and “another step down says the digital base is still leaking.”

surprises.description: Q3 nutrition and other gross margin guidance extends down to 42%, below the preview’s 43% floor for acceptable nutrition margin. Management attributed the expected further decline to lower-priced products and promotions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nutrition and other gross margin dropped about 470 basis points year-over-year to 46.7%, and Q3 guidance calls for a further decline to a 42%-45% range due to lower-priced product mix and promotions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If nutrition margin lands below the 43% floor, the retail pivot’s unit economics come into question.”

surprises.description: Q2 profitability exceeded the guidance ceiling: net income was positive rather than merely at breakeven, and adjusted EBITDA was $6.7 million versus a $6 million high end. The preview expected a fourth consecutive profitable quarter, but the results were better than the provided guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income of $1.4 million and adjusted EBITDA of $6.7 million … both exceeding the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 guidance of “Net income: -$3M to breakeven” and “Adj. EBITDA: $3–6M.”

in_line: Q2 nutrition and other gross margin was 46.7%, within the preview’s expected Q2 gross-margin range of 43%–47%.
The preview expected the fourth consecutive quarter of net income; BODI reported its fourth consecutive quarter of net income.

Retail distribution was broadly in line with the preview’s door-count context: the preview cited about 500 Vitamin Shoppe locations and 100+ Sprouts stores, while the call reported 481 Vitamin Shoppe locations and 131 Sprouts stores.
Cash remained above the preview’s $30 million downside marker and the $22.5 million covenant cash threshold, though it declined from the prior quarter.
Q3 was identified as the first clean year-over-year comparison post-MLM, as the preview anticipated.

surprises.description: GoPro said the strategic-alternatives process is in its later stages and that it has received inquiries from defense, consumer, and financial-sector parties. The preview expected no process update, so this is a meaningful departure from the expected silence, although no transaction or bidder commitment was reported.
surprises.fact_evidence: “inquiries spanning defense, consumer and financial sectors,” and management stated they are “in the later stages of the process.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said it does not intend to provide ongoing updates”; the base case expected “no process update.”

surprises.description: The subscriber attach rate reached a record 69%, up from 54% a year earlier, while retention held at 67%. This is a stronger subscription-engagement signal than the preview’s focus on whether the subscriber base would stabilize or continue to erode.
surprises.fact_evidence: “subscriber attach rate hit a record 69% in Q2, up sharply from 54% in the same period last year, while retention held steady at 67%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether the sub base stabilizes near 2.2M or keeps eroding.”

surprises.description: GoPro is offering a limited-time $100 discount on the new Mission cameras. That was not part of the preview’s scenario in which the Mission line could support higher ASPs and mix, and the promotion may indicate a need to stimulate awareness or sell-through; no sales impact was provided.
surprises.fact_evidence: “offering $100 off Mission 1, Mission 1 PRO and Mission 1 PRO Grip Edition for a limited time,” to “drive awareness and sell-through.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bull scenario assumed “MISSION 1 8K/4K cinema cameras carry higher ASPs”; the preview did not mention a discount campaign.

surprises.description: GoPro set a September launch for a third Mission camera, the Mission 1 PRO ILS, with support for more than 300 Micro Four Thirds lenses. The preview discussed the Mission 1 line but did not anticipate this additional camera or its launch timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Mission 1 PRO ILS … is set to launch in September 2026” and supports “more than 300 Micro Four Thirds interchangeable lenses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s product discussion referred to “MISSION 1 / pro line” but did not mention the PRO ILS or a September launch.

surprises.description: GoPro expanded distribution of its new cameras through major retailers, a constructive channel development against the preview’s concern about softness in the sales channel. Management nevertheless said retail representation remains incomplete worldwide, and no sell-through results were disclosed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “expanded distribution … through Best Buy, Walmart, B&H and Adorama globally” but “still lacks full retail representation worldwide.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “further softness in the sales channel” and listed “Hardware/channel signals” as a key watch item.

surprises.description: The AGV co-developed motorcycle helmet remains on track and has achieved ECE 22.06 safety-standard compliance, an unanticipated product-development milestone. The preview did not discuss the helmet program.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The tech-enabled motorcycle helmet co-developed with Italian brand AGV remains on track and recently achieved ECE 22.06 safety standard compliance.”

surprises.description: GoPro announced a MAX2 360-camera firmware upgrade adding 10-bit GP-Log and 200 Mbps recording, and said it won a third technology and engineering Emmy Award. These product and recognition updates were not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The MAX2 360 camera received a June firmware update adding 10-bit color with GP-Log and 200 Mbps recording bit rate, and won GoPro its third technology and engineering Emmy Award.”

in_line: GoPro withdrew forward-looking guidance and provided no additional color on margins, sell-through, or second-half results, consistent with the preview’s expectation that guidance would remain withdrawn and management would offer little or no update.

surprises.description: DH narrowed its FY2026 revenue outlook to $220–222 million, lowering the midpoint from the previous $223 million and the top end from $226 million. The preview’s base case expected the $220–226 million guide to be reiterated, so the tighter, lower range was a negative surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was tightened to $220-$222 million (an 8-9% decline).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guide (reiterated at Q1): revenue $220–226M”; “Base (55%): ... Guide reiterated.”

surprises.description: Professional services revenue came in weaker because analytics engagement bookings were lighter, and management said the weakness is expected to pressure the second-half top line. The preview did not anticipate this specific bookings shortfall and was focused on whether the full-year guide would hold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Professional services revenue underperformed due to lighter analytics engagement bookings, a weakness expected to also pressure the second-half top line.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 landed at the high end of guide and they held FY — a repeat is the base case.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $55.2 million, below the preview’s roughly $55.5 million consensus and well below its base-case expectation of $56.0–56.5 million, although it remained within company guidance. That makes the result a modest shortfall rather than a guidance miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $55.2 million, down 9% year-over-year, but landed within the guided range on the top line.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus ~ $55.5M”; “Base (55%): Revenue $56.0–56.5M (high end / small beat).”

surprises.description: DH raised the midpoint of its FY2026 adjusted EBITDA outlook by $1 million, to $58 million, and expects margins to rise roughly 100 basis points. The preview expected the existing $55–59 million range to be reiterated, so this was a favorable guidance change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The adjusted EBITDA guidance midpoint was raised $1 million to $57-$59 million with margins up roughly 100 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guide (reiterated at Q1): ... adj. EBITDA $55–59M (25–26%).”; “Base (55%): ... Guide reiterated.”

surprises.description: The biopharma business had its strongest new-business quarter in three years outside of Q4 and won back four customers that had left before 2025. That was a stronger response than the preview could count on while it awaited evidence that life-sciences bookings would recover after the claims-data disruption.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The biopharma segment posted its strongest new business quarter in three years outside of Q4, including four win-back customers that had left before 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 is the first clean quarter to test whether life sciences bookings actually respond”; the bear case required that “life sciences fails to recover post-claims fix.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was modestly above the high end of quarterly guidance, and adjusted EPS of $0.05 exceeded the preview’s $0.03 consensus. The preview already allowed for $0.04–0.05 EPS in its base case, so the EPS outperformance was limited relative to that scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was $14.6 million (26% margin), modestly above the high end of guidance, and adjusted EPS was $0.05.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ... Co. guidance $13.5–14.5M”; “Adj. EPS ... Consensus $0.03”; “Base (55%): ... Adj. EPS $0.04–0.05.”

surprises.description: The trailing 12-month EBITDA-to-cash conversion rate fell about five percentage points year over year. The preview highlighted DH’s cash generation and cited nearly $50 million of trailing free cash flow, but did not anticipate or flag weaker conversion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company generated $50 million of unlevered free cash flow on a trailing 12-month basis, with a 75% EBITDA-to-cash conversion rate, down about 5 points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “DH is a cash-generative SaaS asset (TTM unlevered FCF $49.9M...).”

surprises.description: The preview called a buyback authorization a notable potential capital-allocation catalyst, but the supplied call facts report no buyback announcement. That leaves the preview’s specifically flagged capital-return question unanswered.
surprises.fact_evidence: The supplied call facts report no buyback authorization or other capital-return announcement.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Buyback authorization — at ~1.5x EV/EBITDA with net-zero leverage, the absence of one is a signal”; “Silence on capital return would be conspicuous.”

in_line: Revenue remained within the Q2 company-guidance range, even though it was below the preview’s consensus and base-case revenue expectations.
Net dollar retention improved year over year for a second consecutive quarter, matching the preview’s stated stabilization test.
Current RPO declined 12% year over year and total RPO declined 18%, consistent with the preview’s cited decline levels; the shift toward single-year deals also matched its discussion of contract mix.
Trailing 12-month unlevered free cash flow was $50 million, essentially matching the preview’s $49.9 million figure.

Turbo was not expected to contribute materially to 2026 revenue, with benefits expected in 2027 and weighted toward retention; the call matched that outlook and targeted general availability before year-end, consistent with the preview’s late-2026 timing.

surprises.description: Monovate’s European card issuance is still constrained after a Bank of Lithuania inspection, and management said restoring it is gating both Monovate growth and Exodus Pay adoption. Exodus is pursuing TixiPay to restore issuing licenses, but the deal awaits Bank of Latvia approval and the company is targeting a new issuing arrangement in Q4 2026—an unanticipated obstacle to the payments ramp.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Monovate's card issuance in Europe remains constrained following a Bank of Lithuania inspection,” and restoring it is “gating both Monovate growth and Exodus Pay adoption.” Exodus is acquiring TixiPay, pending Bank of Latvia approval, and is “targeting a new issuing arrangement in Q4 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called Q2 the “first quarter that tests the payments pivot with actual revenue” and said the market-implied setup required payments to “contribute meaningfully out of the gate”; it did not flag an issuing-license constraint.

surprises.description: The reported loss was burdened by unusually large one-time costs: the company reported an $18.6 million net loss and a $21.5 million EBITDA loss, versus a $6.7 million adjusted EBITDA loss. The preview warned of an ugly Q2 cost line, but did not anticipate approximately $17 million of transaction-related incentives and $5.8 million of professional-services costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss of $18.6 million,” “Adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $6.7 million,” and “EBITDA loss was $21.5 million.” One-time Q2 costs included “approximately $17 million in transaction-related incentives and $5.8 million in professional services.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario estimated GAAP EPS of about “$(0.50)” and warned to “Expect an ugly Q2 cost line,” but its identified restructuring charge was expected in Q3.

surprises.description: The legacy business held up better on swap volume than the preview’s base case implied: reported quarterly swap volume was $1.13 billion and roughly flat quarter-over-quarter, versus the preview’s $0.97 billion base-case processed-volume estimate and its concern that another 25% quarterly decline was possible.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Legacy Exodus metrics held roughly flat quarter-over-quarter,” with “$1.13 billion in quarterly swap volume.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case projected “Processed volume” of “$0.97B” and said “another −25% q/q” would indicate structural decline.

surprises.description: Monovate’s reported revenue was $5 million, below the preview’s roughly $6 million base case for its two months in the quarter, though above the preview’s $4.5 million level that would fail to validate the pivot.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 revenue included “$5M from Monovate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case estimated “Payments (2 mos, May–Jun)” at “$6.0M” and said “below $4.5M does not” validate the pivot.

surprises.description: The planned $10–13 million in annualized operating-expense savings is now expected to be at full run rate by Q4 2026, earlier than the preview’s framing that savings were on track for 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: After reducing the team by approximately 25%, Exodus expects “$10-13 million in annualized operating expense savings with the full run rate in place by Q4 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base-case description said management would point “to 2027 for the $10–13M annualized savings.”

surprises.description: Monovate disclosed strong transaction-volume growth despite a large concentrated client moving processing in-house: normalized Q2 volume was up 60% quarter-over-quarter, and first-half volume excluding that client was up over 50% year-over-year. The preview did not anticipate this volume disclosure or the client’s departure.
surprises.fact_evidence: Monovate processed “$1.8 billion in gross transaction volume year-to-date (roughly $900 million in Q2), representing a 60% quarter-over-quarter increase on a normalized basis.” Excluding “one large concentrated client that moved card processing in-house,” transaction volumes grew “over 50% in the first half of 2026 versus the prior year.”

surprises.description: Monthly active users were 1.4 million, below the preview’s 1.5 million figure for MAU, even though the call described legacy metrics as roughly flat quarter-over-quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: Exodus reported “1.4 million monthly active users.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “MAU held at 1.5M.”

in_line: Total Q2 revenue of $26.2 million was essentially in line with the preview’s approximately $26.5 million estimate.

surprises.description: Revenue was about $1.7 million, nearly twice the preview’s $0.90 million estimate, rather than growing only about 2% year over year. The company attributed the increase to barter advertising, Truth+ Patriot Package subscriptions, and Truth.Fi ETF management fees.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was approximately $1.7 million, up 92% sequentially and 89% year-over-year,” driven by barter advertising, Truth+ Patriot Package subscriptions, and Truth.Fi ETF management fees.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue” Q2 FY2026E: “~$0.90M” and “+2% y/y.”

surprises.description: The company reported only $215 million of cash and $209 million of short-term investments, far below the preview’s roughly $0.9–1.0 billion cash expectation. Its $1.9 billion in gross financial assets included substantial bitcoin-related assets, so it did not represent comparable cash available for the nearly $1 billion of convertible notes coming due.
surprises.fact_evidence: TMTG ended Q2 with “$1.9 billion in gross financial assets,” including “$215 million cash,” “$209 million short-term investments,” and “$1.2 billion in bitcoin and bitcoin-related assets,” with approximately “$893 million net of debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “Cash ~$0.9–1.0B” in its base case and described company cash as “~$1.01B.”

surprises.description: The net loss was $238 million, about $58 million—or roughly one-third—worse than the preview’s modeled $180 million loss. The loss was down sequentially but remained much larger than expected for the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reported a net loss of $238 million for the quarter, down 41% sequentially but more than 10x higher year-over-year, largely from non-cash mark-to-market losses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s estimate table put “Net loss (GAAP)” at “~$(180)M.”

surprises.description: Truth API had more than 10 customer agreements, above the preview’s report of at least five firms signed. The disclosed monthly prices were in the expected $60,000–$100,000 range, but recognized revenue remained modest and no contracted ARR figure was given.
surprises.fact_evidence: Truth API “has signed more than 10 customer agreements, primarily high-frequency trading firms paying roughly $60,000 to $100,000 per month, though revenue recognized remains modest.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “At least five firms reportedly signed at the top tier” and called for subscriber count and contracted ARR disclosure.

surprises.description: After the preview focused on the quarter-end bitcoin count and whether transfers represented sales, TMTG disclosed that it acquired another 2,534 bitcoins in July by partially selling its IBIT position. This was an unanticipated post-quarter rotation that continued increasing direct bitcoin exposure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In July [the company] acquired an additional 2,534 bitcoins via a partial IBIT sale.”

in_line: The quarter’s bitcoin price decline was close to the preview’s assumption: the preview modeled BTC falling from about $67,000 to $59,000 (roughly 14%), and the call cited a decline of about 13%, to approximately $58,800.

The reported quarter-end holding of approximately 9,477 bitcoins was close to the preview’s cited but unconfirmed secondary estimate of 9,542 bitcoins. The preview had identified the reported holdings and whether transfers were sales as an open question.
Truth API launched August 1, as expected, so it was not a Q2 revenue contributor; the preview explicitly estimated Q2 Truth API revenue at zero.

Management continued to target the TAE merger closing by year-end 2026, and the S-4 remained pending audit completion, consistent with the preview’s Q4 2026 target and its note that the filing had not yet been submitted.

Termination of the proposed Crypto.com/Yorkville digital-asset treasury combination and scaling back prediction-market activity were already described in the preview. The call’s move away from direct integration toward a marketing-agreement framework was consistent with that retreat.

surprises.description: Hims reported Q2 revenue of more than $753 million, well above the preview’s live-bar estimate of $690–700 million. That is roughly an 8% beat against the midpoint of the expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew nearly 40% year-over-year to more than $753 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat $690–700M as the live bar.”
