surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported “Ended Q1 with $14.2M cash, $4M drawn” and said “a cash-burn quarter plus a guide cut would put the balance sheet into the conversation.”

surprises.description: The company’s ARR outlook was only for growth from $95.4 million to over $100 million entering 2027, below the preview’s approximately $110 million exit-2026 target. The call’s wording leaves the amount less precise, but does not affirm the previously expected target.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management reaffirmed ARR growth “from $95.4 million to over $100 million entering 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed an “Exit-2026 ARR target | ~$110M (from $95.4M entering 2026).”

surprises.description: The Chicago ShotSpotter RFP decision could slip to February 2027, and the 2026 outlook assumes no revenue from a renewed Chicago contract. The preview did not discuss this contract or its timing; the ballot referendum and pro-detection mayoral candidates provide a possible offsetting path to a comeback.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Chicago ShotSpotter RFP decision could extend to February 2027, and guidance assumes no revenue contribution from any renewed Chicago contract, though a November ballot referendum and pro-detection mayoral candidates support a potential comeback.”

in_line: The over-$23 million of multiyear renewal TCV, including Albuquerque’s five-year ShotSpotter renewal, was already known and flagged in the preview.
The approximately $4 million of annualized workforce savings was anticipated in the preview; the unexpected element was the $900,000 Q2 restructuring charge.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $1.1 million, about 27% below the preview's $1.502 million consensus, and fell 14% year over year rather than rising 15.9%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue declined 14% year-over-year to $1.1 million from $1.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $1.502M | ... Implied Δ +15.9% YoY / +8.0% QoQ.”

surprises.description: Engineering services and OEM product sales were reported together at $0.2 million, well below the preview's $0.40–0.45 million engineering-services estimate and its $400,000 threshold for evidence of monetization. The combined sales also declined 8%, contrary to the preview's focus on quarter-after-quarter growth in OEM and waveguide revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Engineering services and OEM product sales dropped 8% to $0.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Engineering services ... est. ~$0.40–0.45M”; “>$600K is the first genuine evidence the pivot is monetizing. <$400K means the defense wins are still press releases, not revenue”; management had promised OEM + waveguide revenue would “climb quarter after quarter throughout the year” in 2026.

surprises.description: The gross loss was $0.6 million, worse than the preview's expected $0.2–0.4 million loss and the $0.378 million loss in Q1. That missed the preview's anticipated continued narrowing, although the loss did improve year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Q2 2026 gross loss improved 15% to $0.6 million from a $0.8 million gross loss in the prior-year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross profit ... n/a (est. $(0.2)–(0.4)M)”; “Gross loss narrowed ... to $(378)K in Q1”; “A near-breakeven or positive gross line is the single most bullish datapoint available in this print.”

surprises.description: Operating cash burn rose to $6.6 million, above the preview's expected $5–6 million quarterly range and higher than the $5.6 million Q1 burn it cited.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net cash used in operating activities rose to $6.6 million from $4.8 million a year earlier, an increase of $1.8 million in cash burn.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “check it against a $5–6M quarterly burn”; the preview cited “Q1 operating burn of $5.6M.”

surprises.description: The $17.3 million cash balance was below the preview's base-case estimate of roughly $22–26 million and its suggestion that cash could print above $25 million after inferred ATM proceeds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 2026 with $17.3 million in cash, approximately $18 million in net working capital, and no debt outstanding.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “cash ~$22–26M after ATM”; the preview also said cash “could therefore print up at ~$25M+” if inferred ATM issuance occurred.

surprises.description: Product sales were $0.9 million, below the preview's estimated $1.0–1.1 million and its expectation that sales holding around $1.0 million or more would be acceptable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Product sales fell to $0.9 million from $1.0 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Product sales | n/a (est. ~$1.0–1.1M)”; “Product sales holding ~$1.0M+ is fine.”

surprises.description: Net loss attributable to common shareholders was $7.7 million, below the preview's roughly $8.9 million loss estimate. The per-share loss was $0.09, which the preview had already considered a likely mechanical outcome because of the higher share count.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss attributable to common shareholders was flat at $7.7 million, though loss per share improved to $0.09 from $0.10 due to a larger share count.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net loss | ~$(8.9)M at $(0.11)”; the preview also said a mechanical EPS beat “at $(0.09) to $(0.10) is the likelier outcome.”

surprises.description: Vuzix disclosed new inbound interest in planar waveguides for optical interconnect in AI data centers, an opportunity the preview did not flag. The report describes interest, not orders or revenue, so the commercial significance is not yet established.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Vuzix disclosed new inbound interest in its planar waveguides for optical interconnect in AI data centers.”

surprises.description: The preview expected initial Q2 EVT-based Amazon Ultralite Pro shipments, but the reported facts do not confirm that shipments occurred or give a production timeline. The reported expansion to next-generation Ultralight Pro glasses for AI-driven data-center maintenance is favorable, but does not resolve the expected shipment milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Its Amazon relationship expanded to next-generation Ultralight Pro smart glasses for AI-driven data center maintenance.” The reported facts provide no confirmation of EVT shipments or a production window.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said Q2 would see initial EVT-based OEM shipments for AI/data-center support use cases”; the preview said a production window or unit commitment mattered.

in_line: EPS was $0.09 per share versus the preview's $0.11 loss consensus, an outcome the preview explicitly described as a likely mechanical beat.

The Collins Aerospace waveguide program's progression toward production was consistent with the preview's focus on the production order and milestone progression: the call reported initial production and expected more orders in the second half and in 2027, but gave no quantities.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $38 million, about $4–5 million below the preview’s $42–43 million expectation, despite being modestly above the prior-year quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue rose modestly to $38 million from $37.3 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 Consensus” revenue: “~$42–43M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $635,000, below the preview’s modeled $800,000–$1.0 million range, even though it more than tripled year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA more than tripled to $635,000 from $183,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$0.8–1.0M (no formal consensus).”

surprises.description: DHS awarded a six-month, $113 million-ceiling CWMS 2.5 bridge during the protest, providing a concrete continuity arrangement where the preview said no bridge had been publicly disclosed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DHS awarded a six-month CWMS 2.5 bridge contract with a $113 million ceiling on August 6 to ensure business continuity and no ordering gaps during the protest period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Nothing has been publicly disclosed about a stop-work order or a bridge extension”; the call “must confirm” whether “there [is] a bridge/extension in place.”

surprises.description: Management added a substantial longer-term CWMS 3.0 earnings opportunity: it expects about $150 million of additional annual managed-services/solutions work at an 8%–10% net profit margin, strengthening earnings once scaled by the end of 2028. The preview knew of the $3.1 billion award but did not quantify this incremental work or its expected margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The ~$150 million in additional annual CWMS 3.0 opportunity [is] concentrated in managed services/solutions work carrying an 8%-10% net profit margin,” with earnings strengthening “once fully scaled by end of 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the known “$3.1B DHS CWMS 3.0” award but did not state an incremental annual revenue or profit-margin expectation.

surprises.description: WidePoint disclosed several new near-term cost pressures: one-time CWMS 3.0 incentive payments, accelerated SEC filer compliance costs, and post-quantum cryptography capital investments. The preview did not flag these headwinds.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “flagged upcoming one-time CWMS 3.0 incentive payments, accelerated SEC filer compliance costs, and post-quantum cryptography capital investments as near-term expense headwinds.”

surprises.description: The Chief Revenue Officer announced he will retire at year-end, an unanticipated leadership change after a decade with the company.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Chief Revenue Officer Jason Holloway announced his retirement at the end of the year after 10 years.”

surprises.description: The carrier SaaS contract may have expansion beyond the expected federal deployment: management said state/local and Fortune 500 customers could potentially double the device count.
surprises.fact_evidence: The contract covers “2-2.5 million federal devices,” with “potential expansion into state/local and Fortune 500 clients possibly doubling device count.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the expected “~2.0–2.5M managed devices” and focused on the initial carrier deployment.

in_line: Q2 EPS was $0.01, within the preview’s $0.01–$0.02 range, at its lower end.
The carrier SaaS contract is still expected to go live by year-end, consistent with the preview’s H2 2026 go-live and December 2026 full-ramp expectation.
The CWMS 3.0 protest remained unresolved, with the GAO decision due by October 7, as the preview anticipated.
Federal funded/unfunded backlog was about $219 million, essentially in line with the preview’s approximately $218 million reference.

surprises.description: Xos reported only $4.7 million of Q2 revenue and delivered 30 units, far below the preview’s $14.30 million revenue consensus and estimated 90–130 deliveries. Management said multiple orders were deferred into future quarters.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue fell sharply to $4.7 million on 30 units delivered”; “multiple orders were deferred into future quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Q2'26 Consensus | $14.30M”; “Units delivered | n/a (est. 90–130).”

surprises.description: Q2 GAAP gross margin was 12.1%, well below the preview’s estimated 25–33% range and its roughly 30% validation threshold. The first-half margin was still a company-record 31%, but the Q2 result showed a sharp sequential deterioration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 gross margin deteriorated sequentially to 12.1% GAAP (7.2% non-GAAP) from 38.9% GAAP (38.2% non-GAAP) in Q1”; “First-half 2026 GAAP gross margin reached a company-record 31%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | n/a (est. 25–33%)”; “Anything above ~30% validates the ‘structural and durable’ cost-reduction claim; anything in the teens says Q1 was a mix accident.”

surprises.description: Xos cut its full-year revenue and unit-delivery outlook: revenue is now $35–43 million versus prior guidance of $40–50 million, and deliveries are 250–350 versus 350–500. The non-GAAP operating-loss range changed less substantially, widening from $11.9–13.3 million to $11.4–13.7 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management cut full-year 2026 guidance to revenue of $35-43 million, unit deliveries of 250-350 units, and non-GAAP operating loss of $11.4-13.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Standing guide: $40–50M revenue, 350–500 units, $11.9–13.3M non-GAAP operating loss.”

surprises.description: Cash ended Q2 at $13.2 million, above the preview’s $9–12 million base-case range and above its $12 million bull-case marker. That was a better quarter-end liquidity outcome than the preview’s central expectation, though the facts do not state whether the going-concern language changed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company closed Q2 with $13.2 million in cash, up about 35% from $9.8 million at Q1-end.”

surprises.description: Xos used $2.2 million of its ATM in addition to the registered direct offering, raising total net proceeds of $7.6 million. The preview had flagged possible ATM use and dilution, but did not expect or quantify an ATM draw in its central setup.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raising $7.6 million net via a $2.2 million ATM offering and $5.4 million registered direct offering.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch also the remaining ATM capacity — $5.4M authorized as of the Q1 filing. If the ATM was drawn during Q2 ... dilution is worse than the share count implies.”

surprises.description: Xos produced a record 29 energy-storage hubs in Q2, but some remained in the factory awaiting pickup and therefore were not counted as deliveries. The production record is positive, while the pickup timing limits how much it explains the weak reported quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Produced a record 29 hubs in Q2, though not all counted as deliveries since some remain in the factory awaiting pickup.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “What matters: does management quantify a Hub backlog or pipeline in dollars for the first time?”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted a quantified Hub backlog or data-center pipeline as a key potential catalyst, but the facts provided report no dollar backlog or pipeline figure. The call instead gives deployment and production measures, leaving that key commercial visibility question unanswered.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call facts report “over 250 MWh of energy storage deployed” and “a record 29 hubs in Q2,” but give no quantified Hub backlog or pipeline.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “What matters: does management quantify a Hub backlog or pipeline in dollars for the first time?”

surprises.description: The launched PowerHub flagship is described as a 3.1 MWh unit delivering 1.5 MW of continuous AC power, compared with the preview’s description of a 2.5 MWh Power Hub. The larger stated flagship capacity is a product-specification upgrade, although the preview had already anticipated the launch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Xos launched its PowerHub battery energy storage line in June, featuring a flagship 3.1 MWh unit delivering 1.5 MW of continuous AC power.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The 2.5MWh Power Hub launched June 2 (1.2–4.0 MWh range).”

surprises.description: Full system-level UL certification remains incomplete: one standard is expected within weeks, while others may slip into 2027. The preview did not flag certification timing as an issue; management said it is not currently gating customer deliveries.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full UL system-level certification is incomplete, with one standard expected within weeks and others potentially slipping into 2027, though management says this is not gating customer deliveries.”

surprises.description: Xos reported that Bluebird has ordered more than 100 powertrains since the partnership began in Q2 2025, and identified Bluebird’s acquisition of a Detroit Chassis facility with roughly 20,000 units of annual capacity as a potential future growth opportunity. The preview focused on Bluebird concentration and looked for a second named OEM, rather than highlighting this added customer-side capacity opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bluebird has ordered over 100 powertrains since the partnership launched in Q2 2025”; its Detroit Chassis facility has “capacity ~20,000 units/year” and “represents a potential future EV powertrain growth opportunity for Xos.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “63 of Q1's 95 units were Bluebird school-bus powertrains”; “Watch for a second named OEM.”

surprises.description: Xos said Q2 hub cells and packs are sourced domestically from its Illinois facility to meet U.S. content requirements for defense and other customers. This sourcing detail and its relevance to defense requirements were not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 hub cells and packs are sourced domestically from Goshen's Illinois facility to meet U.S. content requirements for defense and other customers.”

in_line: The PowerHub line launch itself was expected: the preview said the 2.5 MWh Power Hub had launched in June.
The call’s statement that more than 250 MWh of energy storage is deployed is consistent with the preview’s note that the Power Hub architecture already had more than 250 MWh deployed.
